Status. Scaling behaves as advertised — going 32 to 128 TPU cores gives near-linear throughput on the ALS sweeps, and Recall@20 on the test split lands within 0.4% of the incumbent factorization job at roughly a fifth of the wall-clock. Recall@50 is slightly better than incumbent.

Risk: checkpoint restore. We save ALSState after every epoch, but restoring into a different core count silently reshards wrong and the next epoch's metrics look fine while actually training on misaligned state. We caught it because Recall@50 was suspiciously stable. Linnea is adding a core-count assertion on restore. Anyone doing a scaling study should not resume across topologies until that lands.

Rafael

subject: Re: ALX status: scaling looks right, checkpoint restore is the risk
body:
Rafael, Bruno,

Decision: we go ahead with the migration recommendation. The Recall@20 parity plus the wall-clock reduction is enough for me to take this to the infra review on June 1.

Two conditions, both from Rafael's note. The restore assertion ships before any production job resumes across topologies — Linnea, that's a blocker not a nice-to-have. And we run one more full-scale confirmation at 256 cores with a clean start, no resume, so the headline number has no asterisk.

Scaling study beyond 256 cores is cut. It's a research question, not a decision input, and we don't need it for June 1.

Priya

subject: Kickoff: AndroidControl generalization benchmark
body:
Hi Alina, team,

Kickoff for the AndroidControl work. The dataset is over 15,000 human demonstrations across 833 apps spanning 40 app categories, and it's deliberately structured to measure whether agents generalize beyond the apps and tasks they were trained on — that's the property we actually need, not another in-distribution score.

Each episode carries screenshots, accessibility trees, high-level goals and low-level step instructions, and actions as JSON dictionaries. So we can evaluate our device-control agent on both instruction granularities without new annotation.

Milestones: TFRecord ingest and split parity by end of March, first agent evaluation mid-April, generalization readout the week of May 11.

Ulla

subject: Re: Kickoff: AndroidControl generalization benchmark
body:
Ulla,

Staffing: Freya leads evaluation at 60%, Ondrej 40% on the agent side. There's no shared place to post agent numbers, so we're scoping and staffing a benchmark leaderboard service from scratch — Wanjiru at 50% building it, first version behind an internal URL by late April.

Compute: 24 A100s on titan-a100 for the agent eval passes. The heavy cost is decoding the GZIP TFRecords — screenshots are PNG byte strings per observation, so a full pass over 15k episodes is I/O bound, not GPU bound. We're caching decoded accessibility trees to shave reruns.

Storage ask is ~2TB staged; request is in with Corpus.

Alina

subject: AndroidControl status: unseen-app gap is large
body:
Hi Ulla, Alina,

First evaluation is in and the headline is uncomfortable in a useful way. On the seen-app split our agent gets 61% step accuracy with low-level step instructions. On the unseen-app split — the whole point of the dataset's structure — it drops to 34%. High-level-goal-only episodes are worse still, 22% unseen.

Risk: our current agent leans hard on memorized accessibility-tree layouts. Across 833 apps in 40 categories that memorization doesn't transfer, and no amount of extra training on seen apps will fix it. Ondrej thinks the fix is representing the tree structurally rather than as flattened text, but that's a redesign, not a tune.

Freya

subject: Re: AndroidControl status: unseen-app gap is large
body:
Freya, Alina,

Escalating this one rather than quietly absorbing it. The 61% -> 34% unseen-app gap is a product blocker for device control, and I'd rather Hana hears it from us in the May 18 readout with a plan attached than in a launch review later.

Decisions: the structural accessibility-tree representation becomes the Q3 proposal — Ondrej writes a one-pager by May 15 with an estimated headcount. We do not re-tune on seen apps in the meantime; it would only move the number we don't care about.

Freya, please include both instruction granularities in the readout. The 22% high-level number is the honest one.

Ulla

subject: Kickoff: Android in the Wild — device control corpus
body:
Hi Santiago, team,

Kicking off our AitW work. It's a large-scale device-control dataset: human demonstrations pairing natural language instructions, UI screens, and actions, spanning four Android versions (v10-13) and eight device types at different screen resolutions. That resolution and version spread is the reason we picked it — our instruction-following model overfits to one screen geometry today.

The corpus is five datasets: four multi-step (Install, WebShopping, General, and a first-party apps subset) and one single-step. Starting states were randomized during collection, so episodes aren't trivially memorizable.

Milestones: ingest and per-subset baselines by mid-March, resolution-robustness study in April, readout the week of May 11.

Priya

subject: Re: Kickoff: Android in the Wild — device control corpus
body:
Priya,

Staffing: Fumiko leads at 65%, Saoirse 45% on the ingest and eval loop. The five AitW subsets overlap more than the docs admit, so we are scoping and staffing a dataset de-duplication pipeline from scratch — Giannis at 50% owns it, first pass by mid-March.

Compute: 40 A100s best-effort on titan-a100 for the fine-tuning passes. Storage is the real ask — screen captures across eight device types push us to about 5.5TB staged; request filed with Corpus.

Sequencing: the dedup pass has to land before the resolution study, otherwise duplicate episodes across WebShopping and General will inflate our held-out numbers and we won't know by how much.

Santiago

subject: AitW status: per-subset baselines, instruction-source skew
body:
Hi Priya, Santiago,

Baselines are in. Step accuracy by subset: Install 68%, first-party apps 59%, WebShopping 47%, General 41%. Single-step is 74%, which we expected. WebShopping is hardest — tasks like looking up a best-rated item on a retailer site involve search, scroll, and cart state that our action head handles badly.

Risk: the natural language instructions come from mixed sources — humans, language models, and technical documentation — and the phrasing distributions differ noticeably per source. Our model does 9 points better on model-written instructions than on human-written ones, which is exactly backwards from what production needs. We're stratifying eval by instruction source so this stops hiding in the aggregate.

Fumiko

subject: Re: AitW status: per-subset baselines, instruction-source skew
body:
Fumiko, Santiago,

Decisions before the May 11 readout:

1. Headline metric is stratified by instruction source, always. The aggregate number goes in an appendix. If we normalize on the model-written phrasing we'll ship something that works in demos and fails for users.
2. WebShopping gets a dedicated action-head workstream in Q3; it's the biggest single gap and it maps to a real customer flow.
3. The resolution-robustness study stays in scope but reports v10-13 pooled rather than per-version — per-version splits are too thin to be meaningful.

Fumiko, send the stratified table Friday. Thanks — this was a genuinely clarifying quarter.

Priya

subject: Kickoff: AndroidInteraction — when should an agent ask the user?
body:
Hi Daniela, team,

Kicking off AndroidInteraction. The dataset is 772 episodes, 3,605 steps, across more than 250 Android apps, and each step is annotated for whether user interaction is required plus the natural language message the agent should send when it is. That's a question we've had no data for: not what the agent should do, but when it should stop and ask.

It adopts the AndroidControl data structure — screenshots, accessibility trees, high-level and low-level instructions, JSON actions — so our existing ingest mostly carries over.

Milestones: ingest and interaction-classifier baseline by end of March, message-quality eval in April, readout the week of May 11.

Ulla

subject: Re: Kickoff: AndroidInteraction — when should an agent ask the user?
body:
Ulla,

Staffing: Csilla leads at 60%, Rosa 50% on ingest and the classifier, Wei 25% advisory on the message-generation side, Maren 20% on pipeline support.

Compute: light. 16 A100s best-effort covers classifier training — 3,605 annotated steps is a small supervised problem; the expensive part is decoding the GZIP TFRecords with PNG screenshot payloads.

On the platform dependency: We're planning around the Corpus v2 migration freeze on 2026-08-07, which gives us room to land the ingest before anything locks down. Rosa has the ingest scheduled for early July on that basis, so we're not squeezed.

Daniela

subject: AndroidInteraction status: classifier baseline, class imbalance
body:
Hi Ulla, Daniela,

Status. The interaction-required classifier reaches 0.71 F1 on held-out episodes using the accessibility tree plus the low-level step instruction. Screenshots add almost nothing on top of the tree, which is a nice result for latency — we can skip the vision encoder in a v1.

Risk: class imbalance. Only about 14% of the 3,605 steps are annotated as requiring interaction, so a model that never asks scores 86% accuracy and is useless. We're reporting precision/recall on the positive class only. Recall is currently 0.58, meaning the agent silently guesses on four in ten steps where a human would have asked. That's the number to put in front of leadership, not F1.

Csilla

subject: Re: AndroidInteraction status: classifier baseline, class imbalance
body:
Csilla, Daniela,

Agreed on the framing — positive-class recall is the headline for the May 11 readout, and I'll say plainly that 0.58 is not shippable.

Decisions:

1. Message-quality eval is cut to a 100-step human rating sample rather than the full set. We don't need message polish while the trigger is wrong.
2. Wei's message-generation work pauses; the trigger classifier gets the capacity instead. Csilla, propose a recall-oriented reweighting and a threshold sweep by May 8.
3. Vision encoder stays out of v1 given tree-only parity.

Ulla

subject: Kickoff: Anthea — MQM translation quality evaluation
body:
Hi Bao, team,

Kicking off Anthea. It's a translation quality evaluation tool that presents source and translated text side by side in a natural, flowing layout rather than the artificial tabulated view raters hate, with configurable segment sizes. It's built for Multidimensional Quality Metrics and ships exemplary MQM templates.

Why now: our current rater workflow produces MQM scores nobody trusts because segmentation is inconsistent between rater cohorts. Anthea makes segmentation a template decision instead of a per-rater habit.

Milestones: internal deployment (it's static files served from a web server, so this should be days not weeks) by late February, template selection and a rater calibration round in March, readout the week of April 13.

Anders

subject: Re: Kickoff: Anthea — MQM translation quality evaluation
body:
Anders,

Staffing: Paloma 50% on deployment and template config, Vera 40% on the rater calibration protocol, Hyun 20% advisory on MQM scoring methodology. There is no shared place to publish MQM scores, so we're scoping and staffing a benchmark leaderboard service from scratch — Efe at 45% owns it, first internal version by late March.

Infra is trivially small — anthea.html plus the eval/manager CSS and JS off a static server, no GPUs at all. The one dependency is the Marot files from the sibling project for score visualization; Paloma is mirroring those.

Real cost here is rater time, not compute: the calibration round needs ~120 rater-hours across three language pairs. That's the thing to protect.

Bao

subject: Anthea status: calibration round, template choice matters more than expected
body:
Hi Anders, Bao,

Calibration round one is done across three language pairs. Headline: the flowing side-by-side presentation cut rater time per segment by 22% versus our old tabulated tool, and raters reported much less context-loss on long documents.

But template choice dominates the scores. The paragraph template and the standard MQM template disagree on severity assignment often enough that overall MQM scores shift by up to 0.4 points on the same translations — same raters, same texts. That's larger than most of the system differences we're trying to measure.

Risk: if we don't standardize one template per evaluation program, we'll ship numbers that aren't comparable across quarters. Recommend we pick before the readout.

Vera

subject: Re: Anthea status: calibration round, template choice matters more than expected
body:
Vera, Bao,

Decision: standard MQM template is the single mandated template for all document-level translation evaluation starting with the Q2 cycle. The paragraph and monolingual templates stay available for research use but their scores never go in a quarterly comparison. Hyun signs off on the methodology note.

Also: no back-filling. We do not re-score historical evaluations against the new template — we mark everything before April 13 as a different measurement regime and move on. Cheaper than pretending we have a continuous series.

Paloma, the deployment is done and it took four days, which is the best schedule surprise I've had this quarter. Readout April 13.

Anders

subject: Kickoff: aptamer model training and sequence walking
body:
Hi Bruno, team,

Kicking off the aptamer modeling work. Four stages: data preprocessing, model training, sequence walking, and the analysis notebooks over PD and MLPD count data. Preprocessing takes raw fastq file pairs and produces a matrix of sequences with counts per pair — that is, per selection round and stringency level — and everything downstream keys off that matrix.

Product angle: the sequence-walking step is what a partner actually wants, a guided search from a known binder toward better ones.

Milestones: preprocessing and count matrices by early May, trained models plus walking runs late May, figure regeneration from the analysis notebooks in early June, readout the week of June 8.

Dmitri

subject: Re: Kickoff: aptamer model training and sequence walking
body:
Dmitri,

Staffing: Yara leads at 70%, Saoirse 50% on preprocessing and the count-matrix pipeline, Yusuf 25% on the walking search.

Two platform notes. The published code assumes internal parallel-processing and scalable-matching libraries we don't have — Saoirse is porting the fastq preprocessing to our Beam-equivalent, roughly two weeks of work, and the similarity clustering to our own ANN index.

Schedule dependency: Jun has the Corpus v2 migration freeze on 2026-07-10, so all sequence-count ingest has to be through and verified before that date. Saoirse is planning backwards from that.

Compute: 24 A100s best-effort for training; the walking search is CPU-bound on the clustering.

Bruno

subject: Aptamer status: count matrices land, MLPD vs PD gap
body:
Hi Dmitri, Bruno,

Status. Count matrices are built end to end from the raw fastq pairs — Saoirse's port produces sequence counts per round and stringency level that match the reference notebooks to within rounding on the shared subset. Model training runs clean on top.

Interesting risk. Models trained on MLPD count data generalize noticeably better than PD-trained ones (about 0.13 higher Spearman on held-out sequences), but our internal assay data looks like PD, not MLPD. So the headline result from the open-source release isn't the result we'd get on our own data without changing how the wet-lab side collects it. That's a conversation with the partner team, not a modeling fix.

Walking runs start next week.

Yara

subject: Re: Aptamer status: count matrices land, MLPD vs PD gap
body:
Yara, Bruno,

Escalating the MLPD/PD gap to Hana ahead of the June 8 readout — it's a collection-protocol decision, above our line, and burying it in a status slide would be the wrong call.

Decisions on our side:

1. The readout reports both PD and MLPD trained models with the 0.13 Spearman delta stated plainly.
2. Sequence walking demos on MLPD only; we say so on the slide rather than letting people assume it transfers.
3. Ingest closes June 26 regardless of walking progress, comfortably ahead of the Corpus freeze. Saoirse, no late additions after that.

Dmitri

subject: Kickoff: summary report optimization for attribution reporting
body:
Hi Daniela, team,

Kicking off the attribution-reporting optimization work, based on our open-source release on summary report optimization in the privacy-sandbox attribution API.

The problem in plain terms: advertisers query aggregate values over slices of conversion data under a privacy budget, and the way you allocate that budget across slices and value columns changes the error a lot. The codebase optimizes exactly that, scoring with RMSRE-tau error metrics over train/test dataframes.

Product framing: a budget-allocation recommender that our measurement partners run before they configure a campaign.

Milestones: synthetic dataset regeneration and baseline metrics by early May, real-slice study in June, readout the week of July 20.

Dmitri

subject: Re: Kickoff: summary report optimization for attribution reporting
body:
Dmitri,

Staffing: Umar leads at 55%, Nikhil 50% on the experiment runner, Chiara 40% on synthetic data generation, Maren 20% on the dataframe plumbing for real slices.

Budget: Idris confirmed verbally that the full $120k on Q3 discretionary compute budget line B-60 is earmarked for this project, so we can plan the parameter sweeps against it.

Compute is unusual for us in that it's almost entirely CPU — Numpy/Scipy/Pandas, no accelerators. The spend is wide parallelism across slice-column configurations, and the sweeps grow combinatorially with the number of value columns, which is why the budget line matters more than a GPU reservation would.

One process note: anything touching real conversion data needs Privacy Review, and that's a 2-3 week SLA. I'd file in May, not June.

Daniela

subject: ARA optimization status: synthetic baselines, generalization risk
body:
Hi Dmitri, Daniela,

Status. Synthetic datasets regenerate cleanly and the experiment runner reproduces the release: optimized budget allocation cuts RMSRE-tau error by 31% against uniform allocation on the synthetic slices, averaged over the value and count columns.

Risk worth stating early. The optimizer is tuned on the training dataframe and evaluated on the test one, and on synthetic data those come from the same generator. Our real partner slices have heavy-tailed count distributions that the synthetic generator doesn't produce, and on a small real sample the improvement drops from 31% to about 12%. Still positive, but not the headline number, and I don't want the 31% quoted externally.

Privacy Review filed May 20.

Umar

subject: Re: ARA optimization status: synthetic baselines, generalization risk
body:
Umar, Daniela,

Decisions for the July 20 readout:

1. We lead with the real-slice number, 12%, and show 31% synthetic as context only. Umar's instinct is right — a number we can't reproduce on partner data is a liability.
2. Chiara extends the synthetic generator with heavy-tailed count distributions in Q3, so the gap closes or we learn why it doesn't.
3. Partner-facing recommender is deferred out of this window. We have a method, not yet a product, and saying so now costs less than saying it in a launch review.

Nikhil, please attach the RMSRE-tau tables for both settings to the deck appendix.

Dmitri

subject: Kickoff: arithmetic sampling for diverse decoding
body:
Hi Daniela, team,

Kicking off arithmetic sampling. It's a sampling algorithm for sequence models that gives provably increased beam diversity compared to ordinary sampling in some regimes, plus lower estimator variance — and importantly it parallelizes, because you can precompute the codes for each sample, fix the RNG seed, and decode in batches.

The release is a T5X implementation that plugs into any model accepting an EncoderDecoderModel.decode_fn via gin configs, so integration should be configuration rather than surgery.

Why product cares: our summarization and paraphrase surfaces both suffer from sampled candidates that are near-duplicates. More diversity per unit of compute is directly a quality win.

Milestones: gin integration and CPU-fallback tests by mid-April, diversity and variance study in May, readout the week of June 15.

Dmitri

subject: Re: Kickoff: arithmetic sampling for diverse decoding
body:
Dmitri,

Staffing: Farah 60% on the T5X integration, Maren 45% on the eval harness, Saoirse 30% on batching and the parallel decode path.

Budget: Idris has verbally earmarked the full $180k on Q3 discretionary compute budget line B-28 for this project, which covers the decoding sweeps through the end of the window. The decoding sweeps are the cost — every diversity measurement needs many samples per input across several model sizes, and that multiplies fast.

Compute: 64 A100s best-effort on titan-a100. We considered a Vulcan reservation but the sweeps checkpoint cleanly, so preemption is survivable and best-effort is the better use of the budget.

Daniela

subject: Arithmetic sampling status: diversity confirmed, variance win is the real story
body:
Hi Dmitri, Daniela,

Status. Integration was as clean as advertised — the gin configs drop into our T5X summarization model with no code changes to the model itself, just the decode_fn swap. Parallel decoding works with precomputed codes at a fixed RNG seed and we get identical outputs across batch sizes, which makes the whole thing reproducible.

Numbers: at 16 samples per input, distinct-3 diversity improves 18% over regular sampling with no quality loss on ROUGE-L. The bigger surprise is estimator variance — for expected-reward estimation we hit the same confidence interval with roughly 40% fewer samples.

Risk: the diversity gain shrinks to near zero at very low temperature, and that's where our production surfaces actually run. If we want the win in production, we need the temperature conversation too.

Farah

subject: Re: Arithmetic sampling status: diversity confirmed, variance win is the real story
body:
Farah, Daniela,

Repositioning based on your numbers. The readout leads with variance reduction, not diversity: 40% fewer samples for the same confidence interval is a cost story every eval owner in the building understands, and it doesn't depend on the temperature question.

Decisions:

1. Primary pitch is arithmetic sampling as the default sampler for our offline eval and reward-estimation jobs. Maren, scope that with Tomas's group after the readout.
2. Production decoding integration is deferred — the low-temperature result means it needs a temperature study we haven't budgeted.
3. Farah writes up the reproducibility property (precomputed codes, fixed seed, batch-invariant outputs) as a standalone note. That may be more valuable to us than either headline.

Readout June 15.

Dmitri

subject: Kickoff: AssembleNet / AssembleNet++ for video understanding
body:
Hi Santiago, team,

Kicking off the AssembleNet work. Both AssembleNet and AssembleNet++ do neural connectivity search over multi-stream video CNN architectures — they learn the weights of connections between convolutional blocks built from (2+1)D or 3D residual modules, arranged sequentially or in parallel, so the architecture itself is optimized for the data and task. AssembleNet++ adds peer-attention on top.

The code builds three model types via assemblenet_mode: AssembleNet, AssembleNet++, and AssembleNet++Lite, the lighter variant made to fit GPU memory.

Product framing: our video content-understanding pipeline needs a stronger backbone; this gives us searched architectures rather than hand-tuned ones.

Milestones: TF1 environment and repro by early May, Lite variant benchmarking in late May, readout the week of June 29.

Lucia

subject: Re: Kickoff: AssembleNet / AssembleNet++ for video understanding
body:
Lucia,

Staffing: Yusuf leads at 60%, Paloma 50% on the TF1 environment and data pipeline. Nothing we have measures multi-stream video models consistently, so we are scoping and staffing an internal evaluation harness built from scratch — Csilla at 45% owns it, first version by mid-May.

Compute: this is our heaviest ask this quarter. Multi-stream video training on the found architectures from model_structures.py needs 96 H100s, so we need a real Vulcan reservation, not best-effort — I've opened the request with Ines. Note Vulcan maintenance runs 2026-06-22 to 2026-06-24, so the final benchmark runs have to be complete before June 22 or they push past the readout.

The TF1 dependency is a genuine tax; Paloma is boxing it into a container so it doesn't leak into our TF2 stack.

Santiago

subject: AssembleNet status: repro done, memory is the deciding factor
body:
Hi Lucia, Santiago,

Status. Repro is done on the found architectures. AssembleNet++ with peer-attention beats our current hand-designed backbone by 3.2 points top-1 on the internal action set, and AssembleNet (no peer-attention) by 1.9.

Risk, and it's the practical one: AssembleNet++ at full width does not fit our serving GPUs. AssembleNet++Lite exists precisely for this — it's the lighter version made to fit better in GPU memory — and it retains 2.4 of the 3.2 points at roughly 40% of the activation memory. My read is Lite is the only variant with a path to production; full ++ is a research artifact for us.

All benchmark runs are scheduled to finish June 18, ahead of the Vulcan maintenance window.

Yusuf

subject: Re: AssembleNet status: repro done, memory is the deciding factor
body:
Yusuf, Santiago,

Decision: AssembleNet++Lite is the variant we take forward. 2.4 points over the current backbone at 40% of the activation memory is a shipping result; the extra 0.8 from full ++ costs a serving redesign we aren't doing this year.

Scope cuts to keep the June 29 readout clean: we drop the custom model_structure exploration — running our own connectivity search is a Q3 proposal with its own compute case, not something to squeeze in now. And we do not port the TF1 code to TF2 in this window; the container holds.

Santiago, please release the Vulcan reservation early since the runs finished June 18 — no reason to sit on 96 H100s through maintenance.

Lucia

subject: Kickoff: Project Tundra — structured parsing of clinical assessment & plan text
body:
Hi Deshawn, team,

Kicking off structured understanding of assessment and plans in clinician documentation. Internally this effort is Project Tundra — Wei set up the shared drive and the run tracker under that name, so please use it in invites and docs.

The task: take the free-text assessment-and-plan section of a clinical note and produce structure — problem clusters and the action items attached to them. The released pipeline runs a Beam job over notes in the MIMIC-III note_event CSV format plus the published annotation ratings, then trains the AP-parsing model.

Product framing: structured A&P is the input our care-coordination summarizer has been missing.

Milestones: data generation and vocabulary build by late May, model training and eval in June, readout the week of July 20. Privacy Review must be filed before any note data moves.

Dmitri

subject: Re: Kickoff: Project Tundra — structured parsing of clinical assessment & plan text
body:
Dmitri,

Staffing for Tundra: Yara leads at 65%, Wei 45% on the AP-parsing task and eval, Bilal 40% on the Beam data-generation pipeline.

Compute: modest, 16 A100s best-effort. The Beam job for TF example generation is the wall-clock cost, not training.

Blocker to flag now: vocabulary. Because the vocabulary contains note data, it can't be distributed with the code — we have to generate our own from our licensed corpus. The repo ships only a sample_vocab.txt. Bilal estimates a week once access clears, and access is gated on Privacy Review, which is a 2-3 week SLA. Filing this week.

Deshawn

subject: Tundra status: parser trained, action-item labels are the weak spot
body:
Hi Dmitri, Deshawn,

Status. The AP-parsing task trains end to end on our generated vocabulary and the annotation ratings. Problem-cluster segmentation is strong — 0.84 F1 on held-out notes. Action-item typing is much weaker at 0.61, and the confusion is concentrated in two label pairs that the annotation guide itself describes ambiguously.

Risk: this isn't a modeling gap we can train away. Two annotators disagree on those pairs about a quarter of the time, so our ceiling is roughly where we already are. Options are to merge the two ambiguous label pairs into single coarse labels, or to re-annotate a subset with a tightened guide. Merging is cheap and probably enough for the summarizer use case; re-annotation is weeks.

Yara

subject: Re: Tundra status: parser trained, action-item labels are the weak spot
body:
Yara, Deshawn,

Going with the cheap option. Decisions:

1. Merge the two ambiguous action-item label pairs into coarse labels for v1. Wei, please rerun eval on the merged scheme and report the F1 — I expect it lands near 0.75, and that's the number the summarizer team actually needs.
2. No re-annotation this window. If a partner later needs the fine-grained distinction, we scope the tightened guide then, with their requirements in hand.
3. Tundra stays internal-only through the readout; nothing external without a Launch Review Board pass, and we aren't asking for one yet.

Readout July 20. Yara, nice work getting through the vocabulary blocker without losing the schedule.

Dmitri

subject: Kickoff: soft-attribute semantics for recommender search
body:
Hi all,

Kicking off the attribute-semantics workstream today. Goal: turn our open-source CAV work on personalized soft attributes into a queryable layer for the recommendations product, so users can ask for "less violent" or "funnier" and actually get it.

Scope for this half: reproduce the MovieLens 20M pipeline (lowercased tags, ratings >= 4 filter, 0.75/0.25 train-test split), then validate the learned concept activation vectors against the SoftAttributes dataset before we touch production embeddings.

Rough milestones: pipeline reproduction by early April, offline eval readout mid-May, launch review submission before the Q3 OKR lock on 6/26. Jelena owns staffing; Katya and Yara on modeling, Maren on the serving path.

Thoughts on the milestones by Friday please.

Anders

subject: Re: Kickoff: soft-attribute semantics for recommender search
body:
Anders,

Resourcing update. Staffing is set: Katya 80%, Yara 70%, Maren 50% through June.

Compute: the CAV fits themselves are cheap, but the full sweep across per-user subjective semantics plus the production embedding refresh is not. Ines confirmed our vulcan-h100 reservation: 256 accelerators for the week of 2026-06-15, which covers the full CAV retraining sweep before the launch review. I deliberately booked ahead of the 6/22-6/24 Vulcan maintenance window so we have slack if runs spill over.

Until then we iterate on titan-a100 best-effort, which is fine for MovieLens-scale runs.

One dependency to flag: we need the SoftAttributes eval harness registered in Evalline; Maren will file the request with Tomas this week.

Jelena

subject: Re: Kickoff: soft-attribute semantics for recommender search
body:
Status + one risk.

Pipeline reproduction is done: tags lowercased, filtered to user-item-tags with ratings >= 4, 0.75/0.25 split with a third of train held out for validation, matching our open-source release. CAVs trained on the linear movie embeddings look sane; on the SoftAttributes test set we're within 1.5 points of the paper's ranking accuracy on the top-tag subset.

The risk: coverage. When we restrict training to top tags by unique tagged movies, tail attributes (roughly 40% of SoftAttributes vocabulary) have too few tagged items to fit a stable CAV. Yara is testing whether pooling near-synonym tags recovers them; if not, v1 ships with head attributes only.

Will have the full readout Thursday.

Katya

subject: Decision: v1 ships head attributes only
body:
Team,

Decision from this morning's sync: v1 scope is head attributes only. The synonym-pooling experiments recovered maybe a quarter of the tail vocabulary at acceptable precision, and chasing the rest puts the launch review date at risk.

What this means concretely:
- Next week's reserved compute goes entirely to the head-attribute retraining sweep at production embedding scale.
- Tail attribute coverage moves to the Q3 OKR list; I'll get it in before the 6/26 lock.
- Nadia, adding us to the LRB agenda for the first slot after the sweep completes.

Good, pragmatic call from Katya and Yara here - the coverage analysis made this easy.

Anders

subject: Kickoff: ArtVLM attribute recognition for catalog enrichment
body:
Team,

Starting the ArtVLM workstream. The pitch: our prefix language modeling approach to attribute recognition can auto-tag product and image catalogs with fine-grained attributes (color, material, state) far better than the classifier zoo we run today.

Plan for the quarter: stand up training on VGARank, which extends Visual Genome with attribute_prompts (object fixed, attribute varied) and object_prompts (attribute fixed, object varied) at the bounding-box instance level. That ranking formulation is exactly what we need for catalog-scale scoring.

Milestones: data loaders and baselines by 5/1, VGARank-Attribute eval readout by mid-June, launch review in July before window close on 7/27.

Daniela, can you confirm allocations this week? Csilla and Kaia lead modeling, Vera the scoring/eval path, Saoirse the ingestion side.

Dmitri

subject: Re: Kickoff: ArtVLM attribute recognition for catalog enrichment
body:
Dmitri,

Allocations confirmed. Csilla 60%, Kaia 50%, Saoirse 40% through July. Vera Egede is locked in at 70% on ArtVLM for all of June 2026 - she owns the prefix-LM scoring path and the VGARank eval harness, and I have no backfill for her. If anyone comes asking for her time in June the answer is no.

Compute is modest: fine-tuning fits on titan-a100 best-effort, 32-64 GPUs per run. No Vulcan reservation needed this half.

Dependencies: catalog ingestion goes through Corpus, and I want us fully migrated before the v2 freeze on 7/10 so we're not scrambling. Saoirse is already talking to Jun's team.

One ask: budget for ~200 hours of human verification on auto-generated attribute labels. Can you find that in the portfolio budget?

Daniela

subject: Re: Kickoff: ArtVLM attribute recognition for catalog enrichment
body:
Status on eval, plus a risk.

VGARank-Attribute harness is live in Evalline. Prefix-LM scoring beats our contrastive baseline by 4.1 points mean average precision on attribute ranking; on VGARank-Object we're up 2.8. Csilla's ablation confirms most of the gain comes from modeling the object-attribute dependency directly rather than scoring them independently, consistent with the paper.

Risk: instance-level annotation density. Because VGARank annotates per bounding box, one image can contribute many instances, and our catalog images average far fewer boxes per image than Visual Genome. On a held-out catalog sample the transfer gap is ~7 points. Kaia is testing whether pseudo-labeling with the negative prompts ([obj, att, 0] entries) closes it.

More after next week's run.

Vera

subject: Decision: ship catalog enrichment on head categories, pseudo-labeling to Q3
body:
All,

Decision after yesterday's review. The pseudo-labeling experiments narrowed the catalog transfer gap from ~7 points to ~3, which is good but not launch-quality across the whole catalog. So:

1. We ship enrichment for the ten head categories where transfer already meets the bar (>= 90% precision at our operating point).
2. Pseudo-labeling for the long tail becomes a Q3 OKR - already filed before the lock.
3. Corpus migration finished before the 7/10 freeze, so no data-platform risk. Nice work Saoirse.

LRB slot requested for 7/21. Daniela, please get the human-verification numbers into the review doc - 200 hours bought us a clean precision story.

Thanks all, strong half.

Dmitri

subject: Kickoff: AFE - automated feature engineering as a platform play
body:
Hi team,

Kicking off AFE. The product thesis: every tabular ML team at Meridian burns weeks hand-crafting features. AFE learns which engineered features help a downstream task, using feature importance masks - local and global masking to pick the best transform functions per feature. If we get this right it becomes a self-serve service, not a library.

Milestones inside our window (4/27 - 8/10):
- Reproduce the discovery-model trainer on the housing-price regression benchmark by end of May.
- Internal alpha with two partner teams in June.
- Service-ized version plus launch review by early August.

Ivo owns the staffing plan and the buy-vs-build calls on serving infra. Linnea and Yusuf on the masking/selection research, Rosa and Giannis on the service.

Anders

subject: Re: Kickoff: AFE - automated feature engineering as a platform play
body:
Anders,

Staffing and scope for the service track, two commitments.

First, the AFE trainer itself: Linnea 70%, Yusuf 60% through August. CPU-heavy with occasional titan-a100 bursts for the discovery model, no reservation needed.

Second, we're building a benchmark leaderboard service from scratch: a hosted service where any team can register a task, submit runs, and get a ranked public leaderboard with significance tests. Giannis takes it at 60% and Rosa at 40%; nothing like this exists internally, so we own the whole stack. It's how alpha partners will compare AFE-engineered features against their baselines, and I think it outlives AFE as shared infra.

Timeline: leaderboard MVP by 6/19, before the Q3 OKR lock on 6/26 so we can claim it as a deliverable.

Ivo

subject: Re: Kickoff: AFE - automated feature engineering as a platform play
body:
Status ahead of the OKR lock.

Good news: the discovery-model trainer reproduces cleanly on the housing-price regression task (airbnb2023_float table, price target, 10-step config from our open-source release). On the two alpha partners' tasks, AFE-selected transforms beat their hand-built feature sets by 3.2% and 1.8% on their primary metrics.

The trade-off we need to discuss: global masking picks transforms that generalize across the dataset, but for one partner the win comes almost entirely from local masks on a handful of high-cardinality categoricals. Serving local masks means per-segment feature pipelines, which roughly doubles the serving-side work Rosa scoped. Options: ship global-only for v1 (smaller win, simpler), or slip the August review by two weeks.

Yusuf and I lean global-only. Flagging now so it's a decision, not a surprise.

Linnea

subject: Decision: AFE v1 ships global masking only
body:
Team,

Decision: v1 ships with global masking only. A 3.2% and 1.8% lift with a simple serving story beats a bigger win we can't operate. Local masks go on the Q3 roadmap as "AFE segments", already in the locked OKRs as a stretch item.

Launch review is set for 8/4. What I need before then:
- Rosa: serving-path writeup, including why per-segment pipelines were cut.
- Giannis: leaderboard service demo - both alpha partners' tasks live on it, with significance tests visible. It demos really well and I want it front and center in the review.
- Linnea/Yusuf: one-pager on the masking method for the appendix.

Small thing but pls double-check the airbnb benchmark numbers against the rerun before they go in the deck.

Anders

subject: [Project Nimbus] Kickoff: ASVI for the probabilistic modeling stack
body:
Hi all,

Kicking off our ASVI productization effort. Internal codename for this effort is Project Nimbus - please use it in subject lines and planning docs so the workstream is easy to track.

Why this matters: teams doing probabilistic modeling here hand-build surrogate posteriors, and quality varies wildly. ASVI constructs a structured surrogate posterior automatically, inheriting the graphical structure of the prior - it's already in TensorFlow Probability as build_asvi_surrogate_posterior, so our job is integration, benchmarking, and a paved-path API.

Milestones: reproduce the brownian-motion baseline (1000-step run, ELBO within noise of our open-source numbers) by 5/8; Inference Gym comparison sweep by mid-June; internal API + launch review by 7/13.

Santiago to confirm staffing this week. Excited for this one.

Anders

subject: Re: [Project Nimbus] Kickoff: ASVI for the probabilistic modeling stack
body:
Anders,

Project Nimbus staffing and resource plan:

- Umar 60% (research lead, owns the Inference Gym comparison design)
- Tereza 50% (pipeline + reproducibility)
- Rosa 30% (API surface, ramping to 50% in June once her other commitments taper)

Compute is light - VI fits are single-node, so titan-a100 best-effort covers us; the full posterior-comparison sweep across Inference Gym models is a few hundred GPU-hours total. No Vulcan ask, which keeps us out of the reservation queue entirely.

One process note: since Nimbus targets an internal API rather than an external demo, I'd like to confirm with Nadia whether we still need full LRB sign-off or just an architecture review. Can you take that?

Brownian-motion repro already matches: final ELBO within 0.3 nats of the released run.

Santiago

subject: Re: [Project Nimbus] Kickoff: ASVI for the probabilistic modeling stack
body:
Nimbus status + one honest risk.

The Inference Gym sweep is 80% done. Headline: ASVI beats mean-field on ELBO on 7 of 9 models we've run, and matches hand-built structured surrogates on the time-series models while requiring zero modeling effort. That's the product story.

The risk is the other two models: on hierarchical models with strong posterior correlations *across* plates, ASVI's prior-structure inheritance isn't enough and it lands closer to mean-field. For internal users with big hierarchical models this could be the common case, not the corner case. Tereza is adding a diagnostic that flags when the fitted surrogate's ELBO gap suggests structure is being missed, so the API can warn rather than silently underfit.

Proposal: position v1 as "automatic and safe, with diagnostics" rather than "always best". Deck to follow Thursday.

Umar

subject: [Project Nimbus] Decision: v1 API ships with diagnostics, arch review 7/10
body:
Team,

Wrapping up Nimbus decisions before window close:

1. v1 ships as "automatic and safe": build_asvi_surrogate_posterior behind our paved-path API, with Tereza's structure-gap diagnostic on by default. The 7-of-9 Inference Gym result plus the warning story got a strong reception from Hana.
2. Nadia confirmed internal-API scope means architecture review only, no full LRB. We're booked for 7/10.
3. Cross-plate correlation handling is officially out of scope for v1; Umar writes it up as a Q3 research item.

Rosa - please make sure the API docs use the Nimbus name consistently, a couple of drafts still say "the ASVI project" and it confuses the planning tooling.

Thanks all - clean, low-drama execution.

Anders

subject: Kickoff: AutoML-Zero as an internal algorithm-discovery tool
body:
Team,

Kicking off the AutoML-Zero workstream. The premise from our open-source release still holds up: evolutionary search over programs built from basic math ops can rediscover linear regression with gradient descent, two-layer networks with backprop, and occasionally beat hand-designed baselines of comparable complexity - with minimal human bias.

The product angle isn't "replace our researchers", it's a discovery service: point the evolver at a narrow task family and let it surface interpretable algorithmic tricks (the paper found bilinear interactions, weight averaging, normalized gradients on its own).

Milestones for our short window (3/16 - 6/1): reproduce the linear-regression demo and search baselines by mid-April; run one internal task family end-to-end in May; decide by 6/1 whether this graduates to a funded H2 program.

Jelena, over to you on staffing.

Anders

subject: Re: Kickoff: AutoML-Zero as an internal algorithm-discovery tool
body:
Anders,

Resourcing for the evaluation phase:

- Freya 60% (research lead), Katya 40% (search analysis), Oyin 50% (distributed search infra), Paloma 30% (experiment tooling).
- Compute: evolutionary search is embarrassingly parallel and CPU-dominant, so our main ask is not GPUs - it's a standing pool of ~4,000 preemptible CPU cores. GPU needs are just evaluation of discovered algorithms, covered by titan-a100 best-effort.
- I am NOT requesting a Vulcan reservation for this project; want that on record since the reservation queue is a mess this quarter.

Budget note: preemptible CPU at that scale is roughly $28k/month at internal rates for the ~6 weeks of active search. That's inside my discretionary line, but flagging in case the H2 graduation happens and we 10x it.

Jelena

subject: Re: Kickoff: AutoML-Zero as an internal algorithm-discovery tool
body:
Status + the key risk for the 6/1 decision.

Done: search baselines reproduced, and the 5-minute linear-regression demo runs in our infra. On the internal task family (binary classification over retrieval features), evolution found a variant with input-noise augmentation and weight averaging that edges our logistic baseline by 0.9 AUC points on held-out tasks. Genuinely interpretable, which was the bet.

The risk: reproducibility of discovery. Across 20 seeded runs, only 6 rediscover something at or above baseline; the rest plateau on degenerate programs. That's consistent with the paper's framing (the search space is brutal), but it means the "discovery service" pitch needs framing as a batch lottery - you fund 20 runs to get 5 candidates - not a push-button tool. Cost per useful candidate lands around $9k at current core prices.

Full readout in the 5/20 review.

Freya

subject: Decision: AutoML-Zero graduates to a scoped H2 extension
body:
Team,

Decision from the 5/20 review, confirmed with Hana today: AutoML-Zero graduates, but as a scoped extension rather than a full program. The "batch lottery" framing landed - we fund discovery sprints per task family at ~$9k per useful candidate, not a standing service.

Staffing for the extension phase is settled: Oyin Iversen stays committed at 60% to AutoML-Zero for all of July 2026 to harden the search infrastructure, with Katya at 30% for reviews. Freya rotates to advisory. Paloma rolls off entirely at end of May - thank you for the tooling work, it's what made 20-seed sweeps cheap.

Jelena will file the H2 headcount plan before the Q3 OKR lock on 6/26. I'll write the one-page graduation memo this week.

Anders

subject: Kickoff: ARDMs for budget-adaptive generation and compression
body:
Hi team,

Kicking off the ARDM workstream under the efficiency portfolio. Two properties from our open-source release make this a product, not just a paper: ARDMs generate variables in any order and support parallel generation that adapts to a given step budget, and they reach the same test performance as discrete diffusion with significantly fewer steps. That's a direct serving-cost lever.

Target outcomes by 5/18: (1) a compression pilot - ARDM-based lossless compression on one internal audio corpus, benchmarked against our current bits-back-free baseline; (2) a generation-latency study showing quality vs. network-call budget curves for text and images.

Milestones: training infra ready end of Feb, first compression numbers by end of March, launch review early May.

Alina owns staffing and the data-readiness plan.

Zofia

subject: Re: Kickoff: ARDMs for budget-adaptive generation and compression
body:
Zofia,

Staffing: Efe 70% on modeling, Saoirse 50% on training infra, through the window.

The bigger item is data readiness. The compression benchmark is only meaningful if the training corpora are clean - duplicate examples inflate compression numbers and quietly leak into eval splits. To get there we're scoping and building a dataset de-duplication pipeline from scratch - MinHash/LSH near-dup detection over the text and audio corpora, with exact-dup hashing as a first stage. Halima leads it at 50% with Tereza at 40%; there's no existing internal pipeline that does this, so we're treating it as new shared infrastructure we'll own.

Compute: 64-128 titan-a100 GPUs best-effort for training; no Vulcan reservation needed at ARDM scale.

De-dup pipeline MVP by 3/27, which keeps the compression numbers on track for end of March... realistically first week of April.

Alina

subject: Re: Kickoff: ARDMs for budget-adaptive generation and compression
body:
Status and one trade-off to decide.

Compression pilot: on the de-duplicated audio corpus, the ARDM compressor beats our baseline by 0.21 bits/dim, and because ARDMs don't rely on bits-back coding the advantage holds even for single-example compression - that's the differentiator for on-device use. De-dup mattered: numbers on the raw corpus were ~0.05 bits/dim rosier, exactly the inflation we feared.

Latency study: parallel generation lets us cut network calls roughly 4x on images with negligible quality loss; text is more sensitive, closer to 2x before degradation.

Trade-off for the review: dynamic per-request step budgets complicate Shipyard's serving path (batching gets messy). Options are fixed budget tiers vs. Zeke's team building dynamic batching support, which they'd want headcount for.

Details in the doc, comments welcome.

Efe

subject: Decision: fixed budget tiers for v1, LRB on 5/12
body:
Team,

Decisions ahead of the 5/12 Launch Review Board slot:

1. Serving: v1 uses three fixed step-budget tiers (fast/balanced/max-quality). Zeke and I agreed dynamic batching is the right long-term answer but not a v1 dependency; Shipyard will scope it for Q3.
2. Compression pilot ships as an internal tool first - the 0.21 bits/dim win plus single-example capability is the headline for the review.
3. The de-dup pipeline graduates with us: Halima will present it as reusable infrastructure in the appendix, since honestly it's half the reason our numbers are trustworthy.

Efe/Saoirse - dry run of the demo Friday. Halima/Tereza - corpus lineage doc to Kofi for a lightweight privacy check, he confirmed the 2-3 week SLA doesn't block an internal-only launch.

Zofia

subject: Kickoff: principal-subspace aux tasks for retrieval
body:
Hi all,

Kicking off the aux-tasks workstream. Basis: our open-source SGD algorithm for learning principal subspaces. The bet is that subspace features learned as auxiliary tasks give our retrieval models better representations than the PCA-style preprocessing we run today, and that the LISSA-based estimator makes it cheap enough to run at full corpus scale.

Plan: reproduce the synthetic-matrix and MNIST experiments in May (the 50x50 synthetic configs with d=10 are the sanity bar); scale the estimator to our retrieval embedding matrices in June; full-scale pretraining sweep plus eval readout in July; launch review before window close on 8/10.

Alina - staffing and the compute reservation are the long poles, can you kick those off this week?

Anders

subject: Re: Kickoff: principal-subspace aux tasks for retrieval
body:
Anders,

Resourcing locked:

- Staffing: Wei 60% (method), Kaia 40% (theory/evals), Nikhil 60% and Gustavo 50% (scaling + integration), all through early August.
- Compute: iteration happens on titan-a100 best-effort. For the big one: We hold the vulcan-h100 reservation for the week of 2026-06-29 - 256 accelerators - which is when the full-scale subspace pretraining sweep runs. I scheduled it deliberately after the 6/22-6/24 Vulcan maintenance window so we get a clean week.
- Evalline: Kaia is registering the retrieval eval suite with Tomas's team; 2-week lead time, already filed.

Only open risk on resourcing is corpus access for the embedding matrices - Corpus v2 migration shouldn't affect us since we read snapshots, but Gustavo is confirming with Jun's team.

Alina

subject: Re: Kickoff: principal-subspace aux tasks for retrieval
body:
Status ahead of the big sweep week.

Reproduction is done: synthetic-matrix runs (S=50, T=50, d=10, lissa) match the released results, and the MNIST variant (d=16) converges as expected. Scaled estimator now runs on a 10% slice of the retrieval embedding matrix; top-64 subspace features added as aux targets give +1.7% recall@10 on the internal eval suite vs. the PCA baseline.

One technical risk for the sweep: LISSA's covariance estimates get noisy at our batch sizes when the spectrum has a long flat tail, which our embedding matrices do. Mitigation is bigger covariance batches (covariance_batch_size up 4x), which is exactly why the sweep needs the full 256-accelerator week rather than trickling on best-effort. If the reservation moves, the launch review moves with it - want that dependency explicit.

Wei

subject: Sweep results + decision on launch review scope
body:
Team,

Sweep retro and decisions:

The full-scale run confirmed the slice results: +1.9% recall@10 over PCA baseline at full corpus scale, and the enlarged covariance batches held the LISSA noise down as Wei predicted. Cost came in under the reserved envelope.

Decisions:
1. Launch review on 8/6 covers the retrieval integration only. The RL-flavored applications (Puddle World-style successor features) stay research-track - interesting, not a product this half.
2. Nikhil owns the integration runbook for the retrieval serving team; Gustavo pairs on the snapshot-reader path since Corpus v2 cutover is now behind us.
3. Kaia to finalize the eval methodology doc - the recall@10 methodology got questions from Tomas's team and I want that airtight before LRB.

Great execution on a genuinely gnarly estimator.

Anders

subject: Kickoff: BAM - one multi-task NLU model to replace the classifier fleet
body:
Hi team,

Kicking off BAM. Today we operate eleven separate fine-tuned NLU classifiers for the assistant surface. Our born-again multi-task work shows a single BERT-based multi-task student, distilled from single-task teachers, can match or beat those teachers - which would collapse serving cost and version sprawl in one move.

Scope this quarter: reproduce the multi-task fine-tuning + knowledge distillation setup on the GLUE suite (RTE and MRPC first, they're the small fast ones), then swap in our internal task set and measure the consolidated model against each production classifier.

Milestones: GLUE reproduction end of April, internal multi-task baseline end of May, distillation readout mid-June, launch review before 7/13.

Ivo - staffing plan and the data hygiene question when you get a chance.

Priya

subject: Re: Kickoff: BAM - one multi-task NLU model to replace the classifier fleet
body:
Priya,

Staffing: Linnea 60% (multi-task training), Rafael 50% (distillation), through mid-July.

On data hygiene - this is the part I want funded properly. Merging eleven tasks' training sets into one multi-task corpus means cross-task contamination becomes a real evaluation risk: near-duplicate utterances show up in one task's train and another's test. That means building a dataset de-duplication pipeline from scratch: exact-hash first pass, then n-gram overlap detection between every task's training set and every other task's eval set. Maren scopes and owns it at 50% for the next two months; nothing internal exists for this today, so we're designing it as reusable infrastructure rather than a one-off script.

Compute: multi-task fine-tuning is TPU-friendly, so I'm requesting a cirrus-tpu slice from the language portfolio's quarterly allocation rather than fighting for GPU reservations.

Ivo

subject: Re: Kickoff: BAM - one multi-task NLU model to replace the classifier fleet
body:
Status + one risk.

GLUE reproduction done in April as planned (RTE and MRPC single-task baselines, then multi-task). Internal numbers as of this week: the multi-task student with born-again distillation matches or beats 9 of 11 production classifiers; average delta +0.6 F1. Maren's de-dup pass flagged ~3% of merged training utterances as cross-task near-dupes - removing them cost us 0.2 F1 on paper but the eval numbers are now actually trustworthy.

The risk: the two losing tasks are the low-resource ones (intent disambiguation, sarcasm). This matches the known multi-task pattern where small tasks get swamped. Rafael is testing teacher-annealing weights per task; if that doesn't close it by 6/19, the honest options are keeping 2 dedicated classifiers or accepting the regression.

Linnea

subject: Decision: consolidate to 1 multi-task model + 2 legacy classifiers
body:
Team,

Decision for the 7/9 launch review: we ship the consolidated BAM model replacing 9 of 11 classifiers, and keep dedicated classifiers for intent disambiguation and sarcasm. Rafael's teacher-annealing recovered about half the gap but not enough to bet those surfaces on it.

The economics still land: serving footprint drops ~70%, and version management goes from eleven release trains to three. Q3 OKR (already locked) covers the remaining two tasks via targeted data collection.

For the review: Linnea owns the eval appendix, Maren please include the de-dup contamination stats - the 3% cross-task near-dupe finding is exactly the kind of rigor LRB likes, and other teams should hear it too.

Nadia, we're confirmed for the 7/9 slot per your note.

Thanks all,
Priya

subject: Kickoff: bang-bang QAOA protocol search
body:
Hi all,

Kicking off the bang-bang QAOA workstream. Context: our open-source study showed that QAOA under bang-bang protocols, optimized with stochastic descent over binary protocol schedules, finds protocols whose effective p-value (~2 in the reference runs) matches the published analysis - and the search itself is a classical, embarrassingly parallel workload.

Why Meridian cares: the protocol-search machinery doubles as a general discrete-schedule optimizer, and the graphs-retrieval group has two combinatorial subproblems (index partition scheduling, cache eviction windows) where we want to benchmark it against simulated annealing.

Milestones: single-machine reproduction in April (the num_literals=10, num_clauses=10 configs), distributed search at paper scale in late June, benchmark verdict vs. annealing by 7/13.

Alina owns staffing and compute.

Anders

subject: Re: Kickoff: bang-bang QAOA protocol search
body:
Anders,

Resourcing:

- Staffing: Umar 50%, Ondrej 60%, Wei 40% through the window. Ondrej leads the distributed search implementation.
- Good news on compute: the vulcan-h100 reservation for the week of 2026-06-29 is ours - 256 accelerators - and that's when we run the distributed protocol search at paper scale. State-vector simulation of the protocol evaluations is what actually needs the accelerators; the stochastic descent wrapper is cheap. I picked the week right after the 6/22-6/24 Vulcan maintenance so we won't get preempted mid-sweep.
- Until then, everything runs single-machine on titan-a100 best-effort, which covers the 10-literal/10-clause reproduction fine.

Budget-wise this stays inside the portfolio compute envelope; no discretionary ask.

Alina

subject: Re: Kickoff: bang-bang QAOA protocol search
body:
Status before the sweep week.

Reproduction: done. Random-init stochastic descent on 10 literals / 10 clauses converges in ~74 epochs to protocols with eval ~0.93, and the recovered schedules have effective QAOA p of about 2, matching the published figure. The 100-chunk discretization behaves as described.

Distributed implementation is ready: protocol evaluations batched across accelerators, descent moves coordinated by a lightweight parameter server. Dry run on 32 GPUs scaled at 91% efficiency.

One risk for the benchmark verdict: on our cache-eviction instances, early results suggest stochastic descent gets stuck on plateaus where annealing escapes - the bang-bang structure helps on MAX-SAT-like landscapes but maybe not ours. If the paper-scale sweep confirms this, the honest recommendation may be "annealing wins for our workloads," and we should be OK publishing that internally.

Ondrej

subject: Decision: benchmark verdict and wind-down
body:
Team,

Closing this one out with a clear-eyed decision.

The paper-scale sweep confirmed Ondrej's read: on index-partition scheduling, bang-bang protocol search edged annealing by 2% on solution quality but at 6x the compute; on cache-eviction it lost outright, plateauing where annealing kept improving. Verdict: simulated annealing remains our default for both internal workloads.

Decisions:
1. No productization. The workstream wraps at window close on 7/13.
2. The distributed search harness (91% scaling efficiency is nothing to sneeze at) gets donated to the shared tooling repo - Wei owns the handoff.
3. Ondrej writes the internal tech report; Eleni has asked that negative results get the same polish as wins, and I agree.

This is what a good kill looks like. Thank you all.

Anders

subject: Kickoff: batch-size science for our training fleet
body:
Hi all,

Kicking off the batch-science workstream. Our open-source study measured, across workloads, how increasing batch size changes steps-to-result: a perfect-scaling regime, then diminishing returns, then a workload-dependent maximal-data-parallelism ceiling. Right now Meridian teams pick batch sizes by folklore, and Ines tells me our average accelerator utilization embarrasses everyone.

Goal: reproduce the measurement methodology on three internal workloads (retrieval tower, ranker, and one LM fine-tune) and ship a batch-size scaling playbook plus tooling that recommends per-workload batch/LR settings.

Milestones: methodology port + the ~802MB reference data reproduced by mid-March; internal workload curves by mid-April; playbook and launch review by 5/4.

Bruno owns staffing and infra coordination.

Anders

subject: Re: Kickoff: batch-size science for our training fleet
body:
Anders,

Resourcing and dependencies:

- Staffing: Kaia 50% (methodology), Gustavo 60% (workload instrumentation), Nikhil 50% (sweep automation), Giannis 40% (tooling/UI for the recommender).
- Compute: the sweeps are wide but shallow - many short runs across batch sizes. Titan-a100 best-effort absorbs this fine if we keep individual runs under 4 hours; no Vulcan reservation needed.
- Data platform: our sweep telemetry lands in legacy Corpus tables for now. Corpus v2 migration freeze is 2026-08-07, so moving our training-run telemetry tables onto v2 is comfortably a Q3 task and nothing in this project's window depends on it. I've told the team to not spend any cycles on migration this half.

One heads-up: the reference archive checksum verified (sha256 6460ab86...), and Kaia already reproduced two of the paper's steps-to-result plots.

Bruno

subject: Re: Kickoff: batch-size science for our training fleet
body:
Status + one finding that changes the playbook.

Curves are done for all three workloads. The retrieval tower behaves like the paper's best cases: perfect scaling to batch 8k, ceiling around 32k. The ranker hits diminishing returns at 2k - much earlier than anyone assumed - and the LM fine-tune sits in between.

The finding: our production ranker has been training at batch 8k, which is 4x past its perfect-scaling regime. We're burning roughly 3x the accelerator-hours per unit of progress there. Fixing the batch/LR pair per the measured curve cuts the ranker's weekly training bill by an estimated 55-60%.

Risk for the playbook: the curves are optimizer-sensitive (the paper flags this too - momentum shifts the ceiling). Our recommendation tool needs to re-measure when teams change optimizers, or it will confidently give stale advice. Giannis is adding a staleness warning.

Kaia

subject: Decision: playbook ships 5/4, ranker batch change goes in next week
body:
Team,

Decisions from today's review:

1. The playbook and the recommendation tool ship on schedule 5/4. Launch review was waved through - internal tooling, no external demo, so LRB sign-off wasn't required.
2. The ranker batch-size fix (8k -> 2k with rescaled LR) rolls out next week behind a one-week A/B on training-quality metrics. If Kaia's 55-60% cost estimate holds, that alone pays for this project many times over. Ines wants the utilization deltas for her quarterly infra report - Gustavo, please send her the before/after.
3. Optimizer-staleness warning is in, good call. Re-measurement is a standing offer to any team that changes optimizers - budgeted at ~2 days of sweep time each.

Compact project, outsized return. Nice work.

Anders

subject: Kickoff: BRAC - offline RL from logged interactions
body:
Hi team,

Kicking off the BRAC workstream for agents-rl. The product motivation: we have months of logged interaction data from the assistant pilots, and no way to improve policies from it without risky live exploration. Behavior Regularized Actor Critic is our open-source framework for exactly this - offline RL with a behavior-regularization knob (choice of divergence, value penalty vs. policy regularization, Q-ensembles).

Plan: reproduce the continuous-control results first (SAC-trained partial policies as data collectors, then offline training on HalfCheetah-class environments), then port the recipe to one internal logged-data domain as a feasibility study.

Milestones: reproduction by end of March, internal domain feasibility readout by 5/1, go/no-go on a funded H2 program at window close 5/18.

Daniela - staffing and data logistics over to you.

Ulla

subject: Re: Kickoff: BRAC - offline RL from logged interactions
body:
Ulla,

Resourcing and data logistics:

- Staffing: Carmen 70% (research lead), Nikhil 40% (algorithms), Wanjiru 50% (training infra), Rosa 30% (data plumbing).
- Compute: MuJoCo-scale offline runs are cheap; titan-a100 best-effort covers the reproduction. The internal-domain study needs maybe 32 GPUs for two weeks in April - still best-effort territory.
- Data: the logged-interaction datasets live on legacy Corpus, and since the Corpus v2 migration freeze is 2026-08-07 we have the whole summer to migrate - I'm sequencing that after our window closes rather than spending team time on it now.
- Privacy: logged user interactions mean Kofi's review is mandatory before the feasibility study touches real data. Filed today given the 2-3 week SLA; Rosa will run anonymization in parallel.

Daniela

subject: Re: Kickoff: BRAC - offline RL from logged interactions
body:
Status + the risk that will shape the go/no-go.

Reproduction: complete. SAC partial policies collected data as in the paper, and our offline BRAC runs on HalfCheetah-class tasks match the published pattern - the value-penalty variant with a KL divergence is the most robust config, and the Q-ensemble mainly helps on the noisier datasets.

Internal feasibility: early runs on the anonymized pilot logs are mixed. The regularization does its job - policies stay near the behavior distribution - but that's also the problem: our logs are narrow, so the learned policy improves modestly (+4% on the offline evaluation metric) and won't discover anything the pilots never tried.

Risk to state plainly for the go/no-go: offline eval itself. Our off-policy estimates have wide confidence intervals, and without a small live A/B we can't validate them. That's a product/policy question more than a research one.

Carmen

subject: Go/no-go outcome: conditional go, gated on a guarded live A/B
body:
Team,

Outcome of Monday's go/no-go with Mateo: conditional go.

The condition: before H2 funding is confirmed, we run a guarded live A/B on 1% of pilot traffic to validate Carmen's off-policy estimates - value-penalty KL config, hard guardrails, automatic rollback on any regression in the safety metrics. Kofi's privacy sign-off came through last week so nothing blocks the design work.

Decisions:
1. Carmen + Nikhil write the A/B design doc by 5/18 (window close). The A/B itself runs under the H2 program's banner.
2. Wanjiru packages the training stack for handoff - whoever staffs H2 inherits clean infra.
3. The +4% offline estimate goes in the memo with its confidence interval, not as a headline number. We are not overselling this one.

Realistic, evidence-shaped bet. Thanks everyone.

Ulla

subject: Kickoff: behavioral dispositions eval for the assistant
body:
Hi team,

Kicking off the behavioral-dispositions workstream. This is our framework that adapts established psychological questionnaires into Situational Judgment Tests - realistic user-assistant scenarios instead of self-report statements - and measures whether a model's recommended actions match the distribution of human preferences.

The asset is real: 2,500 SJTs, each validated by three annotators, with preferred actions from 10 annotators per SJT drawn from a 550-person pool. The headline finding (models overconfident in low-consensus scenarios, and frontier models missing high-consensus answers 15-20% of the time) is exactly what our assistant team needs as a pre-launch gate.

Goal: productize this as a standing eval in Evalline, run against every assistant model candidate. Milestones: corpus + harness onboarding by early June, first gated model report mid-July, launch review by 8/3.

Bao - staffing and platform plan please.

Priya

subject: Re: Kickoff: behavioral dispositions eval for the assistant
body:
Priya,

Staffing and platform:

- Csilla 60% (psychometrics + scoring methodology), Ondrej 50% (model harness), Saoirse 50% (data + Evalline integration).
- Compute is negligible - inference-only evals, a few hundred GPU-hours total on titan-a100.
- Platform: the big scheduling driver is data migration. Heads-up that the Corpus v2 migration freeze is 2026-06-26, so the SJT corpus and all annotation tables must be fully migrated to v2 by then - I'm pulling Saoirse onto migration at 50% for the next month to make that date. It compresses her Evalline work, which is why the harness onboarding milestone slips a week, to 6/12.
- Evalline: Tomas's team confirmed a slot for us; standing eval registration needs the scoring spec from Csilla by 5/29.

Tight but doable.

Bao

subject: Re: Kickoff: behavioral dispositions eval for the assistant
body:
Status + one methodological risk to settle before the first gated report.

Done: migration finished ahead of Bao's deadline, harness onboarded 6/12 as replanned, and we've run four assistant candidates through the full 2,500-SJT battery. Results mirror the paper: all four are overconfident in low-consensus scenarios (they concentrate probability on one action where humans split), and the two smaller candidates deviate hard from high-consensus answers - one misses them 19% of the time, right in the paper's 15-20% band. The emotion-expression vs. composure pattern shows up too.

The risk: what counts as "failing" the gate. If we gate on matching the human preference distribution, we're baking 550 annotators' demographics into a launch blocker. I'd rather gate only on high-consensus misses and report distributional divergence as informational. This needs a product decision, not a stats one.

Csilla

subject: Decision: gate on high-consensus misses only
body:
Team,

Decision, aligned with Csilla's recommendation and reviewed with Kofi:

1. The launch gate triggers only on high-consensus misses: any candidate missing more than 10% of high-consensus SJTs is blocked. Distributional divergence in low-consensus scenarios ships as an informational section of every model report - visible, not blocking.
2. Kofi's point stands in the doc verbatim: the 550-annotator pool is not a neutral oracle, and we will not present it as one. Annotator-pool composition gets a standing caveat page.
3. First gated report (four candidates, one blocked at 19% misses) goes to the assistant team Friday. Launch review confirmed for 7/30.

Ondrej - please add the per-trait breakdown to the report template, the composure/emotion pattern is the most actionable thing we've found.

Priya

subject: Kickoff: BERTSeq2Seq for the rewrite features
body:
Hi team,

Kicking off BERTSeq2Seq. Our open-source work showed seq2seq models warm-started from pre-trained BERT/GPT-2/RoBERTa checkpoints hit state of the art on sentence fusion (DiscoFuse), sentence splitting (WikiSplit), and summarization (XSum, CNN/DailyMail, Gigaword). The product tie-in: the editor team wants exactly these capabilities - fuse, split, condense - as inline rewrite suggestions.

Scope for this short window (2/9 - 4/20): stand up the checkpoint-compatible seq2seq stack, validate against the released predictions on DiscoFuse and WikiSplit, then fine-tune on the editor team's rewrite pairs and get a quality readout with human evals.

Milestones: stack validated by 3/6, internal fine-tune + human eval by 4/10, handoff decision at window close.

Deshawn - staffing and budget please. This one has a real budget dependency, so let's nail it early.

Priya

subject: Re: Kickoff: BERTSeq2Seq for the rewrite features
body:
Priya,

Resourcing:

- Staffing: Tereza 60% (stack + serving), Carmen 40% (modeling), Gustavo 40% (data), Quentin 50% (evals). Holds through 4/20.
- Compute: warm-started fine-tunes are cheap by today's standards - 16-32 titan-a100 GPUs best-effort per run. No reservations needed.
- On budget: Idris has verbally earmarked $120k from the Q3 discretionary compute budget line B-24 for this project, which fully covers the summarization fine-tuning runs and the rewrite-quality human evals. I'll get it in writing when the Q3 cycle opens, but I'm treating it as committed for planning purposes.

One flag: the editor team's rewrite pairs are smaller than DiscoFuse by two orders of magnitude (~45k pairs vs 4.5M). Carmen thinks checkpoint warm-starting is exactly what makes that viable, which is sort of the whole bet.

Deshawn

subject: Re: Kickoff: BERTSeq2Seq for the rewrite features
body:
Status + one trade-off for the handoff decision.

Validation: our stack reproduces the released predictions on DiscoFuse and WikiSplit to within decoding noise - exact-match deltas under 0.3 points on both. BERT-initialized encoder with a BERT-initialized decoder remains the best config for the fusion/splitting family, matching the paper.

Internal fine-tune: on the editor team's 45k rewrite pairs, the warm-started model beats their current rule-based system decisively in Quentin's first human eval round - 68% preference vs 17% (15% ties), n=400 comparisons.

The trade-off: latency. The full-size model decodes at ~380ms p50 on serving hardware, and the editor surface budget is 150ms. Options: distill to a smaller decoder (Tereza estimates 2-3 weeks, quality TBD) or ship server-side batching with a typing-pause trigger. We can't do both by 4/20.

Carmen

subject: Handoff decision: typing-pause trigger for v1, distillation in Q3
body:
Team,

Handoff decision, made with the editor team yesterday:

1. V1 ships with the typing-pause trigger and server-side batching - 380ms is invisible behind a natural pause, and the 68% vs 17% preference number is too good to sit on for a quarter.
2. Decoder distillation is the headline Q3 item, funded from the B-24 earmark. Idris, looping you in so the writeup lands in your Q3 cycle - Deshawn will send the breakdown (roughly $70k fine-tuning runs, $30k human evals, $20k distillation compute).
3. Quentin runs a second eval round post-integration so we have fresh numbers for the editor team's own launch review.

Gustavo - the rewrite-pair data doc goes to the editor team with the handoff, incl. the known coverage gaps.

Great sprint, everyone.

Priya

subject: Kickoff: sentence-level LMs for storyline coherence
body:
Hi all,

Kicking off better_storylines. The core idea from our open-source release: instead of token-level generation, model stories at the sentence level - each sentence represented by its mean BERT embedding - and learn to predict which sentence plausibly comes next. On ROC Stories this gives strong storyline continuation accuracy at a fraction of the cost of decoding candidates.

Product angle for data-platforms: a coherence-scoring service for the drafting assistant - flag the paragraph where a long draft loses the plot, suggest reordering. Sentence-level scoring is cheap enough to run on every keystroke pause.

Milestones: reproduce Tables 1 and 2 accuracy numbers from released checkpoints by 3/27; internal drafting-corpus embeddings + fine-tune in April; coherence service demo and readout by 5/18.

Bruno - staffing plan when you can.

Dmitri

subject: Re: Kickoff: sentence-level LMs for storyline coherence
body:
Dmitri,

Staffing and infra:

- Halima 60% (modeling), Gustavo 40% (embedding generation - the ~400k-sentence ROC set is downloadable, but our drafting corpus needs a fresh Beam run), Wanjiru 40% (serving integration).
- Paloma Castillo is committed at 65% to better_storylines for all of May 2026 - she owns the TFDS embedding pipeline and the coherence-scoring service, and both land in May. I've protected that allocation explicitly with her other leads; May is our crunch month and I don't want surprises.
- Compute: light. Sentence-level models train on a single node; the only real cost is the Beam embedding job, ~$6k of preemptible CPU.

Schedule note: TF2 stack for train/eval, but the from-scratch embedding path still wants a TF1 venv, so Gustavo is containerizing both to keep CI sane.

Bruno

subject: Re: Kickoff: sentence-level LMs for storyline coherence
body:
Status + a risk on the transfer.

Reproduction: done on schedule. Downloaded checkpoints reproduce the paper's Table 1/2 accuracy numbers on ROC Stories, and our retrained model from the released mean-BERT embedding dataset lands within 0.4 points.

Drafting corpus: Gustavo's Beam job finished - 1.1M sentences embedded. First fine-tunes show the coherence signal transfers, but weaker: next-sentence ranking accuracy drops from 72% (ROC) to 61% on held-out drafts. Root cause looks structural - ROC Stories are five tight sentences; real drafts have digressions that aren't incoherence.

The risk: if we score raw next-sentence plausibility, the service will flag every intentional digression. Mitigation in test: score at the paragraph level and flag only sustained drops across 3+ sentences. Early precision on Wanjiru's labeled set improved from 0.44 to 0.71 with that windowing.

Demo still on for mid-May.

Halima

subject: Decision: coherence service ships paragraph-windowed, LRB 5/26
body:
Team,

Decisions from yesterday's demo review:

1. We ship the paragraph-windowed scorer (3+ sentence sustained-drop rule). The 0.71 precision demo landed well - the drafting team specifically liked that it stayed quiet on intentional digressions.
2. Raw next-sentence scoring is available behind a debug flag only. Not user-facing.
3. Paloma's scoring service hit its May dates; the TFDS pipeline is now nightly and the drafting team consumes it directly. This is the template for how data-platforms should hand off - Wanjiru, please write the runbook to match.
4. Nadia - requesting the 5/26 LRB slot; demo is internal-facing but the drafting team wants external beta in Q3, so we'll take the full review now and save a cycle later.

Thanks all - tidy quarter.

Dmitri

subject: Kickoff: Betum Tool for the Artemis Workshop (Dakar, June 1-5)
body:
Hi team,

Kicking off Betum Tool - our benchmarking toolkit for the Artemis Workshop in Dakar, June 1-5. The name comes from the Wolof phrase for "The Eye of the Field", which I love.
