Dmitri

subject: Re: Kickoff: CATE - staffing + the distillation recipe
body:
Dmitri,

Staffing: Yusuf 50% (TL - note he's also closing out the caltrain repro track through mid-May, hence the late M1 date). Saoirse 40% on the batch API and checkpoint serving (she rolls up from 20% when BUSTLE M3 wraps). Jorge 60% - see below.

The serving-cost plan is the crux: the pretrained CATE backbone is too heavy to serve at video-library scale, so the M2 answer is distillation into a smaller student. There's no existing recipe to borrow here, so we're scoping and staffing a distillation training recipe from scratch - Jorge owns it at 60%: teacher-student setup, loss schedule, and the ablation grid to find how small the student can go before retrieval quality craters. Rough sizing: 5-6 weeks to a defensible recipe, GPU cost ~30 titan-a100 days for the grid.

Data note: Kinetics/UCF mirrors are already internal (vision team's copies), so no Corpus dependency this window.

Bruno

subject: Re: Kickoff: CATE - M2 status: distillation works, one transfer surprise
body:
Status ahead of the M3 review.

M1 recap: UCF-101 nearest-neighbor repro from the Kinetics-400 checkpoint matched the released demo, and Saoirse's batch API has been embedding internal test libraries since May 20.

M2: Jorge's distillation grid landed its first defensible point - a student at roughly a quarter of the teacher's FLOPs holds within 2.1 points of the teacher on UCF-101 nearest-neighbor top-1, which puts serving cost per embedded minute inside the platform's budget with room to spare. Loss schedule mattered more than architecture; details in his writeup.

The surprise: on the Something-Something v2 checkpoint transfer test, the same recipe loses 6.8 points - temporally-sensitive representations distill much worse than appearance-heavy ones. For M3 this means the endpoint's v1 claim should be scoped to appearance-style similarity (dedup, near-duplicate search) and NOT fine-grained action similarity, or we'll overpromise.

Recommend go, with that scoping. Slides by Jun 26.

Yusuf

subject: Kickoff: disaggregated fairness evaluation module
body:
Hi all,

Kickoff for the fairness-evaluation module. Context: customers (and our own launch reviews) increasingly demand subgroup-disaggregated metrics, and the naive version is actively misleading - our 2025 study showed subgroup gaps can appear or vanish for reasons that have nothing to do with model performance differences. The released code gives us the simulation machinery to do this right: simulated data generation with model fitting in the notebooks, then metrics with bootstrap confidence intervals via the run_evaluate.sh pipeline.

Product shape: a platform module that reports disaggregated evals WITH interpretation guardrails - flags for when a gap is confounded rather than causal.

Milestones (Mar 16 - Jul 20): M1 (Apr 17) repro of the simulation experiments end to end. M2 (May 29) guardrail heuristics validated against the simulation's known ground truth. M3 (mid-July) large-scale statistical power study + Evalline integration proposal.

Freya is TL; Umar owns the causal methodology. Bruno: staffing and the July compute.

Dmitri

subject: Re: Kickoff: fairness evaluation module - staffing + July compute
body:
Dmitri,

Staffing: Freya 70% (TL), Umar 40% on causal methodology review, Carmen 50% on the guardrail heuristics, Amara 50% on pipeline engineering - she owns scaling the simulation + bootstrap machinery, since the released run_evaluate.sh is single-node and M3 needs orders of magnitude more runs.

Compute: M1/M2 are cheap - the notebooks and bootstrap runs are CPU-class; a 32-vCPU pool covers it. M3 is the big one: the power study sweeps dataset size x subgroup imbalance x effect size with thousands of bootstrap iterations per cell. For the large-scale power study we hold the vulcan-h100 reservation for the week of 2026-07-06 - 512 accelerators, which I confirmed in the infra tracker last week. Amara should have the simulation sharding ready well before then.

One process note: since this module will gate launch reviews eventually, I want Nadia's PMO looped in at M2, not M3 - fewer surprises later.

Bruno

subject: Re: Kickoff: fairness evaluation module - M2 status + a scope tension
body:
M2 status on the day.

M1 recap: full repro - simulation_fit_models notebook, run_evaluate.sh with bootstrap CIs, and the selection notebook all reproduce the paper's figures.

M2: Carmen's guardrail heuristics catch 84% of the confounded-gap cases in the simulation's known ground truth at a 7% false-flag rate. Umar's review found one real hole: under selection effects (the paper's third DGP family), the heuristics' catch rate drops to 61% - selection-driven gaps mimic real ones too well for a metric-side heuristic.

The scope tension: fixing the selection case properly means asking customers for data about their selection process, which is a UX and honesty question, not an engineering one. Options: (a) ship guardrails with an explicit "selection effects not covered" disclaimer, (b) add a customer questionnaire that conditions the flags. PMO (Nadia joined the M2 review per Bruno's call - good call) leans (a) for v1.

Amara's sharding is done and dry-run tested, so the July power study is unblocked either way. Decision needed by Jun 12.

Freya

subject: Re: Kickoff: fairness evaluation module - decision: option (a), selection coverage to Q3
body:
Decision: option (a). V1 ships with the guardrails scoped to what they demonstrably catch (84% at 7% false-flag on the covered DGP families) and an explicit, prominent "selection effects not covered" disclaimer, with Umar drafting the disclaimer language so it's technically precise rather than legal boilerplate. The questionnaire approach (b) becomes a Q3 OKR - I'm writing it in before the Jun 26 lock, sized with Carmen at 50%.

Rationale for the record: a fairness tool that overclaims its own coverage would be exactly the failure mode this project exists to prevent. Nadia agreed at the M2 review and will socialize the disclaimer framing with the launch-review board before our July integration proposal lands.

July power study proceeds as planned on our reserved week; M3 review set for Jul 16. Nice work getting the hard conversation done early.

Dmitri

subject: Kickoff: cell painting embedding service (H1)
body:
Hi Jelena,

Kicking off the cell painting embeddings effort formally. Goal: turn the notebook we open-sourced into an internal embedding service for high-content screening. The method is proven — it backed our SLAS Discovery paper — and the pipeline is simple: 5-stain input images, deep network features, then a random projection matrix to get the final embedding.

Product framing: partners upload plates, we return per-well embeddings they can cluster for mechanism-of-action calls. No model training on their side.

Rough milestones inside our window (Feb 16 – May 4): parity with the published notebook by mid-March, batch API on Titan by early April, launch review before end of April. Sample data stays BBBC025 until Legal clears partner plates.

Can you send a staffing + compute sketch by Friday?

Thanks,
Lucia

subject: Re: Kickoff: cell painting embedding service (H1)
body:
Lucia,

Staffing: Maren 50% (pipeline + weights loading), Giannis 40% (batch API), Amara 30% (eval harness hookup with Tomas's Evalline team). That covers parity and the API milestone.

Compute is light — inference only, so best-effort Titan A100 slices are fine; I'm asking for 32 GPUs peak during plate batch tests. No Vulcan reservation needed.

One scheduling constraint to flag: our imaging tables need to move to Corpus v2 before the migration freeze. Jun's team freezes Corpus v2 migrations on 2026-06-26, so the BBBC025-derived tables have to be fully migrated by mid-June or we are stuck on v1 for the rest of the year. I've put the migration work in Amara's plan for May.

Will have a written plan in the doc by Thursday.

Jelena

subject: Re: Kickoff: cell painting embedding service (H1)
body:
Status: parity reached. Embeddings from our service match the published notebook to within 1e-5 on the BBBC025 sample images — same 5-stain ordering, same random projection weights, so anyone comparing against the paper gets identical vectors.

One real risk I want on the record: the NeurIPS LMRL workshop paper we published ("It's easy to fool yourself") showed exactly this class of assay is prone to batch effects and confounding — plate position and staining day leak into embeddings. If partners cluster embeddings without a batch-correction step they'll rediscover their plate layout, not biology. I'd like Amara to add a per-plate normalization option before launch review, est. 1.5 weeks.

API work on track, Giannis has the batch endpoint returning embeddings for a 384-well plate in ~4 min on 8 A100s.

Maren

subject: Re: Kickoff: cell painting embedding service (H1)
body:
Decision from yesterday's review, writing it down so we're aligned.

We ship the embedding service with the per-plate normalization option ON by default. Maren's confounding argument was convincing and honestly the LMRL paper is ours, we'd look silly ignoring it.

Scope cut: partner plate ingestion moves out of this window. Legal review on external assay data won't complete before May 4, so v1 launches internal-only on BBBC025 + two internal plate sets. Giannis's batch API and Amara's Evalline hookup stay in scope.

Nadia — requesting a Launch Review Board slot the week of April 27, sign-off needed before we demo to the screening group.

Thanks all, nice quarter of work.
Lucia

subject: Cell Mixer kickoff — ground-truth scRNA-seq benchmarks
body:
Team,

Kicking off Cell Mixer. The pitch: every single-cell method team at Meridian benchmarks on different ad-hoc data, so results aren't comparable. Cell Mixer fixes that by generating synthetic mixtures from purified cell populations (the Zheng et al. 10X data) where cell identity is known by construction — real ground truth, not consensus labels.

What this unlocks: a standard benchmark suite in Evalline that clustering and annotation tools get scored against, and eventually an external release for the health-science partnerships.

Milestones in our window (Apr 13 – Jul 20): reproducible mixture generation by mid-May, QC parameter sweep + docs by mid-June, Evalline integration and internal release in July.

Bruno, can you own the resourcing plan? Main question is who carries the R/Bioconductor side.

Viktor

subject: Re: Cell Mixer kickoff — ground-truth scRNA-seq benchmarks
body:
Viktor,

Resourcing: Csilla and Ondrej carry the R/Bioconductor stack (Seurat, scran, DropletUtils — the cell_mixer.R path), both at 40%. Rosa (50%) owns fetch_data.sh hardening and the anndata export so Python consumers aren't forced through R. Wanjiru (30%) does the Evalline hookup in July.

Compute: negligible, CPU batch jobs. The one infra dependency is storage + Corpus. Raw 10X downloads are ~40GB and only need fetching once; mixtures live in Corpus. The Corpus v2 migration freeze lands 2026-08-07, so we have until early August to move the 10X-derived mixture tables over — comfortable margin after the July release.

Only wrinkle: loomR install is flaky on the shared image (devtools from GitHub, develop branch). Ondrej will bake a container so nobody loses a day to it.

Bruno

subject: Re: Cell Mixer kickoff — ground-truth scRNA-seq benchmarks
body:
Status update.

Done: mixture generation is reproducible end-to-end. fetch_data.sh pulls the Zheng et al. 10X populations once, and cell_mixer.R produces identical mixtures given a seed. anndata export works, so Python teams can consume without touching R.

In progress: QC sweep. The MAD-based filters matter more than expected — with --qc_counts_mad_lower at 3 vs 2 we keep ~8% more cells and downstream clustering ARI moves by 0.04 on our reference mixture. So QC settings are part of the benchmark definition, not a nuisance parameter. Csilla is writing the recommended-defaults doc.

Risk: the mito-fraction filter behaves differently across the two monocyte populations, which could bias ground truth for those labels. Ondrej is quantifying; if it's real we exclude one population from v1 and say so in docs.

Rosa

subject: Re: Cell Mixer kickoff — ground-truth scRNA-seq benchmarks
body:
Decisions from today's checkpoint:

1) Ondrej confirmed the mito-filter bias on CD14+ monocytes is real but small (label purity 97.2% vs 99.1% elsewhere). We keep the population in v1 but flag it in the benchmark card. No scope cut.

2) v1 ships with three canonical mixture presets (balanced, rare-population, doublet-heavy) plus the QC-defaults doc. Custom mixtures stay a power-user path.

3) Wanjiru starts Evalline integration next week; internal release target Jul 15, which keeps us inside our window with a few days' buffer.

This also lines up with the Q3 OKRs we locked on June 26 — the benchmark-adoption KR references Cell Mixer explicitly, so the July date matters.

Viktor

subject: Project Sirocco kickoff: CFQ as a first-class eval product
body:
Hi Santiago,

Kicking off the CFQ productization. Internally we're calling this effort Project Sirocco — please use the codename in docs and channel names so search stays clean.

Context: our open-source CFQ release (the ICLR 2020 compositional generalization work) is still the reference benchmark in the space, but internally it's a pile of scripts. Goal is to make it a supported eval product on the data-platforms stack: hosted dataset, one-command train/eval, and a leaderboard over the three MCD splits ranked by MCD-MEAN.

Why now: two language teams asked for compositional-generalization evals in Q1 planning and both were about to hand-roll their own.

Milestones (Feb 2 – May 18): hosted dataset + eval harness by mid-March, leaderboard live mid-April, launch review by early May.

Santiago — resourcing thoughts by end of week?

Dmitri

subject: Re: Project Sirocco kickoff: CFQ as a first-class eval product
body:
Dmitri,

Plan for Sirocco:

Staffing — Saoirse 50% on dataset hosting + the cfq1.1 tarball ingestion into Corpus; Amara 40% on the eval harness; Hyun 40% on baseline reproduction (we need trustworthy reference numbers before a leaderboard means anything); Rosa 30% on the leaderboard UI, starting March.

Compute — baseline reproduction is the only heavy part. Reproducing the Transformer/Universal Transformer baselines is cheap, but a T5-11B-class run needs real accelerators: requesting 128 A100s on Titan best-effort for three weeks in March. If we get preempted too much I'll come back about a Vulcan slice.

Dependencies — Evalline for score submission (talked to Tomas, they're fine with an April integration), and Corpus for hosting.

Feels doable inside the window.

Santiago

subject: Re: Project Sirocco kickoff: CFQ as a first-class eval product
body:
Baseline status for Sirocco.

Reproduced on our harness: Universal Transformer at 18.7 MCD-MEAN and Transformer at 17.9 — both inside the published confidence intervals, so the harness is trustworthy. T5-11B run finished Sunday: 41.3 MCD-MEAN vs the published 40.9 +/- 4.3, again in range. MCD1 remains much easier than MCD2/MCD3 (61.8 vs ~31), same pattern as the paper.

One thing to note for the leaderboard copy: the published SOTA is HPD at 67.3 +/- 4.1, and we have NOT reproduced it — it's a specialized architecture and 3 weeks wasn't enough. Proposal: leaderboard launches with reproduced-by-us badges on our four baselines, external numbers marked as reported. Keeps us honest.

Compute note: Titan preemption cost us ~4 days total, tolerable, no Vulcan ask needed.

Hyun

subject: Re: Project Sirocco kickoff: CFQ as a first-class eval product
body:
Wrapping up the Sirocco milestone thread.

Decisions: leaderboard went live internally April 20 with Hyun's reproduced-by-us badge scheme — already 3 submissions from the language portfolio. The hosted dataset serves from Corpus and the harness runs the full MCD-MEAN protocol (average over the three MCD splits with 95% CIs) with one command.

Scope cut: SPARQL-level error analysis tooling moves to a fast-follow. It kept growing and I'd rather hit the window than gold-plate.

Nadia — we'd like a Launch Review Board slot the week of May 11 for sign-off on opening the leaderboard to all portfolios; no external demo yet.

Small typo in the announce draft btw, it's "Compositional Freebase Questions" not "Queries" — fixed.

Dmitri

subject: Kickoff: pre-training vs specialized architectures study
body:
Hi Alina,

Kicking off the semantic parsing generalization study. Basis is our published comparison of pre-training vs. specialized architectures for compositional generalization; the ask from leadership is an updated, internal-model version: does scale-plus-pre-training still beat purpose-built parsers (CGPS and friends) on MCD-style splits, and by how much?

Product angle: this directly informs whether the parsing features in two roadmap items use a fine-tuned general model or a bespoke architecture. A clear answer saves a team-quarter either way.

Milestones (Apr 20 – Jul 13): harness + data prep by mid-May, main sweep done end of June, write-up and recommendation by Jul 10. The original experiments ran on single V100s, so per-run cost is small — it's the sweep breadth that adds up.

Alina, over to you for staffing + compute.

Lucia

subject: Re: Kickoff: pre-training vs specialized architectures study
body:
Lucia,

Staffing plan:

- Gustavo 50% throughout — experiment design, owns the recommendation doc.
- Linnea 40% May–June — T5 fine-tuning lanes.
- Halima 40% May–June — specialized-architecture lanes (CGPS reproduction first, it's the fiddliest).
- Farah Haddad is committed at 60% here for all of July 2026 to carry the final sweep infrastructure. She ramps at 20% in June for handover, then owns the big sweep and results pipeline in July. I've confirmed her calendar is clear for it.

Compute: ~40 concurrent V100-class runs at peak. Titan best-effort covers it; no reservation. Single-GPU jobs, embarrassingly parallel.

Risk to flag now: the reference stack is old (TF 1.15 era images). Halima will containerize week one so we don't fight dependencies in June.

Alina

subject: Re: Kickoff: pre-training vs specialized architectures study
body:
Mid-study status.

Harness and data prep done (Linnea). CGPS reproduction done (Halima) — matches published behavior: strong on the random split, collapses on MCD-style splits. T5 lanes: fine-tuned T5-base already beats CGPS on every MCD split we've run, consistent with the original paper's headline that pre-training closes most of the gap that specialized architectures were built for.

Interesting wrinkle: on our hardest internal split the specialized model wins at small data sizes (<10k examples), crossover around 25k. If that holds it changes the recommendation from "always pre-train" to a data-budget rule.

Risk: the crossover finding needs the full sweep to be trustworthy — 5 seeds x 8 configs x 4 splits. That's the July work Farah is set up to run. Schedule holds.

Gustavo

subject: Re: Kickoff: pre-training vs specialized architectures study
body:
Confirming the July plan after yesterday's sync.

Farah takes over sweep execution today at her planned 60% allocation for the month — she's built the config matrix (5 seeds x 8 configs x 4 splits = 160 runs) with auto-retry on Titan preemptions, and results land in a live dashboard so Gustavo can watch the crossover question settle in real time.

Decision: we are NOT extending the sweep to the two extra model sizes Linnea proposed. It would push past Jul 13 and the data-budget crossover is the decision-relevant question, not absolute SOTA.

Linnea and Halima roll off this week as planned. Write-up review Jul 9, recommendation to Lucia Jul 10.

Alina

subject: Charformer JAX port — kickoff
body:
Hi Bruno,

Kicking off the Charformer effort. Our open-source release is the Mesh-TensorFlow reference implementation of gradient-based subword tokenization — layers that plug into the T5 codebase — and the README has promised a JAX/FLAX implementation "later" for long enough that it's become a running joke. More importantly, tokenizer-free models are back on the roadmap: the multilingual quality team wants GBST for scripts where our current subword vocab is embarrassing.

Goals for Feb 9 – May 4: (1) JAX/FLAX GBST layer with parity against the Mesh-TF reference on a small config, (2) integration into our internal trainer, (3) a base-size training run demonstrating quality on the multilingual eval. Scaled sweeps come in Q3 with real budget.

Bruno — staffing and the budget conversation with Finance are the first blockers. Can you take both?

Priya

subject: Re: Charformer JAX port — kickoff
body:
Priya,

Staffing: Wei 50% (GBST layer + parity, he knows the Mesh-TF code path including the transformer.py injection points), Milan 40% (trainer integration), Emeka 30% (test harness + parity checks), Yara 30% from March (multilingual eval).

Compute, near term: parity runs are small — 16 A100s best-effort on Titan is plenty through April.

Budget, Q3: good news from my sync with Finance yesterday. Idris has verbally earmarked $180k from the Q3 discretionary compute budget line B-57 for our scaled JAX training runs, so the Q3 sweep is funded even before the formal allocation posts. I'll get it in writing when the Q3 books open, but we can plan the sweep sizing around that number now.

cc'ing Idris for visibility.

Bruno

subject: Re: Charformer JAX port — kickoff
body:
Status on the port.

Parity: reached on the base config. Our FLAX GBST layer matches the Mesh-TF reference (the cf_v2_d3_dv_base.gin config) to within float tolerance on forward pass, and end-to-end training curves overlap after 50k steps. The fiddly part was replicating how the reference injects the gradient-subword layers right after the positional embeddings and loops them before the layer stack — order matters more than the paper lets on.

Trainer integration (Milan): done for single-host, multi-host sharding in review.

Risk for the record: at char-level sequence lengths our attention memory blows up ~3.5x vs subword baseline at equal batch. GBST's downsampling recovers most of it but not all; Yara's eval runs will need gradient checkpointing on, which costs ~20% step time. Doesn't threaten the window, does affect Q3 sweep sizing.

Wei

subject: Re: Charformer JAX port — kickoff
body:
Closing out the window, decisions from today's review:

1) Yara's base-size multilingual run cleared the bar: +2.1 average on the low-resource script slice vs our subword baseline, roughly neutral elsewhere. That's the GBST pitch working as advertised.

2) Decision: we upstream the FLAX implementation to our open-source repo — it finally makes good on the README promise, and it's good optics for the release. Emeka owns the cleanup, two weeks.

3) Q3 sweep sizing: per Wei's memory findings we plan the sweep at checkpointing-on step-time numbers, which fits inside the budget envelope Bruno secured. Sweep plan doc due to me by May 15 so it's ready when Q3 OKRs lock June 26.

Good quarter, team.

Priya

subject: CISC kickoff — cheaper self-consistency for reasoning endpoints
body:
Hi Deshawn,

Kicking off CISC productization. Background: self-consistency decoding is our largest serving-cost line on the reasoning endpoints — we sample many long paths and majority-vote. Our CISC work (Confidence-Informed Self-Consistency, the ACL Findings paper) showed a confidence-weighted majority vote reduces required reasoning paths by over 40% on average across nine models and four datasets, at equal or better accuracy.

40% off that serving line is a real number Finance will notice, which is the pitch.

Milestones (Feb 23 – Jun 8): reproduce paper results on our production models by end of March; offline A/B on logged traffic in April; serving integration + shadow deployment in May; launch review early June.

Deshawn, staffing plan when you can. The serving integration is the long pole so let's get that owner named early.

Priya

subject: Re: CISC kickoff — cheaper self-consistency for reasoning endpoints
body:
Priya,

Staffing:

- Katya 50% Mar–Apr: paper reproduction on prod models, owns the eval methodology.
- Umar 40% throughout: confidence-extraction methods (the within-question confidence evaluation from the paper is the part I trust least to transfer, he'll pressure-test it).
- Nikhil 30% Apr: offline A/B harness on logged traffic.
- Jorge Vidal is committed at 60% to this project for May 2026 — he owns the serving-path integration with Zeke's Shipyard team, and I've blocked his calendar accordingly. Shadow deployment can't slip, so I wanted a named owner with real allocation, not spare cycles.

Compute: sampling-heavy but inference-only. Requesting 64 A100s best-effort on Titan for March/April evals; serving-side capacity comes from Shipyard's existing pool.

Deshawn

subject: Re: CISC kickoff — cheaper self-consistency for reasoning endpoints
body:
Reproduction + A/B status.

Good news: on our three production reasoning models, CISC's weighted majority vote hits self-consistency parity at 38–44% fewer sampled paths, right in line with the paper's 40%+ claim. On the internal math suite it's actually accuracy-positive at equal budget.

The caveat Umar predicted: confidence method choice matters a lot, and — exactly as the paper found — the most calibrated method is the least effective for CISC. Our best-calibrated prod confidence head underperforms; the cheap verbalized-confidence prompt wins. Counterintuitive but consistent with the within-question evaluation story: what matters is ranking answers within a question, not global calibration.

Risk: verbalized confidence adds ~35 tokens/path. Net savings still large (~36%) but the headline number shrinks. Nikhil's A/B harness starts on logged traffic Monday.

Katya

subject: Re: CISC kickoff — cheaper self-consistency for reasoning endpoints
body:
Decision checkpoint.

Offline A/B confirmed Katya's numbers: 36% serving-cost reduction at neutral-to-positive accuracy on logged reasoning traffic. We go to shadow deployment.

Jorge's serving integration with Shipyard is on track — confidence-weighted vote runs in the aggregation layer, no model changes needed, and Zeke's team signed off on the latency budget (adds <8ms p99). Shadow deploy targets May 27, two weeks of shadow, then launch review June 8 — Nadia has us penciled for that board.

One scope decision: we ship with verbalized confidence only. Umar's alternative confidence heads go to a fast-follow; the shrunken-but-solid 36% is worth banking now rather than chasing the last few points into Q3.

Priya

subject: CIW kickoff — robust training under label noise as a shared component
body:
Hi Jelena,

Kicking off the CIW effort. Our Constrained Instance and Class reWeighting work formulates label-noise handling as constrained optimization problems with simple closed-form updates for instance and class weights, solved per mini-batch — no need to store weights over the full dataset. That last property is why it can be a drop-in component rather than a research artifact.

Demand is real: three teams flagged noisy-label pain in Q2 planning (weak supervision, crowdsourced labels, scraped data). Goal: a supported library + recommended recipes, validated on the standard CIFAR-10 noise benchmarks and two internal datasets.

Milestones (Apr 13 – Jul 20): library extraction by mid-May; benchmark validation June; big validation sweep early July; docs + internal release by Jul 20.

Jelena — staffing and the compute ask for the July sweep are the open items.

Ximena

subject: Re: CIW kickoff — robust training under label noise as a shared component
body:
Ximena,

Staffing: Leilani 50% (library extraction + API), Emeka 40% (benchmark harness), Giannis 30% (internal dataset integrations), Farah 25% (CI + release tooling through June).

Compute: day-to-day development fits on Titan best-effort. The July validation sweep is the big ask — noise types x noise rates x methods x seeds across CIFAR-10 and both internal sets. Ines confirmed our reservation on vulcan-h100 — 512 accelerators for the week of 2026-07-06 — which covers the full noise-sweep matrix in one shot. I've sized the matrix so it completes in 5 days with headroom, and cc'd Ines so the paperwork trail is in one place.

After the sweep we're compute-light through release.

Jelena

subject: Re: CIW kickoff — robust training under label noise as a shared component
body:
Status.

Library extraction done — the closed-form weight updates are now a standalone module with a keras-style wrapper; Farah's CI runs the CIFAR-10 40% symmetric-noise config as the regression test.

Benchmark validation under way (Emeka): on CIFAR-10 with 40% symmetric noise we match the published CIW numbers, and the CICW variant — using the instance weights to drive mixup — adds a further +1.8 accuracy, consistent with the paper's finding that weighted mixup gives additional gains under noise.

Risk to flag: on one internal dataset the class-weight constraint interacts badly with extreme class imbalance (weights collapse toward the head classes). Giannis is testing the label-smoothing-style relaxation the theory section suggests. If it doesn't resolve by mid-June we ship instance-weighting-only recipes for imbalanced data and document it.

Leilani

subject: Re: CIW kickoff — robust training under label noise as a shared component
body:
Pre-sweep checkpoint and one decision.

Decision: Giannis's relaxation fixed the imbalance collapse on the internal set (head-class weight mass down from 91% to 64%, accuracy +2.3 on the tail), so full CICW recipes ship for imbalanced data too. No scope cut needed.

Sweep logistics: config matrix is frozen at 1,920 runs. We start Monday on our vulcan-h100 week — the 512-accelerator reservation for the week of 2026-07-06 — with Emeka running launch and Farah on-call for the results pipeline. Anything that fails twice gets dropped from the matrix rather than re-queued, we have stats headroom.

If all goes to plan we're writing docs by Jul 13 and release on schedule.

Jelena

subject: CKD kickoff — hallucination-resistant captioning via contrastive distillation
body:
Hi Ivo,

Kicking off CKD. Problem statement: our VLM captioning features still hallucinate objects, and it's the top complaint from the two internal product surfaces using them. CKD is our contrastive knowledge distillation recipe built on the LAVIS stack (patched — the ckd.patch approach from our open-source release) that trains the model to distinguish grounded objects from plausible-but-absent ones.

What it unlocks: measurably lower hallucination rates, scored on POPE-style object-presence evals, without retraining the base VLM.

Milestones (Apr 27 – Aug 3): environment + data downloads (VG, COCO, GQA) by mid-May; training data pipeline by end of June; distillation runs + POPE evals in July; go/no-go for product integration Aug 3.

Ivo — resourcing plan please, the data pipeline is the part I can't size myself.

Lucia

subject: Re: CKD kickoff — hallucination-resistant captioning via contrastive distillation
body:
Lucia,

Sizing done, here's the plan.

The long pole is exactly what you suspected. We're scoping and staffing a synthetic-data generation pipeline from scratch — negative-object mining over the image corpora plus cached model-generated descriptions — since nothing reusable exists in the org for this. Concretely: stage 1 mines plausible negative objects per image (the vg_sample_negatives path), stage 2 generates and caches descriptions from our strongest internal model so training never blocks on inference. Wanjiru and Chiara own it, both at 50% for six weeks starting next week.

subject: CBD kickoff — fixing tail-class accuracy on long-tailed workloads
body:
Hi Santiago,

Kicking off the Class-Balanced Distillation effort. Three internal classification workloads have textbook long-tail problems — great head-class numbers, embarrassing tail. Our published CBD recipe (BMVC 2021) is a two-stage approach: stage one trains teachers with vanilla and augmented setups, stage two distills into a student with class-balanced sampling. It beat prior long-tail methods on ImageNet-LT and iNaturalist18, so we have a strong prior it transfers.

Goal for Feb 16 – Jun 1: reproduce published numbers to validate our harness, then apply to the two highest-priority internal workloads with a go/no-go quality bar of +5 tail accuracy at <1 head regression.

Efficiency angle for the OKR: better tail accuracy means fewer manual review escalations, which is a measurable cost line.

Santiago — staffing + compute plan when ready.

Zofia

subject: Re: CBD kickoff — fixing tail-class accuracy on long-tailed workloads
body:
Zofia,

Plan:

Staffing — Tereza 50% (reproduction: the two-stage config path, stage_one_vanilla then stage two, on ImageNet-LT via tfds-nightly since we added ImageNet-LT and iNaturalist18 to TFDS as part of the release); Linnea 40% (internal workload adaptation); Wanjiru 30% (data plumbing); Fumiko 30% from April (analysis + the go/no-go eval).

Compute — reproduction is moderate: ~64 A100s for the teacher ensembles, Titan best-effort should hold. SimCLR-style augmentation teachers double stage-one cost, budgeted for that.

Budget — flagging the Q3 continuation early: Idris verbally earmarked $180k from the Q3 discretionary compute budget line B-28 for this project's scale-up runs, so we can commit to the larger teacher ensembles in the Q3 plan. Formal allocation lands when Q3 books open; cc'ing Idris so it's on the record.

subject: Re: CBD kickoff — fixing tail-class accuracy on long-tailed workloads

ImageNet-LT: done. Our two-stage runs land within 0.4 of the published CBD overall accuracy, with the expected pattern — big tail-class gains from the class-balanced distillation stage, head classes held by the teacher ensemble. Teacher diversity matters as advertised: dropping the SimCLR-augmented teacher costs 1.9 on tail accuracy.

iNaturalist18: running, ETA next week. No surprises so far.

Internal workload #1 (Linnea): adaptation started. subject: CLAY kickoff — denoising our mobile UI datasets at scale
body:
Hi Jelena,

Kicking off the CLAY adaptation. Context: our internal mobile UI-understanding datasets have the exact pathology our CHI 2022 CLAY paper addressed — raw view hierarchies that don't match what's actually on screen (invisible nodes, mislabeled types, layout drift). The published work showed you can learn to denoise raw mobile UI layouts and improve dataset quality at scale, using a Transformer-based object typing model for the per-node labels.

Goal (Feb 9 – May 11): stand up the denoising pipeline against our internal datasets, quality-gate it against a hand-labeled audit set, and hand data-platforms a repeatable cleaning pass they can run on every ingest.

This is a 3-email-checkin project on my side; keep it lean. Jelena, staffing sketch when you can.

Dmitri

subject: Re: CLAY kickoff — denoising our mobile UI datasets at scale
body:
Dmitri,

Staffing + the one big build item.

People: Kaia 50% (models — denoiser + the object typing model), Katya 40% (audit set + eval), Saoirse 40% and Wanjiru 40% (data engineering).

The build item: our internal screens differ enough from the public CLAY dataset that we need training data reflecting our own noise distribution. So: we're scoping and staffing a synthetic-data generation pipeline from scratch — there's nothing in the org we can reuse for this, so Saoirse and Wanjiru will build the noise-injection and screen-synthesis stages ourselves. Six weeks, starting Mar 2. It's the majority of the eng cost but it's also what makes the cleaning pass repeatable on every ingest.

Compute: light — 16 A100s best-effort on Titan covers training. No reservations.

Jelena

subject: Re: CLAY kickoff — denoising our mobile UI datasets at scale
body:

Pipeline: synthetic-data generation is live — noise injection matches the empirical noise stats Katya measured on the audit set (node-visibility errors and type mislabels within 2% of observed rates). Denoiser trained on it hits 91.4 F1 on invisible-node detection against the hand-labeled audit set; the object typing model is at 87.9 macro-F1 across our 24 internal type classes.

Risk: tablet layouts. They're 9% of ingest volume but 31% of our residual errors — the noise distribution is genuinely different (multi-pane hierarchies). Options: (a) extend synthesis to tablet patterns, ~3 weeks, blows the May 11 window; (b) ship phone-layout cleaning now, gate tablet ingest behind a warning flag, extend in a fast-follow.

subject: CaR kickoff — open-vocabulary segmentation without training data
body:
Hi Jelena,

Kicking off the CLIP-as-RNN productization. The method (CaR, from our open-source release) does open-vocabulary segmentation with zero training — a recurrent loop that proposes masks from CLIP and iteratively filters text queries that don't match the image, so it can segment essentially arbitrary concepts. For product teams this means segmentation for long-tail concepts without anyone collecting a labeled dataset first, which is the entire reason three teams have asked for it.

Milestones (Apr 13 – Jul 6): internal demo endpoint by mid-May; benchmark evals reproduced on our harness by early June; hardened batch API + launch review by Jul 6.

Known constraint from the public demo: the SAM-based mask refinement needs GPU serving, CPU-only won't cut it — so this is a Shipyard conversation early.

Jelena, staffing + infra plan please.

Lucia

subject: Re: CaR kickoff — open-vocabulary segmentation without training data
body:
Lucia,

Plan:

Staffing — Carmen 50% (method owner: the recurrent CLIP loop + mask quality), Bilal 40% (serving + data), Gustavo 40% (eval reproduction on the segmentation benchmarks, config-per-dataset like the release).

subject: Re: CaR kickoff — open-vocabulary segmentation without training data

subject: Project Obsidian kickoff — Cluster-GCN on our entity graphs
body:
Hi Jelena,

Kicking off the Cluster-GCN adoption. We're running this under the internal codename Project Obsidian — use it in channel names and docs.

Why: the retrieval team's entity graph has grown to the point where full-graph GCN training doesn't fit, and neighborhood-sampling approaches are burning GPU-hours. Our Cluster-GCN work (KDD 2019 oral) fixes exactly this: partition the graph with METIS, then train on cluster-induced subgraph batches, which keeps memory bounded and lets us go deeper than 2-3 layers.

Goal (Feb 2 – Apr 13): reproduce the published PPI and Reddit benchmark results to validate the setup, then train on the internal entity graph and hand retrieval a model that beats their sampled-GCN baseline at half the GPU cost.

Jelena — staffing + a quick infra check on METIS in our build, please.

Anders

subject: Re: Project Obsidian kickoff — Cluster-GCN on our entity graphs
body:
Anders,

Obsidian plan.

Staffing: Efe 50% (reproduction: PPI + Reddit, GraphSAGE-format preprocessing per the release); Csilla 40% (internal entity-graph adaptation — she knows the retrieval team's data model); Wei 30% (deep-GCN experiments once reproduction is green); Jorge 30% (infra: METIS builds, training pipeline).

Infra check done: metis-5.1.0 builds clean in our container with the shared-lib config, and Jorge verified the Python interface (part_graph on the example gives sane edgecuts). One gotcha — METIS_DLL has to be set in the job env or imports fail silently at runtime, he's baking it into the base image.

Compute: modest, that's the whole point of the method. 8 A100s best-effort on Titan covers everything including the internal graph.

Jelena

subject: Re: Project Obsidian kickoff — Cluster-GCN on our entity graphs
body:
Obsidian status.

Reproduction: green on both benchmarks. PPI micro-F1 matches the published Cluster-GCN result within noise, Reddit likewise — and the headline property holds: peak GPU memory stays flat as we scale batch count, exactly what the cluster-induced subgraph batching promises. A 5-layer model on Reddit trains on a single A100 where full-batch would OOM.

Internal graph (Csilla): first METIS partitioning of the entity graph done — 1,400 partitions, partition quality looks reasonable (6.2% edge cut). First training runs this week.

Risk to flag: our entity graph's degree distribution is much more skewed than Reddit's. A handful of hub nodes end up with most of their edges cut across partitions, which the paper's stochastic multiple-partition trick mitigates but maybe not fully at our skew. Wei is designing an ablation; if hub-node accuracy lags we may need a hybrid batching scheme for the top 0.1% of nodes.

Efe

subject: Re: Project Obsidian kickoff — Cluster-GCN on our entity graphs
body:
Closing out Obsidian's window — decisions from this morning's review.

Results: internal entity-graph model beats retrieval's sampled-GCN baseline by +3.1 on their ranking eval at 0.45x the GPU cost. Under half. The hub-node concern turned out manageable — Wei's ablation showed stochastic multiple partitions recovers most of it; hub accuracy trails by only 0.8 and retrieval considers that acceptable for v1.

Decisions:
1) Hand off to retrieval as planned. Csilla owns the transition doc; Jorge packages the training pipeline (with the METIS_DLL fix baked in) as a reusable recipe.
2) The hybrid batching scheme for hub nodes is NOT pursued now — parked with Wei's ablation data attached for whoever picks it up.
3) Wei writes a short internal tech note comparing depth: 5-layer vs 2-layer gains on our graph.

Thanks all — textbook project.

Anders

subject: CNC kickoff — learned normalized cuts for corpus clustering
body:
Hi Jelena,

Kicking off the CNC adoption. Today the retrieval side clusters corpus shards with spectral clustering — Laplacian eigenspace embedding, then k-means — and it's both slow at our scale and awkward to update incrementally. Our CNC work replaces that with a model trained to directly minimize a continuous relaxation of the expected normalized cuts objective, unsupervised, outputting cluster probabilities directly. In the paper's motivating example CNC converges to the optimal cut value (0.286 on the toy CIFAR-10 affinity graph), matching spectral clustering without the eigendecomposition.

Goal (Feb 23 – May 25): reproduce published behavior on reference datasets, then a bake-off vs the spectral pipeline on one production corpus shard — quality parity at materially lower cost is the bar.

Jelena, staffing + platform dependencies when ready.

Anders

subject: Re: CNC kickoff — learned normalized cuts for corpus clustering
body:
Anders,

Plan:

Staffing — Umar 40% (method owner, loss + training); Quentin 50% (reproduction and the bake-off harness — good growth project for him with Umar reviewing); Farah 35% through April (training infra); Wanjiru 30% (affinity-graph construction from the production shard, plus the Corpus work below).

Compute — small models, the cost is in affinity-graph construction, which is CPU/data work. 8 A100s best-effort covers all training.

Heads-up on the one platform dependency: the Corpus v2 migration freeze is 2026-06-26, so the affinity-graph tables must be migrated before our window even ends — Wanjiru will run that migration in late May so we're not scrambling. I'd rather eat the week now than discover in July that we're pinned to v1 tables nobody maintains.

Jelena

subject: Re: CNC kickoff — learned normalized cuts for corpus clustering
body:
Status.

Reproduction: done. On the reference setups our CNC loss converges to the expected normalized cuts values and the cluster assignments match spectral clustering's, as in the paper. The end-to-end differentiable formulation trains stably once we got the learning-rate schedule right (it's sensitive early — Umar's warmup fix in the repo).

Bake-off, first pass on the production shard: quality is at parity (within 0.3 on our internal cluster-coherence metric) and inference is where the win is — assigning new documents to clusters is a forward pass, vs re-running the eigenspace embedding. Incremental updates go from a nightly batch job to near-online.

Risk/trade-off: full-graph training on the shard's affinity graph is memory-hungry; we're training on sampled subgraphs and there's a quality wobble (~0.5) depending on sampling rate. Umar wants one more sweep before we lock the recommendation.

Quentin

subject: Re: CNC kickoff — learned normalized cuts for corpus clustering
body:
Decision checkpoint.

Umar's sampling sweep settled it: at 20% subgraph sampling the quality wobble drops to 0.1 — parity for practical purposes — and training fits comfortably on our footprint. So the bake-off verdict is: parity on quality, ~6x cheaper incremental updates, near-online cluster assignment. Retrieval wants it.

Decisions:
1) GO on handover: Quentin and Umar package the training recipe + the warmup fix; target May 22.
2) Scope cut: we do NOT take on replacing the batch re-clustering job itself this window — retrieval owns operationalizing, we deliver the model + recipe. Keeps us honest on the May 25 close.
3) Wanjiru confirmed the affinity-graph tables are migrated and validated — that dependency is closed.

Good project, and Quentin — strong first lead. Noted for calibration.

Anders

subject: CMMD kickoff — replacing FID in Evalline
body:
Hi Daniela,

Kicking off the CMMD rollout. Our "Rethinking FID" work showed FID's weaknesses as a generation metric — Inception features and the normality assumption chief among them — and proposed CMMD: MMD distance computed on CLIP embeddings (ViT-L/14@336px), distribution-free and better aligned with human judgment. Every image-gen team here still reports FID because that's what Evalline serves. Let's fix that.

Goal (Mar 2 – May 11): CMMD as a first-class Evalline metric — JAX implementation productionized, reference sets hosted, side-by-side CMMD/FID reporting during a transition period, then CMMD as the default gate for generation launches.

Coordination with Tomas's team is the critical path; the math is done, the plumbing isn't.

Daniela — staffing + dependency plan please.

Lucia

subject: Re: CMMD kickoff — replacing FID in Evalline
body:
Lucia,

Plan:

Staffing — Katya 50% (metric implementation: the JAX/Scenic path, CLIP weight handling for air-gapped jobs where auto-download fails); Amara 40% (Evalline integration, pairing with Tomas's team); Chiara 30% (reference-set hosting + docs).

Dependencies — Tomas has committed an integration slot in April (cc'd). Reference image sets (COCO-derived and two internal) get hosted in Corpus now; Corpus v2's migration freeze is 2026-08-07, so moving the reference-image sets to v2 is comfortably a post-launch task — I've slotted it for July and we don't need to think about it this window.

Risk — teams gaming the transition by reporting whichever metric flatters them. Proposal: side-by-side is mandatory, cherry-picking isn't an option.

subject: Re: CMMD kickoff — replacing FID in Evalline
body:
Status.

Implementation: done and validated — our production CMMD matches the reference implementation to 4 decimal places on the paper's test cases. The unbiased MMD estimator means no more "FID needs 50k samples" folklore: CMMD is stable at a few thousand images, which alone will save teams real eval compute. Also handled the offline case: CLIP ViT-L/14@336px weights are mirrored internally so air-gapped eval jobs don't attempt the auto-download.

Evalline integration (Amara): metric endpoint merged, side-by-side CMMD/FID reporting works in staging.

One finding worth surfacing: on our internal gen-model leaderboard, CMMD and FID disagree on the #2/#3 ordering. We expected this (it's the paper's whole point — FID can contradict human raters) but expect noise from affected teams. Suggest we pre-brief them rather than let them find out on the dashboard.

Katya

subject: Re: CMMD kickoff — replacing FID in Evalline
body:
Wrap-up decisions.

1) CMMD went live in Evalline Apr 27, side-by-side with FID. The pre-briefing worked — the team affected by the #2/#3 flip re-ran their human-preference study and CMMD's ordering matched raters, which turned our loudest potential critic into the reference customer. Couldn't have scripted it better.

2) Decision: FID is deprecated for launch gates effective with the Q3 cycle; side-by-side reporting continues through end of Q3 for continuity, then FID becomes opt-in. Tomas is aligned.

3) Scope cut: video-generation support (frame-sampling scheme) was floated and is explicitly out — it needs its own design, punting to a Q3 proposal.

Chiara's docs + reference-set hosting are done. Nice tight project, thanks all.

Lucia

subject: CNN quantization kickoff — 4-bit training as a serving-cost lever
body:
Hi Bao,

Kicking off the quantization effort. Our open-source quantization codebase (built on tf_cnn_benchmarks) already demonstrates 4-bit fixed-point quantized training — weights and activations both, via the quant_weight_bits=4 / quant_act_bits=4 path with the ReLU-X activation trick. What it's never had is a vetted, supported recipe with quality bars, and meanwhile vision-model serving cost grew 40% year over year.

Goal (Feb 23 – Jun 29): validate 4-bit quantized training on ResNet50-class models against full-precision baselines, characterize the accuracy/cost frontier at 8/4/2 bits, and publish an internal recipe with go/no-go bars for serving teams.

The big validation sweep in June is the one real compute event; everything before is single-node work.

Bao — staffing + the June compute ask, please.

Zofia

subject: Re: CNN quantization kickoff — 4-bit training as a serving-cost lever
body:
Zofia,

Plan:

Staffing — Maren 50% (owns the codebase: bringing the tf_cnn_benchmarks-based stack up on current nightlies, it's picky about TF versions); Jorge 40% Feb–Apr (training infra + sweep automation); Farah 30% (eval + the accuracy/cost frontier analysis).

Compute — development fits on scraps: single-GPU runs (the resnet50_v2 batch-32 config) on Titan best-effort. subject: Re: CNN quantization kickoff — 4-bit training as a serving-cost lever
body:

Codebase: up on current nightlies (took two weeks of dependency archaeology, the stack really does want the latest nightly TF as the README warns). Frontier so far (Farah's analysis): 8-bit is free (0.2 gap), 4-bit costs ~1 point, 2-bit falls off a cliff (>6 points) on everything we've tried. So the recipe story is shaping up as "8-bit by default, 4-bit where cost dominates."

subject: Re: CNN quantization kickoff — 4-bit training as a serving-cost lever

subject: Cochlear implant pipeline kickoff — from hackathon code to accessibility demo
body:
Hi Bruno,

Kicking off the cochlear implant effort. Our open-source hackathon submission takes input audio — music, speech in noise — applies speech enhancement primarily when music is NOT detected, and generates electrodograms for cochlear implants. The clever bit is the mixing strategy: because enhancement tends to strip music as if it were noise, the pipeline uses YAMNet to estimate music content and causally mix original and enhanced audio.

Why now: the accessibility roadmap has a hearing-assistance line item for H2, and this is our strongest asset. Goal (Feb 16 – Jul 6): productize the notebooks into a pipeline, establish evaluation with vocoder simulation for listening checks, retrain the enhancement model on our current speech corpora, and land a Launch Review-approved internal demo.

Bruno — staffing + compute please. The retraining is the only heavy item.

Goran

subject: Re: Cochlear implant pipeline kickoff — from hackathon code to accessibility demo

Goran,

Plan:

Staffing — Efe 50% (enhancement model + retraining), Milan 40% (pipeline engineering: notebooks → batch pipeline, electrodogram generation), Halima 40% (eval: vocoder-simulation listening workflow + objective metrics, plus the YAMNet mixing-threshold study).

Compute — light until June: pipeline and eval work runs on 8 best-effort A100s. The heavy event is the enhancement-model retrain on our current speech corpora. Ines's team has us down for the vulcan-h100 reservation — 512 accelerators for the week of 2026-06-22 — which is when we retrain the enhancement model at full scale. Mixing-threshold study: the fixed-fraction baseline mixing is clearly worse than YAMNet gating — on our music-plus-speech test set, YAMNet-gated mixing preserves music segments the plain enhancement path strips out, at equivalent speech intelligibility scores (STOI within 0.01). Recommend we drop the fixed-fraction path from the demo entirely, one less thing to explain.
