subject: Re: Project Nimbus kickoff: language-to-policy-code demo plan
body:
Hi Ulla,

Staffing: Freya Ruiz at 50% as research lead, Maren Zhou at 40% on the control-primitive API layer, Halima Toure at 30% on perception integration. Tight but workable for the 4/27 target.

Compute is modest — this is prompting-heavy, not training-heavy. I've asked for 32 A100s best-effort on titan-a100 for sim rollouts and eval batches. No vulcan or cirrus ask this half.

Two dependencies to flag: we need a Shipyard demo slot for the LRB session, and the hierarchical code-gen prompts (recursively generating undefined helper functions) need a stable model endpoint — Freya will pin a version this week so evals stay comparable.

If the LRB date slips past early May we lose the robot lab booking, so let's hold 4/27 firm.

Jelena

subject: Re: Project Nimbus kickoff: language-to-policy-code demo plan
body:
Hi both,

Status: the prompt library is in. LMPs now chain perception outputs into control primitives, and the hierarchical code-gen path (recursively generating helper functions) works — the model writes NumPy/Shapely code for the spatial-geometric cases like "move a bit to the left of the mug" unprompted.

Sim numbers: 46/50 tabletop pick-and-place instructions succeed, including held-out object names. Where it struggles: prescribing precise velocities from ambiguous language ("faster") is context-dependent, and on the real arm our impedance-controller primitive occasionally receives unsafe gain values.

Proposed mitigation: clamp gains in the API rather than trusting generated code, and keep a whitelist of importable libraries. Costs some generality, buys safety sign-off.

Risk to 4/27: real-platform integration is a week behind; Maren and I think it's recoverable.

Freya

subject: Nimbus: LRB demo scope decision
body:
Team,

Decision after yesterday's review with Jelena: we're cutting trajectory-based control from the LRB demo and going with vision-based pick and place plus the reactive impedance behaviors only. The trajectory work continues, it just doesn't gate the demo.

Rationale: the gain-clamping change Freya proposed passed safety review, but only for the clamped primitive set. Rather than rush a second review before 5/4, we show the narrower slice confidently.

LRB is confirmed for 4/29, Shipyard slot booked. Nadia's office needs the demo script by 4/24 — Freya, can you own that? Maren, please freeze the API surface Thursday; no new primitives after that.

Nice work getting Nimbus this far this fast.

Ulla

subject: Kickoff: codistillation as our large-scale training recipe
body:
Hi Alina,

Kicking off the codistillation productionization. The pitch for the efficiency portfolio: online distillation lets us scale distributed training past the point where synchronous SGD stops paying off — replicas train together and distill from each other's predictions, no parameter-server bottleneck. Our open-source release already ships the Common Crawl paragraph-ID subset (delta-encoded CSVs, ~392MB), so the data story is reproducible from day one.

What I want out of this half: (1) the recipe reproduced on our stack, (2) a wall-clock and cost comparison against our standard data-parallel baseline, (3) a go/no-go on making it the default for models above 10B params. That last one is the Q3 OKR candidate, so evidence needs to land before the 6/26 lock.

Staffing and compute proposal by early April?

Zofia

subject: Re: Kickoff: codistillation as our large-scale training recipe
body:
Hi Zofia,

Plan: Tereza Aliyev leads reproduction (50%), Kaia Wolde owns the baseline comparison harness (40%), Efe Lindqvist on data plumbing (30%). Saoirse Eriksen is committed at 65% to this project for May 2026 to build the two-worker prediction-exchange layer — that's the long pole, and May is when it has to land.

Compute: staying on titan-a100 best-effort, 64 GPUs steady state for the paired-replica runs. No reservation ask; if we get preempted the comparison is still fair since both arms run in the same pool.

One dependency: the paragraph-ID tarball decodes with the delta scheme from the release — Efe verified the sha256 — but restitching against the raw Common Crawl snapshot needs Corpus scratch space, roughly 30TB. I've filed the ticket with Jun's team.

Alina

subject: Codistillation status: reproduction + fabric contention
body:
Hi both,

Status on reproduction: the two-replica online distillation run matches our data-parallel baseline's validation loss with 1.7x better wall-clock at equal hardware, consistent with the paper's finding that distillation targets act as a stabilizer at large batch counts. Saoirse's prediction-exchange layer is in; checkpoint-free teacher updates every 500 steps.

Data side is clean — Efe rebuilt the training set from the released paragraph IDs (delta decode, then join against the Crawl snapshot), so our numbers are directly comparable to the paper's setup.

The risk: at 4+ replicas the exchange traffic contends with the input pipeline on titan's shared network fabric. Options are (a) staler predictions, exchanged every 2k steps, or (b) requesting a dedicated slice. (a) costs maybe 2% quality by early measurements; measuring properly this week.

Tereza

subject: Re: Codistillation status: reproduction + fabric contention
body:
Team,

Decisions from Wednesday's review, so we're aligned before OKR lock on 6/26:

1. Go for the OKR: codistillation becomes the recommended recipe for 10B+ training, with the 1.7x wall-clock result as headline evidence. Kaia, please get the comparison memo to Eleni by Tuesday.
2. Staleness over dedicated network: we take option (a), 2k-step exchange, and accept the ~2% quality cost. Requesting dedicated fabric would push us into reservation territory and undercut the cost story.
3. Data refresh is out of scope this half. We keep the released paragraph-ID subset frozen as the eval corpus; a Corpus-v2-based refresh is a Q3 item after the 7/10 migration freeze.

Thanks all — this one moved fast.

Zofia

subject: Kickoff: cognate reflex prediction for low-resource lexicons
body:
Hi Jelena,

Kicking off the cognate reflexes project. Basis is our open-source SIGTYP 2022 shared-task work: two systems, a Cognate Neighbors model (the mockingbird-n1/n2 configurations) and a Cognate Inpainting model that treats reflex prediction like filling in missing cells of a cognate table.

Product framing: predicted reflexes let us bootstrap lexicons for low-resource languages where we have related-language data — the language portfolio's coverage OKR depends on exactly this kind of leverage. Milestones: reproduce shared-task numbers by end of April, pick a winning architecture by early June, hand a scored lexicon sample to the translation team by launch review in July.

Can you get me staffing plus a compute sketch by mid-April? Nothing exotic expected — these models are small.

Thanks,
Priya

subject: Re: Kickoff: cognate reflex prediction for low-resource lexicons
body:
Hi Priya,

Staffing: Wei Ivanov leads modeling at 40%, Nikhil Abebe at 30% on the data and eval harness. Katya Silva is committed at 60% to this project for June 2026 — she'll drive the head-to-head training runs and the lexicon-sample deliverable, which is the crunch month before launch review.

Compute: these are small sequence models; we'll run inside our existing cirrus-tpu portfolio allocation, well under quota. No reservation needed.

One constraint: the shared-task data pipeline assumes an svn export plus the ST2022 repo layout, so Nikhil will spend the first week getting a clean internal mirror with checksums before anyone trains. I'd rather eat that week than debug data drift in May.

Jelena

subject: Re: Kickoff: cognate reflex prediction for low-resource lexicons
body:
Hi both,

Reproduction status: the Neighbors model matches the shared-task submissions. The per-language mockingbird-n1 configs at 25k, 30k, and 100k steps line up with the released numbers, and the 100k run is the best of the three on most languages. The per-language-group n2 variant is close behind at a fraction of the training cost — one model per family instead of one per language.

The inpainting model (mockingbird-i1) is the concern: it reproduces, but it degrades badly on families where the cognate table is sparse, which is precisely our low-resource product case. Neighbors handles sparsity better because it conditions on whatever neighbors exist.

Risk/trade-off to settle in June: n1 quality vs n2 operational simplicity. Katya's head-to-head runs will decide it.

Wei

subject: Decision: Neighbors architecture for launch review
body:
Team,

Decision from this morning's review: we go with the Neighbors architecture and drop inpainting from the launch-review scope. Wei's sparsity results made this straightforward — the product case is exactly where inpainting is weakest. Inpainting stays in the repo as a research artifact.

Within Neighbors, we're taking the n2 per-language-group configuration as default, with per-language n1 fine-tuning reserved for the five highest-priority languages. Katya's runs showed n2 within a point of n1 on the families that matter, and one model per family is far easier for the translation team to consume.

Remaining path to launch review: lexicon sample scored and delivered by 7/1, review the week after. Nikhil, please schedule the Evalline slot with Tomas' team.

Priya

subject: Kickoff: COLA audio embeddings as a platform backbone
body:
Hi Deshawn,

Kickoff for the audio embeddings track. We're standing up COLA — our open-source contrastive audio pre-training method — as the shared audio backbone for data-platforms. The library already supports the three modes we need: SSL pre-training, downstream fine-tuning (DS), and a supervised-from-scratch baseline (SUP), so this is productionizing rather than inventing.

Plan of record: pre-train on LibriSpeech, validate with a linear probe on Speech Commands, then offer frozen-encoder embeddings as a platform service. Success metric for the half: downstream teams get within 2 points of a task-specific supervised model using our frozen embeddings.

Milestones: pre-training reproduced by end of April, downstream evals in May, platform integration decision mid-June. Staffing and compute ask by 4/10?

Thanks,
Dmitri

subject: Re: Kickoff: COLA audio embeddings as a platform backbone
body:
Hi Dmitri,

Staffing: Vera Egede leads at 50%, Leilani Nakamura 40% on the serving/platform side, Wei Ivanov 30% on eval design, Halima Toure 20% for the TFDS input pipelines.

Compute is light — titan-a100 best-effort, 16 GPUs for SSL pre-training runs; COLA is deliberately a simple contrastive setup, no giant batches needed.

Scheduling constraint that shapes everything: the Corpus v2 migration freeze lands on 2026-06-26, so our audio ingestion and any new dataset registrations have to be on v2 before that date. I've sequenced Halima's pipeline work first so we're not registering datasets against a frozen system in July, and the platform integration decision needs to happen by mid-June for the same reason.

Deshawn

subject: COLA status: probe numbers + pipeline risk
body:
Hi both,

Status: SSL pre-training on LibriSpeech (LBS) reproduced cleanly, checkpoints landing under the standard model_dir layout. Downstream: a linear probe on Speech Commands v2 (SPCV2) with freeze_encoder=true gets 93.8%, and full fine-tuning reaches 95.4% — so frozen embeddings sit ~1.6 points off task-specific, inside Dmitri's 2-point success bar.

The trade-off to discuss: frozen-encoder serving is cheap and one-model-for-everything, but two downstream teams (wake-word and audio events) asked about fine-tuned variants, which multiplies serving cost and breaks the single-backbone story.

Risk: our input pipelines are TFDS-based; re-pointing them at Corpus-registered datasets is where Halima is spending most of her time, and it's slower than planned. She thinks two more weeks.

Vera

subject: Re: COLA status: probe numbers + pipeline risk
body:
Team,

Decision from today's review: we ship frozen-encoder embeddings as the platform offering. Vera's numbers (93.8 linear probe vs 95.4 fine-tuned on SPCV2) put frozen inside our quality bar, and one backbone is the whole point of a platform. Wake-word and audio-events teams can fine-tune downstream at their own serving cost — we'll document the DS recipe but not host the variants.

Halima confirmed the audio dataset registrations completed on v2 yesterday, ahead of the Corpus v2 freeze this Friday, so we're clear on the platform dependency.

Remaining: Leilani drives the embedding-service integration through July; Wei owns the eval card in Evalline. Launch review target stays mid-July.

Thanks all,
Dmitri

subject: Kickoff: cold posteriors & calibrated serving
body:
Hi Ivo,

Kicking off the uncertainty-quantification study for the efficiency portfolio. Base is our open-source cold-posterior work: careful SG-MCMC sampling shows the Bayes posterior predictive in deep nets can be systematically worse than plain SGD point estimates, while "cold" posteriors that overcount evidence do better. That result has direct product value — our deployed classifiers need calibrated confidence, and this tells us which posterior to actually serve.

Deliverables this half: reproduce the paper's figures 1-3 on our stack, run the hypothesis experiments on our internal image models, and produce a recommendation memo on temperature selection for serving. Launch-review-adjacent but mostly a research deliverable; final sweeps in July, memo by 7/17.

Staffing and compute by mid-April please — I expect the MCMC chains to be the expensive part.

Zofia

subject: Re: Kickoff: cold posteriors & calibrated serving
body:
Hi Zofia,

Staffing: Umar Costa leads at 50%, Paloma Castillo 40% on the SG-MCMC harness, Nikhil Abebe 25% on eval plumbing.

Compute: the chains are the cost, as you guessed — long sampling runs with many parallel chains to hit the ESS targets. Plan is titan-a100 best-effort through June for development, then the big final sweeps on Cirrus: we hold the cirrus-tpu reservation for the week of 2026-07-06, 128 accelerators, which covers the full temperature grid across both ResNet and LSTM experiments in one shot. That lands two weeks before your 7/17 memo date, with slack for reruns.

One flag: Paloma is also carrying harness maintenance for two other teams, so if her 40% erodes, the harness milestone slips first.

Ivo

subject: Re: Kickoff: cold posteriors & calibrated serving
body:
Hi both,

Status: figures 1-3 reproduce. Our SG-MCMC chains confirm the headline: at temperature T=1 (the true Bayes posterior) the posterior predictive underperforms the SGD point estimate on CIFAR-10 ResNet-20, and cooling to T around 1e-3 gives the best accuracy — the cold-posterior effect is robust on our stack.

Hypothesis experiments underway: prior misspecification looks like the strongest explanation on our internal models; the data-augmentation hypothesis also moves the effect noticeably.

Trade-off for the memo: cold posteriors give better point accuracy but shrink predictive diversity, which is what our calibration story leans on. We may end up recommending different temperatures for accuracy-critical vs calibration-critical serving.

Risk: chain mixing on the internal models is slower than on CIFAR; the July sweep sizing assumed CIFAR-like mixing. Paloma is profiling.

Umar

subject: Decisions ahead of the July sweep
body:
Team,

Ahead of next week's sweep, decisions from Monday's review:

1. Sweep plan is locked for our cirrus-tpu week of 7/6 — Umar, the 128-accelerator layout doc goes to Paloma by Thursday. Given the slower mixing Umar flagged, we cut the LSTM temperature grid from nine points to five and give the reclaimed budget to longer chains on the internal image model.
2. The memo will recommend per-use-case temperatures: cold (around 1e-3) for accuracy-critical serving, milder for calibration-critical paths, with the diversity trade-off quantified.
3. Paloma's harness time is protected through 7/17 — I've told the other teams maintenance waits.

Memo review with Eleni stays 7/17. Good momentum, thanks all.

Zofia

subject: Kickoff: collaborative translation data pipeline
body:
Hi Alina,

Kicking off the translation data-quality effort. Basis is our open-source collaborative-translation collection: 11 different human-machine workflows over WMT test-set sources, each data point carrying (source, target) pairs plus MQM error annotations with severity, category, and span. The finding we're productizing: the right human-machine split beats human-only collection on quality per dollar.

Goal for the half: turn this into Meridian's standard translation-data pipeline — pick the two or three winning collection workflows, wire them into our rater tooling, and produce a costed quality report per workflow. Launch review target late July.

I'd also like a plan for compressing the expensive teacher setup into something we can run continuously — details yours to scope.

Staffing and platform asks by end of April?

Priya

subject: Re: Kickoff: collaborative translation data pipeline
body:
Hi Priya,

Staffing: Gustavo Moreau leads at 50%, Amara Okafor 40% on rater tooling integration, Leilani Nakamura 30% on the data pipeline, Efe Lindqvist 25% on analysis.

On your compression ask: we're scoping and staffing a distillation training recipe from scratch — Gustavo owns the recipe build within his 50%, with Efe supporting — to distill the expensive post-editing teacher setup into a student model we can run continuously. I checked around and nothing in-house covers this, so we're budgeting it as a ground-up build: roughly six engineer-weeks, first trainable version mid-June.

Platform: we need Corpus rater queues for the MQM annotation passes (the 2-3 week privacy SLA applies since raters see source text), and modest titan GPU time for the student training.

Alina

subject: Status: ingestion done, rater throughput risk
body:
Hi both,

Status: the release data is fully ingested — all 11 collection workflows, with MQM annotations preserved down to error spans. Early analysis confirms the paper's direction: post-edited translations carry materially fewer major MQM errors than from-scratch professional translation at roughly 60% of the cost, and the LLM-post-edited workflow is the best quality-per-dollar of the machine-assisted variants.

Distillation recipe v0 is training as of Tuesday — student initialized from our standard MT checkpoint, teacher signals from the post-editing workflow outputs. First eval numbers next week.

The risk is rater throughput: privacy review for the rater queues took the full 3-week SLA, so annotation capacity came online 5/26, not 5/5. That compresses the costed-quality-report timeline. Options: cut two low-priority workflows from the report, or slip a week.

Gustavo

subject: Re: Status: ingestion done, rater throughput risk
body:
Team,

Decisions from Monday's review:

1. Workflow cut: the costed report covers 8 of the 11 collection workflows. We drop the three pure-machine variants — they're dominated on quality and aren't candidates for the standard pipeline anyway. This absorbs the rater delay without moving launch review, which stays the week of 7/20.
2. Pipeline pick, pending final numbers: LLM-assisted post-editing as default, from-scratch human reserved for high-stakes domains. Efe's analysis memo is due 7/15 to lock this.
3. Distillation recipe: v0 student is within 1.1 MQM-weighted points of the teacher — good enough to keep investing; Gustavo continues per the six-week plan.

Amara, please book the Launch Review Board slot with Nadia's office this week.

Priya

subject: Kickoff: ColTran archive colorization
body:
Hi Santiago,

Kicking off the colorization product effort for the vision portfolio. Base is our open-source Colorization Transformer: a three-stage stack — autoregressive colorizer, color upsampler, spatial upsampler — pointed at the photo-archive restoration market. The custom-dataset fine-tuning path already exists in the release, which is exactly what archive customers need.

Half goals: (1) fine-tune on two customer-like archival datasets, (2) hit the quality bar — remembering evaluation must be distribution-level (FID), not per-image SSIM/LPIPS, since any single plausible colorization won't match ground truth — and (3) a Shipyard-hosted demo for Launch Review Board in mid-July.

I'd also like a low-cost serving story; the autoregressive stage worries me for latency. Staffing and compute plan by 5/8?

Lucia

subject: Re: Kickoff: ColTran archive colorization
body:
Hi Lucia,

Staffing: Hyun Traore leads at 60%, Maren Zhou 40% on the fine-tuning pipeline and datasets, Efe Lindqvist 30% on eval and the FID harness.

Compute: titan-a100 best-effort, 48 GPUs for fine-tuning runs — the three stages train separately so we can pipeline them through a modest allocation.

On serving cost: we're scoping and staffing a distillation training recipe from scratch to compress the autoregressive colorizer into a feed-forward student for cheap serving — Hyun owns the recipe design inside his 60%, Maren supports on training infra. There's nothing on the shelf internally we can reuse for this, so I've budgeted it as a fresh build with a first student checkpoint targeted mid-June.

Flag: archive-customer data likely needs privacy review before fine-tuning; filing this week given the 2-3 week SLA.

Santiago

subject: Re: Kickoff: ColTran archive colorization
body:
Hi both,

Status: fine-tuning on the first archival dataset is done using the release's custom-dataset path (pretrained ImageNet checkpoint via pretrain_dir, dataset=custom). FID on the held-out archive split: 21.3 for the fine-tuned model vs 27.8 zero-shot — a clear win for fine-tuning. Per Efe's harness we report FID only; the SSIM numbers people keep asking for are meaningless here and I keep deleting them from decks.

Distillation student v0 trains, but the first checkpoint underperforms: FID 31.5. The autoregressive colorizer's sampling diversity is exactly what the feed-forward student loses. Trying a multi-sample distillation target next.

Risk: the second archival dataset is still in privacy review (filed 5/8, so due imminently). If it clears past 6/19 the two-dataset claim for LRB gets thin.

Hyun

subject: ColTran: LRB scope decisions
body:
Team,

Decisions for the 7/16 Launch Review Board slot:

1. Demo scope: hosted colorization with the fine-tuned three-stage stack only. The distillation student stays out of the demo — v1 improved to FID 26.9 with the multi-sample target, but that's still visibly behind the teacher, and I won't show it against customer archives yet. It remains our serving-cost path for Q3.
2. Dataset claim: privacy review cleared the second archive 6/22, and Maren got the fine-tune done — we present both datasets, FID 21.3 and 22.7.
3. Latency: we demo the batch (non-interactive) flow and are explicit about it; the interactive story arrives with the student model.

Efe, please get the eval card into Evalline by 7/14 for Nadia's packet.

Lucia

subject: Kickoff: Combiner for 32k-token serving
body:
Hi Ivo,

Kicking off the long-context serving effort. Base: our open-source Combiner work — full-attention expressiveness at sparse computation cost, with both JAX (axial, mixture, fixed, logn variants) and TF implementations in the release. Product motivation is direct: the language portfolio's long-document features are gated on attention cost, and Combiner's sub-quadratic structure is our best path to 32k-token contexts without a serving-cost blowup.

Half plan: benchmark the variants against our full-attention baseline through March-April, pick a winner by early May, then hand a serving integration plan to Zeke's Shipyard team. I've put a launch-review checkpoint on 5/8.

Staffing and compute proposal by early March? I expect this one is engineer-heavy rather than compute-heavy.

Thanks,
Priya

subject: Re: Kickoff: Combiner for 32k-token serving
body:
Hi Priya,

Staffing: Yusuf Keita leads the benchmarking at 50%, Nikhil Abebe 30% on the eval harness, Leilani Nakamura 25% on the TF-side parity checks. For the serving handoff: Milan Zapata is committed at 60% to this project for June 2026 to drive the Shipyard integration — he's finishing another commitment in May, and June is when the integration work actually starts, so the timing lines up.

Compute: titan-a100 best-effort, 32 GPUs for the benchmark grid. The variants train on the same toy-through-medium configs, so no reservation needed.

One watch item: the JAX and TF implementations differ in which variants they expose (logn is JAX-only), so if logn wins the bake-off, TF parity becomes real work for Leilani.

Ivo

subject: Combiner bake-off status
body:
Hi both,

Benchmark status: at 8k context the axial variant matches our full-attention baseline's perplexity within 0.3% at roughly 40% of the attention FLOPs; mixture closes the gap entirely but gives back a third of the savings. The fixed-pattern variant falls off at longer contexts, as expected. logn looks best asymptotically but, per Ivo's earlier flag, it's JAX-only.

At 32k (the product target) axial holds: 1.1% perplexity gap, attention cost scaling near sqrt as advertised.

Trade-off for the 5/8 decision: axial (cheapest, tiny quality gap, exists in both frameworks) vs mixture (no quality gap, less savings). My lean is axial — the 0.3-1.1% gap is below what our downstream evals can detect.

Risk: Nikhil found nondeterminism in the TF eval path; being chased this week, doesn't affect the JAX numbers.

Yusuf

subject: Re: Combiner bake-off status
body:
Team,

Decision from today's checkpoint, ahead of Friday's launch-review gate: we adopt the axial variant as Meridian's long-context attention for serving. Yusuf's numbers carried it — a perplexity gap our downstream evals can't detect, at 40% of the attention cost, available in both JAX and TF. Mixture is documented as the fallback if long-document quality regressions show up in production evals.

Consequences:
- Leilani closes out TF parity for axial only; no logn port.
- Nikhil's nondeterminism fix (the TF eval seeding issue) is confirmed merged.
- Milan's June integration scope is now concrete: axial kernels into Shipyard's serving stack, 32k target, plan review with Zeke's team first week of June.

Thanks all — clean bake-off, exactly what the OKR needed.

Priya

subject: Kickoff: COMISR for user-upload enhancement
body:
Hi Bao,

Kicking off compression-informed video super-resolution for the efficiency portfolio. Base is our open-source COMISR work: super-resolution built for compressed video, which matters because real user uploads arrive as CRF-compressed streams, not pristine frames — models trained on clean inputs fall apart there.

Product target: an enhancement pass for user-uploaded video on the serving side. Half plan: reproduce the vid4 evaluation on our stack by mid-April, extend the compression matrix beyond CRF25 in May, code-complete by end of May with a Shipyard demo after Launch Review Board.

Compute should be modest; the model is small by current standards. Staffing plan by 3/9? Note we have five people attached, so I mostly need clarity on fractions and who owns eval vs deployment.

Zofia

subject: Re: Kickoff: COMISR for user-upload enhancement
body:
Hi Zofia,

Fractions: Tereza Aliyev leads at 40%, Leilani Nakamura 30% on the training/eval loop, Emeka Pinto 30% on the ffmpeg compression pipeline, Saoirse Eriksen 20% on serving prep through April. Jorge Vidal is committed at 60% to this project for June 2026 — he owns the eval-and-deployment phase that runs past the May code-complete date, including the Shipyard demo and the post-LRB fixes.

Compute: titan-a100 best-effort, 16 GPUs; this is inference-heavy eval, no reservation.

Dependency: the vid4 test data and pretrained checkpoint come from our public release buckets; Emeka is mirroring them internally with checksums this week so eval is hermetic.

One flag: five people at small fractions is coordination-heavy. If anything slips I'd rather consolidate onto Tereza and Jorge than add people.

Bao

subject: Re: Kickoff: COMISR for user-upload enhancement
body:
Hi both,

Status: vid4 reproduction is done. On the lr_crf25 inputs (calendar, city, foliage, walk) our numbers match the release checkpoint, and against a strong non-compression-aware baseline we're seeing +0.6 dB PSNR average on the compressed inputs — the whole point of the method holding up on our stack.

Emeka's pipeline generates the compression matrix cleanly: lossless x264, then re-encode at target CRF, frames extracted at 10fps — exactly the release recipe. CRF30 and CRF35 sets are built; eval running now.

Early risk: at CRF35 the gains compress to +0.2 dB and temporal shimmer appears in high-motion clips (walk especially). If that holds, the product claim needs a quality floor — "enhancement for moderately compressed uploads" rather than everything. Worth deciding before we write LRB materials.

Tereza

subject: COMISR: scope + LRB decisions
body:
Team,

Decisions from this morning's review:

1. Scope the product claim to CRF <= 30 inputs. Tereza's CRF35 results (+0.2 dB, visible shimmer on high-motion content) don't clear the quality bar, and uploads that degraded are a small tail anyway. The LRB narrative becomes "reliable enhancement for the typical upload," which is honest and demoable.
2. Code-complete holds at 5/29. Remaining items are the CRF30 eval writeup and Emeka's pipeline docs.
3. LRB slot requested for the 6/10 board with Nadia's office; Jorge's June deployment phase starts against that date, Shipyard demo to follow sign-off.

Saoirse rolls off at end of April as planned — thanks for the serving groundwork.

Zofia

subject: Project Kestrel kickoff: CFQ classification guardrail
body:
Hi Ivo,

Kicking off the compositional query-understanding effort — we're tracking this internally as Project Kestrel, so please use that tag in docs and standup notes. Base is our open-source CFQ classification work: convert CFQ into a sentence-pair classification task and train models with structure annotations, which measurably improves compositional generalization.

Why data-platforms cares: our query-understanding services fail on exactly the compositional patterns CFQ measures. A classifier that reliably scores query/parse pairs becomes a guardrail in front of the semantic parser.

Milestones: datasets built by mid-March (including the model-negative variants, which need CFQ baseline beam outputs), trained classifiers with structure annotations by mid-April, integration recommendation by the 5/25 end of window.

Staffing and compute by end of Feb?

Dmitri

subject: Re: Project Kestrel kickoff: CFQ classification guardrail
body:
Hi Dmitri,

Staffing: Linnea Yamada leads at 50%, Nikhil Abebe 30% on dataset generation, Maren Zhou 25% on training infra, Yara Jokic 20% on analysis.

Compute: the classifiers are cheap, but the model-negative dataset isn't — we have to rerun the CFQ baselines (LSTM, transformer, universal transformer) with beam scores enabled to harvest negatives across splits. That's the bulk of the ask: 48 GPUs on titan-a100 best-effort for roughly three weeks, then a trickle for classifier training.

Sequencing per the release scripts: baseline decodes land under cfq_model_outputs per split, then create_cls_dataset.sh with the negative-method and hold-out options. The tree-annotated variant additionally needs the xlink mapping file staged in the output dir — Nikhil hit this already; fiddly but understood.

Ivo

subject: Re: Project Kestrel kickoff: CFQ classification guardrail
body:
Hi both,

Status: datasets are built for the primary CFQ split — rule-based negatives and model negatives from the beam outputs of all three baselines. Classifier results, first pass: without annotations the sentence-pair model sits at 71.4% accuracy on the compositional test split; with structure annotations it reaches 79.8% — a +8.4-point lift, consistent with the paper's core claim that structure is what the vanilla model is missing.

The interesting operational finding: model negatives are much harder than rule-based ones — training on them is what makes the classifier useful against real parser errors.

Risk/trade-off: the tree-annotation pipeline (the xlink mapping dependency) remains brittle, and tree outputs only add ~1 point over flat structure annotations. Recommend we not put trees on the critical path for the integration recommendation.

Linnea

subject: Kestrel: integration recommendation decisions
body:
Team,

Kestrel decisions from today's review:

1. The integration recommendation goes forward on flat structure annotations only. Linnea's numbers (79.8% vs 71.4%, with trees adding barely a point at real pipeline cost) make this easy — the brittle xlink-dependent tree path moves to a Q3 research item, not a launch dependency.
2. Model-negative training is mandatory in the recommended recipe; rule-based-only configs are documented as a fast-start option.
3. Handoff: Yara writes the recommendation memo with Linnea by 5/20; I'll walk it into the query-understanding team's planning ahead of Q3 OKR lock on 6/26.

This one lands inside the window with room to spare — nice work.

Dmitri

subject: Kickoff: environment generation for robust web agents
body:
Hi Jelena,

Kicking off the web-agents robustness effort. Base: our open-source environment-generation work for zero-shot compositional RL — instead of training agents on a fixed set of web tasks, we generate environments of growing compositional difficulty (on the MiniWoB stack) so agents generalize to task combinations they've never seen.

Product motivation: our form-filling agent prototypes are brittle on exactly the compositional cases — new page layouts recombining familiar widgets. Half plan: environment-generation pipeline running by end of May, curriculum-trained agents with zero-shot evals through June and July, and a go/no-go for the agents roadmap at the 8/10 review.

We'll also need a way to get human judgments on agent behavior beyond raw success rate — please scope that with the team.

Staffing and platform asks by early May?

Ulla

subject: Re: Kickoff: environment generation for robust web agents
body:
Hi Ulla,

Staffing: Yara Jokic leads at 50%, Quentin Farkas 40% on the environment-generation pipeline, Halima Toure 30% on agent training.

On human judgments: we're scoping and staffing a human-rating annotation UI from scratch — Vera Egede owns the build at 50%, with Quentin supporting on the trajectory-replay backend — so raters can watch agent episodes and grade them on task completion, efficiency, and safety. I looked and there's nothing in our current tooling that does trajectory-level rating, so we're budgeting it as a ground-up build: first usable version end of June.

Compute: titan-a100 best-effort, 24 GPUs; these agents are small but the curriculum means many parallel environment instances — the cost is CPU-side env serving more than accelerators.

Also filing privacy review early since raters may see generated page content.

Jelena

subject: Status: curriculum results + tooling risks
body:
Hi both,

Status: the generation pipeline is producing compositional web environments end to end — we're on the legacy MiniWoB branch pinned at the release commit, with the 2to3-converted Python bindings, plus the bootstrap-based page templates. Quentin's difficulty scheduler ramps the number of composed primitives per page.

First real result: curriculum-trained agents hit 58% zero-shot success on held-out compositional tasks vs 37% for agents trained on the fixed task set — a +21-point generalization gap in our favor, in line with the original result.

Risks: (1) the legacy MiniWoB dependency is fragile — the 2to3 conversion breaks on two wrappers whenever we bump Python, so Halima pinned the toolchain; (2) rater UI v0 slipped a week (replay backend), now targeting 7/3 — still compatible with the July evals.

Yara

subject: Re: Status: curriculum results + tooling risks
body:
Team,

Decisions from Monday's review, with the 8/10 go/no-go in sight:

1. We narrow the zero-shot eval to the top three task families — form-filling, search-and-filter, and multi-step login flows — instead of all seven. The +21-point generalization result holds across families, but rater capacity doesn't: with Vera's UI live since 7/6, throughput supports deep human evals on three families, not thin ones on seven. Product only cares about those three anyway.
2. Curriculum config freezes 7/24; Halima's toolchain pin becomes the blessed build.
3. For 8/10 I'll present success rates plus the human ratings on task completion and safety — Quentin, please have the rating dashboards exportable by 8/5.

Ulla

subject: Kickoff: compositional-generalization recipe card
body:
Hi Daniela,

Kicking off the training-recipe study. Base is our open-source "Making Transformers Solve Compositional Tasks" work: a systematic sweep over architectural choices — position encodings, copy decoders, weight sharing — showing that the right combination dramatically improves compositional generalization on SCAN, PCFG, COGS, and CFQ, plus the synthetic tasks (Addition, Reversing, Duplication and friends).

Why data-platforms owns it: every internal team training seq2seq models picks these knobs by folklore. Deliverable is a recipe card — evidence-backed defaults — published in the platform docs.

Milestones: harness ported off the notebooks by mid-March, main sweep April-May, recipe card by the 6/8 window close, with an extended repetition matrix continuing into July for statistical confidence.

Staffing and compute by early March?

Dmitri

subject: Re: Kickoff: compositional-generalization recipe card
body:
Hi Dmitri,

Staffing: Carmen Reyes leads at 50%, Fumiko Rossi 40% on the harness port (the release assumes Colab notebooks; we're making it batchable), Katya Silva 25% on dataset staging for SCAN/PCFG/COGS/CFQ, Nikhil Abebe 20% on eval plumbing.

For the extended phase: Wei Ivanov is committed at 60% to this project for July 2026 to run the full repetition matrix — the paper-style num_repetitions sweeps across all dataset/model combinations that give us error bars worth publishing internally. He's lighter (20%) through the main sweep.

Compute: the individual runs are small but the grid is wide — several days end-to-end per the release docs. Asking for 40 titan-a100 GPUs best-effort April-May, similar in July for Wei's matrix.

Daniela

subject: Re: Kickoff: compositional-generalization recipe card
body:
Hi both,

Sweep status: harness is fully off the notebooks (thanks Fumiko) and the first pass over the grid is done. Headline findings match the paper: relative position encodings plus a copy decoder are the difference-makers — COGS exact-match jumps from the mid-30s to low-80s with the right combination, and the SCAN length splits show the same shape. The synthetic tasks (Addition, AdditionNegatives, Reversing, Duplication) are useful smoke tests: any config that fails Reversing fails everything compositional.

Trade-off surfacing for the recipe card: the best COGS config is not the best CFQ config — weight sharing helps small-data compositional splits but costs capacity on CFQ. The card probably needs two profiles rather than one default.

Risk: repetition variance is high on PCFG; single-run conclusions there are unsafe, which is exactly why Wei's July matrix matters.

Carmen

subject: Recipe card: two-profile decision
body:
Team,

Decisions from Friday's review, ahead of window close on 6/8:

1. Recipe card ships with two profiles, per Carmen's finding: "small-data compositional" (relative positions, copy decoder, weight sharing) and "large-data semantic parsing" (relative positions, copy decoder, no sharing). One-default was the goal, but the COGS/CFQ split is real and the card should say so.
2. Card v1 publishes to platform docs 6/5, marked provisional pending error bars.
3. The July repetition matrix is confirmed as the follow-through: Wei runs the full num_repetitions grid and we stamp v1.1 "evidence-final" by end of July. PCFG gets double repetitions given the variance Carmen flagged.

Thanks all — this is the kind of boring-but-load-bearing work the platform exists for.

Dmitri

subject: Kickoff: concept bottleneck policies for auditable agents
body:
Hi Santiago,

Kicking off interpretable multi-agent RL. Base is our open-source Concept MARL work: concept bottleneck policies that extend MultiAgent-PPO (on Acme) with a concept loss, so each agent's policy routes through human-interpretable concepts — positions, held objects, teammate state — instead of an opaque embedding. Environments come from our Melting Pot ports: Collaborative Cooking, Clean Up, Capture the Flag, plus the miniature cooking variants for fast iteration.

Product motivation: the agents roadmap keeps hitting the auditability wall — customers ask why an agent did something and we have nothing. Concept bottlenecks are the credible answer.

Half plan: training reproduced by mid-May, concept-quality evals in June, LRB-ready interpretability demo by the 7/20 window close. Staffing and compute by mid-April?

Ulla

subject: Re: Kickoff: concept bottleneck policies for auditable agents
body:
Hi Ulla,

Staffing: Quentin Farkas leads at 50%, Maren Zhou 30% on the environment wrappers and pixels pipeline, Umar Costa 25% on the concept-quality eval design. Nikhil Abebe is committed at 60% to this project for June 2026 — June is the concept-eval crunch, and he owns the probe suite plus the ablation runs end to end.

Compute: titan-a100 best-effort, 24 GPUs. Multi-agent PPO with the concept loss is sample-hungry but the networks are small; the miniature cooking environments keep iteration cheap.

Sequencing note: the concept-extraction wrapper parses concept values from observation prefixes, so Maren's wrapper work gates everything — she's first in, and Quentin stubs against her interface in the meantime.

Santiago

subject: Re: Kickoff: concept bottleneck policies for auditable agents
body:
Hi both,

Status: Concept PPO training reproduced on the miniature Collaborative Cooking environments — the concept loss integrates into the PPO objective cleanly, and training is stable across seeds. The multi-modal encoder (RGB + position + orientation) works with Maren's wrappers, including the dense pseudo-rewards wrapper for cooking.

Concept quality, first look: probes recover ground-truth concept values at 87% accuracy from the bottleneck on cooking; Clean Up is lower (~78%) — the pollution-state concepts are noisier to extract.

Trade-off we should discuss: the dense cooking pseudo-rewards speed training substantially but shape behavior toward the reward designer's strategy, which slightly undermines the "agent's own interpretable reasoning" story for the demo. Options: demo with sparse rewards (slower training, cleaner story) or dense (better behavior, asterisk in the narrative).

Quentin

subject: Concept MARL: demo scope decisions
body:
Team,

Decisions from Monday's review, aimed at the 7/20 close:

1. Demo environment: Collaborative Cooking only. Nikhil's June probe results (87% concept recovery on cooking vs 78% on Clean Up) make cooking the defensible showcase; Clean Up and Capture the Flag move to the Q3 backlog.
2. Rewards: we demo the sparse-reward agents. Quentin's concern was right — the interpretability story is the whole product pitch, and an asterisk kills it. Dense-reward runs stay as a training-efficiency appendix.
3. The LRB packet leads with the concept-probe dashboard; Umar owns the eval card in Evalline by 7/15, Nadia's office gets the packet 7/16.

Good half, team — this went from paper to demo in fifteen weeks.

Ulla

subject: Kickoff: diffusion concept decomposition & bias audits
body:
Hi Deshawn,

Kicking off the diffusion-interpretability effort. Base is our open-source "hidden language of diffusion models" work: learn a pseudo-token as a sparse weighted combination of vocabulary tokens that reconstructs what the model generates for a concept — which surfaces surprising structure, like "a president" being dominated by specific individuals.

Product angle is bias detection and mitigation for our image-generation offering: trust review keeps asking how we audit concept representations, and this is a concrete, demoable answer. Single-image decomposition and semantic manipulation are secondary demos.

Half plan: pipeline reproduced on Stable Diffusion by end of March, concept audits April-May, a large final concept sweep in early June, launch review by the 6/15 window close.

Staffing and compute by mid-Feb? The sweep will need a real reservation.

Priya

subject: Re: Kickoff: diffusion concept decomposition & bias audits
body:
Hi Priya,

Staffing: Giannis Sato leads at 50%, Farah Haddad 40% on the pipeline and infra, Katya Silva 30% on the audit methodology.

Compute, two phases: development runs on titan-a100 best-effort (16 GPUs — per-concept pseudo-token optimization is cheap individually). For the final sweep we hold the vulcan-h100 reservation for the week of 2026-06-01, 256 accelerators, confirmed through Ines' reservation process — that week covers the full concept vocabulary at multiple sparsity levels, which is what the bias-audit claims need for launch review.

Note the timing is deliberate: vulcan's maintenance window is 6/22-6/24 and our LRB is 6/15, so the 6/1 week is effectively our only shot at scale. No slack behind it.

Deshawn

subject: Re: Kickoff: diffusion concept decomposition & bias audits
body:
Hi both,

Status: the decomposition pipeline reproduces on Stable Diffusion. Pseudo-tokens trained per concept reconstruct generated images faithfully, and the qualitative findings hold on our stack — "a composer" decomposes into a handful of specific-individual tokens plus style terms, while abstract concepts like "happiness" mix concrete tokens ("family", "laughter") with abstract ones. Single-image decomposition works and is honestly the best demo material we have.

Audit progress: Katya's methodology scores concepts by how concentrated their decomposition is on protected-attribute or specific-person tokens; a first pass over 200 profession concepts flags 31 for review.

Trade-off: sparsity level matters a lot — at 10 tokens the decompositions are readable but reconstruction suffers; at 50 they reconstruct well but audits get noisy. The June sweep should cover both regimes, which doubles its size; worth confirming the reservation covers it.

Giannis

subject: Pre-sweep decisions: sparsity, LRB scope
body:
Team,

Decisions from today's pre-sweep review:

1. Sweep design: we cover both sparsity regimes (10 and 50 tokens) across the full concept set, per Giannis' trade-off. Farah re-sized the job: it fits our vulcan-h100 week of 6/1 at 256 accelerators, at about 85% utilization — tight but no descoping needed.
2. Launch review scope: bias audit is the headline, single-image decomposition is the live demo, semantic manipulation is out (trust review flagged it needs its own privacy pass; not before 6/15).
3. Katya's 31 flagged profession concepts go to Kofi for counsel review in parallel — findings, not conclusions, in the LRB packet.

Sweep kicks off Monday 6/1, LRB on 6/15. Bring it home.

Priya

subject: Kickoff: typology prediction for coverage planning
body:
Hi Deshawn,

Kicking off the typology-prediction project. Base: our open-source NEMO work from the SIGTYP 2020 shared task — frequentist inference for predicting a language's typological features (from WALS) given only a handful of observed ones.

Product motivation: the language portfolio's coverage planning currently treats unknown languages as blank slates. Predicted typological profiles (word order, morphology type, etc.) let the i18n teams pick tokenizers, segmentation defaults, and eval sets for languages we've never shipped — before collecting data.

Half plan: reproduce shared-task numbers by mid-April, extend to the full WALS matrix in May-June with a big imputation sweep; the deliverable is a typology-profile service proposal by the 7/6 window close.

Staffing plus compute sketch by mid-March? The full-matrix sweep may need reserved capacity.

Priya

subject: Re: Kickoff: typology prediction for coverage planning
body:
Hi Priya,

Staffing: Umar Costa leads at 40%, Oyin Iversen 35% on the data tooling (the shared-task setup wants a clean WALS staging area — she's building it properly), Quentin Farkas 25% on modeling, Maren Zhou 20% on infra.

Compute: development is trivial — NEMO is classical frequentist machinery, laptops-and-CPUs territory. The exception is the full-matrix imputation sweep with the neural comparison arms: for that we hold the cirrus-tpu reservation for the week of 2026-06-22, 256 accelerators. Timing works out — vulcan is down for maintenance 6/22-6/24 anyway, so cirrus that week is the right home for it, and results land two weeks before window close.

Flag: WALS licensing is CC-BY, but Kofi should still glance at the service proposal before it leaves the building.

Deshawn

subject: Re: Kickoff: typology prediction for coverage planning
body:
Hi both,

Status: NEMO reproduction is complete. Our runs match the shared-task submission — the frequentist approach (per-feature estimators with typological-constraint filtering) beats the majority-class baseline comfortably on the blind test set, and per-family accuracy tracks the paper.

Beyond reproduction: Quentin added two neural comparison arms (a feature-embedding MLP and a graph-propagation model over language families). In the sparse-observation regime that matters for our product — five or fewer observed features per language — NEMO still wins; the neural arms only pull ahead past ~15 observed features, which real unknown languages rarely have.

Risk for the sweep: WALS sparsity is brutal — many features have <300 attested languages — so the full-matrix imputation confidence intervals will be wide. Oyin is adding per-feature reliability scores so the i18n consumers know which predictions to trust.

Umar

subject: Decisions: sweep + service proposal shape
body:
Team,

Decisions from today's review, one week out from the sweep:

1. Sweep is confirmed for our cirrus-tpu week of 6/22 with the full 256-accelerator layout — Maren's job configs are done, and the neural comparison arms run alongside NEMO for the full matrix. Umar, please freeze the estimator configs by 6/18.
2. Service proposal shape, based on Umar's results: NEMO is the default predictor with per-feature reliability scores; the neural arms are documented but not proposed for serving — they don't win in the observation regime our users are actually in.
3. Kofi reviewed the WALS licensing question — attribution requirements only, no blocker.

Proposal draft to me by 7/1 for the 7/6 close. Nearly there.

Priya

subject: Kickoff: romanized input for South Asian languages
body:
Hi Daniela,

Kicking off romanized-input support for South Asian languages. Base is our open-source context-aware transliteration work: users type Hindi, Bengali, or Tamil in the Latin alphabet, and context-aware models map it into native script far better than word-by-word transliteration. The release ships FST-based transliteration via Nisaba with released models, generated text resources, and neural checkpoints on the way.

Product target: a transliteration layer for the language portfolio's input stack — romanized input is how a huge share of South Asian users actually type, and our coverage there is embarrassing.

Plan: FST baseline reproduced by end of May, context-aware neural comparison in June-July, integration recommendation by the 8/3 window close.

Staffing and platform dependencies by mid-May?

Priya

subject: Re: Kickoff: romanized input for South Asian languages
body:
Hi Priya,

Staffing: Yara Jokic leads at 40%, Wanjiru Horvat 35% on the FST/Nisaba integration, Rosa Mensah 30% on the evaluation harness and text-resource staging.

Platform dependency worth calling out: the released text resources and our eval corpora need to move onto Corpus v2, and the Corpus v2 migration freeze is 2026-08-07 — so we have until early August to finish registrations, which comfortably covers the whole window. Rosa will do the migration alongside the harness work in June rather than as a scramble later.

Compute: negligible — FSTs are CPU-bound and the neural checkpoints are inference-only for our comparison. No reservations.

One flag: Nisaba version pinning matters; Wanjiru hit a grammar incompatibility on the newest release and is pinning to the version the models shipped against.

Daniela

subject: Re: Kickoff: romanized input for South Asian languages
body:
Hi both,

Status: the FST baseline is fully reproduced — Wanjiru has the Nisaba pipeline running with the released models (pinned version, per her earlier flag), and our numbers match the paper's FST tables on the released test sets. Rosa's harness scores both word-level accuracy and full-sentence transliteration, which is where context should pay off.

Neural comparison: the released checkpoints are staged; early single-language runs show the context-aware neural model beating the FST clearly on ambiguous romanizations — cases where the same Latin string maps to different native-script words depending on context, exactly the paper's motivation.

Risk for the recommendation: FST wins on latency and footprint by a wide margin; neural wins on ambiguous-context accuracy. The integration answer is probably a hybrid (FST default, neural rerank on ambiguity), which is more engineering than either alone. I'll bring sized options to the 7/23 review.

Yara

subject: Contrack kickoff - entity repository as the assistant memory layer
body:
All,

Starting Contrack today. The bet: our open-source context tracking work already treats entity recognition, attribute classification, coreference and plural-mention resolution as one end-to-end task over an entity repository, instead of four bolted-together models. That repository is exactly the thing our assistant team keeps hand-rolling badly, and because it updates incrementally turn-by-turn it stays cheap on long sessions - which is the whole product argument.

Milestones inside the window (Apr 13 - Jun 22):
- Apr 30: reproduce the published numbers on our internal dialogue set.
- May 22: turn-by-turn repository update running under 40ms p95 on a 60-turn session.
- Jun 12: integration spike with the assistant runtime, demo-ready for launch review.

Bruno owns staffing and will come back with the resourcing plan next week. Fumiko, you are tech lead.

Anders

subject: Re: Contrack kickoff - entity repository as the assistant memory layer
body:
Anders,

Resourcing, as promised.

Compute is modest: ~600 GPU-hours on titan-a100 best-effort for the training sweeps, no Vulcan reservation needed. The bottleneck is data, not silicon. Real multi-party transcripts with clean plural-mention annotations basically do not exist in our corpus, and buying them is a 12-week procurement.

So we are building a synthetic-data generation pipeline from scratch. Csilla Nassar owns it at 50% from May 4 through the end of the window, with Linnea Yamada at 25% on the templating and validation side. Scope: scenario templates, entity/attribute samplers, a coreference-chain generator with controllable ambiguity, and a validation pass that rejects degenerate dialogues. Target 80k synthetic sessions by May 29.

Fumiko stays at 60% on the model itself. Ines has confirmed the titan quota, nothing to escalate there.

Bruno

subject: Contrack status - plural mentions are the long pole
body:
Status through May 25.

Good: the incremental repository update holds. 60-turn session, p95 update latency 31ms, memory flat at ~4MB per session because we never re-encode the full history. Entity recognition and attribute classification are both within a point of the published numbers.

Bad: resolving plural mentions. Anything of the form "both of them" or "the two engineers" where the antecedents were introduced 8+ turns apart drops to 0.58 F1 against 0.79 for singular coreference. The synthetic generator makes plenty of plural cases but they are too clean - the ambiguity distribution doesn't look like real dialogue, so we're overfitting to easy ones.

Trade-off for you Anders: I can either spend two weeks widening the generator's ambiguity model, or we ship the Jun 12 integration spike with plural mentions behind a flag and fix it in Q3. I lean flag-it, but it's your call on what the demo needs to show.

Fumiko

subject: Re: Contrack status - plural mentions are the long pole
body:
Decision: flag it.

The Jun 12 spike shows singular coreference + attribute tracking over a 60-turn session, which is the story that actually sells - persistent memory that doesn't blow up latency. Plural mentions ship disabled, and we say so plainly in the review deck rather than getting caught on it. Nadia, that's what's going to the board, please slot us for the Jun 18 session.

Fumiko - do not spend the two weeks on the generator now. Write up the ambiguity gap as a Q3 OKR candidate instead; I'd rather fund it properly than half-fix it before OKRs lock.

One ask: in the deck, give me the 0.58 vs 0.79 F1 split explicitly. Reviewers trust us more when we hand them the weak number ourselves.

Thanks both, this has been a clean quarter.

Anders

subject: Kickoff: contrastive RL as our goal-conditioned baseline
body:
Team,

Kicking off the contrastive RL workstream. The claim in our open-source release is the interesting one for us: apply contrastive representation learning to action-labeled trajectories and the inner product of the learned representations *is* the goal-conditioned value function. No auxiliary losses, no data augmentation, and it still beats the non-contrastive baselines on image-based tasks.

Why I care as PM: our current goal-conditioned stack is three losses in a trenchcoat and every new task needs someone to retune the augmentation pipeline. If this holds up, we delete a whole category of tuning work.

Milestones in the Apr 6 - Jul 27 window:
- May 8: reproduce state-based success rates on the standard goal-conditioned suite.
- Jun 19: image-based tasks, no augmentation, head-to-head vs our current agent.
- Jul 17: recommendation memo - adopt, or park.

Deshawn will send resourcing. Hyun is tech lead.

Ulla

subject: Re: Kickoff: contrastive RL as our goal-conditioned baseline
body:
Ulla,

Staffing + infra:

- Hyun Traore 70%, algorithm and the head-to-head evaluation.
- Carmen Reyes 40%, image-based environments and the offline data pipeline.
- Jorge Vidal, see below.

Compute: 96 GPUs on vulcan-h100, reserved through Ines for the May and June sweeps. Note vulcan is down 2026-06-22 to 2026-06-24 for maintenance, so the image-task sweep has to land before the 19th anyway.

The part that needs your sign-off: to make the head-to-head credible across five environments and three seeds each we need somewhere to put the results that isn't a spreadsheet. We are building a benchmark leaderboard service from scratch - submission API, run registry, per-task success-rate tables, and a public-facing web view. Jorge Vidal owns it at 50% from April 20 through the end of June. It's about six weeks of work and it outlives this project.

Deshawn

subject: Contrastive RL status - reproduced state-based, image tasks are noisier than advertised
body:
Update ahead of the Jun 19 milestone.

State-based: reproduced. Averaged over the five goal-conditioned tasks we get 71% success vs 63% for our current non-contrastive agent, three seeds, and we did not touch augmentation or add an auxiliary loss. That's the paper's claim and it holds.

Image-based is where it gets interesting. Mean success is still ahead (+6 points) but seed variance is large - one task swings 22 points between seeds. The representation collapses early in maybe one run in six, and when it collapses the inner-product value function is basically flat, so the policy never gets a gradient worth following. Carmen has a fix candidate (temperature schedule on the contrastive loss) but it needs another sweep.

Risk: vulcan is out Jun 22-24, so if we want the extra sweep before your Jun 19 checkpoint I need the decision this week, not next.

Hyun

subject: Re: Contrastive RL status - recommendation and scope cut
body:
Recommendation, going into the Jul 17 memo: adopt for state-based goal-conditioned tasks, hold on image.

The +8 points on state-based with no augmentation and no auxiliary loss is a real simplification win and I want it in the default agent config for Q3. Image-based, a 22-point seed swing is not something I can put in front of a customer, even with the temperature schedule cutting collapse rate to roughly 1 in 20.

Scope cut: we are dropping the third image environment from the memo entirely rather than reporting it half-measured. Hyun, please write the collapse analysis up as its own note - Eleni, this is the piece I think is genuinely publishable, separate from whether we adopt.

Deshawn, keep Carmen at 40% through the end of the window to finish the schedule ablation. Everything else winds down after the 17th.

Ulla

subject: Kickoff - seq2seq coref as the multilingual backbone
body:
Hi all,

Formally kicking off coref_mt5. The pitch: instead of searching over candidate spans, we treat coreference as a text-to-text transition system on mT5 and predict mentions and links jointly. Our open-source version reports 83.3 F1 on CoNLL-2012, which is state of the art, and because the backbone is multilingual T5 we get non-English for free-ish rather than as a separate model per language.

Product angle: document understanding has been asking for entity threading across long contracts and support transcripts in six languages. One model instead of six is the whole business case.

Window is Apr 13 - Jul 27. Checkpoints:
- May 15: decoder running against our own checkpoint server, English parity with the published F1.
- Jun 26: two non-English languages measured, serving path benchmarked.
- Jul 20: launch review packet.

Daniela has staffing. Yusuf is tech lead.

Priya

subject: Re: Kickoff - seq2seq coref as the multilingual backbone
body:
Priya,

Staffing for the window:

- Yusuf Keita 60%, transition system, evaluation against CoNLL-2012 and our internal sets.
- Katya Silva 45%, fine-tuning runs and the non-English data prep.
- Chiara Olsen is at 65% on coref_mt5 for the whole of June 2026 - she owns the decoder service and the transition-state serialization, and June is when both have to be production-shaped. She's at 30% in April/May ramping in.

Infra: the XXL checkpoint needs a real server, not a notebook. Zeke has us penciled in on Shipyard for a June serving slot. Inference is the cost driver here, not training - we are fine-tuning, not pre-training, so 32 GPUs on vulcan-h100 covers us.

One caveat I want on record: 65% of Chiara in June is the plan of record. If that slips the serving benchmark slips with it.

Daniela

subject: coref_mt5 status - accuracy is fine, the decoder is the problem
body:
Status.

Accuracy: 82.9 F1 on CoNLL-2012 with our own fine-tune, against 83.3 published. Close enough that I'm calling English parity done. Katya has the first non-English set through and it looks encouraging, no numbers I'd defend yet.

The problem is decoding cost. The transition system emits one action sequence per document and long documents mean long output sequences - a 40-page contract decodes in 190 seconds on a single accelerator. Search over spans was expensive but it parallelized; seq2seq decoding is inherently serial. For batch document processing that's tolerable, for anything interactive it is not.

Two options: chunk documents and stitch entity chains across chunk boundaries (accuracy risk on long-range links, which is exactly what we're selling), or scope the product to batch-only. Chiara is prototyping chunking this month but I'd rather we decide on positioning than engineer around it.

Yusuf

subject: Re: coref_mt5 status - positioning decision, batch-only for v1
body:
Decision, after talking to the document understanding folks and to Hana.

v1 is batch-only. We position entity threading as an overnight enrichment job, not an interactive feature, and we stop apologising for 190 seconds a document. That number is fine for a nightly pipeline and pretending otherwise is how we end up shipping chunking we don't trust.

Consequences:
- Chunking prototype stops. Yusuf, keep the write-up, kill the branch.
- Zeke, we still want the Shipyard slot but the SLA we're asking for is throughput, not latency - Daniela will send revised numbers.
- Launch review packet on Jul 20 goes in with 82.9 F1 English, two non-English languages, and an explicit batch-only scope line. Nadia, please don't let anyone re-litigate interactive in the room; it's decided.

Good work getting to parity, genuinely.

Priya

subject: Kickoff: Wasserstein batch-effect correction as a corpus-wide layer
body:
Team,

Starting this one today. Our open-source release corrects batch effects in high-content imaging embeddings by minimizing a Wasserstein distance between batch distributions, validated on the BBBC021 set with both CellProfiler embeddings and deep-network embeddings.

My interest is broader than cell imaging. Every embedding corpus we own has nuisance structure - collection run, labeling wave, vendor - and today teams paper over it with ad hoc normalization. If the Wasserstein approach transfers, it becomes a standard de-batching step in the corpus pipeline rather than a biology trick.

Mar 30 - Jul 6. Milestones:
- Apr 24: reproduce the paper on BBBC021, both embedding types, using the ljosa preprocessing path.
- May 29: apply to one non-imaging Meridian corpus, measure whether downstream retrieval improves.
- Jun 26: go/no-go on productizing as a Corpus pipeline stage.

Alina on resourcing, Umar tech lead.

Anders

subject: Re: Kickoff: Wasserstein batch-effect correction as a corpus-wide layer
body:
Anders,

Resourcing:
- Umar Costa 55%, method work and the transfer study.
- Linnea Yamada 35%, preprocessing - percentile-matching normalization and the factor analysis step, i.e. the ljosa path end to end.
- Amara Okafor 30%, pipeline integration.

Compute is small, ~250 GPU-hours on titan-a100. The TensorFlow implementation is old but it runs.

Schedule dependency worth flagging: the non-imaging corpus we want for the May 29 milestone has to be re-ingested with per-run metadata attached, otherwise we have no batch labels to correct against. The Corpus v2 migration freeze is 2026-07-24, so we have the whole of July to land the re-ingest before anything locks; I've planned the embedding re-export backwards from 2026-07-24. That gives Amara comfortable float and means I don't need to fight anyone for priority in May.

Alina

subject: Status - BBBC021 reproduced, transfer is the open question
body:
Reproduction is done and it was less painful than expected. On the CellProfiler embeddings, after percentile-matching normalization plus factor analysis, the Wasserstein-corrected representation recovers mechanism-of-action clustering at 0.71 vs 0.52 uncorrected. Deep-network embeddings land in the same neighbourhood. Both within noise of the paper.

The risk is the transfer claim in Anders' kickoff. The imaging case has a clean nuisance variable - the plate - and hundreds of samples per plate. Our text corpus has labeling waves of wildly uneven size, some with 40 documents. The Wasserstein estimate is badly biased at that sample size, and in the first run the correction erased about as much signal as noise: retrieval nDCG moved -0.4 points, i.e. nothing, with wider variance.

Linnea is testing whether pooling small waves into synthetic batches helps. If it doesn't, my honest read is that this is an imaging tool, not a corpus layer.

Umar

subject: Re: Status - go/no-go call: scoped yes
body:
Go/no-go, as promised for the 26th.

It's a scoped yes. We productize the correction as an opt-in Corpus pipeline stage with a hard guardrail: minimum 200 samples per batch, otherwise the stage refuses to run rather than silently destroying signal. Umar's -0.4 nDCG result is the reason the guardrail exists and I want that in the doc, not buried.

We are NOT claiming this as a general de-batching layer. That was my framing in March and Umar's numbers didn't support it.

Alina - the re-ingest with per-run metadata still needs to happen for the pilot corpus. You've got it planned against the 2026-07-24 Corpus v2 freeze, which leaves float, so let's use some of it: I'd rather Amara land it in the first half of July than sprint. Jun, flagging you for visibility on the ingest ask.

Anders

subject: Kickoff - encoder + compartmental forecasting as a platform template
body:
Morning all,

Kicking off the epidemiology forecasting workstream. What we're actually after isn't disease forecasting - it's the architecture. Our open-source release puts learnable encoders inside an extended SEIR compartmental model, so the network learns the rates while the compartmental structure enforces conservation. Forecasts stay physically plausible even when the data is thin.

That pattern generalizes to half a dozen constrained forecasting problems on the data platform: capacity, inventory, queue depth. Anything where an unconstrained network happily predicts a negative population.

Window Feb 23 - Jun 1:
- Mar 20: reproduce the US state-level model, evaluation metrics matching the published notebook.
- Apr 24: strip out the COVID-specific model definitions and land a reusable BaseModelDefinition-style template.
- May 22: one platform forecasting use case ported onto the template.

Alina has resourcing. Halima is tech lead. Note we will need privacy review since the source data is health-adjacent - I'll open that with Kofi early.

Dmitri

subject: Re: Kickoff - resourcing and the Corpus dependency
body:
Dmitri,

Staffing:
- Halima Toure 60%, model definitions and the encoder work.
- Farah Haddad 40%, data pipeline and feature preprocessing.
- Maren Zhou 35%, evaluation harness against the published metrics.
- Milan Zapata 25% from April, porting the platform use case.

Compute: trivial by our standards, ~120 GPU-hours on titan-a100. These are small models; the cost is data wrangling.

Which brings me to the dependency. The platform use case at the May 22 milestone reads its history from Corpus. Jun's team holds the Corpus v2 migration freeze at 2026-07-10, and I've built the ingest schedule around that date - everything we need from Corpus has to be in before 2026-07-10 or it waits for the other side of the migration. Since our window closes June 1 that's comfortable, but I don't want anyone assuming we can slip into July.
