subject: Status - US state model reproduced, the template is harder than it looks
body:
Status through Apr 15.

Reproduction: done, state level. Our numbers track the published evaluation notebook within ~3% on the 14-day horizon. The Japan prefecture model we skipped deliberately - different constructor, no value for us.

The Apr 24 milestone is the one at risk. "Strip out the COVID-specific parts and leave a reusable template" sounded clean in the kickoff, but the compartmental structure isn't a plug-in - the encoders are wired to specific rate parameters, and the shared helper functions in the base definitions assume epidemiological features (population density, mobility). For a queue-depth forecast there is no analogue of an infection rate, so you're not reusing the model, you're reusing a design pattern plus about 200 lines.

My recommendation: retarget Apr 24 to a written design pattern + a worked port, and stop pretending we're shipping a framework. Maren agrees. It's less impressive and more true.

Halima

subject: Re: Status - scope cut agreed, and privacy timing
body:
Halima - agreed, and thank you for saying it in April rather than in the June retro.

Scope cut, effective now: no framework. We deliver (a) the reproduced state-level model as a reference implementation, (b) a design-pattern write-up on wiring learnable encoders into a conservation-constrained model, and (c) exactly one worked port - Milan's queue-depth forecast. If a second team wants the pattern they read the doc and copy the 200 lines. That is a fine outcome.

Kofi - the privacy review is on the reference implementation only, since the ported use case touches no health data at all. That should shorten the SLA on your side; can you confirm we're clear before Jun 1?

Alina, no staffing change, I just want Milan's port finished properly rather than three ports done badly.

Dmitri

subject: Kickoff - VHH design workflow as our sequence-design reference
body:
All,

Starting the VHH design workstream. The open-source release covers high-throughput ML-guided design of diverse single-domain antibodies against SARS-CoV-2 - notebooks for the data, the plots, and critically a model that scores candidate sequences, the same one used to design the third library.

We are not going into antibodies as a business. What I want is the workflow: propose, score, select for diversity, measure, feed back. That loop is the reusable asset, and today every sequence-design conversation here restarts from zero.

Mar 2 - Jun 1:
- Mar 27: notebooks running against our infra, scoring reproduced on the released third-library sequences.
- Apr 30: diversity-selection step reimplemented as a standalone library with our own distance metric.
- May 26: internal write-up + one design round on a non-antibody sequence problem.

Bruno on resourcing, Gustavo tech lead. Deliberately small team - this is a study, not a product.

Anders

subject: Re: Kickoff - resourcing, small as requested
body:
Anders,

Keeping it small as you asked:
- Gustavo Moreau 30%, scoring model and the design loop.
- Wanjiru Horvat 35%, notebook-to-pipeline conversion and the diversity library.
- Linnea Yamada 20%, distance metric and evaluation.

No cluster reservation. The scoring model is tiny by our standards and runs comfortably on titan-a100 best-effort; the notebooks were written to run in a free hosted environment, which tells you the scale.

One small platform item: the released sequence tables need registering in Corpus so the design-round results are queryable alongside everything else. Corpus v2 freezes on 2026-07-24, which is well clear of anything we do, so the sequence tables can be re-registered any time up to 2026-07-24 without a fight. Wanjiru will file the ticket but it is not on the critical path.

Bruno

subject: Status - scoring reproduced; diversity is the interesting failure
body:
Quick status.

Scoring: reproduced. Running the released model over the third-library sequences we match the published scores to 4 decimal places, so the port is faithful. Wanjiru got the notebooks off hosted colab and onto our pipeline, which was most of the actual work.

The interesting part is diversity selection. Naively picking top-scored candidates gives you a library that is 80% minor variants of two backbones - high predicted affinity, almost no coverage. The published design used an explicit diversity constraint and now I understand why: the scoring model's confidence is highest exactly where its training data was densest, so score-greedy selection is a feedback loop that eats its own tail.

Our reimplemented selector with a Hamming-distance floor of 6 gets predicted mean score down ~9% but triples backbone coverage. I think that trade is the actual finding, and it transfers to any model-guided design problem. Slight risk it makes the May 26 write-up longer than you wanted.

Gustavo

subject: Re: Status - make the diversity result the headline
body:
Gustavo - flip the write-up. The reproduction is table stakes; the score-vs-coverage trade is the thing worth other people's attention. Lead with the -9% mean score / 3x backbone coverage number and the explanation of why score-greedy selection collapses. That paragraph is the most useful thing this project produced.

Decision on scope: we are dropping the non-antibody design round from May 26. Two weeks isn't enough to pick a problem, get data and run a round honestly, and a rushed one would undercut the diversity argument. Instead the write-up names three candidate problems and what each would need. Bruno, that frees Wanjiru back to 15% from May 11.

Hana, cc'ing you because I think this is a two-page internal note that a lot of teams should read, not a project post-mortem.

Anders

subject: Kickoff - hypercube unfoldings, and why data-platforms cares
body:
Team,

Yes, this is a combinatorics project in a data-platforms portfolio. Bear with me.

The open-source enumerator generates all unfoldings of the n-dimensional hypercube by representing each one as a pair (T, P) - a tree on 2n nodes plus a perfect matching in the complement of that tree - and treating two pairs as equivalent when an isomorphism maps both simultaneously. It leans on nauty for the trees and their automorphism groups, and it computed the sequence out to dimension 10.

What I want is the machinery, not the tesseracts. We have graph-shaped records - dependency graphs, schema lineage - where "are these two the same thing up to relabeling" is asked constantly and answered badly. Canonical forms plus automorphism-aware dedup is exactly that problem.

Apr 20 - Jul 27:
- May 15: build and reproduce counts up to n=8 on our infra.
- Jun 19: canonicalization extracted as a library, benchmarked on our lineage graphs.
- Jul 17: recommendation on adopting it in the dedup path.

Bruno on staffing; Kaia is tech lead.

Dmitri

subject: Re: Kickoff - staffing, CPU not GPU, and one schema deadline
body:
Dmitri,

Staffing:
- Kaia Wolde 50%, canonicalization library.
- Rafael Duran 40%, the enumeration port and the n=8..10 verification.
- Vera Egede 30%, build system - nauty, gtest and GNU parallel all have to work in our CI, which is not free.
- Efe Lindqvist 25%, lineage-graph benchmark.

No GPU ask at all, which will make a change for you. This is CPU and memory: the n=10 run needs roughly 900 core-hours and about 60GB peak, and we'll shard it with parallel like the original does.

Deadline that does bind us: writing canonical forms alongside the lineage records means a new column. Corpus v2 migration freeze is 2026-07-10 per Jun's platform note, so the canonical-form column has to be written into the graph tables before 2026-07-10; after that date the schema is closed until the migration completes. That pulls Kaia's library milestone forward, not the Jul 17 recommendation.

Bruno

subject: Status - counts verified through n=9, and a trade-off on labels
body:
Status before the Jun 19 checkpoint.

Rafael has verified the published counts through n=9 on our build; n=10 is running and will take another nine days of wall clock. Vera got nauty and gtest into CI, which sounds boring and was the single biggest time sink of the quarter.

On my side the canonicalization library works, with a caveat Dmitri should hear before Jul 17. The hypercube setting has unlabeled, uncolored nodes - that's what makes the tree-plus-matching equivalence clean. Our lineage graphs have typed nodes and edge attributes. Canonicalizing with full labels means we almost never find duplicates (0.4% of pairs); canonicalizing on structure alone finds 11% but a chunk of those are structurally identical graphs doing genuinely different things.

So the honest answer is that automorphism-aware dedup is a *candidate generator*, not a decision procedure. It needs a cheap second-stage check on attributes. That's a real design, just not the one in the kickoff.

Kaia

subject: Re: Status - adopting it as a candidate generator only
body:
Recommendation for the 17th, so nobody is surprised in the room:

We adopt the canonicalization as a candidate generator in the dedup path, with a second-stage attribute comparison that Kaia will spec but that we build in Q3, not now. 11% candidate recall at near-zero cost is worth having even if precision needs a second pass. We do not claim dedup accuracy numbers until the second stage exists - Kaia, please make sure the doc says that in the first paragraph rather than the appendix.

The canonical-form column landed before the freeze, so we are not blocked on Corpus. Thank you Vera and Bruno for taking that seriously in May instead of the week before.

n=10 finished and matched, which is a nice footnote and, to be clear, not why we funded this.

Dmitri

subject: CuBERT kickoff - a code encoder for review triage
body:
Hi team,

Kicking off CuBERT. Our open-source release gives us BERT-style models pre-trained on deduplicated Python and Java corpora from public GitHub, plus vocabularies, fine-tuned checkpoints and the run_classifier.py harness for the classification tasks - exception type prediction being the one I keep pointing at in decks.

Product goal: review triage. Given a diff, predict which reviews need a human immediately. Today that's keyword heuristics and it's embarrassing.

Apr 13 - Aug 3:
- May 22: fine-tune the released Python checkpoint on our internal review-outcome labels, get a first accuracy number.
- Jun 26: our own pre-training corpus from the internal monorepo, deduplicated with the released process.
- Jul 24: head-to-head vs the keyword baseline; launch review packet.

Alina will send resourcing this week. Gustavo is tech lead. One thing up front: the deduplication step is not optional - the release is explicit that near-duplicate files inflate results, and I don't want a number we have to retract.

Priya

subject: Re: CuBERT kickoff - resourcing
body:
Priya,

Plan of record:

- Gustavo Moreau is committed at 70% to cubert for May 2026 - he is running the deduplication rebuild and the first fine-tuning sweep, both of which have to happen in May or the June milestone is dead. He tapers to 40% from June.
- Katya Silva 45% across the window, label pipeline from review outcomes.
- Oyin Iversen 40%, corpus extraction from the monorepo.
- Halima Toure 20% from June, evaluation.

Compute: fine-tuning the released large checkpoint is cheap - about 300 GPU-hours. Pre-training our own is not. Ines has us down for 128 GPUs on vulcan-h100 for the last two weeks of June, and I've told her we can work around the 2026-06-22 to 2026-06-24 maintenance window by starting the run on the 25th.

Gustavo's May allocation is the thing I'd defend hardest if anything comes up.

Alina

subject: CuBERT status - fine-tune result, and a dedup surprise
body:
Status.

May milestone hit, just. Fine-tuning the released Python checkpoint on 41k internal review outcomes gives 0.68 F1 on "needs human review" vs 0.51 for the keyword baseline. That's the number I'd put in front of anyone right now.

The surprise is dedup. Running the released deduplication process over our monorepo extraction removed 34% of files. Not 5%, 34% - generated clients, vendored dependencies, copy-pasted test scaffolds. When I evaluated the fine-tune on the pre-dedup split I got 0.79 F1, which would have been a lovely slide and complete fiction: the same file was in train and test.

So the 0.68 is the honest number and I want to be clear it went *down* because we did this properly.

Risk for June: 34% smaller corpus than I sized the pre-training run against. Either we accept a weaker in-domain model or we widen the extraction to other repos, which is a scope change.

Gustavo

subject: Re: CuBERT status - decision: ship the fine-tune, drop our own pre-training
body:
Decision for the Jul 24 packet.

We ship review triage on the fine-tuned released checkpoint. 0.68 F1 vs 0.51 keyword baseline is a real improvement and it exists today. We are dropping in-house pre-training from this project entirely - a 34%-smaller corpus was never going to buy back its cost, and widening the extraction is a quarter of work that has to compete for Q3 OKRs on its own merits, not sneak in as a milestone.

Gustavo, two asks for the packet: state the 0.79 -> 0.68 dedup story explicitly, and give Nadia the false-positive rate at the operating threshold, because that's the first question the board will ask.

Alina - release the vulcan reservation for the last week of June, we don't need it. Please do that today so someone else can use it.

Good, disciplined quarter.

Priya

subject: Project Nimbus kickoff - offline control without reward labels
body:
Team,

Kicking off our Contrastive Value Learning work. Internally this is Project Nimbus - use that on decks, calendar invites and the tracker, not "the CVL thing".

The substance: CVL learns an implicit multi-step dynamics model that can be trained without reward functions, and the model directly indicates the value of each action - no TD learning in the loop. Because the multi-step transitions stay implicit it never has to predict high-dimensional observations, which is exactly why it scales where 1-step model-based methods fall over.

Why it matters to us: our offline control datasets are large and almost entirely unlabeled for reward. Every method we've tried starts by demanding a reward model we don't have.

Apr 20 - Aug 3:
- May 29: reproduce on the continuous control benchmarks, offline only.
- Jul 3: run on our own unlabeled manipulation logs.
- Jul 31: adopt/park memo.

Alina has staffing. Rafael is tech lead.

Ulla

subject: Re: Project Nimbus kickoff - staffing and compute
body:
Ulla,

Everything below is filed under Project Nimbus in the tracker.

Staffing:
- Rafael Duran 50%, algorithm and benchmark reproduction.
- Rosa Mensah 40%, data pipeline over the manipulation logs (about 1.9TB of trajectories, no reward column, which is the point).
- Vera Egede 25%, evaluation tooling and run bookkeeping.

Compute: 64 GPUs on vulcan-h100 for May and June sweeps, confirmed with Ines. Offline RL is cheap on environment interaction and expensive on data loading, so Rosa's pipeline is the real bottleneck, not the accelerators.

One process note: Ines asked me to be precise about which effort the reservation belongs to when I filed it, so it's booked against Project Nimbus. If anyone sees a Nimbus line item on the infra report, that's us.

Alina

subject: Nimbus status - benchmarks reproduced, coverage is the catch
body:
Status.

May milestone done. On the continuous control suite we're within 2 points of the published offline returns, averaged over 4 seeds, and training genuinely used no reward labels. Not having a TD bootstrap in the loop makes these runs boringly stable compared to what we're used to - the training curves are almost dull, which I mean as a compliment.

The catch is on our own logs. CVL's implicit model estimates action value from what the data shows is reachable. Our manipulation logs are ~85% successful demonstrations of six routine motions. So the model is confident and roughly correct in a narrow tube and confidently wrong outside it, and the policy proposes actions in that outside region far more often than I'd like - 12% of steps in the first eval.

We either need coverage (deliberate exploration data we don't have) or an uncertainty gate on the value estimate. I'd like Vera's tooling time redirected to measuring the gate before we promise Jul 3.

Rafael

subject: Re: Nimbus status - memo landing Friday, one scope cut
body:
Wrapping up. The Project Nimbus recommendation memo goes out Friday and says: adopt for offline evaluation and candidate ranking, do not put it on a robot yet.

Rationale is Rafael's coverage finding. Reward-free training on 1.9TB of unlabeled logs is genuinely valuable to us and the benchmark reproduction is solid. But 12% of proposed steps landing outside the data's support is a safety conversation, not a metrics conversation, and the uncertainty gate is a Q3 item with its own owner.

Scope cut: the Jul 3 "run on our own logs" milestone shipped as a measurement study, not a deployed policy. I've already told the robotics folks, so nobody is expecting a demo.

Eleni - the reward-free stability result is the part I think is worth a broader read.

Thanks all, this was a well-run one.

Ulla

subject: Kickoff - discrete diffusion for structured record generation
body:
Team,

Kicking off D3PM. Our open-source release does denoising diffusion in discrete state spaces, with structured transition matrices rather than Gaussian noise, and it ships three tracks: image space evaluated in bits-per-dimension, text space, and the insertion/deletion variant from the follow-up work.

What I want out of it is the text and categorical side. We generate synthetic records constantly - for testing, for privacy-preserving sharing - and autoregressive generation is slow and produces suspiciously fluent garbage. A diffusion process over discrete states can be conditioned on partial records and refines the whole record in parallel.

Mar 2 - Jun 15:
- Mar 27: image track reproduced, bits-per-dimension matching the paper. This is our sanity check, not the goal.
- Apr 30: text track running on our schema-constrained record corpus.
- Jun 5: quality + speed comparison vs our autoregressive generator.

Deshawn on staffing, Carmen tech lead. FID/IS are not available in the release, so plan evaluation around bits-per-dimension and our own metrics.

Dmitri

subject: Re: Kickoff - staffing and the compute shape
body:
Dmitri,

Staffing through Jun 15:
- Carmen Reyes 55%, diffusion process and transition matrix design for our schema.
- Ondrej Bergstrom 40%, text track.
- Yusuf Keita 30%, evaluation and the autoregressive baseline.
- Farah Haddad 35%, data plumbing and the record corpus.

Compute: 64 GPUs on vulcan-h100 through May, agreed with Ines. Note diffusion sampling is the expensive bit at inference - 1000 denoising steps per sample by default - so the Jun 5 speed comparison needs to be honest about step count, not just wall clock on a tuned config.

One thing I want visibility on early: if the text track works, the insertion/deletion variant is the obvious follow-on, and that is not in this window. I'd rather plan it than discover it in June.

Deshawn

subject: D3PM status - text track works, fixed-length is the wall
body:
Status.

Image track reproduced in March, bits-per-dimension within 0.02 of published, we've left it alone since.

Text track on our record corpus: working, and the parallel refinement story is real. Generating a 40-field record takes 1.4s at 200 denoising steps against 6.8s autoregressive, and schema validity is 94% vs 91% - because we can bake schema constraints into the transition matrices rather than hoping the decoder respects them.

The wall is length. The base D3PM formulation diffuses over a fixed-length sequence. Real records have repeated groups - line items, addresses - so we currently pad to a maximum and the model wastes capacity learning to emit padding. About a third of our validity failures are length-related.

This is exactly what the insertion/deletion variant in the release addresses, and Ondrej and I both think it's the right next step rather than a hack around padding. Not in this window though.

Carmen

subject: Re: D3PM status - follow-on staffing for the insert/delete work
body:
Dmitri, closing out the window and pre-committing the follow-on so we don't lose momentum over the summer.

The Jun 5 comparison landed: 1.4s vs 6.8s per record, 94% vs 91% schema validity, with the length caveat Carmen described. I'm happy to call that a success and you should feel comfortable saying so.

For the insertion/deletion variant: I have Farah Haddad at 65% on d3pm for July 2026 to build the insertion/deletion evaluation - that is agreed with her and it is the plan of record for July. Carmen stays at 30% to supervise the transition-matrix changes; Ondrej is off the project after the 15th.

That's the whole ask - no new compute, we'll reuse the May reservation pattern. Shout now if July doesn't work for you, because I'm telling Farah it's confirmed.

Deshawn

subject: Kickoff - DAC for learning from operator demonstrations
body:
All,

Kicking off the DAC workstream. The open-source release addresses the two things that always kill adversarial imitation learning for us: reward bias, where the learned reward implicitly rewards or punishes termination, and sample inefficiency, which it fixes by going off-policy instead of throwing away every trajectory after one update.

Our use case: we have thousands of hours of operator demonstration logs for pipeline remediation, and no reward function anyone can agree on. Imitation is the right frame, we've just never had a method that learns from a realistic number of demonstrations.

Feb 9 - Jul 20, deliberately long because the data prep is the risk:
- Mar 20: reproduce the published results with the standard expert trajectories.
- May 15: our demonstration logs converted into the same trajectory format.
- Jul 10: final imitation sweep and a recommendation.

Alina has staffing and compute. Rosa is tech lead on the data side, Carmen on method.

Dmitri

subject: Re: Kickoff - resourcing incl. the July sweep reservation
body:
Dmitri,

Staffing:
- Rosa Mensah 45%, trajectory conversion pipeline and the expert-data import (the release's import script takes 1-2 hours on their data; ours is a lot bigger).
- Carmen Reyes 25%, discriminator and absorbing-state handling.
- Hyun Traore 20%, evaluation worker and baselines.

Compute has two phases. Development runs sit on titan-a100 best-effort, roughly 400 GPU-hours a month, no reservation needed - DAC is off-policy so we get a lot per environment step.

The final sweep is the one that needs booking. We hold the cirrus-tpu reservation for the week of 2026-07-06 - 128 accelerators, the full week, booked for the final imitation sweep. That's 9 environments x 3 seeds x 2 discriminator variants and it does not fit anywhere else in the quarter.

Alina

subject: DAC status - conversion done, our demos are not expert demos
body:
Status on the May 15 milestone - late by four days, done now.

Reproduction went fine back in March; off-policy training gives us the sample efficiency the paper claims and the absorbing-state fix visibly removes the survival bias in the learned reward.

The problem is our data. "Expert trajectories" in the benchmark means a trained policy executing cleanly. Our operator logs are humans, and humans backtrack, pause for 40 minutes, and occasionally fix the wrong thing first. The discriminator learns to distinguish human hesitation from policy behaviour, which is trivially easy and completely useless - it saturates in 2k steps and the actor gets no gradient signal.

Carmen's mitigation is filtering to trajectories with no backtracking, which leaves us 2,900 of 14,000 demonstrations. That may still be enough, DAC's whole point is working from few demos, but it changes what we're claiming: we imitate clean operators, not operators.

Rosa

subject: Re: DAC status - final sweep is a go, with the narrower claim
body:
Agreed on the narrower claim: we say "learns from clean operator demonstrations" and we report the 2,900 of 14,000 filter openly. Rosa, put the hesitation-saturation finding in the write-up - it's the kind of thing the next team needs to know before they spend three months discovering it.

Sweep is confirmed: the 128 accelerators on cirrus-tpu for the week of 2026-07-06 are ours and the sweep starts Monday morning. Rosa, please have the trajectory shards staged by Friday close so we are not burning reservation time on data movement. Nine environments, three seeds, two discriminator variants as planned - no adding a variant this late.

Recommendation memo lands Jul 17 either way. If the sweep says the filtered demos aren't enough, that is also a result and I'd rather publish it than pad the window.

Dmitri

subject: Kickoff - DARC, closing the sim-to-production dynamics gap
body:
Team,

Kicking off DARC. The idea in our open-source release is elegant and I want us to take it seriously: instead of trying to make the simulator match production, you train auxiliary classifiers that tell source-domain transitions from target-domain ones, and fold their output into the reward. The agent gets penalized for exploiting dynamics that only exist in simulation. No simulator engineering required.

For us the source domain is our traffic simulator and the target is a few thousand logged production episodes. Today policies trained in sim look great and then do something absurd in week one, because they learned to lean on a simulator artifact.

Apr 6 - Jun 15, short window on purpose:
- Apr 30: reproduce the published transfer results on the standard off-dynamics tasks.
- May 22: classifiers trained on our sim vs production transitions.
- Jun 10: policy comparison, DARC-corrected vs uncorrected, with human plausibility ratings.

Deshawn on resourcing. Yara is tech lead.

Ulla

subject: Re: Kickoff - resourcing, and we need a rating tool
body:
Ulla,

Staffing:
- Yara Jokic 55%, DARC implementation and the classifier training.
- Milan Zapata 40%, production transition extraction.
- Chiara Olsen 30%, simulator harness.
- Paloma Castillo, see below.

Compute: 32 GPUs on titan-a100, best-effort is fine, these are small policies.

The gap in your Jun 10 milestone is "human plausibility ratings". We have no tooling for that. Sending raters a folder of rollout videos and a spreadsheet is how you get unusable labels.

So we are building a human-rating annotation UI from scratch: side-by-side rollout playback, a 5-point plausibility scale, keyboard-driven navigation, rater agreement tracking and an export path into our eval store. Paloma Castillo owns it at 50% from April 20; first usable build April 30. It's about three weeks and we'll want it for every transfer project after this one.

Deshawn

subject: DARC status - the classifier is too good, which is a problem
body:
Status ahead of Jun 10.

Reproduction: done on time, transfer results match the paper on the off-dynamics tasks.

Our setting is where it gets awkward. The domain classifiers hit 99.4% accuracy separating simulator transitions from production ones - not because the dynamics differ in interesting ways, but because production transitions carry timing jitter and our simulator emits perfectly regular intervals. The classifier found the clock, not the physics.

The consequence is that the reward correction is essentially a constant penalty on every simulated transition, which does nothing useful. Once Milan added matched jitter to the simulator, classifier accuracy dropped to 71% and the correction started penalizing the things we actually care about - the aggressive retry patterns that only work when the simulated backend never rate-limits.

So: real result, but it took two weeks of the window to find, and I'm not confident there isn't a second such artifact. Rating study starts Jun 2 on the jittered runs.

Yara

subject: Re: DARC status - closing out, and a checklist I want kept
body:
Closing the window on the 15th. Where we land:

DARC works for us, conditional on the simulator not leaking trivial signal. Rated plausibility on the corrected policy is 3.9/5 vs 2.7/5 uncorrected, 4 raters, agreement 0.72 - that is a result I'm happy to take forward.

The durable output is not the policy though, it's Yara's clock-artifact lesson. Before any future DARC-style run: check classifier accuracy first, and if it's above ~95% assume you have an artifact rather than a triumph. Yara, please write that as a short checklist, three bullets max.

Tomas - Paloma's rating tool has rater agreement tracking built in and worked well; worth a look for Evalline.

No extension. Q3 OKRs lock on 2026-06-26 and if we want the second-artifact hunt funded it goes in as its own line, not as a quiet rollover.

Ulla

subject: Kickoff - DBLE as our calibration layer
body:
Team,

Kicking off DBLE. The premise from our open-source release: adapt prototypical learning so the representation space has a usable metric, then calibrate confidence by how far a sample sits from its class center. Since you don't have ground-truth labels at inference, you train a second confidence model - and crucially you train it only on the mis-classified training samples, which the paper shows is what makes it work.

Why now: three teams route automated decisions off classifier confidence, and all three are using raw softmax, which is famously overconfident. A model-agnostic calibration layer that works on MLPs, VGG and ResNet alike is worth a quarter of our time.

Apr 27 - Aug 10:
- Jun 5: reproduce the reported calibration improvements, ResNet-50 on the standard image sets.
- Jul 10: apply to two internal classifiers, measure expected calibration error against temperature scaling.
- Aug 5: recommendation + integration plan.

Alina has resourcing. Carmen tech lead.

Dmitri

subject: Re: Kickoff - staffing for dble
body:
Dmitri,

Staffing:
- Efe Lindqvist is on dble at 60% for May 2026 - the prototypical training rewrite is his and it has to be finished inside May for the June calibration numbers to mean anything. He drops to 30% in June and July.
- Carmen Reyes 35% across the window, method and the confidence-model training.
- Maren Zhou 40%, evaluation harness - expected calibration error, reliability diagrams, temperature-scaling baseline.
- Gustavo Moreau 25% from June, integration with the two internal classifiers.

Compute: 24 GPUs on titan-a100 best-effort. These are CIFAR-scale reproductions, then fine-tunes of existing internal models - nothing that needs a vulcan reservation.

The May dependency on Efe is the schedule's single point of failure. Flagging it now rather than in June.

Alina

subject: dble status - reproduced, but the training cost is the real story
body:
Status.

Jun 5 milestone met (a week late). ResNet-50: expected calibration error 0.021 with DBLE vs 0.068 uncalibrated and 0.034 with temperature scaling. So it beats the cheap baseline meaningfully, which is the bar that matters.

The caveat Dmitri should hear before the Aug 5 memo: DBLE is not a layer you bolt on. It changes how the classifier is trained - prototypical learning, distance-based decision rule, plus the jointly trained confidence model. You cannot take an existing production classifier and calibrate it this way; you retrain it. Temperature scaling, for all its weakness, needs a validation set and ten minutes.

Maren's numbers on our first internal classifier show ECE 0.019 vs 0.041 temperature-scaled - real, but that cost a full retrain plus two weeks of Efe's rewrite.

So the honest framing is: DBLE for new classifiers where accuracy of the confidence matters. Not a retrofit.

Carmen

subject: Re: dble status - recommendation: new classifiers only
body:
Recommendation, going out tomorrow:

DBLE is recommended for new classifiers whose confidence drives an automated action, and explicitly not recommended as a retrofit. Carmen's framing is right and I'd rather ship a narrow recommendation people follow than a broad one they quietly ignore.

Numbers for the memo: ECE 0.019 vs 0.041 temperature-scaled on our first internal classifier; 0.021 vs 0.034 on the reproduction. Both with the retrain caveat stated in the same paragraph, not a footnote.

Scope cut: we are dropping the second internal classifier. Gustavo's integration time in July went almost entirely into the first one, and a second data point bought with a rushed retrain would be worse than no second data point.

Hana - the interesting open question is whether the confidence model can be trained against a frozen backbone. That's a Q4 question, not a this-window one.

Dmitri

subject: Kickoff - abbreviation expansion via reverse substitution
body:
Team,

Short, sharp project: Mar 2 - May 11.

The open-source release we're working from expands clinical abbreviations without training on sensitive records. The trick is reverse substitution: take ordinary text, take a curated abbreviation-expansion dictionary, and mechanically *insert* abbreviations to manufacture training pairs. Evaluation then uses a small clinician-written set of snippets containing real abbreviations.

Our version of this problem is internal jargon - ticket text, incident reports, and about 900 acronyms that mean different things per team. Same shape, no patient data, and Kofi will confirm we can skip the heavier review path because we never train on the sensitive corpus.

Milestones:
- Mar 27: dictionary assembled for our top 3 teams, reverse substitution running.
- Apr 17: model fine-tuned, evaluated on a hand-written internal snippet set.
- May 8: results write-up and a call on whether this becomes a service.

Deshawn on resourcing. Halima is tech lead.

Dmitri

subject: Re: Kickoff - resourcing, and we need somewhere to put results
body:
Dmitri,

Staffing for a 10-week window:
- Halima Toure 50%, reverse substitution and fine-tuning.
- Amara Okafor 40%, dictionary assembly - this is mostly interviewing three teams and arguing about what SLR means.
- Milan Zapata 25%, snippet set collection.
- Oyin Iversen, below.

Compute: negligible, ~200 GPU-hours titan-a100 best-effort.

The thing that isn't in your milestone list: we have no consistent way to score and track these runs. Right now every project here rolls its own notebook and the numbers aren't comparable week to week.

We are building an internal evaluation harness from scratch - dataset registry, per-example scoring with pluggable metrics, run comparison, and regression alerts when a metric moves more than a configured threshold. Oyin Iversen owns it at 50% from March 16, first version by April 3. It's not free but it pays back inside two projects.

Deshawn

subject: Status - reverse substitution works, ambiguity is where we lose
body:
Status.

Reverse substitution is running and the dictionary covers 612 acronyms across the three pilot teams, which is more than I expected Amara to get in a month.

Model results on our internal snippet set (287 snippets, hand-written, roughly the size of the clinician set in the release): 88% expansion accuracy overall. But that number hides the split. Unambiguous acronyms - one expansion in the dictionary - are at 96%. Ambiguous ones, where the same three letters mean different things in platform vs support vs finance, are at 61%.

That's not a model problem so much as a context problem: the snippets often don't contain enough signal to disambiguate, and neither would a human without knowing which team wrote the ticket. Adding the authoring team as a feature took ambiguous accuracy to 79% in a quick test.

Recommendation: make team-context a required input rather than pretending we can do this from text alone.

Halima

subject: Re: Status - decision for the May 8 write-up
body:
Decision, so Halima can finish the write-up:

1. Team context becomes a required input. 61% -> 79% on ambiguous acronyms is too big to argue with, and any caller who can't tell us which team authored the text probably shouldn't be expanding their jargon anyway.
2. This does not become a service this quarter. It becomes a library plus the dictionary, which the ticket-search team can call. A service means an SLA and an on-call rotation for an 88% feature.
3. Dictionary maintenance is the real long-term cost. Amara should hand over an owner per team before we close out, otherwise it rots in six months.

Kofi - confirming for the record that we never trained on the sensitive corpus, only on reverse-substituted ordinary text, so no further review is expected. Correct me this week if that's wrong.

Good project. Short, honest, done on time.

Dmitri

subject: Kickoff - DEDAL and learned alignment scoring
body:
All,

Kicking off DEDAL. The core idea in our open-source release: rather than using a fixed substitution matrix and hand-set gap penalties, the model predicts *contextual* Smith-Waterman parameters per sequence pair - substitution scores plus gap open and gap extend - and outputs alignment scores, homology logits and the predicted alignment path.

My interest is the pattern, applied to our own long symbolic sequences: event streams, command histories, config lineages. Every one of those we currently align with an edit distance that treats all substitutions as equal, which is obviously wrong and nobody has had time to fix.

Mar 16 - Jul 6:
- Apr 17: released model running in both alignment and embedding mode, homology detection reproduced.
- May 29: our own sequence type, learned scoring vs fixed-cost edit distance.
- Jun 26: recommendation.

Ivo has resourcing. Katya is tech lead. Note the 512-token input limit including EOS - our event streams are longer than that, so chunking or a windowed scheme is on the critical path, not an afterthought.

Anders

subject: Re: Kickoff - resourcing for dedal
body:
Anders,

Staffing:
- Katya Silva 45%, model work, alignment/embedding modes and the windowing scheme for sequences over 512.
- Rosa Mensah 20%, data extraction for the event-stream pairs.
- Wei Ivanov, below.

Compute: 32 GPUs on titan-a100 best-effort. Fine-tuning only. The memory shape is the thing to watch - the predicted alignment paths come back as B x 512 x 512 x 9 tensors, so batch size is bounded by that, not by the encoder.

Separately, and I'd argue this is the more durable investment: we have no shared place to compare alignment methods across teams. We are building a benchmark leaderboard service from scratch - task registry, submission endpoint, automatic scoring against held-out pairs, versioned result tables and a browsable ranking view. Wei Ivanov owns it at 45% from March 30 with a first cut live by May 8. Roughly five weeks of work.

Ivo

subject: dedal status - learned scoring wins, the 512 limit hurts
body:
Status for the May 29 milestone, a couple of days early.

Homology reproduction was clean back in April. On our own event streams, learned alignment beats fixed-cost edit distance by a distance: 0.81 vs 0.62 on our pair-matching task. The contextual gap penalties are doing the work - our streams have long runs of retries that a fixed gap-extend penalty punishes indiscriminately, and the learned parameters figure out that a long homogeneous gap is cheap while a short heterogeneous one is expensive. That's a genuinely nice result.

The cost is the 512 limit. Median stream is 1,900 events, so we window at 480 with 32-event overlap and stitch. Stitching is where the errors live - about 70% of our remaining failures are pairs whose true alignment crosses a window boundary. Memory is also tight because of the 512x512x9 path tensor, so we can't just widen the window.

Anders, worth deciding whether we invest in a hierarchical scheme or accept the ceiling.

Katya

subject: Re: dedal status - accept the ceiling, ship the recommendation
body:
Accept the ceiling. 0.81 vs 0.62 is a large enough win that shipping it windowed beats spending Q3 on a hierarchical scheme for the tail. Katya, put the boundary-crossing failure rate in the recommendation as a known limitation with a number attached - "about 70% of residual errors" - so whoever picks up the hierarchical work later starts from evidence.

One scope cut: we are not doing the third sequence type (config lineages) in this window. Q3 OKRs lock on 2026-06-26 and I would rather it appear there as a funded item than as an unstaffed bullet in our closeout.

Ivo - Wei's leaderboard has three teams submitting now, which is more adoption than I expected in six weeks. Please make sure it has an owner after this project closes; unowned shared infrastructure is how we end up rebuilding it next year.

Anders

subject: Kickoff - predicting generalization gap before we pay for training
body:
Team,

Kicking off DEMOGEN. The dataset is 756 trained models - CNN variants and ResNet-32, across weight decay, dropout, normalization, width and learning rate - each with its train and test performance. Test accuracies span 60% to 90.5% and generalization gaps span 1% to 35%, which is exactly the spread you need to learn a predictor. The release also ships the margin-distribution and total-variation utilities from the original work.

The product question: can we rank candidate configs by predicted generalization gap using only quantities measurable early in training? If yes, we stop burning cluster time on configs that were never going to generalize. That is a straight cost argument, which is why I expect it to get funded.

Mar 30 - Jul 6:
- Apr 30: margin-distribution predictor reproduced on DEMOGEN.
- Jun 5: our own model zoo - ~200 internal configs trained and measured.
- Jun 30: predictor evaluated on our zoo, cost-saving estimate.

Daniela on resourcing and the budget. Umar tech lead.

Dmitri

subject: Re: Kickoff - resourcing and the B-81 funding
body:
Dmitri,

Staffing:
- Umar Costa 50%, predictor and the margin/total-variation feature work.
- Ondrej Bergstrom 40%, model zoo training harness.
- Hyun Traore 20%, evaluation and the cost model.

The expensive part is our own zoo. Training ~200 internal configs to convergence is roughly 41,000 GPU-hours. That does not fit in best-effort titan capacity without pushing everyone else out, so it needs real money.

Idris has verbally earmarked the full $120k available on Q3 discretionary compute budget line B-81 for demogen - that is the whole line, and it covers the model-zoo training in May and June. I have not seen it in writing yet but he was unambiguous on the call.

If that funding moves, the Jun 5 milestone moves with it and we fall back to a 60-config zoo, which weakens the predictor evaluation considerably.

Daniela

subject: demogen status - predictor reproduced, transfer to our configs is shakier
body:
Status.

April milestone done. Using margin distributions at the hidden layers plus total variation, the predictor gets rank correlation 0.87 with true generalization gap across the 756 DEMOGEN models. Comfortably reproduces the published result.

Ondrej's zoo is at 118 of 200 configs trained. Early read on those: rank correlation drops to 0.61. Two reasons I can see. First, DEMOGEN's variation is mostly regularization strength with fixed data; ours varies dataset mixture too, and margin distributions don't see data-mixture effects at all. Second, our gaps are compressed - most internal configs sit between 4% and 11% gap, so there's much less signal to rank than the 1-35% spread in DEMOGEN.

0.61 still saves money if we use it as a coarse filter (drop the bottom quartile) rather than a ranking. That is a weaker claim than the kickoff made and I'd rather say so in May than in June.

Umar

subject: Re: demogen status - shipping it as a filter, and closing the budget loop
body:
Decision for the Jun 30 write-up: we ship it as a coarse filter, not a ranker. Drop the bottom quartile of candidate configs before training. On last quarter's actual sweep volume that would have saved about 9,000 GPU-hours with one config wrongly dropped out of 84. I can defend that trade; I could not defend claiming a ranking at 0.61.

Umar - please state the DEMOGEN 0.87 and our 0.61 side by side, with the data-mixture explanation. The gap between them is the most useful paragraph in the doc.

Idris, closing a loop: the $120k on Q3 discretionary compute budget line B-81 is ours for Q3, as you confirmed verbally back in April. We've spent about $74k of it on the zoo, 176 configs trained in the end. I'd like the remaining ~$46k held on the same line for the filter's integration work rather than returned. Can you confirm in writing this week - Q3 OKRs locked Friday and I don't want this floating.

Dmitri

subject: Kickoff: dense entity retrieval for the knowledge assistant
body:
Team,

Kicking off the entity retrieval track. The plan is to take the dense-representations work from our open-source release and make it the linking backbone for the internal knowledge assistant. Concretely: a dual encoder that retrieves entities directly in embedding space, evaluated against the 2018 Wikinews annotations we regenerate with parse_wikinews.py from the Jan 1, 2019 dump.

Ivo, can you come back with staffing and a compute ask this week? OKR language due to Hana by Friday.

Thanks,
Anders

subject: Re: Kickoff: dense entity retrieval for the knowledge assistant
body:
Anders,

Staffing plan for May, confirmed with everyone yesterday. Rafael Duran is committed at 65% to this project for May 2026 to own the dual-encoder training runs. Vera takes the Wikinews regeneration pipeline at 40%, Wanjiru covers the retrieval serving path at 30%, and Tereza floats for evals.

That keeps May 15 realistic for baseline reproduction.

subject: Re: Kickoff: dense entity retrieval for the knowledge assistant

Status as of this morning: baseline is reproduced. Rafael's dual-encoder runs land at recall@1 of 86.4 on our regenerated Wikinews set, against 87.1 published, so we are inside the 2-point envelope Anders set.

Two things to watch. subject: Decision: scope for entity retrieval LRB pre-read

Following the June 12 review, decisions for the LRB pre-read the week of July 6:

subject: Kickoff: DePlot chart QA for the analytics suite
body:
Hi all,

Starting the DePlot workstream today. The pitch: DePlot translates a chart image into a linearized table in one shot, and once you have the table, any of our reasoning models can answer questions over it. That decomposition is what makes it a fit for chart QA in the analytics suite -- we do not need to fine-tune a giant multimodal model per dashboard.

Scope for this half: fine-tune from the released checkpoints (they are fully compatible with the Pix2Struct codebase, which saves us a rewrite), stand up an internal demo on Shipyard, and hit an LRB slot in late June.

Daniela owns feasibility and staffing; first checkpoint review May 8.

Anders

subject: Re: Kickoff: DePlot chart QA for the analytics suite
body:
Anders,

Feasibility and resourcing:

Staffing: Maren leads modeling at 50%, Bilal on the data pipeline at 50%, Vera 30% on evals, Giannis 40% on the Shipyard demo path.

Compute: this trains on TPU, so I am requesting a Cirrus slice from the graphs-retrieval quarterly allocation -- one v5 slice for fine-tuning is plenty since we start from released checkpoints. The gin configs come from Pix2Struct, so environment setup is mostly cloning that repo and exporting PIX2STRUCT.

Data: We are planning around the Corpus v2 migration freeze on 2026-06-26, so the chart-table pretraining shards have to be fully ingested before that date. Bilal's ingestion plan works backward from there: synthetic chart corpus in by May 29, human-annotated dashboards by June 12.

First checkpoint review May 8 stands.

Daniela

subject: Re: Kickoff: DePlot chart QA for the analytics suite
body:
Status: fine-tuning from the released DePlot checkpoint is working end to end on Cirrus. On our internal dashboard eval, plot-to-table exact structure match is at 71%, and downstream QA accuracy is 64% when we chain the table into the reasoning model.

The main risk is derendering quality on our densest chart types. DePlot's strength is standard bar/line/pie; our stacked area charts with more than 8 series lose rows in the linearized table, and every dropped row is an unrecoverable QA error downstream. MatCha-style pretraining on chart derendering would likely help, but that is real pretraining compute, not fine-tuning.

Proposal: keep fine-tuning only, and scope stacked-area out of the June demo. Will bring numbers to the next review.

subject: Re: Kickoff: DePlot chart QA for the analytics suite
body:
Decision time, since the LRB slot is June 25 and OKR lock is the 26th.

1. Stacked-area charts are out of scope for the demo and for the Q3 commit. Maren's numbers make the case: 71% structure match overall but under 40% on 8+ series stacked area. We demo bar, line, and pie.

3. Giannis, please have the Shipyard demo frozen by June 22 so Nadia's team can dry-run it.

Thanks all -- good half so far.

subject: Kickoff: unsupervised depth + motion for AR occlusion
body:
Jelena, team,

Kicking off the depth-and-motion track. What the research unlocks: joint training of a depth model and a motion model using only pairs of RGB images -- no depth sensors, no semantic labels. The depth net infers a dense map from a single image; the motion net gives us 6-DoF camera motion plus a 3D translation field for every pixel. Camera intrinsics can be learned, which matters because our AR partners cannot guarantee calibrated devices.

Product target is the occlusion layer in the AR SDK, with robot perception as the second customer. Milestones: training reproduced on our driving corpus by June 5, quality bar review July 10, LRB pre-read early August.

Jelena to follow up on staffing and infra.

Lucia

subject: Re: Kickoff: unsupervised depth + motion for AR occlusion
body:
Lucia,

Staffing and infra plan.

Modeling: Katya at 60% on training and the intrinsics-learning path. Data: our driving corpus needs converting into Struct2depth format, which is what the trainer expects -- Giannis takes that first.

Evaluation is the gap. There is no repeatable way today to score depth and motion-field quality across checkpoints, and the July 10 quality bar review is meaningless without one. We are scoping and staffing an internal evaluation harness built from scratch: Leilani Nakamura leads the build at 50% from mid-May, with Giannis Sato supporting at 25%. Scope: automated depth-metric suite, motion-field error vs. held-out ego-motion, and regression dashboards per checkpoint.

Compute: 32 A100s on Titan best-effort covers training; init from a pretrained ImageNet checkpoint keeps runs short.

Jelena

subject: Re: Kickoff: unsupervised depth + motion for AR occlusion
body:
Status: training reproduced, four days late but done. With ImageNet init (init_ckpt_type=imagenet) and Giannis's Struct2depth-format conversion, depth error on our driving held-out set is within 6% relative of the reference implementation.

The interesting risk is the motion field. Because the model predicts a full 3D translation field for every pixel, it will happily explain away moving objects as depth errors in scenes with lots of dynamics -- our urban clips are exactly that. The learned-intrinsics path also converges slower than specified intrinsics, roughly 1.4x steps to the same error.

Mitigation I want to try: stronger motion-field regularization for the first 20k steps. Leilani's harness is what will tell us if it actually helps -- her depth-metric suite is running, motion metrics land next week.

Katya

subject: Decision: depth+motion scope for the August LRB pre-read
body:
Team,

Decisions from the July 10 quality bar review, now that the follow-up runs are in:

1. AR occlusion ships on specified-intrinsics mode only. Learned intrinsics stays a research track -- the 1.4x convergence cost and the residual scale drift are not worth carrying into the SDK this half.
2. Katya's motion-field regularization is in: it cut dynamic-scene depth outliers by 23% on the harness metrics with no static-scene regression.
3. Leilani's evaluation harness becomes the gate for every checkpoint we promote; Giannis will wire it into the release pipeline by August 7.

LRB pre-read is August 12. I will circulate the narrative doc Friday.

Lucia

subject: Kickoff: depth from unknown cameras (video-in-the-wild)
body:
Alina, team,

Kicking off the video-in-the-wild depth track. The differentiator here is unknown cameras: because the model can learn intrinsics rather than requiring them, we can train on and serve depth for arbitrary user-uploaded video -- YouTube-style footage, dashcams, old phone clips. That is the unlock for the media-tools depth feature, where we control nothing about the capture device.

Mechanics per the ICCV release: training takes triplets of RGB frames with possibly-moving objects masked out, and produces 6-DoF camera motion plus a dense translation vector field.

Milestones: masking + data pipeline live May 22, baseline quality review June 15, intrinsics ablation and LRB readout the first week of July.

Alina owns staffing; note we share people with other vision tracks, so let's be explicit about allocations.

Lucia

subject: Re: Kickoff: depth from unknown cameras (video-in-the-wild)
body:
Lucia,

Allocations, as requested, explicit:

May-June: Quentin 60% on the masking pipeline (we need moving objects masked out of every training triplet, so this is the critical path), Rosa 50% on the data plumbing and TFRecord generation, Wanjiru 40% on serving experiments, Katya 20% advisory since she is deep on the sister depth track.

July: Rafael Duran is committed at 60% to this project for July 2026 to run the learned-intrinsics ablation study. That ablation -- learned vs. specified intrinsics across camera types -- is the centerpiece of the LRB readout, and Rafael wrote the original intrinsics code, so I want him properly resourced, not squeezed in at 20%.

Compute: 48 A100s on Titan, short runs from an ImageNet checkpoint.

Alina

subject: Re: Kickoff: depth from unknown cameras (video-in-the-wild)
body:
Status on the masking pipeline, six days late vs. the May 22 milestone but now live.

What shipped: automated segmentation masks for possibly-moving objects over our in-the-wild corpus, emitting Struct2depth-format triplets the trainer consumes directly. Throughput is about 40 clip-hours per day, so the full corpus is masked by June 9.

The risk worth flagging: mask quality drives everything downstream. On a 500-frame audit, 7% of frames had a moving object partially unmasked, and those frames are exactly where the depth net learns wrong geometry -- the paper's whole training setup assumes movers are masked out. Rosa and I are adding a dilation pass plus a confidence filter, which should cut leakage under 3%.

Baseline training starts Monday regardless; June 15 review holds.

Quentin

subject: Decision: July plan for video-in-the-wild depth
body:
Team,

Outcomes from the June 15 baseline review, plus July commitments:

1. Baseline quality is good enough to proceed: with the dilation+confidence masking fix, depth error on uncalibrated clips is within 9% of the calibrated-camera baseline. That gap is the whole story for the LRB.
2. The learned-intrinsics ablation is confirmed as the July centerpiece per Alina's staffing plan. Deliverable: a camera-type breakdown (phone, dashcam, action cam) of learned vs. specified intrinsics by July 8.
3. Scope cut: no real-time serving demo this half. Wanjiru's latency numbers say we would need a distilled model, and I would rather show honest offline quality than a laggy demo.

LRB readout targeted for July 9.

Lucia

subject: Kickoff: Dichotomy of Control for reliable automation agents
body:
Deshawn, team,

Kicking off the DoC evaluation track. Why it matters for us: return-conditioned agents like Decision Transformer quietly take credit for lucky outcomes in stochastic environments, which is exactly the failure mode we cannot afford in the ops-automation agents. Dichotomy of Control separates what the policy controls from what the environment decides, and the released code makes the contrast easy to demonstrate -- flipping algo_name from doc to dt in run_tabular.sh shows the dramatic performance drop on the tabular benchmarks.

Scope for the half: reproduce the Bandit and FrozenLake results from the offline datasets, then a neural DoC run on one internal ops simulator, wrapping by June 8 with a go/no-go recommendation for Q3 adoption.

Deshawn to size staffing and infra.

Ulla

subject: Re: Kickoff: Dichotomy of Control for reliable automation agents
body:
Ulla,

Sizing is done. This is CPU-and-small-GPU work, so no cluster reservations needed -- a handful of Titan A100s best-effort covers the neural runs.

Staffing March-May: Jorge 50% on environment setup and the dice_rl dependency (the offline datasets for Bandit and FrozenLake come from create_dataset.sh once dice_rl is installed, but its pinned deps fight our base image -- he is containerizing it). Carmen 40% on reproducing the tabular results and the DoC-vs-DT comparison. Linnea 30% ramping on the neural DT path, scaling up in the final month.

One feasibility note: the ops simulator is much noisier than FrozenLake, so if DoC's advantage does not transfer, that is a legitimate finding, not a failure. Framing it that way now so June is not a fire drill.

Deshawn

subject: Re: Kickoff: Dichotomy of Control for reliable automation agents
body:
Status heading into the final stretch.

Done: Carmen reproduced the tabular results. On Bandit, DoC holds near-optimal return where the dt baseline collapses, matching the paper's reported gap; FrozenLake reproduces as well from the create_dataset.sh offline sets.

In flight: the neural DoC run on the ops simulator. First runs show DoC ahead of DT by 12% mean return but with high seed variance, so we need the full 5-seed sweep before we can call it. Linnea Yamada is committed at 60% to this project for June 2026 to land the neural DoC runs before the June 8 wrap.

Risk: if two of the five seeds land inside DT's variance band, the go/no-go gets murky. My recommendation would then be 'adopt for high-stochasticity workflows only'. Flagging now so the June readout language is no surprise.

Deshawn

subject: Kickoff: dictionary learning for embedding-table compression
body:
Team,

Kicking off a small but high-leverage track: embedding-table compression via the dictionary learning implementation from our open-source release. The method factors an embedding table into a dictionary (row_percentage controls how many dictionary words we keep) and a sparse code (col_percentage controls nonzeros per row). The reference example recovers a synthetic matrix at about 11% relative error with row_percentage=0.5 and col_percentage=0.3 -- if we can hold error in that range on the production retrieval tables, serving memory drops by more than half.

Goal for the half: a validated compression recipe for the two largest retrieval embedding tables, plus a serving integration plan, feeding the Q3 serving-cost OKR.

Jelena to propose staffing and the sweep plan.

Anders

subject: Re: Kickoff: dictionary learning for embedding-table compression
body:
Anders,

Plan and staffing.

April: Efe characterizes the method on synthetic tables -- error vs. row_percentage/col_percentage curves, plus sensitivity to n_iterations (the default 32 may be low for our table sizes). Wanjiru pulls anonymized copies of the two production tables.

May is the heavy month: Saoirse Eriksen is committed at 65% to this project for May 2026 to own the factorization sweeps and the serving integration spike. Leilani supports at 25% on the eval side, measuring retrieval quality (not just reconstruction error) on compressed tables.

June: integration plan and writeup before the Q3 OKR lock on June 26.

Compute is trivial for once -- this is CPU/NumPy work, no cluster ask. The scarce resource here is people, hence the explicit May allocations.

Jelena

subject: Re: Kickoff: dictionary learning for embedding-table compression
body:
Status + one real trade-off.

Synthetic characterization is done and matches the reference: on the documented example setup we reproduce error = 0.1128 almost exactly (0.113 on our seeds). On the production tables, results are more nuanced. Table A (entity embeddings) compresses beautifully: row_percentage=0.5, col_percentage=0.3 gives 0.14 reconstruction error and only -0.4 points recall@10 on Leilani's retrieval eval. Table B (query embeddings) is the problem child -- at the same settings error is 0.31, and we need col_percentage=0.5 and n_iterations=64 to get anywhere reasonable, which halves the sparsity win.

Trade-off to decide by end of May: ship Table A only (still ~55% of the memory savings), or spend Saoirse's remaining May sweeps chasing Table B configs.

Efe

subject: Decision: compression scope for Q3 OKRs
body:
All,

Decisions, so we are clean before the June 26 OKR lock:

1. We commit Table A compression to the Q3 serving-cost OKR. Saoirse's sweeps confirmed Efe's May numbers hold at full table scale: 0.14 error, -0.4 recall@10, roughly 55% memory reduction on the biggest table in the retrieval fleet.
2. Table B is explicitly out of the OKR. The col_percentage=0.5 / n_iterations=64 configs erase most of the sparsity benefit. It stays as an exploration item with no committed number.
3. Saoirse's serving integration spike showed decode overhead is negligible at query time, so Wanjiru writes the integration plan with the serving leads by July 3.

Good, boring, shippable result. My favorite kind.

Anders

subject: Kickoff: Didi digital-ink benchmark hosting
body:
Ivo, team,

Kicking off the Didi benchmark track. The dataset gives us digital ink drawings of diagrams with full dynamic drawing information -- stroke timing included -- collected via prompted drawing sessions, with the prompts available in png, dot, and xdot form. That combination (ink + ground-truth graph structure) is rare, and it is the right substrate for the interactive diagram-understanding features the notes product wants.

Goal for this short window: host the dataset internally on Corpus, ship the TFRecord conversion path from the reference notebook as a supported pipeline, train a baseline model on the paper's train/validation/test split, and give researchers a standard way to compare results.

Milestones: data hosted March 13, pipeline + baseline April 10, wrap May 8.

Dmitri

subject: Re: Kickoff: Didi digital-ink benchmark hosting
body:
Dmitri,

Resourcing update. Data hosting is on track: Amara has the raw NDJSON ink mirrored into Corpus and the TFRecord conversion running as a scheduled pipeline; the png/dot/xdot prompt files land this week.

On 'a standard way to compare results' -- that needs real software, not a spreadsheet. We are scoping and staffing a benchmark leaderboard service built from scratch: Chiara Olsen at 60% and Farah Haddad at 40% through April to design and build it. Feature set: submission upload, automatic scoring against the held-out test split, per-task breakdowns, and an internal results page. Katya stays 30% on the baseline model so the leaderboard has a reference entry on day one.

Compute ask is minimal, a few Titan A100s for the baseline.

One watch item: scoring rules need to be nailed down before submissions open, else early numbers wont be comparable.

Ivo

subject: Re: Kickoff: Didi digital-ink benchmark hosting
body:
Status for the April 10 milestone.

Pipeline: done. NDJSON to TFRecord conversion is a supported scheduled job, and the paper's train/validation/test split is materialized as fixed manifests so every consumer trains on identical data.

Baseline: Katya's model trains end to end; recognition accuracy on the validation split is 71.8%, which is in the plausible range given we have not tuned.

Risk worth escalating: prompt-to-ink alignment. About 4% of drawings reference dot/xdot prompt files with node labels that do not match what the participant actually drew -- prompted collection is messy like that. If we score strictly against the xdot graph structure, those samples systematically penalize honest submissions. Proposal: flag the 4% as an 'alignment-noisy' subset and exclude them from the headline leaderboard metric. Need a decision before submissions open.

Amara

subject: Re: Kickoff: Didi digital-ink benchmark hosting
body:
Decisions to close out the half:

1. Amara's proposal is approved: the 4% alignment-noisy subset is excluded from the headline metric but published as a separate diagnostic split. Transparent and defensible.
2. Scoring rules freeze this Friday, May 1. Chiara, please version them in the service so a rule change can never silently reshuffle historical entries.
3. The leaderboard service opens to internal submissions May 8 with Katya's 71.8% baseline as entry #1. Demo at the data-platforms all-hands the following week.

Nice execution on a tight window, everyone. This gives the diagram-understanding work a real yardstick going into Q3.

Dmitri

subject: Kickoff: Differentiable Data Selection for vision training
body:
Bao, team,

Kicking off the DDS evaluation. The method is a two-step recipe: first train a normal model on CIFAR-10 with Wide-ResNet-28-10, then use it as the representation for a learned DDS scorer that reweights training examples during a second training run. If the published gains transfer to our internal vision corpora, this becomes a standing data-curation lever -- better models from the same data budget, which is the cheapest win we ever get.

Important constraint up front: the implementation only runs on TPUs, so this lives on Cirrus, not the GPU pools.

Milestones: CIFAR-10 reproduction by April 24, internal-corpus pilot by June 5, Q3 investment recommendation before OKR lock.

Bao to size the TPU ask and staffing.

Lucia

subject: Re: Kickoff: Differentiable Data Selection for vision training
body:
Lucia,

Sizing and money.

Staffing: Quentin 50% on reproduction and the scorer training, Bilal 40% on porting our internal corpus into the input pipeline, Amara 30% on infra and the Cirrus scheduling glue.

Compute: reproduction fits in the vision portfolio's Cirrus quarterly allocation -- the reference runs use batch 1024 at 32x32, which is modest. The internal-corpus pilot is the expensive part: images are 4x larger and the DDS recipe means training essentially twice (scorer model, then the DDS run). My estimate is it exceeds our remaining quarterly allocation by roughly 40%.

On covering that gap: Idris Osei has verbally earmarked $120k from Q3 discretionary compute budget line B-13 for this project. I want to convert that to a written commitment before we schedule the pilot burns -- verbal is verbal.

Bao

subject: Re: Kickoff: Differentiable Data Selection for vision training
body:
Status, a bit late for the April 24 milestone but with a clean result.

Reproduction: done. Baseline WRN-28-10 on CIFAR-10 matches the reference setup (cosine decay, EMA 0.9999, 100k steps, bfloat16 on Cirrus), and the DDS run on top shows +0.6 accuracy over the baseline, consistent with the paper's reported effect size.

The fiddly part was scorer stability: with the documented scorer_lr=1e-06 the scorer barely moves early on, but raising it 10x made example weights oscillate and hurt final accuracy. We landed back on 1e-06 with scorer_clip=0.5 doing the real stabilization work. Writing this up so the pilot doesn't rediscover it.

Risk for the pilot: our internal corpus has label noise CIFAR does not, and DDS's value should be larger there -- but the scorer checkpoint quality becomes critical. Bilal's pipeline is ready.

Quentin

subject: Re: Kickoff: Differentiable Data Selection for vision training
body:
Decisions ahead of the June 26 OKR lock.

1. The pilot ran on the partial budget we had confirmed in writing: two of the four planned internal-corpus configurations. Result: +1.1 accuracy on the noisy-label corpus, which supports Quentin's hypothesis that DDS earns more where data quality is worse.
2. Q3 recommendation: adopt DDS for the two noisiest training corpora only. I am writing a scoped OKR around those, not a blanket rollout.
3. The remaining two pilot configurations run in Q3 only if the B-13 funding is confirmed in writing -- Bao, please push to close that with Finance this week; it has been pending too long.

Thanks all. Solid, evidence-shaped half.

Lucia

subject: Kickoff: node-level DP GNNs for interaction-graph features
body:
Deshawn, team,

Kicking off the DP-GNN track. The problem: our recommendation and abuse teams want features computed over the user-interaction graph, and Legal will only sign off if we can bound what any single node contributes. The node-level DP-GNN work gives us exactly that -- a JAX DP-GCN with per-node privacy guarantees, with a clean training setup driven by config files under configs/ and config_flags overrides for sweeps.

Plan: reproduce on ogbn-arxiv first (the download script handles it), then re-run on an anonymized interaction subgraph. Deliverable is an epsilon-vs-utility curve Legal and the feature teams can negotiate over.

Milestones: ogbn-arxiv reproduction May 1, interaction-graph runs mid-June, recommendation doc July 10.

Deshawn to size staffing and data needs.

Dmitri

subject: Re: Kickoff: node-level DP GNNs for interaction-graph features
body:
Dmitri,

Staffing: Maren 50% on the DP-GCN training and the epsilon sweeps, Emeka 40% on the interaction-subgraph extraction and anonymization, Bilal 30% on eval tooling and the utility metrics.

Compute is light -- these graphs fit on single hosts, a few Titan A100s best-effort.

Data timeline is the real planning constraint. The interaction subgraph and both benchmark graphs get ingested through Corpus, and the pipelines we build now need to be re-run once on migrated v2 storage. The Corpus v2 migration freeze is 2026-07-24, which gives us headroom to re-ingest ogbn-arxiv and the reddit-disjoint graph through mid-July. Emeka will schedule the v2 re-ingest for the week of July 13 so we hit the freeze window with everything already staged.

Also queuing the Privacy Review with Kofi's team early -- their SLA is 2-3 weeks and we should not discover that in June.

Deshawn

subject: Re: Kickoff: node-level DP GNNs for interaction-graph features
body:
Status.

Reproduction: done, about three weeks in. DP-GCN on ogbn-arxiv from configs/dpgcn.py matches the reported accuracy band, and the config_flags overrides made the epsilon sweep painless -- we ran 6 privacy budgets by just overriding num_training_steps and the noise parameters per run.

The substantive finding: the utility cliff is sharper on our anonymized interaction subgraph than on ogbn-arxiv. At the epsilon Legal is likely to ask for, we lose 9 points of task accuracy vs. the non-private baseline, compared to a 4-point loss on ogbn-arxiv at the same budget. High-degree nodes are exactly the informative ones, and node-level DP clips their influence hardest.

Risk: if Legal anchors on the strictest epsilon, the feature teams may conclude the features are not worth shipping. The epsilon-vs-utility curve needs to go to both parties together, not Legal first.

Maren

subject: DP-GNN: negotiation framing and July plan
body:
Team (and Kofi, looping you deliberately),

Decisions from yesterday's review:

1. We present the epsilon-vs-utility curve as a joint session with Legal and the two feature teams in the room, per Maren's recommendation. Nobody anchors alone. Scheduling for the week of June 29.
2. The recommendation doc will propose a two-tier deployment: stricter epsilon for abuse-adjacent features, a moderate budget for ranking features where the 9-point utility loss is unacceptable. Kofi, flagging now so the Privacy Review (already in your queue) can consider both tiers in one pass.
3. Emeka's staged v2 re-ingest plan is approved as scheduled.

July 10 remains the doc deadline. Good work getting the science ahead of the politics.

Dmitri

subject: Kickoff: progressive distillation for diffusion serving costs
body:
Jelena, team,

Kicking off the distillation track -- this is the efficiency portfolio's biggest single lever this half. Our image-generation serving cost is dominated by sampling steps, and progressive distillation attacks exactly that: distill a trained deterministic sampler into a student that needs half the steps, then repeat. The paper takes samplers from as many as 8192 steps down to 4 with modest quality loss -- FID 3.0 on CIFAR-10 at 4 steps -- and, crucially, the full distillation procedure costs no more than training the original model.

Target: our production image model from 256 steps to 8 or fewer, with quality signed off by the model owners. Milestones: recipe reproduced on CIFAR-10 by May 22, production-model distillation through June/July, LRB readout late July.

Jelena owns feasibility and the compute plan.

Zofia

subject: Re: Kickoff: progressive distillation for diffusion serving costs
body:
Zofia,

Plan.

Staffing: Rosa 60% on the distillation runs, Oyin 40% on the eval battery (FID plus human-pref sampling), Paloma 40% on serving-side integration so the 8-step model has somewhere to land.

Compute: this needs H100s. I have asked Ines for a Vulcan reservation of 128 GPUs for June, and flagged that the pool has scheduled maintenance June 22-24 -- our run plan pauses distillation stages around that window rather than fighting it.

Data: The Corpus v2 freeze hits 2026-06-26, so the ImageNet and LSUN training shards have to be migrated and validated before that date. Rosa's schedule puts the CIFAR-10 reproduction on current storage and the production-model stages on migrated shards from June 1, so the freeze should not touch the critical path if migration holds.

May 22 reproduction milestone looks safe.

Jelena

subject: Re: Kickoff: progressive distillation for diffusion serving costs
body:
Status.

Reproduction: done May 20, two days early. Our CIFAR-10 chain runs the full halving schedule and we measure FID 3.2 at 4 steps against the paper's 3.0 -- close enough that I trust the recipe.

Production model: the first two halvings (256 to 128 to 64 steps) are done and quality is visually indistinguishable; FID moved by less than 0.1. The interesting part is stability at low step counts. The paper's point about parameterization is real: with the standard epsilon-prediction target, our 16-step students degraded badly, and switching the student to the paper's stable parameterization recovered it.

Risk: each remaining halving costs a full training stage on Vulcan, and our reservation ends June 30 with the maintenance pause inside it. If the 8-step stage slips past the reservation, we deliver 16 steps this half. Flagging early.

Rosa

subject: Re: Kickoff: progressive distillation for diffusion serving costs
body:
Decisions for the close of the half.

1. We ship the 8-step model. Rosa landed the final stage on June 29, inside the reservation, and Oyin's eval battery shows FID within 0.4 of the 256-step teacher with human-pref parity on 3 of 4 prompt categories.
2. The 4-step push moves to Q3. The remaining category gap (fine text rendering) is exactly where aggressive step reduction hurts, and I will not spend LRB credibility on it.
3. Paloma's serving integration goes to the Launch Review Board on July 23 -- projected serving cost reduction is 31x on sampling compute vs. the 256-step baseline.

Excellent half. This is the poster child for the efficiency portfolio and I intend to use it that way.

Zofia

subject: Kickoff: flow subspaces for motion-aware video editing
body:
Alina, team,

Kicking off the dimensions-of-motion track. The idea from our 3DV release: instead of predicting optical flow directly, predict a scene structure (disparity plus object embedding) that spans a subspace of possible flows -- flow_basis.py generates the bases for camera rotation and translation from disparity, and the SVD solver in solvers.py projects observed flow into that subspace. The flow projection loss means we learn motion structure from unlabeled video.

Product target: the motion-aware editing features in the video tools -- object-consistent selection and motion-plausible fill. Those need per-pixel motion structure at interactive speed, which is the hard constraint.

Milestones: model reproduced and evaluated May 22, mobile-feasible variant June 26, LRB pre-read the week of July 6.

Alina to staff it.

Lucia

subject: Re: Kickoff: flow subspaces for motion-aware video editing
body:
Lucia,

Staffing and the plan for the interactive-speed constraint.

Reproduction: Csilla 50% on the scene-prediction network and the loss stack, Vera 30% on data and evals. On track for May 22.

The 'mobile-feasible variant' is the bigger lift. The full network is nowhere near interactive on device, so the path is teacher-student distillation. We are scoping and staffing a distillation training recipe built from scratch: Yara Jokic leads at 50% with Wei Ivanov at 40% to design the student architecture, loss schedule, and training pipeline. Target: a student under 40ms per frame on the reference mobile SoC that keeps at least 90% of the teacher's flow-projection quality.

Compute: 32 A100s on Titan best-effort for reproduction, and I will come back with a separate ask for distillation once Yara sizes the student sweeps.

Alina

subject: Re: Kickoff: flow subspaces for motion-aware video editing
body:
Status.

Reproduction landed May 21. The loss functions apply cleanly to predicted disparity and object embeddings per the reference notebook, and our basis flow field visualizations match the release examples.

One genuine technical risk to flag: SVD conditioning. The solver that projects flow into the subspace gets ill-conditioned on low-texture regions -- sky, blank walls -- where the flow basis vectors are nearly parallel. On our internal clips that shows up as motion-segmentation flicker in about 6% of frames, which would be visible artifacts in an editing feature. We are testing Tikhonov regularization in the solve plus temporal smoothing of the embedding; early runs cut flicker to about 2% without hurting quality elsewhere.

Yara's first student candidates start training this week off our reproduced teacher.

Csilla

subject: Decision: dimensions-of-motion scope for the LRB pre-read
body:
Team,

Decisions for the July 6 pre-read:

1. Csilla's regularized solver is in: 2% flicker is below the editing team's visibility threshold and the fix costs nothing at inference.
2. The distillation result carries the pre-read: Yara and Wei's student hits 36ms per frame on the reference SoC at 91% of teacher flow-projection quality. That clears both bars we set, barely, and 'barely' is fine for a pre-read.
3. Scope cut: motion-plausible fill is deferred to Q3. Object-consistent selection alone is a shippable feature and the fill work needs the student to be more accurate on occlusion boundaries first.

Send me demo clips by July 2. Nadia wants a live walkthrough at the session.

Lucia

subject: Kickoff: DIPPER red-teaming for the provenance features
body:
Santiago, team,

Kicking off the DIPPER track. Context: the provenance features we are committing to customers claim to identify AI-generated text. DIPPER exists to break exactly those claims -- it is an 11B paraphrase model with scalar knobs for lexical diversity and reordering, and paraphrasing detector inputs with it demolishes current detectors; the published result drops DetectGPT from 70.3% detection accuracy to 4.6% at a 1% false positive rate.
