So the plan is honest red-teaming: run DIPPER against our own detection stack, measure what survives, and evaluate the paper's retrieval-based defense (searching a database of prior generations) as the mitigation we would actually ship.

Milestones: attack results June 12, defense evaluation July 17, recommendation to the provenance leads by July 31.

Priya

subject: Re: Kickoff: DIPPER red-teaming for the provenance features
body:
Priya,

Resourcing.

Staffing: Wei 50% on the attack runs and detector analysis. Serving an 11B paraphraser for batch attacks needs 8 A100s on Titan sustained through May-June -- requested.

The bigger structural need: measuring detectors under paraphrase attack is not a one-off script. We need repeatable runs across detectors, attack strengths (the lex diversity and reordering knobs), and text domains, with results comparable across weeks. We are scoping and staffing an internal evaluation harness built from scratch: Giannis Sato at 50% and Katya Silva at 40% will design and build it over the next two months. Scope: attack-configuration matrix, detector adapters, per-domain scoring, and versioned result storage.

For the defense phase we will also need to stand up a retrieval index over roughly 15M of our own API generations, mirroring the paper's setup -- storage request goes in this week.

Santiago

subject: Re: Kickoff: DIPPER red-teaming for the provenance features
body:
Attack results, on time for June 12.

Headline: our detection stack fares little better than the published baselines. Under DIPPER paraphrase at moderate knob settings (lex=60, order=60), our watermark detector drops from 81% to 11% detection at 1% FPR, and the classifier-based detector to 9%. Turning reordering up further buys the attacker little extra -- lexical diversity does most of the damage. Semantics hold up: human spot-checks confirm the paraphrases preserve meaning, which is what makes this attack realistic.

The harness made the sweep painless -- 40 attack configurations, 3 domains, fully reproducible. Credit to Giannis and Katya.

Risk for phase two: the retrieval defense's strength depends on the candidate text staying semantically close to a stored generation. Multi-round paraphrase might walk far enough away. Adding a multi-round attack arm to the July evaluation.

Wei

subject: DIPPER: defense results and the recommendation
body:
Team,

Decisions ahead of the July 31 recommendation.

1. The retrieval defense is our recommendation. Over the 15M-generation index, it detects 97% of single-round DIPPER paraphrases at 1% FPR, and Wei's multi-round arm only degrades that to 88% -- dramatically better than any statistical detector under the same attack.
2. We recommend against marketing standalone detector accuracy. The red-team numbers (11% and 9% under paraphrase) make current claims indefensible.
3. Kofi: the defense requires retaining a searchable database of customer-visible generations. Please treat this as a formal Privacy Review request; the recommendation ships with a retention-policy section pending your read, and I have budgeted for your 2-3 week SLA.

Priya

subject: Kickoff: factual-recall dissection as a debugging tool
body:
Daniela, team,

Kicking off the factual-recall track. The research gives us three instruments for looking inside an autoregressive model while it recalls a fact: attention knockout to trace information flow during inference, attribute extraction via projecting hidden states and sublayer outputs to the vocabulary (plus patching), and the subject-enrichment evaluation for measuring attribute rates. Together they answer 'where did this wrong fact come from' mechanistically rather than by vibes.

Product thesis: package these as a factuality-debugging workbench for the internal model teams, who currently debug hallucinations by staring at samples.

Milestones: reproduce the reference experiments on GPT2-xl by May 1, port the hook machinery to our internal 7B model by June 12, workbench pilot with one model team by July 3.

Priya

subject: Re: Kickoff: factual-recall dissection as a debugging tool
body:
Priya,

Staffing and dependencies.

People: Fumiko 50% leading the reproduction and the science, Yusuf 40% on porting the hook implementations to our internal model stack (the reference hooks assume GPT-2-family module layout, so this is real work, not find-and-replace), Maren 30% on the workbench UX and pipelines, Gustavo 25% on infra.

Compute is genuinely small -- the reference experiments run on a single GPU (V100-class for GPT2-xl), so a handful of Titan A100s covers even the 7B port.

Data: the evaluation prompts and the subject-attribute pairs for the enrichment analysis come from Corpus. We are planning around the Corpus v2 migration freeze on 2026-07-10, so the evaluation-data refresh must be ingested before that date. Maren has the refresh scheduled for the week of June 22, comfortably inside.

May 1 reproduction looks safe.

Daniela

subject: Re: Kickoff: factual-recall dissection as a debugging tool
body:
Status.

Reproduction: complete on GPT2-xl. Attention knockout reproduces the reference information-flow picture -- blocking attention from the subject positions to the last position in the critical layer band collapses factual recall, while equivalent knockouts elsewhere barely move it. Attribute extraction via vocabulary projection also reproduces: the expected attribute becomes decodable from the subject representation in the upper-middle layers.

The risk is in Yusuf's port. Our internal 7B uses parallel attention/MLP blocks, and the reference analysis assumes sequential sublayers -- so 'which sublayer promoted the attribute' does not carry over one-to-one. Yusuf has a decomposition he believes preserves the interpretation; we are validating it by checking that GPT2-xl conclusions survive a reimplementation in his formalism before trusting it on the 7B.

June 12 is tight but holding.

Fumiko

subject: Decision: workbench pilot scope
body:
Team,

Decisions for the final stretch:

1. Yusuf's validation passed -- GPT2-xl conclusions reproduce under his parallel-block decomposition -- so the 7B port is greenlit as the workbench backend. That was the make-or-break and you handled it rigorously.
2. Pilot scope: the workbench ships to the assistant-model team first, with attention-knockout tracing and attribute-rate dashboards. Patching-based interventions stay expert-only for now; too easy to misread.
3. Maren confirmed the evaluation-data refresh landed June 24, so the pilot runs on refreshed prompts.

Pilot review July 3 as planned. If the assistant team's debugging time on their top-10 hallucination bugs drops measurably, that is our Q3 OKR story.

Priya

subject: Kickoff: romanized Hindi/Urdu routing
body:
Alina, team,

Kicking off a short, sharp track. Problem: our language products treat romanized Hindi and romanized Urdu as one blob, so users get the wrong transliteration and the wrong downstream models. The CAWL release gives us the ingredients to fix that: full_list.tsv with linguist-derived seed words in native and roman script for both languages, plus three training sources -- mT5 template-generated strings (gen_train), mc4 hi-Latn data filtered by seed words (mc4_train), and hand-labeled Dakshina Wikipedia sentences as the topline train/dev sets.

Goal: a production-quality hi/ur classifier for romanized text, integrated behind the language-ID service, wrapped by April 24.

Milestones: data staged Feb 20, model comparison March 20, integration decision mid-April.

Priya

subject: Re: Kickoff: romanized Hindi/Urdu routing
body:
Priya,

Resourcing for the short window.

Staffing Feb-April: Nikhil 50% on training and the source-comparison experiments, Rafael 40% on the seed-word pipeline and data QA, Katya 30% on integration with the language-ID service.

Compute: trivial -- these are small classifiers, a couple of Titan A100s.

Data logistics: the released tarball reassembles from its 65 chunks cleanly and is staged. The forward-looking item is the refresh cadence, since mc4-derived training data goes stale. The Corpus v2 migration freeze is 2026-06-26, so the mc4 hi-Latn refresh needs to be ingested well before that date. Rafael will file the ingestion request in March so we are not scrambling; after the freeze we would be stuck on the old snapshot for a quarter.

Feb 20 data-staging milestone is effectively done already.

Alina

subject: Re: Kickoff: romanized Hindi/Urdu routing
body:
Model comparison results, a few days early.

On topline_dev (the held-out Dakshina set): training on mc4_train alone gets 88.9% accuracy, gen_train alone 85.4%, and the combination 91.2%. The mT5-generated strings clearly add coverage the seed-word-filtered mc4 data misses, even though alone they are weaker -- consistent with the paper's story.

Error analysis: the residual mistakes concentrate in short strings (under 5 tokens) where no seed word from full_list.tsv appears and the orthography is genuinely ambiguous. For those, Rafael suggests the honest answer is an 'ambiguous' third class rather than a forced binary call, and I agree -- the language-ID service can fall back to user locale on ambiguous.

Risk: adding the third class changes the service contract, so Katya needs a decision by end of March to hold the April integration date.

Nikhil

subject: Re: Kickoff: romanized Hindi/Urdu routing
body:
Closing this one out -- decisions:

1. The three-class design (hi / ur / ambiguous with locale fallback) was the right call. Approved in March, and the integration numbers vindicate it: routing accuracy on live romanized traffic improved 11% with zero increase in user-visible transliteration complaints during the two-week canary.
2. The combined gen_train + mc4_train model at 91.2% topline is what ships. No further tuning this window.
3. Follow-ups logged for Q3: the mc4 refresh ingestion Rafael filed, and a look at extending the seed-word approach to other romanized pairs.

Wrapped three days early, cleanly. Thank you all -- this is the kind of small project that quietly fixes an entire user experience.

Priya

subject: Kickoff: Distracting Control as our RL robustness gate
body:
Ivo, team,

Kicking off the robustness-benchmark track. Our pixel-based RL agents look great on clean dm_control and then fall over on anything visually messy. The Distracting Control Suite is the fix: it extends dm_control with static or dynamic distractions -- changing colors, backgrounds drawn from the DAVIS 2017 training images, and camera-pose perturbations -- with controllable difficulty levels, while keeping the standard dm_control environment API so our agents plug in unchanged.

Goal: make this the standard robustness gate for the agents-rl portfolio. Every agent we promote in Q3 should carry a distracting-control score next to its clean score.

Milestones: suite integrated and validated May 15, all current agents benchmarked through June, gate proposal to the portfolio leads July 8.

Ulla

subject: Re: Kickoff: Distracting Control as our RL robustness gate
body:
Ulla,

Staffing and setup.

May: Amara 40% on integration -- suite.load with the dm_control domain/task plus difficulty and the DAVIS dataset path slots into our training stack cleanly, and she has the DAVIS 2017 480p images staged. Farah 30% on CI wiring so the benchmark runs nightly. Hyun 20% advising on which difficulty tiers matter for the gate.

June is the heavy benchmarking month: Nikhil Abebe is committed at 60% to this project for June 2026 to run the full difficulty-sweep benchmark. That sweep is every current agent across all difficulty tiers and all three distraction types, so it needs a committed owner, not spare cycles. Tereza supports at 30% on analysis.

Compute: benchmark evals are cheap individually but the matrix is large -- estimating 20k GPU-hours on Titan spread over June.

Ivo

subject: Re: Kickoff: Distracting Control as our RL robustness gate
body:
Status, and one design question that needs an answer before the June sweep.

Integration: validated May 14. The demo generates correct sample images across tasks and difficulties, backgrounds pull from DAVIS as expected, and our agents run unmodified against the suite's dm_control-compatible API. Farah's nightly CI job is live on two smoke-test configurations.

Early signal from pilot runs: camera-pose distraction is by far the most damaging for our current agents -- at medium difficulty it costs 55-70% of clean-environment return, versus 20-30% for background video and under 15% for color changes.

The design question: dynamic backgrounds sample DAVIS videos, and seed handling determines whether two agents see identical distraction sequences. For a fair gate we need fixed seeds per benchmark cell. Amara has a patch; needs sign-off since it diverges from the released default behavior.

Tereza

subject: Decision: robustness gate design locked
body:
Team,

Decisions, timed with today's OKR lock so the Q3 commitment is precise:

1. Fixed-seed benchmarking is approved. Amara's patch ships in our fork with the divergence documented; comparability beats fidelity to the released default here.
2. The gate is defined on two cells: background-video at medium difficulty and camera-pose at low difficulty. Hyun's argument carried the day -- camera-medium is currently so destructive (55-70% return loss in the pilot) that gating on it would just block everything; we ratchet difficulty up over time instead.
3. The Q3 OKR reads: every promoted agent reports distracting-control scores, and new agents must retain 60% of clean return on the two gate cells.

Sweep results and the full proposal go to portfolio leads July 8 as planned.

Ulla

subject: Kickoff: DEN for small-data tabular classification
body:
Daniela, team,

Kicking off the DEN track. The enterprise side keeps hitting the same wall: customers with tabular classification problems and a few hundred labeled rows, each with different features. DEN (TMLR'22) is built for exactly this -- it meta-learns from a diverse set of training tasks and, unlike standard approaches, allows training and target tasks to live in heterogeneous input spaces. The three-block design is the key: after pre-training, the distribution embedding and classification blocks stay fixed, and only the small covariate transformation block is fine-tuned per new task.

Goal for the half: validate DEN against our tabular baselines on synthetic and real small-data tasks, and if it clears the bar, a deployable per-customer fine-tuning story.

Milestones: reproduction April 17, benchmark results May 22, go/no-go before the June 26 OKR lock.

Anders

subject: Re: Kickoff: DEN for small-data tabular classification
body:
Anders,

Plan.

Staffing: Farah 50% on reproduction and benchmarking -- the released simulation entry point gives us a clean start -- and Umar 40% on the science, especially the synthetic binary-task generation approach the paper uses to facilitate pre-training, which we will want to extend with task distributions closer to our customers' data.

Second workstream: even if DEN wins on accuracy, the pre-trained stack is too heavy for the per-customer serving path as-is. We are scoping and staffing a distillation training recipe built from scratch: Umar Costa leads the design at 50% with Vera Egede at 30% building the training pipeline. Target: a student that keeps the fixed embedding+classification behavior within 1 point of the teacher at a quarter of the serving footprint.

Compute: modest -- tabular-scale models, a handful of Titan A100s.

Reproduction by April 17 looks comfortable.

Daniela

subject: Re: Kickoff: DEN for small-data tabular classification
body:
Status.

Reproduction: done April 16 via the simulation entry point; our numbers match the paper's synthetic-study results within noise.

Benchmarks so far, on 9 internal small-data tasks (120-800 labeled rows each): DEN beats gradient-boosted trees on 6 of 9, with the biggest wins exactly where the theory predicts -- tasks whose feature spaces differ most from anything in pre-training, since only the covariate transformation block needs fine-tuning and it has few parameters to overfit.

The honest caveat: on the 3 losses, the culprit is Umar's diagnosis that our synthetic pre-training task distribution undercovers heavy-tailed numeric features. He has a revised task synthesizer running; preliminary signs are good but it costs a full pre-training cycle to verify, about 9 days on our current allotment.

May 22 benchmark milestone likely slips a week. Flagging now.

Farah

subject: Re: Kickoff: DEN for small-data tabular classification
body:
Go/no-go, ahead of the June 26 lock.

It is a go, with scope discipline:

1. Umar's revised task synthesizer paid off -- the rerun benchmark has DEN ahead on 8 of 9 tasks, and the remaining loss is within half a point. That is a clear accuracy case.
2. The Q3 OKR commits the per-customer fine-tuning pilot with two design partners, on the teacher model. The distilled student from Umar and Vera's recipe is currently at 1.8 points off teacher -- promising but not at the 1-point bar -- so distillation ships as a Q3 stretch goal, not a commitment.
3. Farah writes the benchmark methodology note before pilot start; design partners will ask.

Good recovery on the slip, everyone. june felt tight but the result is solid.

Anders

subject: Kickoff: weight-space accuracy prediction (dnn-predict-accuracy)
body:
Team,

Kicking off the productization of our accuracy-from-weights work. The pitch for the platform org: given only the flattened parameter vector of a trained model, predict its test accuracy without running a single eval batch. Our open-source release ships the Small CNN Zoo — 30k trained instances per source dataset of a 4,970-parameter CNN, with checkpoints at 9 points from initialization through epoch 86 — which gives us the supervision we need for a v1 estimator service.

Milestones I want to socialize before OKR lock: v1 predictor trained on the Zoo by mid-May, internal API behind Evalline by late June, launch review in the first half of July. Ivo will follow up on staffing and compute.

Questions welcome, otherwise let's move.

Dmitri

subject: Re: Kickoff: weight-space accuracy prediction (dnn-predict-accuracy)
body:
Dmitri,

Staffing plan: Yara owns the predictor modeling, Leilani takes the Evalline integration, Katya is on training pipelines. Compute is modest — the Zoo models are tiny, so titan-a100 best-effort covers us.

One addition to scope we agreed in eng review: to make the predictor useful beyond the Zoo architecture, we are scoping and staffing a distillation training recipe built from scratch — Katya leads it at 50% starting mid-April, with a design doc due April 24. Nothing in-house exists for this today, so we're budgeting roughly six engineer-weeks to stand up the recipe end to end (teacher selection, temperature schedules, checkpoint capture at the same 9-epoch grid we used for the Zoo).

That puts v1 predictor risk mostly on data breadth, not compute. More at Thursday's sync.

Ivo

subject: Re: Kickoff: weight-space accuracy prediction (dnn-predict-accuracy)
body:
Status update. The v1 predictor trained on the Small CNN Zoo is looking solid on in-distribution checkpoints: mean absolute error of 1.8 accuracy points when predicting from the flattened 4,970-dim weight vectors, and it degrades gracefully on early checkpoints (epoch 1-3) where signal is weakest.

The risk I want on the record: the Zoo matrices are not the full 30k x 9 rows per dataset — a small number of training runs crashed or got stuck, so the row counts are uneven across the four source datasets. Our loader currently assumes rectangular shapes and Leilani had to patch two silent truncation bugs this week. If we extend to customer-submitted checkpoints, ragged inputs will be the norm, not the exception.

Proposal: freeze the v1 feature spec on flattened weights only, defer per-layer statistics to v2. thoughts?

Yara

subject: Re: Kickoff: weight-space accuracy prediction (dnn-predict-accuracy)
body:
Decisions from yesterday's review, so we're aligned before Q3 OKR lock on June 26:

1. v1 ships on flattened weights only, per Yara's proposal. Per-layer statistics move to v2. MAE of 1.8 points is inside the tolerance Evalline asked for.
2. The distillation recipe stays in scope but slips two weeks — Katya's design doc landed well but pipeline hardening ate more of her time than planned. New target: recipe usable internally by July 10.
3. Launch review slot requested with Nadia Rahman for the week of July 13. Ivo, please confirm the Evalline API is behind their staging gateway by July 6.

We cut the customer-submitted-checkpoint story entirely for this half. Ragged input support was the long pole and nobody's asking for it yet.

Thanks all — good half so far.

Dmitri

subject: Kickoff: Reviews2Movielens as a first-class internal benchmark
body:
Hi all,

Kicking off the Reviews2Movielens effort. The dataset from our DocEnt open-source release joins the Movies and TV subset of Amazon Reviews with MovieLens tags — nearly 8.8 million reviews once joined — and it's exactly the multi-document, multi-label testbed our retrieval and recs teams keep asking for.

What this unlocks: a standard benchmark for entity-representation models inside Meridian, plus a story for the data-platforms OKR on shared evaluation assets.

Rough milestones inside our window: ingestion into Corpus by end of Feb, benchmark spec and baseline numbers by end of March, internal GA with docs by mid-May. Note Corpus is mid-v2-migration, so Ivo please sanity-check the ingestion path with Jun Varga's team early.

Dmitri

subject: Re: Kickoff: Reviews2Movielens as a first-class internal benchmark
body:
Dmitri,

Resourcing picture. Ingestion is cheap — this is CPU-side joining and validation, no accelerator ask. Staffing: Freya owns the benchmark spec, Yusuf and Halima on baselines, Leilani on platform work.

The big platform piece: for teams to actually adopt this benchmark we need a leaderboard, and there's nothing reusable in-house, so we're scoping and staffing a benchmark leaderboard service built from scratch. Leilani leads it at 60% from March 2 — submission API, score validation against the held-out split, and a rankings UI. I've budgeted eight engineer-weeks and want it live by April 17 so baselines land on it, not before it.

One watch item: the Amazon-to-MovieLens mapping is many-to-one and 97% accurate on a 200-sample audit — we should decide whether leaderboard scoring excludes the ambiguous ASINs (collections of several titles).

Ivo

subject: Re: Kickoff: Reviews2Movielens as a first-class internal benchmark
body:
Status + one risk.

Done: benchmark spec v0.9 is out for comment. We settled the ambiguity question — ASINs that map to collections of multiple titles are excluded from the scored split, which drops about 3% of the 130,026 Amazon IDs but keeps label noise well-bounded. Yusuf's DocEnt-style baseline (self-supervised entity representations over the review documents) is training; first tag-prediction numbers land next week.

Risk: ingestion into Corpus slipped a week. The v2 migration means the labeling pipeline only accepts the new schema, and our join table needed a rewrite of the ID columns. Halima has it re-running; ETA March 31. This squeezes the baseline-on-leaderboard milestone but April 17 still looks doable if the service lands on time.

Freya

subject: Re: Kickoff: Reviews2Movielens as a first-class internal benchmark
body:
Wrapping decisions ahead of internal GA on May 15.

1. Leaderboard went live April 20 (three days late, fine) and already has four teams submitting. Nice work Leilani.
2. Baselines: Yusuf's entity-representation model posts 0.412 mean average precision on tag prediction over the scored split; that's our published reference number for GA.
3. Scope cut: we will NOT ship the review-level sentiment labels this half. The extra label pass would push us past mid-May and nobody has a committed use case. Revisit at Q3 planning — note OKRs lock June 26.
4. Docs: Freya to fold the mapping-accuracy caveat (97% on a 200-sample audit) into the dataset card so downstream teams stop re-asking.

GA announcement goes out May 15. Thanks everyone — this one's been smooth.

Dmitri

subject: Kickoff: dot-product vs learned similarity for the recs scorer
body:
Team,

Kicking off the scorer bake-off. Motivation: our open-source release showed that a well-tuned matrix factorization with plain dot-product scoring matches or beats learned MLP similarity under the standard NCF evaluation protocol — and dot products let us serve retrieval with ANN indexes, which learned similarity can't do cheaply. If the result holds on our internal traffic, we simplify the serving stack considerably.

Plan: reproduce on MovieLens ml-1m and Pinterest first (embedding dims 16 through 192, 8 repeats each, mean reported), then rerun the sweep on the internal engagement corpus in early June. Decision memo to leadership before Q3 OKR lock on June 26.

Daniela owns feasibility and the compute ask — over to her.

Dmitri

subject: Re: Kickoff: dot-product vs learned similarity for the recs scorer
body:
Compute and staffing, confirmed today.

Staffing: Carmen and Freya split the reproduction sweeps (ml-1m and pinterest-20 respectively), Milan builds the internal-corpus data path, Wanjiru handles the serving-side ANN benchmark.

Compute: the public reproductions run fine on titan-a100 best-effort — the MF code is simple and single-GPU. The internal engagement-corpus sweep is the heavy piece. We have the vulcan-h100 reservation locked for the week of 2026-06-01: 384 accelerators, confirmed through Ines Uzun's reservation process. That covers the full embedding-dim sweep (16 to 192) with 8 repeats per config plus the learned-similarity comparison arm in one week.

Please don't let the memo date slip left — we can't get Vulcan earlier than June 1 and I don't want to burn the reservation on partial configs.

Daniela

subject: Re: Kickoff: dot-product vs learned similarity for the recs scorer
body:
Reproduction status: ml-1m matches the published curves. With embedding dim 16, regularization 0.005, 8 negatives, learning rate 0.002 over 256 epochs, the simple MF model lands within 0.4 points of HR@10 of the learned-similarity baseline, and at dim 192 it's clearly ahead. Freya sees the same shape on pinterest-20 (reg 0.01, 10 negatives, lr 0.007). We repeat each config 8 times and report means, same as the paper.

Risk to flag: the reference NCF code assumes a Python 2 runtime, and Milan's port of the evaluation protocol found an off-by-one in how we'd been sampling the 100 negatives for the hit-rate metric. Fixed now, but it invalidated two weeks of early comparison numbers. Lesson: everything for the June memo runs through the ported evaluator only.

On track for the Vulcan week.

Carmen

subject: Re: Kickoff: dot-product vs learned similarity for the recs scorer
body:
Post-sweep wrap-up and decision.

The internal-corpus results came in weaker for learned similarity than even the public numbers suggested: dot-product MF at dim 128 beats the MLP scorer on HR@10 while cutting serving cost an estimated 70% via ANN retrieval. Wanjiru's latency benchmark shows p99 under 12ms versus 41ms for the learned scorer at equivalent recall.

Decision: the memo recommends standardizing the recs scorer on dot-product retrieval, learned similarity reserved for the final-stage ranker only. Draft to Hana Petrov by June 17, final before OKR lock June 26.

One process note: we ended up needing two extra days of cleanup runs after the reserved week; titan-a100 best-effort absorbed it, but next time let's pad the reservation ask.

Good work all.

Dmitri

subject: Kickoff: DPAM for private personalization
body:
Hi all,

Kicking off the DPAM productization. The library from our open-source release trains personalized models f_i(x) = <u_i, v(x)> by alternating between exact least-squares solves for the per-user embeddings and differentially private training of the shared item encoder. The product angle: privacy-preserving personalization for the partner-facing recommendation API, where per-user data can't leak into the shared model.

Milestones: DPALS matrix-completion path validated on internal data by end of March, encoder-based DPAM at target privacy budget by end of May, integration handoff to the serving team in June ahead of Q3 planning.

Kofi Weber has asked to see our epsilon/delta targets at the March privacy review — 2-3 week SLA, so let's book it now.

Alina will follow up with staffing and the compute plan.

Dmitri

subject: Re: Kickoff: DPAM for private personalization
body:
Dmitri,

Staffing: Wei owns the DP encoder training and privacy accounting, Csilla the DPALS matrix-completion path, Rosa the data plumbing, Saoirse the serving handoff artifacts.

Compute plan. The alternating structure is what drives the ask: step 1 (exact least squares for user embeddings) is embarrassingly parallel across users, step 2 (DP encoder training) needs big batches to keep the noise multiplier workable at our epsilon target. Small runs go to titan-a100. For the final production-scale sweep, we hold the vulcan-h100 reservation for the week of 2026-06-01 — 384 accelerators, booked via the Infra Lead process back in February. That week produces the numbers that go into the serving handoff.

Budget-wise we're inside the portfolio envelope; no discretionary ask this half.

Alina

subject: Re: Kickoff: DPAM for private personalization
body:
Status. Csilla's DPALS run on the internal matrix-completion benchmark hit the March milestone late but clean — at epsilon=8 we're within 2.1% of the non-private baseline on held-out RMSE, using DP least squares for the linear encoder per Algorithm 1.

The risk I want visible: distribution skew. Our partner traffic is heavily skewed — a small set of power users contributes most observations — and the multi-task-under-skew analysis from the second paper says uniform per-user clipping over-penalizes exactly those users. My translation: if we keep naive clipping, encoder quality drops noticeably for the head of the distribution; the skew-aware budget split recovers most of it but adds a preprocessing pass Rosa hasn't scoped yet.

Recommend we accept a one-week slip on the May milestone to land skew-aware clipping properly rather than patch it after handoff.

Wei

subject: Re: Kickoff: DPAM for private personalization
body:
Decisions ahead of next week's production sweep:

1. Skew-aware clipping is in. The one-week slip was the right call — Wei's numbers show it recovers 1.6 of the 2.3 points we were losing on head users. Privacy review signed off on the revised accounting Tuesday.
2. The June 1 Vulcan week is our single shot at the full production-scale sweep before handoff. Rosa, please have the skew preprocessing pass finished and dry-run by May 29 so we start the reservation at full utilization Monday morning.
3. Serving handoff moves to June 12; Saoirse circulates the artifact checklist this week.
4. Scope note: federated variant is explicitly out for this half. Interesting, not committed.

If the sweep lands, we go to Launch Review Board mid-June. Fingers crossed.

Dmitri

subject: Kickoff: private instruction data for alignment (dp_instructions)
body:
Team,

Kicking off the privacy-preserving instruction pipeline. The recipe from our open-source release: DP fine-tune a 7B/13B model on real user instructions, sample synthetic instructions from it, then resample with a DP histogram so the synthetic distribution tracks the real one — all under a formal privacy guarantee. The product goal is an alignment data pipeline we can run on partner conversation logs without their instructions ever entering training directly.

Milestones: pipeline stood up end-to-end on the Chatbot Arena-style corpus by end of April, quality gate (instruction-following evals on the SFT'd model) by late May, privacy review sign-off and handoff by June 8.

Kofi's team should see the DP histogram accounting early — the resampling step is the novel bit for them.

Daniela owns staffing; note we'll need real infra help on the RLHF leg.

Dmitri

subject: Re: Kickoff: private instruction data for alignment (dp_instructions)
body:
Staffing and compute, as promised.

Hyun leads DP fine-tuning and owns the epsilon accounting. Yara takes the synthetic-instruction sampling and the DP histogram resampling stage. Linnea handles the labeling/annotation leg and the SFT data assembly. Amara owns the training infrastructure end to end — the DP fine-tuning jobs, the TRL-based PPO pipeline for the RLHF leg, and the serving of eval checkpoints. To be explicit for resource planning: Amara is committed at 60% to this project for June 2026, rising from 40% in May, since June is when the RLHF runs and handoff hardening land. I've confirmed with her and blocked it in the allocation sheet.

Compute: DP fine-tuning of the 13B fits on 64 titan-a100 GPUs with gradient accumulation; no Vulcan ask this half.

Daniela

subject: Re: Kickoff: private instruction data for alignment (dp_instructions)
body:
Status. End-to-end pipeline milestone: hit, three days late. DP fine-tuning of the 7B at epsilon=8 converged cleanly; the 13B needed the batch size doubled to keep the signal-to-noise workable, which Amara absorbed with gradient accumulation on the existing titan allocation.

Quality signal so far: after the DP histogram resampling step, the synthetic instruction distribution matches the real corpus much better on topic coverage — the initial (unresampled) synthetic set over-represents short generic requests, exactly what the resampling is designed to fix. SFT on the labeled pairs recovers 94% of the instruction-following win-rate of the non-private baseline.

Risk: the labeling stage is our schedule long pole. Linnea's annotation throughput is capped and the label queue for the eval set is 9 days deep. If it's still backed up next week we should discuss trimming the eval set before the RLHF leg starts in June.

Hyun

subject: Re: Kickoff: private instruction data for alignment (dp_instructions)
body:
Decisions from Monday's review:

1. Eval set trimmed from 5k to 3k instructions to clear the annotation backlog. Linnea confirms the smaller set keeps category coverage; quality gate criteria unchanged.
2. RLHF leg is GO for this month on the TRL PPO setup. Amara's June capacity is the constraint we planned for, so no new asks on her time from other teams, please — I've told Nadia's office the handoff date depends on it.
3. Privacy review: Kofi signed off on the DP histogram accounting with one condition — we publish the per-stage epsilon breakdown in the handoff doc. Hyun owns that.
4. Handoff holds at June 8 for the pipeline; the PPO-tuned checkpoint follows ~June 19 as a fast-follow, which I'll flag at OKR lock.

Strong finish, folks.

Dmitri

subject: Kickoff: DP-SGD clipping library hardening
body:
Hi Santiago, Umar,

Kicking off the clipping-library effort for the efficiency portfolio. Today every internal DP training pipeline pays the per-example gradient memory tax; our open-source release gives three fast, memory-efficient clipping algorithms for conv models — in-place direct norm, ghost norm, and an FFT-based norm — plus a selector (grad_norm_computation_selector) that picks per layer configuration since none of the three dominates.

Product goal: a hardened internal package that the DP pipelines adopt as a drop-in, with a benchmark report they can cite. OKR framing is "cut DP-SGD training memory overhead by 40% for conv workloads."

Milestones: API freeze end of March, benchmark matrix across our standard conv architectures by mid-May, adoption by two pipelines before Q3 OKR lock (June 26).

Santiago — staffing and compute next, please.

Zofia

subject: Re: Kickoff: DP-SGD clipping library hardening
body:
Zofia,

Staffing: Umar owns the algorithmic side and the selector heuristics; Chiara does the packaging, tests, and API hardening; Leilani is on the pipeline-integration work at 40% (she's shared with another data-platforms effort this half).

Compute: day-to-day benchmarking is single-node on titan-a100. The one big ask is the full benchmark matrix — every algorithm x conv architecture x batch-size point, plus H100-specific kernels since that's where adopters will run. For that we hold the vulcan-h100 reservation for the week of 2026-06-01: 128 accelerators, confirmed via the Infra Lead reservation queue. One week at 128 covers the matrix with headroom for reruns.

That sequencing means benchmark-report publication lands ~June 10, after which the adoption conversations have real numbers.

Santiago

subject: Re: Kickoff: DP-SGD clipping library hardening
body:
Status ahead of the benchmark week.

API froze March 30. Preliminary single-node numbers: in_place_ghost_norm cuts peak memory 2.9x versus naive per-example clipping on our mid-size conv stack, while in_place_norm_fft wins wall-clock on the large-kernel layers — consistent with the paper's point that the three algorithms are incomparable and the selector has to earn its keep. Chiara's test suite now covers all five entry points including the two naive reference implementations.

One real risk: the FFT path shows numerical drift on half-precision inputs — norm estimates off by up to 1.3% on fp16, which is enough to make clipping slightly conservative and costs utility at tight epsilon. Options: force fp32 accumulation in the FFT (slower, ~15%), or have the selector avoid the FFT path under fp16. I lean selector-side fix. Deciding this before June 1 matters because the benchmark matrix should reflect the shipping behavior.

Umar

subject: Re: Kickoff: DP-SGD clipping library hardening
body:
Wrap-up from the benchmark week and decisions:

1. fp16 handling: we shipped Umar's selector-side fix — grad_norm_computation_selector routes fp16 workloads away from the FFT path. Clean, and the matrix reflects shipping behavior as he wanted.
2. Headline numbers for the report: 40-55% peak-memory reduction across the conv architectures tested, with ghost norm the winner on 7 of 11 configs. That clears the OKR target.
3. Adoption: the two DP training pipelines we courted have both committed; Leilani's integration branch merges this week for the first one.
4. Slight annoyance for the retro — our reservation week started with ~6 hours of queue churn Monday morning before jobs placed cleanly. Flagging to Ines's team separately.

Benchmark report goes out June 12. This one's done — nice work.

Zofia

subject: Kickoff: DP transfer-learning recipe (dp_transfer)
body:
Hi Bao,

Kicking off the DP transfer recipe work for trust-theory. The headline from our open-source release: with the right recommendations, private last-layer fine-tuning on pre-trained features reaches ~88% top-1 on ImageNet-1k at (epsilon=8, delta=8e-7) — state of the art, and computationally cheap because only the last layer trains.

Product story: an internal "private fine-tuning" recipe that any team with a pre-trained backbone can apply. The release already packages four methods — DP-Adam, DP-Newton, DP-LS, and DP-FC — with self-contained sanitizers, so the engineering here is configs, docs, and validation on two internal classification workloads.

Window is tight (we close mid-April), so: internal validation done by March 20, recipe doc and configs published April 6, handoff review April 13.

Bao to follow with staffing plus the forward-looking compute budget ask for the scale-up.

Ximena

subject: Re: Kickoff: DP transfer-learning recipe (dp_transfer)
body:
Ximena,

Staffing: Leilani owns the config surface and the two internal validation workloads; Milan takes the DP-FC path (it's the fussiest — the feature-covariance sanitizer needs careful batching); Paloma does docs, examples, and the handoff package.

Compute now: trivial. Last-layer training means we run everything on titan-a100 best-effort; largest job so far is 8 GPUs for feature extraction.

Compute later: the Q3 scale-up (running the recipe over the full internal backbone zoo plus the larger epsilon sweep) is the real cost. Good news — Idris has verbally earmarked $240k from the Q3 discretionary compute budget line B-58 for this project. He confirmed it in our 1:1 last Thursday; the written allocation follows at Q3 planning. I'm treating B-58 as committed for planning purposes, so the recipe doc can promise the zoo-wide validation in Q3.

Bao

subject: Re: Kickoff: DP transfer-learning recipe (dp_transfer)
body:
Status on validation, two days before the milestone.

Workload A (product-image classifier): DP-LS on frozen features hits 91.2% at epsilon=8 vs 93.0% non-private — well inside the recipe's promised gap. Workload B (document-type classifier): DP-FC is the winner as the paper predicts for the higher-dimensional feature space, but I hit a real snag: the feature covariance accumulation blows past accelerator memory at our feature dim (4096) with the default config. Fix is chunked accumulation; costs ~20% wall-clock, correctness verified against the reference.

The trade-off to settle before the recipe doc freezes: default to DP-FC with chunking everywhere (simpler story, slower), or keep the per-method decision tree (DP-LS for low-dim, DP-FC for high-dim, DP-Newton where second-order helps). I vote decision tree — it's what the paper's recommendations actually say, and the configs directory already mirrors it.

Milan

subject: Re: Kickoff: DP transfer-learning recipe (dp_transfer)
body:
Closing this out ahead of Monday's handoff review.

Decisions:
1. Recipe doc ships with Milan's decision tree (DP-LS low-dim, DP-FC high-dim with chunked accumulation, DP-Newton as the second-order option), not a single default. Published April 6 as planned.
2. Both validation workloads are in the doc with full epsilon/delta reporting; the 91.2% at epsilon=8 number is our internal headline.
3. Q3 zoo-wide validation is committed in the doc on the strength of the B-58 funding — Bao, please make sure that line survives Q3 planning as discussed, since two teams have already asked when their backbones get covered.
4. Small scope cut: we drop the JAX-to-PyTorch config translator; Paloma documents the manual mapping instead. Nobody blocked on it.

Thanks all — clean landing on a short window.

Ximena

subject: Kickoff: DPOK fine-tuning for the image-gen stack
body:
Hi both,

Kicking off DPOK adoption for agents-rl. The method from our open-source release fine-tunes text-to-image diffusion models with online policy-gradient RL, using a reward model (ImageReward in the release) plus a KL term to keep the policy anchored — the knobs are reward_weight and kl_weight, and the reference config uses reward weight 10 with KL weight 0.01.

Why we care as product: our internal image-gen demo consistently loses side-by-sides on prompt fidelity. DPOK is the cheapest lever we have — no new base model, just RL fine-tuning against our internal preference reward model.

Milestones: single-prompt training reproduced on our stack by end of March, multi-prompt runs through April, a Launch Review Board slot for the improved demo in mid-May (sign-off is required before we show it externally).

Alina owns staffing and the money conversation for the scale-up.

Ulla

subject: Re: Kickoff: DPOK fine-tuning for the image-gen stack
body:
Ulla,

Staffing: Tereza leads the RL training loop and reward integration, Rosa owns the multi-GPU scaling work, Chiara the eval harness plumbing and demo packaging.

Compute reality check: policy batch size 4 fits a single A100, but the moment we go multi-GPU the whole UNet has to be shared and we drop to batch 2 per accelerator — so multi-prompt training at demo quality is 32-48 GPUs for a couple of weeks. Q2 we can squeeze out of titan best-effort. The Q3 scale-up (full prompt distribution plus reward-model refresh cycles) needs its own funding: Idris has verbally earmarked $180k from the Q3 discretionary compute budget line B-85 for this project — confirmed to me by phone Friday, paperwork to follow at Q3 planning. I'm planning the Q3 run rate against that line.

One dependency: our accelerate/torch_xla version pin is fragile (known issue in the release), Rosa is baking a fixed container image.

Alina

subject: Re: Kickoff: DPOK fine-tuning for the image-gen stack
body:
Status + a trade-off that needs a call.

Single-prompt reproduction: done (March 27). With reward weight 10 and kl_weight 0.01, ImageReward scores on the held-out renders improve 21% over the base model, and the KL term is doing its job — samples stay on-distribution instead of collapsing to reward-hacky textures.

Multi-prompt is where the trade-off bites. Our internal preference reward model is noisier than ImageReward; at kl_weight 0.01 the policy starts drifting on faces and text-in-image prompts around step 8k. Raising kl_weight to 0.03 stabilizes it but gives back about a third of the fidelity win. Options: (a) accept 0.03 and a smaller but robust win for the May demo, (b) hold 0.01 with early stopping per prompt cluster, more babysitting but bigger wins.

Also hit the documented hang — fixed exactly as the release notes say, uninstall torch_xla and pin accelerate 0.17.0. Rosa's container has it baked now.

Tereza

subject: Re: Kickoff: DPOK fine-tuning for the image-gen stack
body:
Decision time, with LRB on May 14.

We go with option (a): kl_weight 0.03, the robust setting. Rationale: the Launch Review Board cares more about "no embarrassing failure modes" than peak side-by-side wins, and Tereza's drift examples on text-in-image prompts are exactly the kind of thing that gets a demo pulled. The measured win at 0.03 — +13% internal preference score, up from the base model, across the full prompt distribution — is still a clear story.

Option (b) doesn't die: Chiara will keep the per-cluster early-stopping branch alive as the Q3 path, funded under the scale-up line Alina secured.

Scope cut for this half: no reward-model refresh before the demo. Frozen reward model, frozen eval set, boring and defensible.

See everyone at the dry run Tuesday.

Ulla

subject: Kickoff: honest privacy accounting for our DP-SGD pipelines
body:
Team,

Kicking off the batch-sampler accounting effort. The uncomfortable finding from our open-source work: most DP-SGD implementations shuffle their data but report privacy guarantees computed under Poisson subsampling, and the two can diverge meaningfully — "How Private are DP-SGD implementations?" is literally the title. We also have the balls-and-bins sampler with accounting that gets the practical benefits of shuffling with provable bounds.

Product goal: every internal DP training pipeline reports epsilon computed for the sampler it actually uses. Deliverables: the accounting library integrated with the dp_accounting package interface, a sampler audit of the four internal DP pipelines, and a migration rec per pipeline.

Milestones: library API stable end of March, audit done mid-May, recs and leadership readout before Q3 OKR lock June 26.

Jelena — staffing/compute over to you.

Ximena

subject: Re: Kickoff: honest privacy accounting for our DP-SGD pipelines
body:
Ximena,

Staffing: Yara owns the accounting math and the shuffling-vs-Poisson comparison surfaces; Farah integrates against the dp_accounting interfaces; Leilani builds the pipeline audit tooling; Amara supports the empirical validation runs (she's fractional here — heads-down on another data-platforms project most of this half).

Compute: the accountants themselves are numpy/scipy on CPU — negligible. The empirical validation is the ask: to show the reported bounds are tight in practice we rerun two production-scale DP training jobs under each of the three samplers (shuffle, Poisson, balls-and-bins). For that we hold the cirrus-tpu reservation for the week of 2026-06-01 — 128 accelerators from the trust-theory portfolio allocation, confirmed with the Infra side. One week covers both jobs times three samplers.

Audit tooling design review is April 3 if you want to sit in.

Jelena

subject: Re: Kickoff: honest privacy accounting for our DP-SGD pipelines
body:
Audit results are in, and they're spicy.

Of the four internal DP pipelines: two shuffle but report Poisson-subsampling epsilon. For pipeline P2 the honest shuffling bound puts effective epsilon at roughly 1.9x the reported value at their noise multiplier — that's a compliance conversation, not a rounding error. P1's gap is smaller but real. The other two genuinely Poisson-subsample; their reports stand.

Recommendation shaping up: migrate P1/P2 to balls-and-bins sampling — implementation-wise it's close to what their input pipelines already do, and our accounting for it gives bounds close to Poisson. Farah's dp_accounting integration passed review last week, so the accountants they'd need are already importable.

Risk: P2's team will push back on any noise increase before their July launch. The June validation runs matter precisely to show the utility cost is small — please keep that reservation week protected.

Yara

subject: Re: Kickoff: honest privacy accounting for our DP-SGD pipelines
body:
Post-validation decisions, for the record before the leadership readout June 18:

1. Validation runs completed in the reserved week. Headline: balls-and-bins matches Poisson-level bounds with under 0.4% utility delta on both production jobs. That kills P2's main objection.
2. Decision: P1 and P2 migrate to balls-and-bins sampling in Q3, with epsilon reported from our accountants. Kofi is aligned and wants the corrected epsilon figures in the next privacy review cycle — the 1.9x gap on P2 goes in the readout, framed as "found and fixed."
3. The library is now the mandated accounting path for new DP pipelines; Farah publishes the integration guide Friday.
4. Deferred: extending the audit to the two federated pipelines. Q3 candidate, not committed.

This is exactly the kind of result trust-theory should be known for. Well done.

Ximena

subject: Kickoff: grasping benchmark revival (dql_grasping)
body:
Hi all,

Kicking off the grasping-benchmark revival. Context: the manipulation roadmap needs a common yardstick before we commit Q3 OKRs, and our open-source grasping release is the right starting point — simulated grasping environments at several difficulty levels, with customizable DQL, MC, Supervised, Corr-MC, DDPG, and PCL learners, plus ready-made scripts for off-policy data collection and hyperparameter grid search.

What product gets out of it: an apples-to-apples comparison of the six algorithm families on our environments, so the roadmap picks a lane on evidence instead of vibes.

Milestones: environments and data-collection pipeline modernized by end of March, small-scale comparisons through May, the full grid-search sweep in late June, readout the first week of July.

Alina owns staffing and the compute reservation for the big sweep.

Ulla

subject: Re: Kickoff: grasping benchmark revival (dql_grasping)
body:
Ulla,

Staffing: Efe leads algorithms (he knows the PCL and Corr-MC corners best), Nikhil owns the environment modernization and sim throughput, Wanjiru the data/eval infrastructure, Quentin runs the comparison experiments.

Compute: the small-scale May comparisons run on titan-a100 best-effort — sim is CPU-heavy anyway, so we're renderer-bound more than GPU-bound there. The June grid search is different: six algorithm families x hyperparameter grid x multiple difficulty tiers x 5 seeds. For that we hold the vulcan-h100 reservation for the week of 2026-06-22 — 512 accelerators, locked in through the Infra Lead reservation process. It's a big ask but one intense week beats dribbling it out over six, and the readout date depends on it.

Risk to note early: the release's data-collection scripts assume an old virtualenv/python2-era toolchain; Nikhil is porting rather than patching.

Alina

subject: Re: Kickoff: grasping benchmark revival (dql_grasping)
body:
Status on the small-scale comparisons.

On the easy-tier environment with random-policy bootstrap data, early numbers: DQL reaches 78% grasp success, plain MC returns trail at 71% but are the most stable across seeds, DDPG is sample-efficient early then plateaus at 74%, and supervised is the floor at 66%. Corr-MC with eligibility traces is the interesting one — the biased-returns trick from the paper closes most of the MC-vs-DQL gap on the medium tier. PCL still has a divergence issue Quentin is chasing; likely a learning-rate interaction with our ported replay buffer.

Risk for the June sweep: sim throughput. Nikhil's port is functionally done but we're at about 60% of the frames/sec we budgeted, renderer-side. If we can't close it by June 12, the grid needs a trim — I'd cut the hardest difficulty tier before cutting seeds; five seeds is the minimum for the readout to mean anything.

Efe

subject: Re: Kickoff: grasping benchmark revival (dql_grasping)
body:
Decisions before next week's sweep, since we're out of slack:

1. Throughput landed at 85% of budget — good recovery Nikhil — but not 100%, so per Efe's recommendation we cut the hardest difficulty tier from the grid and keep all 5 seeds. The tier comes back as a follow-up run in July on best-effort.
2. PCL stays in the sweep: Quentin's fix (decoupling the replay-buffer sampling from the ported eligibility-trace code) held for two weeks of soak. If it diverges mid-sweep we drop it and say so in the readout, we don't rerun.
3. Readout moves from July 2 to July 6 to give Wanjiru time to build the comparison dashboards off the sweep output directly.

Our reservation week is what everything hangs on now — Alina, please reconfirm the booking with Infra today and make sure our job configs are staged by Friday.

Ulla

subject: Kickoff: Dream Fields 3D asset demo
body:
Team,

Kicking off the Dream Fields effort for vision. The method from our open-source release generates 3D object geometry and color from a text prompt alone — no 3D supervision — by optimizing a NeRF so that renders from many camera views score highly against the caption under a pre-trained CLIP model, with sparsity-inducing transmittance regularization and scene bounds keeping the geometry clean.

Product target: an internal demo where a designer types a prompt and gets a usable textured mesh for prototyping. The creative-tools group is the sponsor.

Milestones: reproduce release quality in our environment by mid-May (the NGC-container Docker path should make this quick), quality/latency improvements through June, demo assets and Launch Review Board submission early July.

Deshawn follows up on staffing, compute, and the data-platform dependency for the caption set.

Lucia

subject: Re: Kickoff: Dream Fields 3D asset demo
body:
Lucia,

Staffing: Tereza leads optimization quality (CLIP guidance, transmittance regularization tuning), Saoirse owns the training/render pipeline, Chiara the mesh-extraction and designer-facing packaging, Rosa the data path.

Compute: each object is a per-prompt NeRF optimization — GPU-hungry per asset but parallel across prompts. Titan best-effort covers development; I'll size a modest Vulcan ask for the June quality push separately.

Data dependency, the important one: our curated caption/prompt corpus lives in Corpus, and the v2 migration freeze is scheduled for 2026-08-07. That gives us comfortable room — we plan to land the expanded prompt corpus ingestion in late July, after the demo ships, and the freeze lands well after our window closes. So no migration risk on the critical path this half; Rosa will schedule the late-July ingestion with Jun Varga's team accordingly.

Deshawn

subject: Re: Kickoff: Dream Fields 3D asset demo
body:
Status.

Reproduction: done May 13 via the NGC container path. On our 40-prompt eval set we match release quality on CLIP retrieval score for 34/40 prompts; the misses are thin structures (chairs legs, wire objects) where geometry gets wispy.

Quality work since: the transmittance regularization weight is the big lever — raising it aggressively early then annealing gives us solid geometry on 5 of the 6 thin-structure failures without hurting the rest. Multi-view consistency holds up in turntable renders. Chiara's marching-cubes extraction produces usable meshes for about 80% of prompts; the rest need manual cleanup, which is fine for a designer-in-the-loop demo.

The honest risk for LRB: per-asset cost. We're at ~35 GPU-minutes per object at demo quality. Fine for the demo, not a product price point — the readout should frame the roadmap around distillation/amortization, not per-prompt optimization forever.

Tereza

subject: Re: Kickoff: Dream Fields 3D asset demo
body:
Decisions ahead of the July 2 LRB submission:

1. Demo scope locks at 60 curated prompts across the categories the creative-tools folks care about. Thin-structure prompts stay in — Tereza's annealing schedule made them presentable and they show honesty about limits.
2. Per-asset cost goes in the readout exactly as Tereza framed it: ~35 GPU-minutes per object today, distillation/amortization as the Q3 roadmap. I'd rather set that expectation now than get it as an LRB question.
3. Mesh cleanup stays manual for the demo; Chiara documents the workflow rather than automating it this half.
4. Data plan unchanged: expanded prompt corpus ingestion stays parked for late July per Deshawn's schedule with the Corpus team — nothing about the migration timeline affects the demo.

Submission goes in Monday. Really pleased with where this landed.

Lucia

subject: Kickoff: DReG estimators in the LVM training toolkit
body:
Hi all,

Kicking off the DReG integration. Quick framing for those newer to it: multi-sample IWAE bounds get tighter with more samples, but the standard inference-network gradient estimator counterintuitively degrades as samples grow. Our open-source DReG work showed the popular "sticking the landing" style estimator is actually biased, and that a second application of the reparameterization trick removes the bias and slashes gradient variance. Free accuracy for anyone training latent-variable models.

Product goal: DReG as the default inference-network estimator in the internal LVM toolkit, with variance telemetry so teams can see the win, plus applicability to reweighted wake-sleep style training.

Milestones: estimator module + unit-level variance benchmarks by end of March, two internal adopter models converted in April, toolkit release mid-May.

Bao owns staffing and the (small) compute picture.

Zofia

subject: Re: Kickoff: DReG estimators in the LVM training toolkit
body:
Zofia,

Staffing: Csilla owns the estimator module and the bias/variance test suite, Efe the adopter conversions, Katya the variance telemetry, Saoirse the toolkit release engineering.

Compute: small. Everything here runs on titan-a100 best-effort; the variance benchmarks are single-GPU jobs.

One genuinely new build in scope: for the adopter models the automated metrics don't settle arguments — the generative-quality deltas from lower-variance gradients are subtle — so we're scoping and staffing a human-rating annotation UI built from scratch. Saoirse leads it at 50% starting March 16: pairwise sample comparison, rater queues, agreement stats, export to the eval store. There's no existing internal tool for this, so I've budgeted five engineer-weeks with a target of April 20 so the April adopter conversions get human-rated before the toolkit release.

Bao

subject: Re: Kickoff: DReG estimators in the LVM training toolkit
body:
Status.

Estimator module landed March 27 with the bias test Katya suggested: we empirically reproduce that the Roeder-style estimator carries measurable bias at k=64 samples while DReG stays centered, and gradient variance on the inference network drops by an order of magnitude at large k. Telemetry shows it live per-run now, which has already been fun in demos.

Adopter one (the doc-topic VAE) converted cleanly: +0.9 nats test log-likelihood at identical step budget, purely from swapping the estimator. Adopter two (speech LVM) is mid-conversion; their reweighted wake-sleep variant hits the exact case the paper flags, so Efe is being careful with the score-function term.

Risk: the annotation UI slipped a week — rater-queue auth took longer than planned — new ETA April 27. That compresses the human-rating window for adopter two to under three weeks. Doable, but zero slack before the May 18 release cut.

Csilla

subject: Re: Kickoff: DReG estimators in the LVM training toolkit
body:
Release decisions:

1. Toolkit ships May 22 (four days late — I'll own that upward) with DReG as the default inference-network estimator and the variance telemetry on by default. The order-of-magnitude variance reduction chart is the first thing in the docs.
2. Adopter two makes the release. The human-rating round on the compressed window came back 62/38 preferring the DReG-trained samples with decent inter-rater agreement (0.71) — enough to publish internally alongside the +0.9 nats number from adopter one.
3. Scope cut: the jackknife variant of the estimator stays out of v1. Csilla documents it as experimental.
4. The annotation UI graduates to a maintained tool under Saoirse — the rater-queue piece is obviously reusable for future evals, and I want it in our OKR story for the half.

Thanks all, genuinely tidy execution.

Zofia

subject: Kickoff: DrJAX as our parallel-computation authoring layer
body:
Hi Jelena, Yusuf,

Kicking off DrJAX adoption for the efficiency portfolio. The library embeds a MapReduce programming model directly into JAX: a simple authoring surface for map/reduce computations, execution that leans on JAX's sharding machinery for datacenter-scale efficiency, and — the differentiator — full differentiability through the communication primitives themselves, broadcasts and reductions included. That last part is what our large-scale training teams keep hand-rolling badly.

Product goal: DrJAX becomes the sanctioned way to author these computations internally, replacing three divergent homegrown wrappers I know of.

Milestones: internal wheel + CI green by mid-April, two pilot teams migrated by end of May, adoption guide and readout by end of June, ahead of Q3 OKR lock on the 26th.

Jelena — staffing and platform asks to you.

Zofia

subject: Re: Kickoff: DrJAX as our parallel-computation authoring layer
body:
Zofia,

Status on the setup plus resourcing.

Staffing: Yusuf leads the technical adoption and the differentiability test coverage, Paloma owns packaging/CI (wheel builds via python -m build are green as of Friday, run_test.sh wired into CI), Tereza and Rosa split the two pilot migrations.

Compute: adoption work itself is cheap — correctness runs on small titan slices; the pilots bring their own training budgets.

New scoped build: to prove the migrations don't regress anything, we need side-by-side correctness and performance comparisons run continuously, so we're scoping and staffing an internal evaluation harness built from scratch — Rosa leads at 50% from April 20, covering benchmark definitions, sharded-vs-baseline numerical diffing, and scheduled regression runs with a report artifact. Nothing off the shelf fits the differentiable-communication cases, so I've budgeted six engineer-weeks, targeting a working harness by June 1.

Jelena

subject: Re: Kickoff: DrJAX as our parallel-computation authoring layer
body:
Status + one risk before the readout.

Pilot one (Tereza, the federated-analytics style workload) migrated fully: authoring went from ~700 lines of hand-rolled pmap orchestration to ~120 lines of DrJAX map/reduce, and differentiating through the reduction — previously a custom-VJP minefield — is now just jax.grad. Performance within 3% of the tuned original on the same sharding.

Pilot two (Rosa's) surfaced the real risk: their computation mixes DrJAX reductions with manual collective ops, and the sharding annotations fight each other — we saw a 2.2x slowdown until we rewrote the offending block DrJAX-native. Lesson for the adoption guide: incremental mixed-mode migration is a trap; migrate whole computation blocks or don't.

The regression harness has caught two numerical diffs since going live June 2, both benign accumulation-order issues, both now documented. Readout drafting starts next week.

Yusuf

subject: Kickoff: Project Riverbed (DSelect-k for multi-task ranking)
body:
Team,

Kicking off what we're calling Project Riverbed internally — please use the codename in docs and standups so search stays clean.

Substance: our multi-task ranking models currently use softmax-style MoE gating, which is dense (every expert runs) or top-k (non-differentiable selection). DSelect-k from our open-source release gives us differentiable selection of a fixed number of experts — the reference example gates 2 of 4 experts via a DSelectKGate keras layer — so we get sparse inference cost with clean end-to-end training.

Product goal: land DSelect-k gating in the two production multi-task rankers, targeting equal quality at materially lower serving FLOPs.

Milestones: gate layer integrated in the ranker training stack by mid-April, offline A/B quality parity by late May, serving-cost readout before June 15.

Daniela follows up on staffing.

Dmitri

subject: Re: Kickoff: Project Riverbed (DSelect-k for multi-task ranking)
body:
Dmitri,

Riverbed staffing and resourcing:

Wei owns the gating research questions (expert-count sweeps, entropy regularization interplay); Maren integrates the DSelectKGate layer into ranker A's training stack; Giannis mirrors for ranker B; Bilal builds the FLOPs/latency measurement rig so the serving-cost readout isn't hand-waving.

Compute: ranker retraining fits our existing titan-a100 allocation — biggest job is 32 GPUs for the full-data retrain. No Vulcan or TPU ask this half, which given what I hear about the June reservation crunch is a blessing.

One planning note: I've registered "Project Riverbed" with the PMO tracker under data-platforms so Nadia's office routes launch-review paperwork correctly.

Budget: nothing discretionary; all inside the portfolio envelope.

Daniela

subject: Re: Kickoff: Project Riverbed (DSelect-k for multi-task ranking)
body:
Riverbed status ahead of the readout.

Ranker A: DSelect-k selecting 2 of 6 experts matches the dense-gate baseline on all four task heads (largest delta 0.15% AUC, within noise) at 41% lower gate-side serving FLOPs per Bilal's rig. Offline parity milestone: met.

Ranker B is the tricky one and the risk to flag: with 8 experts and the same num_nonzeros=2 setting, training is sensitive to the gate's initialization — two of five seeds collapse to a single expert early and never recover. The paper's smoothness knobs help; what worked best is a brief dense warmup then annealing into sparse selection, which recovers 5/5 seeds but adds ~8% training time. Recommend we ship the warmup schedule as the default and document the trade-off rather than chase a cleverer init before June 15.

One ask: can the readout deck use the Riverbed name only? Easier for the LRB paper trail.

Wei

subject: Kickoff: DualDICE for off-policy evaluation
body:
Hi Bruno, Halima,

Kicking off DualDICE adoption. Why it matters: teams keep wanting to evaluate a new policy from logged data where we don't know the behavior policy that generated the logs. DualDICE from our open-source release estimates discounted stationary distribution corrections behavior-agnostically — no behavior-policy knowledge needed — which is exactly the situation our logged partner-interaction data is in.

Product goal: an off-policy evaluation module in the trust-theory toolkit with confidence-caveated estimates, validated first on tabular and non-tabular GridWalk (the release's reference environments), then on one internal logged dataset.

Milestones on the short window: GridWalk validation by March 13, internal-data pilot by April 10, toolkit module and handoff note by April 27. Productionization would be a Q2/Q3 follow-on, which we should staff-plan for now.

Bruno — staffing next please.

Ximena

subject: Re: Kickoff: DualDICE for off-policy evaluation
body:
Ximena,

Staffing: Halima leads the method work and owns the GridWalk validation matrix (tabular and non-tabular, per the release's run configurations); Farah does the toolkit module and API; Oyin owns the data plumbing for the internal pilot and the productionization runway.

On your follow-on staffing ask — settled it with Oyin and her lead this morning: Oyin is committed at 60% to this project for May 2026 to carry the productionization phase, with the remaining 40% on her platform maintenance duties. I've logged that in the allocation sheet so nobody grabs her for Q2 firefighting.

Compute is a non-issue — GridWalk runs are laptop-scale, the pilot is a few dozen CPU-heavy jobs, nothing needing reservations.

One process item: the internal logged dataset touches partner data, so I'm filing the privacy review this week given their 2-3 week SLA — it must clear before the April 10 pilot.

Bruno

subject: Re: Kickoff: DualDICE for off-policy evaluation
body:
Validation status, two weeks in.

Tabular GridWalk: estimates match the oracle within 1% across the policy pairs we tested — remembering the release's caveat that the printed target rewards are themselves estimates, so we bumped num_trajectories to 1000 for a fair oracle.

Non-tabular is where the practical lessons live. Joint optimization of nu and zeta is unstable exactly as documented; the nu/zeta learning-rate pair dominates everything else (we landed on 0.0001/0.001, same as the reference), and lower gamma makes optimization noticeably easier. For the toolkit defaults I'm encoding: start from the reference learning rates, expose gamma prominently, and surface a divergence warning when the nu loss oscillates.

Risk for the pilot: our logged partner data has much longer horizons than GridWalk; at gamma close to 1 the correction estimates get high-variance. Farah and I are adding a variance-based confidence caveat to every estimate the module emits — better to say "low confidence" than be quietly wrong.

Halima

subject: Re: Kickoff: DualDICE for off-policy evaluation
body:
Closing decisions before Monday's handoff:

1. Pilot verdict: on the internal logged dataset, DualDICE estimates for the two candidate policies agreed with the (expensive) holdout A/B directionally and within the stated confidence bands. The variance caveat fired on the longest-horizon slice, exactly as designed. This is a credible OPE story.
2. The toolkit module ships April 27 with Halima's defaults (reference nu/zeta learning rates, prominent gamma, divergence warning).
3. Deferred to the May productionization phase: batched estimation for policy sweeps and the deterministic_env stabilization path. That phase is staffed per Bruno's plan — Oyin at 60% through May carries it, so please protect her allocation; the handoff note names her as owner.
4. Privacy review cleared April 6, for the record.

Good, tight project. Thank you all.

Ximena

subject: Kickoff: dual-pixel depth for the imaging pipeline
body:
Hi all,

Kicking off the dual-pixel depth effort. Our open-source release showed you can learn single-camera depth estimation from dual-pixel data — the DPNet model with affine invariance is the reference — and the released dataset (95G train, 29G test, with RGB, dual-pixel images, and depth maps) is big enough to train production-grade models.

Product target: depth-driven features in the on-device imaging pipeline — portrait relighting and defocus effects — without any additional hardware, since dual-pixel sensors are already in the camera stack.

Milestones: reproduce the paper's metrics on the released test split by end of April, mobile-feasible model by end of May, integration decision with the imaging platform team at the June 15 review.

The affine-invariant eval matters here: depth up to affine transform is fine for defocus, trickier for relighting — Fumiko, let's dig into that early.

Bruno owns staffing/compute.

Lucia

subject: Re: Kickoff: dual-pixel depth for the imaging pipeline
body:
Lucia,

Staffing: Fumiko leads modeling and owns the affine-invariance question, Kaia the dataset pipeline and reproduction, Linnea the mobile-sizing work, Saoirse the on-device runtime path.

Compute: reproduction and ablations fit titan-a100 best-effort — DPNet-scale training is 16 GPUs for ~3 days per run.

The key scoped build: the mobile milestone needs the big DPNet compressed into something that fits the imaging pipeline's latency budget, so we are scoping and staffing a distillation training recipe built from scratch — Linnea leads it at 70% starting April 20. Teacher-student setup against DPNet, affine-invariant distillation losses, quantization-aware fine-tuning at the end. Nothing exists in-house to reuse for this, so I've budgeted seven engineer-weeks with the recipe producing its first mobile-sized student by May 22.

Dataset note: the released set is slightly smaller than the paper's, so expect reproduced metrics to match the updated reference numbers, not the original table.

Bruno

subject: Re: Kickoff: dual-pixel depth for the imaging pipeline
body:
Status.

Reproduction: done April 28. Kaia's runs of DPNet with affine invariance on the released train split land within 2% of the reference metrics on the test split across the board — consistent with the release notes saying the public dataset is slightly smaller than the paper's.

Affine-invariance investigation: as suspected, affine-ambiguous depth is fully sufficient for defocus but relighting needs metric-ish scale. Good news — using the camera's autofocus metadata as a weak anchor resolves the ambiguity well enough on 87% of our internal validation captures. I propose we scope relighting v1 to captures where the anchor is confident and fall back to defocus-only otherwise.

Risk: the distillation recipe's first student (May 8, two weeks ahead of plan — credit Linnea) is 14x smaller but loses more accuracy on the affine-invariant metrics than expected in the far-depth range. Next iteration weights the loss by inverse depth; if that doesn't close it, we may need a slightly larger student than the latency budget wants.

Fumiko

subject: Re: Kickoff: dual-pixel depth for the imaging pipeline
body:
Decisions for Monday's integration review:

1. We take the slightly larger student. Linnea's inverse-depth weighting closed most of the far-range gap, but the last bit costs 1.8ms over the original latency budget — and Saoirse's runtime numbers show we can absorb that by moving the preprocessing to the ISP path. 11x smaller than DPNet, quality within tolerance on all affine-invariant metrics.
2. Relighting scopes to confident-anchor captures per Fumiko's proposal; defocus is unconditional. This is the story we take to the imaging platform team.
3. Scope cut: no low-light specialization this half. The dataset skews well-lit and I won't promise what we haven't measured.
4. Distillation recipe gets written up as a reusable asset under Linnea's name — it's the piece I expect other vision teams to come asking for.

See you Monday.

Lucia

subject: DVRL kickoff - data valuation as a product surface
body:
Team,

Kicking off the DVRL productization effort today. The pitch: our open-source DVRL release scores individual training examples with a reinforcement-learned data value estimator, and customers keep asking us which 10% of their data is hurting their models. We ship that answer.

Scope for this half covers three of the four applications in the codebase: data valuation, corrupted sample discovery with robust learning on tabular data, and domain adaptation. The image transfer-learning variant is a stretch goal.

Rough milestones: internal demo on a customer-shaped tabular dataset by June 8, Launch Review Board pre-read by July 6, decision on external pilot by end of window (Aug 3). Deshawn will follow up on staffing and compute; Wei owns the modeling track.

OKR framing for Q2: "identify 80%+ of injected corrupted labels at 20% noise on two tabular benchmarks." We beat that in the paper setting, now we need it repeatable.

Thanks,
Lucia

subject: Re: DVRL kickoff - data valuation as a product surface
body:
Lucia,

Staffing and resource plan, as promised.

People: Wei 80% on the data value estimator and reward shaping, Rosa 50% on the pipeline and eval harness, Gustavo 70% on data tooling. That's tight but workable for a June 8 demo.

The big gap is test data. To stress corrupted-sample discovery at controlled noise rates we need clean, labeled synthetic corpora we can corrupt on demand. Nothing internal fits, so I want us to scope and staff a synthetic-data generation pipeline from scratch: Gustavo owns the design, Rosa pairs on the serving path, and I'm budgeting six weeks of build time before the DVRL reward loop can consume it. It's a real chunk of the schedule but it de-risks every downstream eval.

Compute is modest: Titan A100 best-effort covers training, no Vulcan reservation needed. I'll file the Corpus ingestion request for the tabular benchmarks this week.

Deshawn

subject: DVRL status: corrupted-sample numbers in, domain adaptation lagging
body:
Hi both,

Status ahead of the June 8 demo. Good news first: on the two tabular benchmarks, the corrupted-sample discovery run (main_corrupted_sample_discovery path) flags 87% of injected corrupted labels at 20% noise, comfortably above the 80% OKR line. Robust-learning accuracy holds within 0.6 points of the clean-data ceiling when we drop the bottom-valued 15% of examples.

The risk is domain adaptation. The main_domain_adaptation pipeline is sensitive to the source/target split, and value estimates get noisy when target data is scarce - we're seeing swings of 3-4 points between seeds. I need another two weeks of reward-shaping work before I'd show it to anyone external.

Proposal: demo data valuation + corrupted-sample discovery on the 8th, and mark domain adaptation "in validation". Rosa's harness makes the ablations easy to re-run, so no schedule risk there.

Wei

subject: Re: DVRL status: corrupted-sample numbers in, domain adaptation lagging
body:
Team,

Decision from yesterday's review: we're cutting the image transfer-learning application from v1 entirely, not just deprioritizing it. The LRB pre-read goes in with data valuation and corrupted-sample discovery as the launch scope, domain adaptation as a fast-follow once Wei's seed-variance issue is under 1.5 points.

Rationale: the demo landed well (the 87%-at-20%-noise number did the work), and the feedback was uniformly "ship the tabular story first." Adding an image pipeline now buys us risk, not signal.

Deshawn - please rebalance Gustavo toward hardening the data tooling for pilot customers, and keep Rosa on the eval harness through the Aug 3 decision point. I'll draft the LRB doc this week and circulate for comments by Friday.

Good work everyone, this one's in decent shape.

Lucia

subject: EBP kickoff: energy-based processes -> 3D capture cleanup
body:
Hi all,

Kicking off the EBP effort. Our open-source Energy-Based Processes release showed EBPs capture multi-modality on exchangeable data where GPs, Neural Processes, and Variational Implicit Processes flatten it out. The product thesis: point-cloud denoising with the learned energy function is exactly what our 3D capture partners need for cleaning noisy scans, with point-cloud generation via the RNN sampler as a second act.
