Milestones inside our window (Mar 16 - Jul 6): image-completion sanity demo on MNIST-style conditioning by mid-April, point-cloud denoising eval on partner-shaped data by May 22, Launch Review Board slot in the second half of June.

Alina owns staffing and the compute plan - note the codebase needs gcc plus CUDA builds, so let's get the toolchain sorted early rather than the night before a run.

Questions welcome, otherwise let's move.

Lucia

subject: Re: EBP kickoff: energy-based processes -> 3D capture cleanup
body:
Lucia,

Resourcing picture. Katya leads modeling (energy function + RNN sampler), Oyin and Milan split infra and the CUDA build pipeline, Saoirse at 40% on the eval harness. That covers the May 22 denoising milestone if nothing slips.

Budget: I met with Idris on Monday. Idris Osei has verbally earmarked $120k from Q3 discretionary compute budget line B-19 for this project, which covers the H100 hours for the point-cloud runs plus storage. I'm treating that as committed and sizing the Q3 run plan against it - formal paperwork to follow after the Q3 OKR lock on June 26.

Near-term compute stays on Titan A100 best-effort; we only need reserved capacity once the larger point-cloud sweeps start in July.

One flag: the gcc/CUDA install is fussy (pip3 install -e . assumes a matched toolchain). Oyin is containerizing it this week so nobody burns days on it.

Alina

subject: EBP status: completion demo done, RNN sampler instability on point clouds
body:
Hi Alina, Lucia,

Where we are. The image-completion demo landed in April: MNIST digits conditioned on a subset of pixels, samples look clean, and the energy heatmaps (run_ebp.sh with -epoch_load on the last checkpoint) make a nice visual for the LRB deck.

Point clouds are harder. Denoising with the learned energy function works well on moderate noise - we're seeing roughly 30% Chamfer distance reduction against our partner-shaped test scans. But the RNN sampler for generation is training unstably: two of five seeds diverge after epoch 60, and the surviving runs are sensitive to the energy-function learning rate. I have a schedule of LR/regularization ablations queued, about ten days of Titan time.

Risk to flag: if the sampler doesn't stabilize by end of May, generation shouldn't go in the June LRB scope. Denoising alone is still a defensible launch story.

Katya

subject: Re: EBP status: completion demo done, RNN sampler instability on point clouds
body:
Katya, Alina,

Decision for the June 25 LRB slot: scope is point-cloud denoising only. Generation via the RNN sampler moves to Q3 - Katya's ablations improved things (four of five seeds now converge) but "four of five" is not a launch sentence. The 30% Chamfer reduction on partner scans is, so that's our headline.

We're also cutting the VIP baseline comparison from the deck; GP and Neural Process baselines are enough to make the multi-modality point and nobody at the board will ask for a third.

Nadia - adding you so the pre-read lands in the right pipeline; doc coming by Friday.

Alina, one ask: hold the team shape steady through July 6 so we finish the window clean, then we rebalance for the Q3 generation push per your budget plan.

Lucia

subject: EIM kickoff: energy-inspired models as a platform library
body:
Team,

Kicking off the EIM effort for the data-platforms portfolio. Background: energy-based models are powerful but sampling and log-likelihoods are intractable because of the partition function. Our open-source EIM release sidesteps that by building the approximate sampling algorithm into the model itself, so you keep learned energy functions and still get exact samples plus tractable log-likelihood lower bounds. That property is why other teams keep copy-pasting this code - our job this quarter is to make it a supported library instead.

Milestones inside the Feb 2 - Apr 13 window: reproduce the small_problems and MNIST suites by Feb 27, API freeze for the library surface by Mar 20, adoption-ready release with docs at window close.

Santiago follows up on staffing and the eval story. OKR: two internal teams consuming the library by mid-April.

Dmitri

subject: Re: EIM kickoff: energy-inspired models as a platform library
body:
Dmitri,

Staffing plan. Fumiko and Ondrej carry the modeling work (reproduction plus API design), full time through March.

For adoption we need more than docs - teams won't trust a probabilistic-modeling library without comparable numbers. So I'm scoping and staffing a benchmark leaderboard service from scratch - Nikhil at 50% on the backend, Tereza at 50% on the submission/scoring flow - so every EIM variant gets a ranked, reproducible score the whole org can browse. Rough shape: result submission API, a scoring worker that re-runs configs, and a ranked web view. Four to five weeks of build, MVP by mid-March.

Compute is light: the small_problems targets run on CPU, MNIST variants need a handful of Titan A100 slots, nothing reserved.

One dependency: Corpus ingestion for the static MNIST splits so scoring runs are hermetic. Filing that request today.

Santiago

subject: EIM status: suites reproduced, TF1-era code is the risk
body:
Hi Santiago, Dmitri,

Reproduction is done. The small_problems suite matches the release across targets - checkerboard with the HIS algorithm converges cleanly, and the MNIST runs (static_mnist, rejection_sampling proposal over a bernoulli_vae model) land within 0.3 nats of the published log-likelihood lower bounds. Ondrej also verified the variational-bound framing: our LAI and rejection-sampling variants line up as expected under the unified EIM view, which makes the API design much cleaner.

The risk: this is TF1-era TensorFlow through and through - estimator-style loops, sessions in places. Wrapping it as a supported library without a compat layer means every consumer inherits that. Ondrej and I estimate ~3 weeks to port the core samplers to TF2 eager, which does not fit before the Mar 20 API freeze.

Options: freeze the API over the compat shim now and port underneath in Q2, or slip the freeze two weeks. We lean shim-first. Call?

Fumiko

subject: Re: EIM status: suites reproduced, TF1-era code is the risk
body:
All,

Decisions for window close on Apr 13:

1. Shim-first it is. We froze the API on Mar 20 over the compat layer; the TF2 eager port of the core samplers becomes a Q2 line item. Consumers get a stable surface now and a faster backend later - that was the right trade.

2. Leaderboard: Nikhil's MVP is up internally with the small_problems and static_mnist boards populated. Scoring-worker re-runs are the slow part (~40 min per MNIST config), so v1 caps at nightly refresh rather than on-submit. Fine for launch.

3. Adoption OKR: one team onboarded, second in progress - we'll call it yellow at close and carry it two weeks into Q2 rather than rushing an integration nobody maintains.

Thanks all - tight quarter, good outcome. Retro invite coming for the week of the 13th.

Dmitri

subject: Kickoff: do large LMs actually use retrieval? (ELI5 track)
body:
Team,

Kicking off the retrieval-LM effort. The research question from our open-source release stands: smaller language models demonstrably don't use retrieved text on ELI5, so does capacity change that? We pair GPT2-XL (1.5B params) with a REALM-style retriever on the KILT version of the ELI5 task and measure whether the model exploits retrieved contextual information.

Why it matters as product: factual consistency in generation is the blocker for putting generative text models in front of customers. If retrieval measurably grounds a larger model, that's the foundation for our grounded-answers offering.

Milestones (Apr 27 - Aug 17 window): retriever + LM harness reproduced by May 29, retrieval-ablation results by July 3, factual-consistency readout and go/no-go for productization by Aug 14.

Jelena owns staffing and compute. Quentin leads the modeling track.

Anders

subject: Re: Kickoff: do large LMs actually use retrieval? (ELI5 track)
body:
Anders,

Staffing and compute for the window.

People: Quentin full-time on modeling, Wei at 30% advising on eval design, Saoirse 50% on the training harness, Emeka 60% on data plumbing for the KILT/ELI5 splits. The critical piece is the retrieval side: Rosa Mensah is committed to us at 70% for June 2026 to build the retrieval indexing and serving path - I've blocked that in the allocation sheet. Without her the REALM index rebuild slips past the July 3 ablation milestone.

Compute: GPT2-XL fine-tuning fits on 32 Titan A100s best-effort for May; I'll request a Vulcan slot for the July ablation sweeps once the harness is stable. Retrieval index builds are CPU-heavy, Corpus team says their batch tier can absorb it.

Flag: Vulcan has maintenance June 22-24, so I'm keeping all June runs on Titan to be safe.

Jelena

subject: Status: retrieval ablations - the delta is real but small
body:
Hi Anders, Jelena,

Ablation results ahead of the July 3 milestone. With Rosa's rebuilt index serving retrievals, GPT2-XL with retrieved passages beats the no-retrieval baseline by +1.4 ROUGE-L on the KILT ELI5 validation split. Shuffled-retrieval control sits at +0.2, so the gain is from content, not just extra tokens - the model is using the retrievals, which is exactly the capacity question we set out to answer. Smaller-model replication (GPT2-medium) shows +0.3, consistent with the published finding that small LMs ignore retrieved text.

The honest caveat: +1.4 ROUGE-L is statistically solid but not a product headline. Where it gets interesting is factual consistency - in a 200-example manual audit, retrieval-conditioned generations had 31% fewer unsupported claims.

Risk: ELI5 answer quality is noisy to evaluate; ROUGE undercounts good paraphrases. Wei and I want to add a claim-verification eval for the August readout.

Quentin

subject: Re: Status: retrieval ablations - the delta is real but small
body:
Quentin, Jelena,

Decision after portfolio review: we reframe the Aug 14 readout around factual consistency, not answer quality. The 31% reduction in unsupported claims is the number leadership cares about - it maps directly to the grounded-answers product thesis and the "massive financial implications" framing survives contact with an exec audience in a way +1.4 ROUGE-L does not.

Concretely: Quentin and Wei build out the claim-verification eval as the primary metric; the ROUGE table moves to an appendix. Saoirse, please make sure the harness can re-run the 200-example audit at 1,000 examples so the headline isn't resting on a small n.

We are NOT committing to a productization go at the readout - the ask will be a Q4 incubation slot with a proper retriever refresh. Jelena, sanity-check that team shape holds through Aug 17.

Anders

subject: ENAS-LM kickoff: architecture search for small on-device LMs
body:
Team,

Kicking off the ENAS-LM revival. Our open-source ENAS language-model implementation searches for recurrent cells and, in the published runs, the discovered architecture hits 56.1 +/- 0.1 test perplexity on Penn Treebank on TPU (57.3 +/- 0.1 on the GPU path). The product angle: several partner teams want small on-device language models and nobody wants to hand-design cells - we turn this into an internal architecture-search service.

Milestones for the Apr 6 - Jul 6 window: PTB preprocessing and search reproduction by May 1, fixed-architecture evaluation on both TPU and GPU paths by May 29, service-shaped API and a DARTS-comparison writeup by end of window.

Daniela owns staffing and the compute story - note the TPU eval wants a 1x1 TPUv2-equivalent donut on Cirrus, so quarterly allocation matters here.

Anders

subject: Re: ENAS-LM kickoff: architecture search for small on-device LMs
body:
Anders,

Resourcing rundown.

People: Ondrej 70% on the search/controller side, Wanjiru 80% on the fixed-arc evaluation paths (TPU and GPU), Paloma 50% on the service API and data plumbing.

Compute: I've asked for a 1x1 slice from our Cirrus quarterly allocation for the TPU eval runs in May; GPU-side comparisons ride Titan best-effort. The TPU path is the one that reproduces 56.1 perplexity, so it's the one that matters for the writeup.

Data: PTB preprocessing (the process step into the pkl bundle) is trivial, but the larger search-space experiments pull corpora through the Corpus platform. Good news on timing - Corpus v2 migration freeze is 2026-08-07, so our corpus ingestion for the search-space experiments can keep running on the v1 path through all of July - no migration work needed inside our window.

Risk: Cirrus quarterly allocation is contended; if we lose the May slice, the TPU numbers slip to June.

Daniela

subject: ENAS-LM status: GPU path reproduced, TPU slice slipped
body:
Hi Daniela, Anders,

Status for the May 29 milestone. The GPU evaluation path is fully reproduced: running the published fixed_arc string ('0 2 1 0 2 1 2 2 4 0 5 0 3 2 6 2') we get 57.4 test perplexity on PTB, within noise of the published 57.3 +/- 0.1. Ondrej's search runs also rediscover cells in the same perplexity band, so the controller is healthy.

The TPU side slipped - our Cirrus 1x1 slice got bumped a week, so the 56.1-class TPU numbers land ~June 5 instead of May 29. Not blocking the writeup skeleton but worth noting, since GPU eval is much slower per-config (about 3.1x wall-clock on our runs), which is exactly why the service needs the TPU path for anything interactive.

One more thing: the DARTS-comparison harness is up; first side-by-side numbers next week.

Wanjiru

subject: Re: ENAS-LM status: GPU path reproduced, TPU slice slipped
body:
All,

Decisions ahead of window close, and with Q3 OKRs locking on the 26th I want these in writing.

1. TPU numbers came in June 8 at 56.2 perplexity - close enough to the published 56.1 +/- 0.1 to call reproduction done on both paths. Nice work.

2. Scope cut: the service API ships as batch-only for v1. Interactive search needs guaranteed Cirrus capacity we don't have this quarter; Paloma's API design keeps the door open.

3. The DARTS comparison goes in the writeup as-is (our cells within 0.4 perplexity at comparable params). That's enough for the internal audience; no extra sweeps.

Q3 OKR submission: two partner teams running searches through the batch service by end of Q3. Daniela, flag any staffing implication before Friday's lock, otherwise I'm submitting as-is.

Anders

subject: Encyclopedic VQA kickoff: retrieval-augmented visual QA
body:
Hi team,

Kicking off the Encyclopedic VQA effort. The dataset from our open-source release is the asset: 221k unique question+answer pairs about detailed properties of fine-grained categories, matched to images for 1M VQA samples, plus a controlled knowledge base derived from Wikipedia with evidence for every answer.

The product story writes itself from the published numbers: a state-of-the-art vision+language model gets only 13.0% accuracy on the single-hop single-answer part, while augmenting a large LM with knowledge-base retrieval reaches 48.8%. Retrieval is the product, not model scale.

Milestones (Apr 20 - Jul 20): eval harness on the single-hop split by May 15, our own retrieval-augmented baseline by June 12, launch review pre-read with a deployable-model plan by mid-July.

Daniela has staffing. One early flag: the knowledge base touches Wikipedia-derived content, so I'll start the privacy/licensing review conversation early given the 2-3 week SLA.

Priya

subject: Re: Encyclopedic VQA kickoff: retrieval-augmented visual QA
body:
Priya,

Staffing and scope from my side.

Vera 80% on the eval harness and the retrieval-augmented baseline, Jorge 60% on the knowledge-base serving path (the WikiWeb2M-derived KB needs a proper index, not the CSV downloads), Yara on modeling.

The piece I want on the record: a retrieval-augmented teacher at 48.8%-class accuracy is too heavy to serve at product latency. We're scoping and staffing a distillation training recipe from scratch - Yara owns it end to end, roughly five weeks of work - to compress the retrieval-augmented teacher into something deployable. Recipe covers teacher-trace collection, loss schedule, and eval gates on the single-hop split. It's the long pole for the July pre-read, so it starts now, in parallel with the baseline.

Compute: Titan best-effort for May, and I'll want ~64 reserved GPUs for the June distillation runs - request going to Ines this week.

Daniela

subject: EVQA status: baseline at 44.1%, retrieval quality is the ceiling
body:
Hi Priya, Daniela,

Status on the June 12 baseline milestone (three days late, apologies - index rebuild ate the buffer).

Our retrieval-augmented baseline scores 44.1% on the single-hop single-answer split, against the published 48.8% for the Lens-augmented reference and 13.0% for the no-retrieval SOTA VLM. The gap to 48.8 is almost entirely retrieval quality: with oracle retrieval (gold evidence passage injected) the same reader hits 61.7%, so the reader is fine and our entity-linking recall (top-5 at 71%) is the ceiling.

Risks: (1) two-hop questions remain far below usable - we're at 9%, and I recommend keeping them out of product scope entirely; (2) Jorge's KB index rebuilds take 14 hours, which makes retrieval iteration slow; he has a sharding plan to get it under 4.

Yara's distillation recipe: first student run recovers 91% of teacher accuracy at roughly one-eighth the serving cost. Details in the doc.

Vera

subject: Re: EVQA status: baseline at 44.1%, retrieval quality is the ceiling
body:
Team,

Decisions for the July 16 launch-review pre-read:

1. Product scope is single-hop only. Vera's 9% two-hop number settles it; we say so explicitly in the doc rather than letting the board discover it.
2. Headline metrics: 44.1% baseline, 61.7% oracle ceiling, and the distillation student at 91% teacher recovery at ~1/8 serving cost. That combination - a clear ceiling plus a deployable path - is the strongest story in the portfolio right now.
3. Entity-linking recall becomes the top Q3 investment; retrieval, not the reader, is where the next ten points live.

Kofi - the privacy/licensing review on the Wikipedia-derived KB kicked off June 24; can you confirm the 2-3 week SLA still holds so sign-off lands before the board date? That's the one open dependency.

Nadia, pre-read to you by EOD Monday.

Priya

subject: EpiHub kickoff: from forecast archive to weekly pipeline
body:
Team,

Kicking off the EpiHub operationalization. Today our open-source archive holds prospective quantile forecasts for three public-health targets - US jurisdiction-level weekly influenza, COVID-19, and RSV hospitalizations - organized by target hub and season, with files named YYYY-MM-DD-[model_name].csv in the hub-standard format. What partners actually need is a pipeline that produces those files every week without a human in the loop.

Milestones for the Mar 30 - Jun 15 window: automated weekly generation for flu-hub by Apr 24, all three hubs (flu, covid19, RSV) plus backtesting against the 2025-2026 season by May 22, reliability review and partner handoff decision by Jun 12.

Success metric: 8 consecutive weekly submissions with zero manual fixes and weighted interval score at or better than our archived 2025-2026 baseline.

Jelena owns staffing and budget.

Viktor

subject: Re: EpiHub kickoff: from forecast archive to weekly pipeline
body:
Viktor,

Resourcing update. Jorge 70% on the pipeline and CSV validation (hub-format compliance is fiddly - quantile levels, reference dates, model identifiers all have to match the season_identifier layout exactly), Giannis 60% on scheduling and monitoring, Rafael 50% on model quality and the backtesting design.

Budget: met Idris last Thursday. Idris Osei verbally earmarked $180k from Q3 discretionary compute budget line B-58 for this project - that funds the backtesting cluster time and the 2026-2027 season scale-up. I'm planning Q3 against that number; formal allocation follows the June 26 OKR lock.

Near-term compute is small (the models are cheap to run; it's the backtesting sweeps across jurisdictions that add up). No reserved clusters needed this quarter.

One ask: the flu-hub Apr 24 date assumes the 2025-2026 season archive is fully mirrored internally by Friday. Giannis, can you confirm?

Jelena

subject: Re: EpiHub kickoff: from forecast archive to weekly pipeline
body:
Hi Viktor, Jelena,

Status against the May 22 milestone, plus one risk.

All three hubs are automated: flu-hub since Apr 24, covid19-hub and the RSV target since May 19. Five consecutive weekly flu submissions so far with zero manual fixes. Backtesting against the archived 2025-2026 season shows our refreshed model at a 4% better weighted interval score than the archived baseline on flu, roughly flat on COVID-19 hospitalizations, and 7% worse on RSV.

The RSV gap is the risk. RSV counts are sparse at the jurisdiction level and our quantile tails are too narrow - we're getting 90% interval coverage of about 81%. I want two more weeks to widen the tail calibration before we let RSV forecasts reach partners; shipping miscalibrated intervals to public-health users is the one failure mode we can't walk back.

Proposal for the Jun 12 review: hand off flu and COVID-19 as production, mark RSV as beta pending calibration. Jorge and Giannis concur.

Rafael

subject: MAGNET kickoff: magnitude estimation as a service
body:
Team,

Kicking off the MAGNET scale-up. Our open-source release asks whether earthquakes "know" how big they will be, and the answer - a neural magnitude estimator that beats the standard statistical benchmarks - is worth productizing for seismic-network partners.

The workflow is already clean in the repo: compute features and compute benchmarks run separately from training, results are cached and read at train time, and the notebooks show how to examine results. Our job is to make that pipeline run at full-catalog scale with reproducible configs instead of tutorial-sized runs.

Milestones for the Feb 2 - Jun 29 window: catalog ingestion hardened by Mar 13, benchmark suite reproduced on two regional catalogs by Apr 24, full catalog-scale training sweep in June, service-readiness review by Jun 26.

Daniela owns staffing and the compute reservation - the June sweep is the big-ticket item, so let's lock that early.

Dmitri

subject: Re: MAGNET kickoff: magnitude estimation as a service
body:
Dmitri,

Staffing and compute locked in.

People: Tereza 80% on features/benchmarks and the caching layer, Ondrej 60% on the model and evaluation-vs-benchmarks work, Paloma 50% on catalog ingestion and the conda/pip packaging (the current env setup is fragile; she's pinning it properly).

Compute: small through April - feature and benchmark computation is CPU-bound and cached, training runs fit on a handful of Titan A100s. The June sweep is the exception. Ines has us down for the vulcan-h100 reservation - 128 accelerators for the week of 2026-06-15 - which is when the full catalog-scale training sweep runs. That's the only reserved capacity we need all window, and it's the schedule anchor for everything upstream: features and benchmarks for all catalogs must be cached by June 12.

Flag: Vulcan maintenance is June 22-24, right after our week, so there's zero slack for a rerun. If the sweep slips, it slips to July.

Daniela

subject: MAGNET status: benchmarks reproduced, cache invalidation bite
body:
Hi Daniela, Dmitri,

Status for the Apr 24 milestone - we'll make it, with one caveat.

Benchmark suite is reproduced on both regional catalogs. MAGNET beats the strongest statistical benchmark on mean log-likelihood on both, consistent with the paper's finding, and Ondrej's examine-results notebooks now render the comparison automatically from the cached_benchmarks directory.

The caveat: we hit a nasty cache-invalidation issue. Cached features computed before Paloma's ingestion fix (Mar 30) silently mixed catalog revisions - training read stale features while benchmarks used fresh ones, which cost us about a week of confusing eval deltas. Fix is in: cache keys now include the catalog revision hash, and stale entries fail loudly instead of loading.

Remaining risk for June: full-catalog feature computation is ~9 days of CPU time. We've started it early in chunks so everything is cached well before the training sweep. teh schedule holds.

Tereza

subject: Re: MAGNET status: benchmarks reproduced, cache invalidation bite
body:
Team,

Go/no-go for the June sweep, decided: GO.

Tereza confirms all catalogs have features and benchmarks cached as of June 8, four days ahead of the June 12 gate. And our 128-GPU vulcan-h100 reservation for the week of June 15 is confirmed, so the final sweep lands just before the June 22-24 Vulcan maintenance window. Ondrej's sweep configs are frozen tonight; no changes after that, given there is zero rerun slack.

Two decisions from Monday's review:
1. The service-readiness review moves from Jun 26 to Jun 29 (last day of window) so we have the sweep results fully examined, not just landed.
2. Scope cut: real-time streaming ingestion is out for this phase. Batch catalog updates only; Paloma documents the streaming design as a Q3 proposal instead.

Appreciate the disciplined run-up - this is what a boring, on-schedule big run should look like.

Dmitri

subject: ES-ENAS kickoff: compact RL controllers without extra cost
body:
Team,

Kicking off ES-ENAS hardening. The headline from our open-source release: combining evolution strategies with neural architecture search costs nothing extra - the controller proposes topologies (edges or partitions) to the same workers that evaluate ES perturbations, collecting rewards under weight sharing. For partners who need compact RL policies on constrained hardware, that's the pitch: smaller controllers, same training bill.

What's missing is production plumbing. The release ships client.py (aggregator) and server.py (workers) but leaves client-server communication as an exercise. We build the gRPC layer properly, plus repeatable experiment configs for edge mode (NumpyEdgeSparsityPolicy with the aggregate_edges search space) as the default.

Milestones for Feb 2 - May 4: gRPC comms layer by Feb 27, edge-mode benchmark suite by Mar 27, partition-mode + writeup and a follow-on plan by window close.

Santiago has staffing. Freya leads research side.

Anders

subject: Re: ES-ENAS kickoff: compact RL controllers without extra cost
body:
Anders,

One dependency to note: the topology controller in the release leans on a proposal-generation library that isn't open-sourced yet, so Freya is treating the code as a template and swapping in our internal evolutionary controller for suggest/feedback. That's a real chunk of her March.

Feb 27 comms milestone looks safe - Rosa has the proto definitions drafted already.

Santiago

subject: ES-ENAS status: edge-mode suite running, controller swap cost us
body:
Hi Anders, Santiago,

Status for the Mar 27 milestone. The edge-mode benchmark suite is running end to end on Rosa's gRPC layer - 2,000 workers, stable for 72-hour runs, aggregator restarts are clean. On our three locomotion benchmarks, edge-mode search (aggregate_edges space) finds policies matching the dense-baseline reward with 64% fewer edges on average. That's the compact-controller story we wanted.

The honest part: swapping the non-open-sourced proposal library for our internal evolutionary controller took three weeks, not two. Suggest/feedback semantics were easy; matching the weight-sharing behavior during topology updates was not - early runs regressed reward by ~15% until we fixed update ordering.

Risk for the partition-mode milestone: partition search spaces are larger and my current runs are converging slowly. May need to cap v1 at edge mode and document partitions as experimental. Will have a firm recommendation by Apr 10.

Freya

subject: Re: ES-ENAS status: edge-mode suite running, controller swap cost us
body:
All,

Close-out decisions for May 4, plus the follow-on plan.

Nice work all. This one ended where the kickoff said it would, which is rarer than it should be.

Anders

subject: ES-MAML kickoff: Hessian-free meta-learning for fast adaptation
body:
Team,

Kicking off the ES-MAML productization. Our open-source ES-MAML release does simple Hessian-free meta-learning via blackbox optimization, and the published follow-up showed rapidly adaptable legged-robot policies - that adaptation speed is what two robotics-adjacent partners are asking us for.

Scope: both algorithm families ship - Zero Order with its custom adaptation operators (blackbox operators like MCBlackboxOptimizer and DPP sampling) and First Order - behind one config surface (everything currently lives in config.py; that becomes a real experiment spec).

Milestones for Mar 16 - May 25: gRPC comms rebuilt and both algorithms running distributed by Apr 10, adaptation benchmark suite by May 8, partner-readiness review by May 22.

Deshawn owns staffing and budget - the meta-learning sweeps are worker-hungry, so fleet sizing is the first conversation.

Dmitri

subject: Re: ES-MAML kickoff: Hessian-free meta-learning for fast adaptation
body:
Dmitri,

Resourcing plan.

People: Umar 70% leading the algorithm work across Zero Order and First Order, Halima 80% on the distributed layer - regenerating the pb2/pb2_grpc bindings from the zero_order and first_order protos is day-one work, then the aggregator/worker fleet - and Maren 50% on the config-to-experiment-spec surface.

Budget: sorted this with Idris on Tuesday. Idris Osei has verbally earmarked $180k from Q3 discretionary compute budget line B-58 for this project, covering the adaptation-benchmark fleet and the July sim-to-real study. I'm building the Q3 fleet plan against that figure; paper allocation follows the OKR lock.

In-window compute: CPU worker fleet on the batch tier (ES workers, same pattern as our other blackbox stacks), roughly 1,500 concurrent workers at peak for the May benchmark suite. No GPU reservations needed.

Apr 10 looks achievable - Halima already has zero_order protos compiling.

Deshawn

subject: ES-MAML status: distributed runs green, zero-order adaptation wins
body:
Hi Dmitri, Deshawn,

Status ahead of the May 8 benchmark milestone.

Distributed is green: Halima's rebuilt gRPC layer runs both algorithm families across the fleet, hit the Apr 10 date, and has been stable through three 48-hour soak runs since.

Early benchmark reads: on our four-task locomotion adaptation suite, Zero Order with the MCBlackboxOptimizer adaptation operator reaches 85% of post-adaptation reward within 25 rollouts of a new task, versus 40+ rollouts for First Order at matched compute. DPP sampling for perturbation selection helps most in the low-rollout regime, which is exactly the sim-to-real-friendly region partners care about.

Risk: First Order results are noisier than published expectations at our worker count - gradient estimates degrade when worker returns arrive very asynchronously. Maren is adding a staleness cutoff to the aggregator. If that doesn't settle it by May 8, my recommendation is we lead with Zero Order for the partner review and mark First Order as tuning-in-progress.

Umar

subject: Re: ES-MAML status: distributed runs green, zero-order adaptation wins

Decisions from yesterday's partner-readiness review, ahead of the May 22 gate:

subject: Project Kestrel kickoff: ETC as our long-document encoder
body:
Team,

Kicking off the ETC standardization effort. Internally this effort is Project Kestrel - please use that name in docs, channels, and cluster job tags so everything rolls up cleanly.

The why: half the portfolio hits the same wall - Transformers that can't encode long or structured inputs. Our open-source ETC release solves exactly that (it's the EMNLP 2020 "Encoding Long and Structured Inputs in Transformers" work), and the repo already separates core Keras layers - compatible with both TF1 and TF2 - from the fine-tuning and example-generation code. We make it the paved path.

Milestones for Mar 2 - May 18: layers packaged with the unit-test suite (the discover -s etcmodel -p '*_test.py' set) green in CI by Mar 27, fine-tuning recipe reproduced on one long-document dataset from the release by Apr 24, adoption guide + review by May 15.

Santiago owns staffing and TPU capacity.

Dmitri

subject: Re: Project Kestrel kickoff: ETC as our long-document encoder
body:
Dmitri,

Kestrel resourcing.

People: Jorge 70% on packaging, CI, and the adoption guide; Umar 50% on the fine-tuning reproduction; Tereza 40% on example generation and dataset plumbing. All Kestrel jobs are tagged kestrel-* on the cluster side per Dmitri's ask.

Compute: fine-tuning wants TPU - the repo's cloud-TPU path (cloud-tpu-client) maps cleanly onto Cirrus, and I've requested a slice from our data-platforms quarterly allocation for April. CI and unit tests run on CPU; note the tests assume the working directory is the parent of the etcmodel folder, which bit us on day one, so the CI image pins that.

Risk to flag early: the Cirrus April window is shared with two other portfolio requests, and if we're bumped, Umar's Apr 24 reproduction milestone moves roughly a week. I'll know by Mar 20.

subject: Kestrel status: CI green, fine-tune under way, one packaging trade-off
body:

Kestrel status.

subject: Re: Kestrel status: CI green, fine-tune under way, one packaging trade-off

Strong finish, everyone.

subject: SpICE kickoff: intelligibility assessment as a service
body:
Team,

Kicking off the SpICE productization. Our open-source SpICE models take speech samples and output intelligibility on a 0-4 scale (typical, mild, moderate, severe, profound). The training base is what makes this defensible: 551,176 disordered-speech samples from 468 speakers, and published generalization without further training - 100% accuracy on TORGO, 0.93 correlation on UASpeech, 0.81 AUC on ALS-TDI PMP.

Product goal: a clinical-partner-facing assessment API with confidence reporting, starting from the released Keras classification model.

Milestones for Mar 9 - Jun 15: serving wrapper plus eval battery reproduced by Apr 17, realistic-speech validation (the unprompted-speech style set) by May 15, retrained pooled-corpus model and launch-review readiness by Jun 12. Privacy review starts now - disordered-speech audio is sensitive data and the SLA is 2-3 weeks.

Ivo owns staffing and the compute reservation.

Goran

subject: Re: SpICE kickoff: intelligibility assessment as a service
body:
Goran,

Resourcing and compute.

People: Linnea 80% on model work and the eval battery (TORGO, UASpeech, ALS-TDI PMP plus our realistic-speech set), Milan 70% on the serving wrapper and API, Paloma 40% on data pipelines, Emeka 50% on partner integration and the confidence-reporting layer.

Compute: inference-scale work rides Titan best-effort through April. The big item is the June retrain: we hold the cirrus-tpu reservation - 128 accelerators for the week of 2026-06-01 - for the full retraining run on the pooled corpus. That's sized from the half-million-utterance training base; one week covers the retrain plus two eval passes if configs are frozen beforehand.

Dependencies: privacy review filed Mar 16 (Kofi's queue). Also the released PyTorch variant is still "coming soon" upstream, so everything v1 is Keras/TFHub-based - fine for serving, worth noting for partners with torch stacks.

Apr 17 milestone looks solid.

Ivo

subject: SpICE status: eval battery reproduced, realistic speech is the hard part
body:
Hi Goran, Ivo,

Status.

Eval battery: reproduced on schedule in April. Our serving-wrapped model matches the published generalization numbers - TORGO at 100%, UASpeech correlation 0.93, ALS-TDI PMP 0.81 AUC - so Milan's wrapper isn't distorting anything.

Realistic speech is where it gets honest. On our unprompted-speech validation set (built to mirror the ~2,300-sample realistic set from the release, with dysarthric and control speakers), exact five-class agreement drops meaningfully versus prompted utterances - most confusion is between adjacent classes, mild vs moderate especially. Within-one-class agreement stays above 95%, which clinicians tell us is the operationally meaningful bar.

Recommendation: the API reports the predicted class plus an adjacent-class confidence band rather than a bare 0-4 score. Emeka has a mock partners liked.

Risk: pooled-corpus retraining configs need to freeze by May 29 for the June run. Any eval-battery change after that waits for the next cycle.

Linnea

subject: Re: SpICE status: eval battery reproduced, realistic speech is the hard part
body:
Team,

Decisions before the retrain window:

1. Confidence bands are in: the API ships predicted class + adjacent-class confidence, per Linnea's recommendation. The within-one-class >95% figure becomes our headline clinical metric, and we say plainly that exact-class on unprompted speech is weaker.
2. Retrain is a GO: our cirrus-tpu week (128 accelerators, week of June 1) starts Monday, and the retraining configs are frozen tonight. Linnea's freeze discipline made this easy - thank you.
3. Privacy: Kofi's review cleared May 20 with one condition, on-device redaction of any transcribable content in partner uploads. Paloma owns the implementation; it gates the launch review, not the retrain.

If the retrained model holds the eval battery, we walk into the June 12 launch-review checkpoint with a complete story.

Goran

subject: EvaNet kickoff: evolved video architectures for activity recognition
body:
Hi team,

Kicking off EvaNet productization for the vision portfolio. Our open-source release ships pretrained models from evolving space-time neural architectures, and the ensemble - RGB and optical-flow streams combined - hits 77.2% on the Kinetics-400 validation set (~19,200 videos in the November 2018 snapshot the release documents). Two partner teams want exactly this for activity recognition on their video archives.

Milestones for Apr 20 - Jul 27: inference reproduction of the released ensemble (the rgb1/rgb2/flow1/flow2 checkpoint combo) by May 22, partner-data evaluation with a served pipeline by Jun 26, launch review pre-read by Jul 20.

Known hard part going in: the flow stream needs precomputed optical flow (the release's sample data ships .npy flow inputs), and partners have raw video only. That pipeline is a first-class deliverable, not a footnote.

Deshawn owns staffing.

Lucia

subject: Re: EvaNet kickoff: evolved video architectures for activity recognition
body:
Lucia,

Staffing plan against the milestones.

Yusuf 70% on ensemble reproduction and eval methodology, Giannis 60% on serving, Halima 40% on partner-data ingestion. On the hard part you flagged: Rafael Duran is committed at 60% for May 2026 to own the optical-flow pipeline and the ensemble-evaluation work - that allocation is in the sheet and it's what makes the June milestone possible. Flow computation at partner-archive scale is the schedule driver, so his May is the whole ballgame.

Compute: inference reproduction is cheap (checkpoints run on a handful of Titan A100s). The June partner-data evaluation is bigger - flow precompute across ~40k archive videos - but still batch-friendly on Titan best-effort. No reservations requested.

One watch item: checkpoint download and the label_map/data assets moved when we mirrored the release internally; Giannis is checksumming everything so we don't silently eval with mismatched weights.

Deshawn

subject: EvaNet status: ensemble reproduced, flow cost is the trade-off
body:
Hi Lucia, Deshawn,

Status.

Reproduction: done May 20. Running the released four-checkpoint ensemble (rgb1, rgb2, flow1, flow2) through our mirrored assets gives 77.1% on Kinetics-400 validation - within noise of the published 77.2%, checksums clean. The HMDB cricket sample runs end to end through Giannis's serving path as a smoke test.

Partner eval: Rafael's flow pipeline is processing the archive now - throughput is at plan after he moved flow computation to batched GPU kernels (was 4x too slow on CPU).

The trade-off to line up for the pre-read: flow computation is ~70% of total inference cost. RGB-only (rgb1+rgb2) scores 74.3% on our partner validation slice vs 76.8% for the full ensemble. So the question for launch is whether 2.5 points buys a 3x cost multiplier. My lean: ship both modes, default RGB-only, flow as a "high-accuracy" tier.

Full partner-data numbers by Jun 24, two days ahead of gate.

Yusuf

subject: Re: EvaNet status: ensemble reproduced, flow cost is the trade-off
body:
Team,

Decision for the Jul 20 pre-read: adopting Yusuf's two-tier proposal exactly. Default tier is RGB-only at 74.3%, high-accuracy tier runs the full RGB+flow ensemble at 76.8%, priced to reflect the ~3x inference cost. Partners choose per-workload; the pre-read presents it as a cost/accuracy dial, not a compromise.

Also decided at portfolio review:
1. The June partner evaluation numbers held up (both partners saw within 0.5 points of our validation slice on their own archives), so the pilot commitment goes in the pre-read as evidence, not aspiration.
2. Scope cut: no fine-tuning on partner data in v1. Pretrained checkpoints only. Fine-tuning becomes the fast-follow with its own eval plan - trying to squeeze it in before Jul 27 was making the doc worse.

Deshawn, staffing shape holds through window close; nothing changes.

Thanks all - clean execution on this one.

Lucia

subject: Experience replay kickoff: replay-ratio guidance for every RL stack
body:
Team,

Kicking off the experience-replay standardization effort for agents-rl. Our open-source study revisited replay fundamentals - how replay capacity and the ratio of new-to-old experience drive value-based agent performance - and internal teams are still configuring buffers by folklore. We turn the findings into defaults.

Concretely, the released code exposes the levers cleanly: replay_capacity (1M in the reference config) and the replay ratio via oldest_policy_in_buffer (250k default), with the ElephantDQNAgent runner on Atari. Our deliverable is a sweep across those knobs on three internal environments plus Atari references, and a config guide with recommended settings per workload class.

Milestones for Apr 20 - Jun 29: sweep harness running by May 15, full sweep results by Jun 12, published guidance + adoption by two internal RL teams by window close.

Jelena owns staffing and data. Q3 OKR ties to adoption, so end date matters.

Ulla

subject: Re: Experience replay kickoff: replay-ratio guidance for every RL stack
body:
Ulla,

Staffing and dependencies.

People: Vera 70% on the sweep design and analysis, Milan 60% on the harness (gin-config plumbing around the ElephantDQNAgent runner, plus our internal envs), Saoirse 40% on results tooling and the guide.

Compute: the sweep is wide but each cell is cheap - I've sized it at 320 concurrent Titan A100 slots at peak in late May. Best-effort is fine; replay sweeps checkpoint well, so preemption costs us little.

Data: trajectory datasets for the internal environments come through Corpus. Timing works out - the Corpus v2 migration freeze is 2026-08-07, so our trajectory-dataset ingestion stays on the v1 path for the whole window and the migration lands after we're done. No v2 porting work on our plate.

Risk: the three internal environments have inconsistent episode-boundary conventions; Milan found two already. Harness normalizes them, but that's the likeliest source of a late surprise.

Jelena

subject: Re: Experience replay kickoff: replay-ratio guidance for every RL stack
body:
Hi Ulla, Jelena,

Sweep results, four days late against Jun 12 (one internal env needed a rerun after an episode-boundary fix - Jelena called that risk in May).

Headlines: the published finding replicates internally. Increasing replay capacity from 1M upward helps or is neutral in every configuration we tested, and performance is far more sensitive to the replay ratio than to capacity - moving oldest_policy_in_buffer from 250k to 2.5M swings our internal envs by up to 23% final return, dwarfing any capacity effect. Uniform sampling with a well-chosen ratio beat prioritized replay with defaults on two of three internal envs, which will surprise people.

Guidance doc structure: three workload classes, each with a recommended capacity/ratio pair and a "when to deviate" note. Draft to Saoirse's tooling Friday; on track for adoption conversations the week of Jun 22.

One trade-off for the guide: the largest-capacity configs cost 2x memory for <1% return. We recommend against them explicitly.

Vera

subject: Explainable routing kickoff: 'why is my route different today?'
body:
Team,

Kicking off the explainable-routing effort. Our open-source release implements the "Why is My Route Different Today?" algorithm, generating explanations for route selection over a collection of synthetically-generated traffic scenarios on OSM-derived graphs - the release ships processed Baden and Washington region graphs. Mapping and logistics partners keep telling us the same thing: users don't distrust reroutes because they're wrong, they distrust them because they're unexplained.

Deliverable: an explanation service over our internal routing testbed, with quality evaluation on both released regions plus one partner-shaped scenario set.

Milestones for Apr 6 - Jul 6: C++ build productionized (it's currently a CMake/Abseil research build with hand-run steps) and scenarios reproducing by May 1, explanation-quality eval framework by May 29, partner demo with the plotly-based visualizations replaced by a real front end by Jun 26.

Daniela owns staffing.

Anders

subject: Re: Explainable routing kickoff: 'why is my route different today?'
body:
Anders,

Resourcing for the window.

Milan 60% on the build productionization and service scaffolding, Gustavo 50% on the scenario tooling and the subgraph caching (cached subgraphs are what make repeated runs fast, so that layer needs to be solid), Wei 30% advising on eval methodology. The anchor: Rafael Duran is committed at 60% for May 2026 to drive the explanation-quality evaluation and the scenario-generation extensions - I've booked him at that level in the allocation sheet. The May 29 eval-framework milestone is his deliverable.

Compute: trivial by portfolio standards - this is CPU-bound graph computation. The one infra ask is a beefy-memory batch tier for the Washington-region runs; loading is much faster with compiler optimizations (Release build) but memory is the constraint.

Risk: the partner-shaped scenario set doesn't exist yet, and Rafael can't start eval design against it until Gustavo's generator handles partner road-network densities. Sequencing is tight in early May.

Daniela

subject: Explainable routing status: both regions reproducing, eval design question
body:
Hi Anders, Daniela,

Status. Milan hit the May 1 build milestone: the CMake/Abseil build is containerized, Release-mode only (the compiler-optimization difference on graph loading is dramatic - about 6x on Washington), and both released regions - baden-processed and washington-processed - reproduce the reference explanation outputs. Gustavo's subgraph caching brings repeated scenario runs from ~40 min to under 4.

Rafael's eval framework is mid-flight for May 29. One design question we want a PM read on: explanation quality has two axes - faithfulness (does the explanation reflect the actual cost differences that flipped the route?) and comprehensibility (would a user accept it?). Faithfulness we can score automatically against scenario ground truth; comprehensibility needs human raters. A 300-explanation rater study adds roughly two weeks and modest cost.

My recommendation: do it. A partner demo claiming "explanations" with no human-acceptance number invites the obvious question.

Wei

subject: Re: Explainable routing status: both regions reproducing, eval design question
body:
All,

Decisions:

1. Rater study approved - Wei's argument won on contact. To protect the Jun 26 demo date we run it at 200 explanations instead of 300 and in parallel with demo prep, results folded in by Jul 2. The demo itself leads with faithfulness numbers (Rafael's framework scores 96% faithful on Baden, 93% on Washington) and cites the rater study as "in flight".
2. Scope cut: the partner-shaped scenario set covers one partner density profile, not both. Gustavo's generator handles the denser urban profile first; the sparse-rural profile becomes a Q3 item. Sequencing risk from April basically forced this and I'd rather cut it cleanly.
3. Front end: Milan's replacement for the plotly flow is good enough - we're not polishing further before the demo.

Q3 OKR framing lands next week; flag conflicts before Friday.

Anders

subject: Risk-explanation kickoff: explaining why risk went up, not just that it did
body:
Team,

Kicking off the risk-explanation productization. Our open-source release trains a model that generates a sequence of risk predictions over clinical observation records and - the part hospital partners actually want - explains increases as weights over the inputs. A risk score that jumps overnight with no explanation gets ignored by clinicians; one that says "these three observations drove it" gets used.

The codebase already speaks the right dialect: tf.SequenceExample in TFRecord format with FHIR-style observation features (Observation.code, value.quantity, harmonized valueset names) and labels like in_hospital_death. Partners are FHIR shops, so ingestion is genuinely close.

Milestones for Mar 23 - Jun 22: training reproduction on the reference data by Apr 17, explanation-quality review with a clinical advisor by May 22, partner-pilot readiness (including privacy sign-off - health data, so we file immediately) by Jun 19.

Jelena owns staffing and platform dependencies.

Dmitri

subject: Re: Risk-explanation kickoff: explaining why risk went up, not just that it did
body:
Dmitri,

Staffing and dependencies.

People: Vera 60% on the observation-sequence model and explanation weights, Bilal 70% on ingestion and the TFRecord/SequenceExample pipeline (batch sizes 64 train / 128 eval per the reference input_fn setup carry over fine), Gustavo 40% on eval tooling and the clinical-review packet.

Platform dependencies: our reference and partner-shaped data flows through Corpus. On timing - Corpus v2 migration freeze is 2026-07-24, which gives us two clear weeks after window close to port our SequenceExample ingestion to the v2 path - so no migration work lands inside this project's schedule. I've planned Bilal's quarter on that basis.

Compute: light. Training the observation sequence model is a single-node job; a dozen Titan A100 slots at peak for the hyperparameter passes.

Privacy: filed Mar 26 with Kofi, so the 2-3 week SLA has sign-off landing around mid-April, well before any partner data touches us.

Jelena

subject: Risk-explanation status: reproduction done, explanation stability is the real question
body:
Hi Dmitri, Jelena,

Status.

Reproduction landed Apr 15: the observation-sequence model trains cleanly on the reference in_hospital_death task (20k train steps as in the example config), AUC within 0.4 points of our expected band, and the explanation weights over input observations look sensible on spot checks - dense_sequence_feature attributions concentrate on the harmonized observation values you'd clinically expect.

The deeper issue for the May 22 clinical review: explanation stability. When we retrain with a different seed, the risk predictions barely move but the attribution weights shift noticeably - top-3 attributed observations overlap only ~70% across seeds. Clinicians will (rightly) ask why the same patient gets different explanations from "the same" model.

Plan: Gustavo is adding an ensemble-attribution mode (average weights over 5 seeds), which lifts top-3 overlap to 91% in early tests at 5x explanation-time cost. Explanation latency isn't clinical-loop critical, so I think that trade is right. Review packet will show both modes.

Vera

subject: Re: Risk-explanation status: reproduction done, explanation stability is the real question
body:
Team,

Decisions ahead of the Jun 19 pilot-readiness gate:

1. Ensemble attribution is the only mode we ship. The clinical review on May 22 was unambiguous - the advisor said single-seed explanations would erode trust within a week, and the 91% top-3 overlap number was the difference between a polite meeting and an engaged one. Single-seed stays as an internal debug mode.
2. Pilot scope: one partner, retrospective data only, no live clinical use. That matches Kofi's April sign-off conditions exactly (thanks for the tight turnaround, Kofi - cleared Apr 14, inside the SLA).
3. Scope cut: multi-label support (beyond in_hospital_death) moves to the next phase. Bilal's ingestion generalizes already, but validating explanations per label is real work we shouldn't rush.

Vera, Gustavo - the review packet was the best clinical-facing doc this portfolio has produced. Reuse it as the template.

Dmitri

subject: Kickoff: extreme-memorization diagnostics track (Feb-May)
body:
Hi Ivo, team,

Kicking off the extreme-memorization workstream under data-platforms. Goal: turn the initialization-scale findings into a training-diagnostics feature for Corpus customers — specifically, surface the representation and gradient alignment scalars our open-source release already logs to TensorBoard as an early-warning signal for memorization.

Milestones: repro on CIFAR-10 and SVHN by end of Feb; alignment-metric API draft mid-March; internal dogfood by Apr 20; launch review before May 4.

Ownership: Amara and Saoirse take the tfrecord ingestion path, Rafael the MLP/convnet sweeps, Bilal the TensorBoard plumbing. I'll send a milestone doc Friday — flag anything that makes the end-of-Feb repro unrealistic.

Thanks,
Dmitri

subject: Re: Kickoff: extreme-memorization diagnostics track (Feb-May)
body:
Dmitri — resourcing picture from my side.

Staffing: Amara 50%, Saoirse 40%, Rafael 60%, Bilal 30% through April. Compute is modest — the sweeps are MLP/convnet scale, so titan-a100 best-effort covers us; I'm asking for ~64 A100s peak during the stddev sweep (we vary the w_1 custom_init stddev from 1e-3 upward, per the paper's setup).

Two constraints. First, storage: the shuffled_labels runs double our checkpoint volume, so I've requested 40TB scratch. Second, sequencing: the Corpus v2 migration freeze lands 2026-07-10, so all of our tfrecord re-ingestion for cifar10/cifar100/svhn has to be finished well before that freeze — Jun Varga's team confirmed the date. Plan assumes no new asks after the Q3 OKR lock.

Ivo

subject: Status: alignment-metric repro + one risk
body:
Quick status.

Repro is in decent shape: the MLP with relu at 1024 hidden units matches the paper's memorization curve on CIFAR-10, and the sin-activation runs reproduce the extreme-memorization regime once we push the custom_init stddev high. Gradient alignment scalars are flowing into TensorBoard from every run, and Bilal's exporter maps them into the API draft schema.

Risk worth flagging: on shuffled-labels CIFAR-100 the alignment signal goes noisy late in training, so the early-warning threshold we pitch to Corpus customers will likely need per-dataset calibration — call it two extra weeks of sweeps. Also, SVHN ingestion is behind; the extracted archive layout differs from the cifar sets and Amara had to rewrite the loader.

Propose we hold the Apr 20 dogfood date but decide on SVHN by end of March.

Rafael

subject: Re: Status: alignment-metric repro + one risk
body:
Thanks Rafael. Decision from yesterday's sync: we cut SVHN from the May scope. Dogfood on Apr 20 ships with CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 only; SVHN moves to a fast-follow once ingestion stabilizes. Rationale: the per-dataset calibration risk you raised is the real work, and I'd rather spend Amara's cycles there than on a third loader.

For launch review (Apr 29 slot with Nadia's board) I need: the alignment-threshold writeup, the two-dataset dogfood results, and a one-pager on how this lands in the Corpus dashboard. Ivo — please confirm staffing holds through the review; no change to the 40TB scratch ask.

One more thing: keep the word memorization out of customer-facing copy until legal has seen it. "Training diagnostics" is fine.

Dmitri

subject: Kickoff: FNet low-cost encoder track (Q2)
body:
Team — kicking off the FNet productionization track.

Why we care: FNet swaps every self-attention sublayer for an unparameterized Fourier transform, which makes it a natural fit for the low-cost encoder tier data-platforms wants to offer — near-Transformer quality at a fraction of serving cost.

Plan inside the Q2 window: (1) env bring-up and the f_net unit-test suite green by Mar 31; (2) the C4 pre-training run in early June on our TPU reservation; (3) GLUE fine-tuning matrix by Jun 15; (4) launch review before Jun 22.

Ownership: Hyun modeling, Kaia the pre-training config, Nikhil evals, Jorge infra. Jelena will follow up on the compute picture. First sync Thursday 10:00.

Dmitri

subject: Re: Kickoff: FNet low-cost encoder track (Q2)
body:
Dmitri — compute and staffing for the plan.

Staffing: Hyun 60%, Kaia 50%, Nikhil 40%, Jorge 30% (Jorge also carries the cloud-tpu-client tooling).

Compute: the C4 pre-training run is sized for a TPU v5 slice. We hold the cirrus-tpu reservation for the week of 2026-06-01 — 384 accelerators — and Ines's team has it in the books, so the full pre-train fits in that window with roughly 20% headroom. Fine-tuning is cheap; GLUE runs go to titan-a100 best-effort.

Dependencies: the SentencePiece c4_bpe vocab model is already mirrored internally, and the Jax/Flax stack matches what Shipyard serves, so no new serving work.

One constraint: if pre-training slips past that week we're into quarterly reallocation territory, so Mar 31 env bring-up is a hard date.

Jelena

subject: Status: FNet GLUE dry runs + eval harness quirk
body:
Status on evals.

Using the small-scale checkpoint Kaia pre-trained on the C4 sample, GLUE dry runs look consistent with the paper's story: we're within about 2.5 points of our BERT-size baseline on the dev average while training steps run roughly 6x faster on the same hardware.

Two flags. First, the released test harness assumes the working directory is the parent of the f_net folder — Evalline's runner doesn't do that by default, so Tomas's team gave us a shim; fine for now, but our numbers aren't yet in the shared leaderboard format. Second, the MNLI fine-tunes are the long pole (~4h each on best-effort A100s); if titan is congested in late May the matrix slips. Mitigation: run MNLI and QQP first.

Nikhil

subject: Re: Status: FNet GLUE dry runs + eval harness quirk
body:
Team — decisions from this morning's checkpoint.

The June pre-train completed within the reserved window, so we're committing to the launch-review slot on Jun 18 with Nadia's board. Scope decision: we present the low-cost encoder tier on the full GLUE matrix minus WNLI (tiny, noisy, not worth a slide). Nikhil's final numbers land Jun 15; Kaia writes the model card from the C4 pre-training config.

On serving, Zeke's team will host the demo endpoint on Shipyard staging — Jorge, please hand them the checkpoint by Jun 12.

Known risk we disclose at review: the quality gap versus the attention baseline is real, about 2-3 GLUE points. Our pitch is cost, not parity.

Nice work getting the pre-train through cleanly.

Dmitri

subject: Kickoff: SQIF factoring evaluation (Q2)
body:
Team — kicking off the SQIF factoring assessment.

Context: our open-source release implements the Schnorr-plus-quantum-optimization factoring approach, with a QAOA method and a classical bruteforce method for finding low-energy states of the hamiltonian. Leadership wants a sober internal read on how far this actually scales before anyone quotes it externally.

Deliverables inside the window: reproducible conda environment and CLI harness by Mar 16; bruteforce baselines across bitsizes through April; qaoa_depth and lattice-parameter sweeps in June; a written evaluation with Launch Review Board sign-off by Jun 29.

Ownership: Rosa the harness, Farah the baselines, Giannis sweep automation, Halima the analysis. Bruno follows up on staffing and compute.

Lucia

subject: Re: Kickoff: SQIF factoring evaluation (Q2)
body:
Lucia — resourcing for the plan.

Staffing: Rosa 50%, Farah 40%, Giannis 40%, Halima 60% through June.

Compute: bruteforce baselines are CPU-bound and run on standard pools. The June QAOA sweeps are the expensive part — we simulate circuits across qaoa_depth 1-8 with num_samples up to 10k per configuration — and we've sized that to the big accelerator slice: we hold the cirrus-tpu reservation for the week of 2026-06-15, 384 accelerators, which covers the full sweep grid with margin.

Ask: freeze the sweep configs by Jun 8 so we don't burn reserved capacity on config churn. One more line item — 5TB object storage for sampled low-energy states.

If the harness slips past Mar 16 the whole tail compresses, so flag early.

Bruno

subject: Status: baselines done, QAOA pilot read
body:
Status on the evaluation.

Baselines: with the bruteforce method we factor test integers reliably up to the low-30s bitsize range; runtime is dominated by the lattice search and results are stable across seeds.

QAOA pilot: at qaoa_depth 2 the sampler recovers usable low-energy states on maybe half the seeds for 16-20 bit inputs, and outcomes are very sensitive to the precision_parameter — small changes flip success to failure. Honest read: nothing yet contradicts the skeptical takes on this method's scaling, and our report should say so plainly.

Risk for June: if the depth>4 sweeps behave like the pilot, most of the reserved capacity produces null results — still a publishable answer, but we should pre-agree the framing with Lucia so the report can't be spun as a capability claim.

Halima

subject: Re: Status: baselines done, QAOA pilot read
body:
Halima, all — decisions after yesterday's readout.

We frame the June results exactly as measured: the QAOA path does not demonstrate scaling beyond small bitsizes, and the classical bruteforce baseline remains the stronger method at every size we tested. The report title drops "quantum advantage" entirely.

Scope cut: no sweeps beyond depth 6 — the depth-5/6 grids already show the null pattern Halima predicted, and burning more reserved time doesn't change the conclusion.

Remaining work: Giannis finalizes the seed-variance appendix; Rosa tags the harness release so external folks can reproduce our numbers with the documented main.py flags. Launch Review Board sign-off is booked for Jun 26; Kofi has already seen the claims language.

Thanks for keeping this one honest.

Lucia

subject: Kickoff: city relighting track (May-Aug)
body:
Team — kicking off the city relighting track.

The research decomposes stacks of street panoramas into intrinsic components — log reflectance and log shading — and can relight the same scene under new illumination. Product-wise that's the missing piece for consistent map imagery across capture times.

Plan: (1) repro the pretrained checkpoint on the NYC sample stack by May 15 — note the code pins Python 3.7-era deps, so environments are their own task; (2) alignment pipeline for our own capture stacks by end of June — the release runs twenty gradient-descent steps with frozen weights per new stack; (3) internal relighting demo mid-July; (4) launch review before Aug 3.

Daniela follows up on staffing. Carmen owns decomposition quality, Wanjiru and Oyin the pipeline, Chiara env/tooling, Bilal the eval harness.

Dmitri

subject: Re: Kickoff: city relighting track (May-Aug)
body:
Dmitri — staffing and infra for the relighting track.

Allocations: Carmen 50% throughout; Wanjiru 40% May-June rising to 60% in July for the demo push; Chiara 30%; Bilal 30% from June. And Oyin Iversen is committed at 60% to this project for July 2026 — she's the only person here who has run the alignment optimization at scale, so the July demo critically depends on that allocation holding.

Compute is light: decomposition and alignment fit on 8-16 A100s best-effort on titan. Storage: 12TB for panorama stacks.

One dependency — our own capture stacks come through Corpus ingestion, and with the v2 migration freeze on 2026-07-10 I want our stack imports done by early July so we're not importing during the freeze.

Daniela

subject: Status: repro clean, alignment on our stacks is harder
body:
Status.

Repro: the pretrained checkpoint reproduces the paper's decomposition on the NYC sample — reflectance layers are stable across the stack and shading captures the illumination variation. Bilal's harness scores reconstruction PSNR within 0.3dB of reference.

Our own stacks are harder. Capture intervals are longer than the NYC data, and the stock twenty alignment steps with frozen weights aren't always enough — on 4 of our 15 pilot stacks, alignment settles into a visibly wrong local minimum. Wanjiru is testing 40-step schedules plus a coarse pre-align; early signs are good but it doubles per-stack cost.

Risk: if we end up needing manual QA per stack, the July demo shrinks to a curated subset. Recommend we decide demo scope by Jul 1.

Carmen

subject: Re: Status: repro clean, alignment on our stacks is harder
body:
Carmen, all — decision from Monday's review: the July demo runs on a curated set of 40 stacks that pass automatic alignment cleanly. The 40-step schedule with coarse pre-align becomes the default, and full no-touch automation moves to next quarter. Nobody outside the team sees the four bad-minimum examples until we can show the fix.

For the Aug launch review I need: the demo reel, the PSNR table against the open-source checkpoint, and a cost slide — the doubled per-stack alignment cost matters for the productization story.

Oyin and Wanjiru, the demo pipeline is yours through July as staffed. Bilal — freeze the eval harness by Jul 24 so the numbers in the deck are final.

Good trajectory, everyone.

Dmitri

subject: Kickoff: Project Basalt — unified dataset interface
body:
Team — kicking off what we're calling Project Basalt internally: productizing our unified TFDS interface that fronts 20 segmentation and detection datasets (ADE20K, COCO, CityScapes, Mapillary, and the rest) behind standardized feature names.

The pitch for data-platforms: one loader, one schema — image, segmentation, boxes, person_keypoints — so experiment code runs unchanged across datasets, including the MSeg universal-taxonomy channel where every dataset shares one label space.

Milestones: feature-parity audit against fids_features.py by Feb 27; licensing review of all 20 sources by mid-March (WildDash is already excluded from redistribution; Kofi should confirm the others); Corpus integration prototype in April; launch review by May 4.

Bruno owns the resourcing follow-up. Please use the Basalt name on docs and threads so search works.

Dmitri

subject: Re: Kickoff: Project Basalt — unified dataset interface
body:
Dmitri — Basalt resourcing.

Staffing: Csilla 50% (taxonomy and feature audit), Rosa 50% (loaders and TFDS packaging), Quentin 30% (MSeg universal mapping QA), Umar 30% (Corpus integration).

Compute is negligible — this is an ingestion project — but storage isn't: mirroring the 19 redistributable datasets runs about 9TB raw plus 4TB in TFDS-prepared form, so I've filed a 15TB Corpus quota request with Jun's team.

Dependencies: Corpus integration has to land while the v2 APIs are still moving toward the 2026-07-10 migration freeze. We're well ahead of it, but Umar's prototype should target the v2 write path directly rather than v1 to avoid a rewrite.

Ask from you: a prioritized list of which datasets the first Corpus customers actually need, so Rosa doesn't burn March packaging long-tail sets.

Bruno

subject: Status: Basalt feature audit + licensing risk
body:
Status on the audit.

Good news: the standardized schema holds up — id/image/segmentation features are consistent everywhere, background is always class 0 with dataset-specific classes above it, and the segmentation_mseg_universal channel gives us the single shared label space we promised.

Gaps to know about: person_keypoints exists only where the source provides it (COCO being the main one), and box_labels one-hot dimensions differ per dataset, so downstream code needs the per-dataset class count from the feature spec — Rosa is adding that to loader metadata.

Risk: licensing. Beyond WildDash (already excluded), two more sources carry research-only clauses that may block Corpus redistribution. Kofi's review is the gate and his SLA is 2-3 weeks, which puts an answer mid-April — tight against the integration prototype. Suggest Umar builds against the unambiguous sets first.

Csilla

subject: Re: Status: Basalt feature audit + licensing risk
body:
Csilla, all — decisions from the Basalt sync.

We go to launch review (Apr 29 slot) with a tiered scope: v1 exposes the twelve datasets Kofi has cleared unconditionally; the research-only sources ship behind an internal-use flag with the license text surfaced in the loader; WildDash stays out entirely.

Quentin's MSeg mapping QA gets one more week — the universal-taxonomy channel is our headline feature and I don't want mapping bugs in the demo. Umar, the integration prototype targets the cleared twelve only; Rosa, cut the packaging long-tail per the priority list.

One admin note: keep tagging everything Project Basalt in docs and the tracker — a couple of untagged threads went missing last week.

Nice work getting the audit done early.

Dmitri

subject: Kickoff: fair submodular selection for retrieval slates
body:
Team — kicking off the fair submodular selection track for graphs-retrieval.

The research gives us streaming submodular maximization under a matroid constraint with fairness guarantees — exactly the machinery we need for retrieval slates that must balance coverage against per-group quotas. Product framing: a candidate-selection library the retrieval stack can call, with fairness constraints declared per surface.

Plan for the window: (1) port the C++17 reference into our build by Feb 27; (2) reproduce the maximum-coverage experiment on the Pokec social graph, including the attribute-extraction preprocessing, by end of March; (3) benchmark against our current re-ranker on internal retrieval logs in April; (4) integration proposal plus launch-review pre-read by May 25.

Freya owns algorithms, Umar experiments, Fumiko the internal-logs benchmark. Ivo will cover staffing and budget.

Anders

subject: Re: Kickoff: fair submodular selection for retrieval slates
body:
Anders — resourcing notes.

Staffing: Freya 50%, Umar 50%, Fumiko 40% through May; no hires needed.

Compute for the repro phase is trivial — the streaming algorithms are single-machine C++, and the Pokec preprocessing (extract-attributes, color-vertices, the BMI graph cleanup) runs on a workstation. The real cost is the April benchmark on internal retrieval logs: replaying a month of logs through candidate selection at scale needs a proper batch allocation, and that lands in Q3 procurement cycles.

On that: Idris has verbally earmarked $180k from Q3 discretionary compute budget line B-74 for this project, which covers the log-replay benchmark plus a production shadow test. I'll get it in writing before the Q3 OKR lock on Jun 26.

Storage: 2TB for graph artifacts. Constraint: Fumiko is out the last week of March.

Ivo

subject: Status: Pokec repro matches, internal logs bind harder
body:
Status.

The port compiles clean under C++17 and the oracle interfaces (SubmodularFunction / Matroid subclasses) mapped onto our retrieval scoring with less than a day of glue.

Repro: on Pokec maximum coverage we match the paper's pattern — the fair streaming algorithm gives up single-digit-percent coverage versus unconstrained greedy while satisfying the per-group constraints exactly; our runs land within noise of the reference implementation.

Internal-logs pilot (Fumiko): early replays show the fairness constraint binds much harder on our data than on Pokec — group skew is worse — so the utility cost is closer to 8-9% on some surfaces. That's the number product will care about; we should present it per-surface, not averaged.

Risk: partition-matroid config per surface is manual right now. Freya's config-generation tool is the fix but adds a week.

Umar

subject: Re: Status: Pokec repro matches, internal logs bind harder
body:
Umar, all — wrapping decisions for the window.

We take the integration proposal to the May 21 pre-read as per-surface opt-in: surfaces adopt the fair selector where the measured utility cost clears their quality bar, with the 8-9% worst-case number stated up front rather than the blended average. Freya's config-generation tool is in scope — manual matroid config would kill adoption, worth the extra week.

Fumiko, the pre-read needs the per-surface table plus the Pokec repro as an external-validity anchor.

Two carries into Q3: the shadow test on live traffic and the log-replay benchmark at full scale, both funded from the discretionary line Ivo secured. I'll ask Nadia for a Launch Review Board slot early in Q3.

Good, disciplined quarter.

Anders

subject: Kickoff: fast gradient clipping for DP-SGD
body:
Team — kicking off the fast gradient clipping adoption track.

Context: DP-SGD's per-example gradient clipping is the tax every privacy-sensitive training job pays, and our open-source release of the unified fast gradient clipping framework shows how to cut it substantially. Goal for the window: land the framework in the internal DP training stack and publish before/after cost numbers privacy teams can budget against.

Milestones: repro the paper's runtime-profiling experiments (fully connected, embedding, and BERT targets) by May 1; integration behind a flag by May 29; adoption guide plus a cost memo to the privacy council by Jun 19, ahead of the Q3 OKR lock on Jun 26.

Leilani owns integration, Bilal profiling, Csilla the correctness review, Vera the BERT-scale runs. Bruno follows up on staffing.

Zofia

subject: Re: Kickoff: fast gradient clipping for DP-SGD
body:
Zofia — resourcing.

Staffing: Leilani 50% through the window, Bilal 40% (profiling then integration support), Csilla 25% for the correctness review. And Vera Egede is committed at 60% to this project for June 2026 for the BERT-scale runs and the cost memo — those runs are the deliverable the privacy council actually reads, so I've protected that allocation explicitly.

Compute: the profiling replays (fc1/fc2, emb1, bert1 targets) fit on 8 A100s best-effort; the June BERT-scale comparison wants 64 A100s for about ten days — filed on titan, no reservation needed.

One gap flagged in the repo: peak-memory profiling assumes internal tooling we don't have, so Bilal will wire our own profiler into the get_compute_profile functions in profiling_tools.py.

Heads-up: vulcan maintenance Jun 22-24 doesn't touch us since we're on titan.

Bruno

subject: Status: profiling repro + an integration snag
body:
Status on profiling and integration.

Repro: runtime results line up with the paper — the fast clipping path shows clear gains over naive per-example clipping on the fully connected targets (fc1), and especially on the embedding-layer experiment (emb1), where the gap widens with vocab size. Our profiler is now wired into get_compute_profile and get_train_bert_model_compute_profile, so we get peak-memory curves the public repo can't produce. On bert1, fast clipping keeps peak memory roughly flat where the naive path grows with batch size — that's the headline for the cost memo.

Risk: Leilani's integration flag currently conflicts with our momentum-optimizer wrapper — in one code path gradients get clipped after accumulation instead of before. Fix is understood but touches the optimizer interface; adds maybe four days. Still tracking May 29 for the flag.

Bilal

subject: Re: Status: profiling repro + an integration snag
body:
Team — decisions from today's review.

The integration ships this week default-off, with the optimizer-ordering fix Leilani and Bilal landed; privacy-sensitive teams opt in per job.

Vera's June runs are far enough along to commit headline numbers to the cost memo: at BERT scale we're seeing the DP-SGD clipping overhead cut roughly in half, with peak memory flat across batch sizes — and Csilla signed off on correctness. The memo goes to the privacy council Jun 18, and I'm writing the Q3 OKR proposing default-on for new DP jobs, which needs to land before the Jun 26 lock.

Remaining risk is adoption, not tech: teams distrust anything touching gradients, so the memo leads with the correctness review.

Thanks all — textbook quarter so far.

Zofia

subject: Kickoff: sparse convnets on-device track
body:
Team — kicking off the sparse convnets on-device track.

Our open-source release ships TF-Lite models where sparse MobileNetV1 at width 1.0 hits 68.4% top-1 at 90% sparsity with 31ms latency on a Snapdragon 835 — numbers that make an edge-inference tier credible.

Goals this window: (1) validate the published latency table on our current device-lab hardware by May 15; (2) stand up the conversion pipeline for customer models with the paper's sparsity recipe — block size 4 in the last inverted-residual block for V1; (3) run a human-rating study on perceived quality of on-device classifications versus the dense baseline, since top-1 deltas undersell perceived regressions; (4) go/no-go readout by Jul 24.

Vera owns models, Freya the sparsity recipe, Paloma tooling, Nikhil evals. Alina follows up on staffing.

Zofia

subject: Re: Kickoff: sparse convnets on-device track
body:
Zofia — resourcing.

Staffing: Vera 40% (heavily committed elsewhere in June, so her model-validation work front-loads into May), Freya 50%, Nikhil 40%, Paloma 50%.

Device lab: two weeks of exclusive time on the Snapdragon rigs in May — booked. Compute for retraining sparse variants: 32 A100s best-effort, fine on titan.

The biggest new line item is the human-rating study: there's no shared tool for side-by-side image-classification ratings, so we're scoping and building a human-rating annotation UI from scratch. Paloma has the design doc — roughly six engineer-weeks covering rater queues, pair presentation, and agreement stats — targeting a working tool by mid-June for a July rating round. Raters come through the vendor pool Nadia's PMO manages.

Flag if six weeks feels heavy, but I'd rather own the tool than bodge spreadsheets.

Alina

subject: Status: latency table doesn't transfer 1:1, accuracy does
body:
Status.

Latency validation: on current device-lab hardware the sparse models are consistently faster than dense equivalents, but the published SD835 table doesn't transfer linearly — on newer SoCs the sparse MobileNetV2 1.15 (85% sparsity) shows a smaller relative win because dense baselines got better silicon support. We'll publish our own table rather than quoting the paper's.

Accuracy repro is clean: mbv1 at width 1.0 and 90% sparsity lands at 68.4% top-1 as documented. Conversion pipeline: Freya's recipe reproduces the block-sparse structure (block size 2 from inverted-residual block 11 onward for V2), and Paloma's tooling now converts a customer model end-to-end.

Risk: the annotation UI is a week behind — rater-queue auth took longer than scoped — which squeezes the July rating round to two weeks. Recommend holding scope: pairs-only rating, no free-text.

Nikhil

subject: Re: Status: latency table doesn't transfer 1:1, accuracy does
body:
Team — decisions from the go/no-go prep.
