We proceed to the Jul 24 readout recommending the edge-inference tier, on the strength of our own latency table — device-lab numbers only, with the paper's SD835 figures as historical reference.

The rating round ran the trimmed pairs-only protocol on the new UI; with about 1,900 rated pairs, human-perceived quality of the 85-90% sparse models is statistically indistinguishable from dense on our demo distribution, which closes the perceived-regression question.

Scope cuts final: no free-text feedback this round, and the EfficientNet variants move to Q4 — fully unstructured sparsity needs different kernels than the MobileNet path.

Paloma — package the annotation tool docs; other teams will want it. Readout deck reviews Wednesday.

Zofia

subject: Kickoff: federated vision benchmark suite
body:
Team — kicking off the federated vision benchmark track for trust-theory.

Our open-source splits give us realistic non-IID client distributions — Landmarks-User-160k with 1,262 users over 2,028 classes, and the iNaturalist splits with both per-user and geographic partitions — which is exactly what our federated-learning claims need to be evaluated against, instead of synthetic CIFAR shards.

Goal: a Meridian-internal federated eval suite on Evalline with these splits as the default benchmark, plus ingestion of partner-contributed imagery into the same user-partitioned format.

Milestones: splits ingested and TFF-compatible by May 8; Evalline harness integration by Jun 5; partner-data pipeline (with de-dup and QA) by early July; readout Jul 17.

Bilal and Emeka own ingestion, Gustavo the TFF harness, Halima analysis. Alina follows up on resourcing.

Ximena

subject: Re: Kickoff: federated vision benchmark suite
body:
Ximena — resourcing for the benchmark track.

Staffing: Bilal 40%, Emeka 50%, Gustavo 50%, Halima 30% rising in June for analysis. Compute: federated simulation rounds on the Landmarks split are surprisingly cheap — 16 A100s best-effort covers the baseline matrix. Storage: 6TB for the public splits plus partner imagery.

The real build is data quality. Partner imagery overlaps heavily with itself and with the public sets, and duplicate leakage across simulated clients would corrupt every non-IID claim we make — so we're scoping and staffing a dataset de-duplication pipeline from scratch: Emeka leads, near-duplicate detection via perceptual hashing plus embedding similarity, batch mode first, about five engineer-weeks with a target of mid-June. I looked for an off-the-shelf internal tool and didn't find one that handles cross-client leakage.

Flag if the five weeks needs a trade.

Alina

subject: Status: Evalline integration live, de-dup throughput risk
body:
Status.

Evalline integration: the TFF-compatible loaders are wired into the harness and the baseline matrix ran end-to-end last week. Numbers behave as the paper leads you to expect — models that look fine on IID shards drop hard under real user partitioning; on Landmarks-User-160k our FedAvg baseline loses double-digit accuracy versus centralized training, and the iNaturalist-Geo partition is harsher still at the extreme client sizes (down to 11 examples per client at the small end). That gap is the point of the benchmark, so the harness reports both partitionings side by side.

Risk: Emeka's de-dup pipeline works but throughput is about 4x slower than planned on the embedding-similarity stage; at current speed partner ingestion finishes Jul 10, leaving one week of slack before readout. Options: GPU-batch the embedding stage, or drop to hash-only for this round.

Gustavo

subject: Re: Status: Evalline integration live, de-dup throughput risk
body:
Gustavo, all — decisions.

De-dup: GPU-batch the embedding stage rather than dropping to hash-only. Cross-client leakage is the one flaw that would invalidate the benchmark, so we spend 8 A100s for a week rather than weaken detection — Emeka confirmed the batching change is two days of work.

Readout scope for Jul 17: public splits fully integrated (Landmarks plus both iNaturalist partitionings); partner imagery included only if it clears de-dup and QA by Jul 13 — otherwise it's a Q3 follow-on and we say so plainly.

Halima, lead the analysis section with the IID-versus-user-partition gap; that's the argument for making this suite the default in Evalline. And book Tomas for the readout — adoption is his call as much as ours.

Ximena

subject: Kickoff: Felix assisted-rewrite track
body:
Team — kicking off the Felix track.

The approach decomposes text editing into tagging (choose and order the input tokens to keep) and insertion (in-fill the missing tokens with a bi-directional model), which makes it a strong fit for the assisted-rewrite feature language wants: edits stay close to the user's own words, unlike free generation.

Plan for the window: (1) reproduce the DiscoFuse sentence-fusion pipeline end-to-end — label map construction, data conversion, fine-tuning both models — by Mar 6; (2) adapt to our internal rewrite corpus by early April; (3) quality evaluation, including human ratings, through April; (4) launch-review pre-read by May 8.

Tereza owns modeling, Fumiko evaluation, Maren the data pipeline. Bao follows up on staffing and eval logistics.

Priya

subject: Re: Kickoff: Felix assisted-rewrite track
body:
Priya — resourcing for Felix.

Staffing: Tereza 60%, Fumiko 40%, Maren 50% through the window. Compute: fine-tuning the tagging and insertion models is BERT-scale, so 16 A100s best-effort on titan covers the DiscoFuse repro and the internal-corpus runs.

The bigger item is human evaluation. Rewrite quality doesn't reduce to exact-match metrics, and we have no tool for side-by-side sentence ratings, so we're scoping and staffing a human-rating annotation UI from scratch — Maren leads the build at roughly 50% for four weeks: paired original/rewrite presentation, 5-point fluency and meaning-preservation scales, rater-agreement tracking. Target: tool ready by end of March so April ratings aren't blocked. Rater budget: about $6k through the vendor pool.

One dependency: the internal rewrite corpus comes via Corpus, and I want extraction done well before their migration crunch.

Bao

subject: Status: DiscoFuse repro done, insertion drift on long rewrites
body:
Status.

DiscoFuse repro is done end-to-end: label-map construction with pointing enabled, data conversion, and fine-tuning both models off the BERT checkpoints — our exact-match numbers land within half a point of the paper's reported fusion results, so the pipeline is faithful.

Internal rewrite corpus: tagging transfers well — the keep/delete/reorder decisions look sensible almost immediately — but the insertion model is the weak link. On longer rewrites it in-fills fluent text that drifts from the source meaning, which is exactly what the meaning-preservation scale in Maren's rating tool should catch. The tool itself is on track for Mar 31; Fumiko has the rating protocol drafted.

Risk: if human ratings confirm the drift at scale, we'll need a constrained-insertion variant, which doesn't fit before May 8 — flagging now so the pre-read can frame it honestly.

Tereza

subject: Re: Status: DiscoFuse repro done, insertion drift on long rewrites
body:
Tereza, all — decisions for the pre-read.

Ratings from the April round (612 rated pairs, decent inter-rater agreement per Fumiko) confirm the pattern: short rewrites score 4.2+ on both scales, long rewrites drop to 3.4 on meaning preservation.

So the launch-review pre-read proposes shipping assisted rewrite scoped to short edits — where the tagging-plus-insertion decomposition is demonstrably strong — and holds long-form rewrites for a constrained-insertion variant in Q3. That's a scope cut and I'll own the messaging: better a sharp small feature than a mushy big one.

Maren, include the rating tool's agreement stats in the appendix; they preempt the "are the ratings real" question. Pre-read goes out May 6 for the May 8 review.

Thank you — this one moved fast and stayed honest.

Priya

subject: Kickoff: FinanceHarness analyst-assist pilot
body:
Team — kicking off FinanceHarness productization for graphs-retrieval.

The release gives us a model-agnostic deep-research agent — web research as a search, visit, cite loop, plus an equity slice with fundamentals, comps, and DCF/WACC — with a headless core we can run behind any backbone via the providers config.

Product target: an analyst-assist service for the internal strategy and finance teams, exposed through the HTTP+SSE service rather than the CLI.

Milestones: backbone profiles wired to our internal endpoints by Mar 6; retrieval grounded in our licensed market-data corpus by early April; a skill library (SKILL.md format) for our recurring report types by end of April; a pilot with Idris's org and a launch-review pre-read by May 8.

Halima owns the agent core, Wei evaluation, Leilani serving, Paloma skills. Ivo follows up on resourcing.

Anders

subject: Re: Kickoff: FinanceHarness analyst-assist pilot
body:
Anders — resourcing.

Staffing: Halima 50%, Wei 40%, Leilani 40% (serving plus the SSE deployment on Shipyard staging), Paloma 50% for the skills library. Compute is light — this is orchestration, not training; the cost line is backbone inference, budgeted at $9k/month during the pilot.

The dependency that worries me is data: our licensed market-data corpus is being migrated under Corpus v2, and the migration freeze is 2026-06-26 — so although our window closes May 11, any follow-on ingestion work we hand to Q3 has to be specced assuming no corpus changes after Jun 26. I've told Paloma to treat the corpus schema as fixed from that date in the skills design.

Also: privacy review for the pilot (internal data, but agent logs cite external pages) has a 2-3 week SLA — filing this week.

Ivo

subject: Status: eval results + backbone variance risk
body:
Status on evaluation.

Research mode: on our 40-question internal benchmark the agent's cited reports check out well — citation-support rate (does the cited page actually support the sentence) is 91% with the primary backbone profile, and the search-visit-cite loop rarely dead-ends now that Halima capped revisits.

Equity slice: DCF outputs are reproducible run-to-run once we pinned the WACC assumptions in the profile. Comps selection is the weak spot — it occasionally pulls a peer from the wrong sector — so Paloma is encoding sector guardrails as a bundled skill, which the discovery precedence picks up with no code changes.

Risk: backbone variance. The same prompt through the two configured profiles differs materially in report depth; for the pilot we should pin one profile and say so, or Idris's team will read variance as unreliability.

Serving: the SSE endpoint is stable on staging.

Wei

subject: Re: Status: eval results + backbone variance risk
body:
Wei, all — decisions ahead of the pre-read.

The pilot ships with one pinned backbone profile — the primary one from your evals — and profile switching stays an internal capability, not a user-facing option. The 91% citation-support number goes in the pre-read with the eval methodology attached.

Pilot scope: research mode plus the equity slice with sector guardrails, five bundled skills covering Idris's recurring report types; the auto-mode router stays off until we've seen real usage.

Leilani — production SSE deployment needs Zeke's sign-off, book it this week. Privacy review cleared Monday with one condition: agent logs retain cited-URL lists for 30 days max.

Pre-read goes out May 8; pilot starts the following week if the board doesn't object. Sharp work on the evals, Wei.

Anders

subject: Kickoff: Fisher-BRC offline RL baseline track
body:
Team — kicking off the Fisher-BRC adoption track for agents-rl.

The method regularizes the critic with a Fisher divergence penalty, which in the paper's benchmarks stabilizes offline RL where naive Q-learning collapses — and offline is the setting our product teams actually live in: they have logged interaction data and no appetite for live exploration.

Plan: (1) repro the paper's results on the D4RL locomotion suite — hopper-medium-expert-v0 and friends — by Apr 24, including the Mujoco licensing setup; (2) port the training loop onto our internal logged-interaction datasets in May; (3) a recommendation memo by Jun 12 on whether Fisher-BRC becomes the default offline baseline in our RL toolkit, feeding the Q3 OKR discussion.

Gustavo owns repro, Freya the internal-data port, Bilal infra, Linnea evaluation. Ivo follows up on staffing.

Ulla

subject: Re: Kickoff: Fisher-BRC offline RL baseline track
body:
Ulla — resourcing.

Staffing: Gustavo 50%, Freya 50% from May, Bilal 30%. And Linnea Yamada is committed at 60% to this project for July 2026 — the recommendation memo will trigger a follow-on evaluation round against our internal baselines, and July is when that lands, so I've locked her allocation now before Q3 planning eats everyone.

Compute: modest — the D4RL repro runs on single-GPU jobs, and 16 A100s best-effort covers the seed matrix (5 seeds per task, per the paper's protocol). The annoying dependency is Mujoco licensing for the repro environments; procurement says two weeks, so Gustavo starts on the tasks that clear first. Storage: 1TB for logged-interaction snapshots.

If the memo recommends against adoption we release Linnea's July allocation back — but I'm not planning on it.

Ivo

subject: Status: D4RL repro matches, tuning caveat for the memo
body:
Status.

Repro: the D4RL locomotion suite matches the paper within seed noise — on hopper-medium-expert-v0 we hit the reported score band on 4 of 5 seeds, and the Fisher divergence penalty clearly does the work: ablating it collapses the critic exactly as described. Mujoco licensing cleared with only a few days' delay.

Internal port (Freya): first runs on our logged navigation dataset are promising but expose a gap — our behavior data is much narrower than D4RL's medium-expert mixtures, and with narrow data the regularizer strength needs retuning per dataset; default hyperparameters underfit noticeably. That tuning burden is the honest caveat for the memo: Fisher-BRC works, but it isn't config-free on real logs.

Linnea is building the evaluation grid so the July round quantifies tuning sensitivity properly. On track for the Jun 12 memo.

Gustavo

subject: Kickoff: flare removal for the imaging pipeline
body:
Team — kicking off the flare removal track for the vision portfolio.

The ICCV method trains networks to remove lens flare, and the released code gives us both training and a standalone testing script (remove_flare.py). Product target: a post-capture cleanup feature for the imaging pipeline.

Milestones: (1) repro the released model's behavior by Apr 24 — note the repo's known history: a training-code issue was reported and a VGG-loss fix landed, so we validate that current code trains to published quality rather than assuming it; (2) retrain on our own capture data with our lens profiles through May; (3) on-device feasibility assessment in June; (4) launch-review pre-read by Jul 3.

Tereza owns training, Rafael data and quality, Farah infra, Yusuf the on-device path. Alina follows up on resourcing.

Lucia

subject: Re: Kickoff: flare removal for the imaging pipeline
body:
Lucia — resourcing.

Staffing: Tereza 50%, Farah 40%, Yusuf 30% until June then 50% for the feasibility work. And Rafael Duran is committed at 60% to this project for July 2026 — the pre-read lands Jul 3 and the quality bar for the imaging pipeline sits with him, so July is exactly when we need his depth on data and perceptual evals.

Compute: retraining needs 32 A100s for roughly three weeks in May — titan best-effort should hold, and vulcan's Jun 22-24 maintenance doesn't affect us. Data: capturing our own flare stacks with production lens profiles needs the optics lab for two weeks — booked from Apr 20.

One flag: the training-code history Lucia mentioned makes the Apr 24 repro milestone genuinely load-bearing. If current code doesn't reach published quality we escalate immediately rather than debugging silently into May.

Alina

subject: Status: repro validated post-VGG-fix, on-device gap
body:
Status.

Repro: good news — with the VGG-loss fix in place, training converges to quality consistent with the published results; our retrained checkpoint matches the released one within 0.4dB PSNR on the flare test images, so the historical training-code issue is behind us. The testing path (remove_flare.py) was never affected and we use it as the reference implementation for evals.

Own-data retraining: the semi-synthetic compositing recipe transfers, but our production lenses produce flare geometries — long radial streaks — underrepresented in the released flare library, so Rafael is capturing an extension set in the optics lab, about 600 additional flare images.

Risk: model size. Yusuf's first look suggests the full network misses the on-device latency budget by ~3x, so June feasibility likely lands on a distilled or tiled variant. Flagging so the pre-read doesn't promise on-device this year.

Tereza

subject: Re: Status: repro validated post-VGG-fix, on-device gap
body:
Tereza, all — decisions from Friday's review.

The Jul 3 pre-read proposes shipping flare removal server-side in the imaging pipeline first: quality is there — with Rafael's 600-image lens-profile extension set, streak-flare cases improved visibly in this week's evals — and the on-device variant moves to Q4 as a distillation project with Yusuf's 3x latency gap stated plainly.

Scope cut: video flare removal is out entirely this cycle. Frame-consistency is unsolved and I won't hint at it in the review.

For the pre-read I need: the PSNR table against the released checkpoint, before/after panels on production-lens captures, and the on-device feasibility one-pager. Rafael's July evaluation round is the last gate before the board sees it.

Solid, honest quarter so far — keep it boring.

Lucia

subject: Kickoff: FLOAT part-level scene parsing
body:
Team — kicking off the FLOAT scene-parsing track.

FLOAT factorizes object attributes for multi-object multi-part parsing — the CVPR 2022 work — and part-level segmentation is what the imagery-understanding roadmap needs next: object masks alone don't cut it for the editing features downstream teams are asking about.

Plan for the window: (1) environment and repro by Apr 10 — the release ships training and inference notebooks with preset settings, and datasets come from the Zenodo archive, so this should be mechanical; (2) convert the notebooks into a proper training pipeline by mid-May (notebooks don't survive contact with our cluster scheduler); (3) evaluate on our internal part-annotated set through May; (4) integration recommendation by Jun 12.

Csilla owns modeling, Gustavo training infra, Tereza evals, Wei analysis, Katya the internal-dataset work. Deshawn follows up on resourcing.

Lucia

subject: Re: Kickoff: FLOAT part-level scene parsing
body:
Lucia — resourcing for FLOAT.

Staffing: Csilla 40%, Gustavo 50%, Tereza 30% (she's splitting with the flare work), Wei 30%. And Katya Silva is committed at 60% to this project for June 2026 — the internal part-annotated evaluation is the whole basis for the integration recommendation, and Katya built that dataset originally, so her June allocation is the one I'll defend if anyone comes asking.

Compute: repro fits the published preset settings on 16 A100s; the May training-pipeline runs want 32, still best-effort on titan. Environment note: the release pins python 3.7.10 in conda — Gustavo is containerizing so the scheduler doesn't fight the old deps.

Storage: 3TB for the Zenodo dataset versions plus our internal set. No exotic asks this quarter; the risk is people, not machines.

Deshawn

subject: Status: repro done, taxonomy mapping is the critical path
body:
Status.

Repro: done via the released notebooks with preset settings — our runs reproduce the paper's part-parsing results on the Zenodo benchmark data within normal variance, and the factorized attribute heads behave as described: the object/part factorization is where the gains come from, and ablating it drops part mIoU noticeably.

Gustavo's pipeline conversion is about 80% there — training now runs headless under the scheduler in the containerized 3.7 environment, with checkpointing the notebooks lacked.

The real issue is our internal part-annotated set: our part taxonomy doesn't align one-to-one with the paper's — we split some parts finer and merge others — so Katya is building a mapping layer plus adjudication rules for the ambiguous classes before the June evals can be trusted.

Risk: that mapping work is the critical path. If it slips past Jun 1, the Jun 12 recommendation slips with it.

Csilla

subject: Re: Status: repro done, taxonomy mapping is the critical path
body:
Csilla, all — decision time ahead of Jun 12.

Katya's taxonomy mapping landed Jun 1 as hoped, and the June evals on the internal set are clean enough to call: FLOAT beats our current parser meaningfully on part-level metrics under the mapped taxonomy, with the biggest wins exactly where the factorization should help — multi-object scenes with repeated part types.

Recommendation: adopt FLOAT as the part-parsing backbone for the imagery-understanding stack, with a Q3 integration plan owned jointly with Deshawn's team.

Two caveats stated plainly in the memo: the aging python 3.7 dependency stack is a maintenance liability until we port it, and fine-grained classes where our taxonomy splits differ remain adjudicated rather than fully automatic.

Memo goes to Hana's staff Thursday. Thanks all — clean quarter.

Lucia

subject: Kickoff: FM4TLP transfer benchmark track
body:
Team — kicking off the FM4TLP track for graphs-retrieval.

The work benchmarks transferring an inductive temporal link prediction model from a training graph to a test graph with zero node overlap — precisely the cold-start problem our graph products hit whenever we onboard a new domain: no shared nodes, only structure. Goal: establish whether transfer-based TLP can replace per-domain training in our recommendation stack.

Milestones: (1) env bring-up by Mar 20 — nontrivial, the repo needs a conda graph-tool environment with a pinned torch 2.3.0/cu118 stack and some documented python-binary oddities; (2) reproduce the benchmark transfer results by end of April; (3) run the transfer protocol on two internal graph domains in June; (4) recommendation readout by Jul 10.

Rosa owns infra, Ondrej modeling, Gustavo experiments, Bilal data plumbing. Daniela follows up on resourcing.

Anders

subject: Re: Kickoff: FM4TLP transfer benchmark track
body:
Anders — resourcing.

Staffing: Rosa 40% front-loaded for the env work, Ondrej 50%, Gustavo 50%, Bilal 30% from April. The conda/graph-tool environment is as fiddly as advertised — Rosa already hit the documented issue where the activated env doesn't pick up the right python binary, so she's baking the working alias into a container image for everyone.

Compute: the April repro runs on titan best-effort (single-node, the pinned torch 2.3.0+cu118 stack). The June internal-domain runs are the heavy part — full transfer matrices across both domains with per-epoch retraining — and for that we hold the cirrus-tpu reservation for the week of 2026-06-29, 256 accelerators, which Ines's team confirmed against our portfolio's quarterly allocation.

Storage: 4TB for temporal graph snapshots. Constraint: the June experiment grid must be final by Jun 19 so the reserved week is fully productive.

Daniela

subject: Status: benchmark repro + June critical path
body:
Status.

Repro: benchmark numbers reproduced for the main transfer setting — models trained on the source graph and evaluated on disjoint-node test graphs degrade exactly as the benchmark documents, and the mitigation strategies in the release recover a good share of the gap on most dataset pairs.

The interesting internal question is which regime our domains fall into: structural similarity between source and target predicts transfer quality strongly in our repro, and our two candidate internal domains differ a lot on that axis. Gustavo's prep suggests domain A (session graphs) should transfer well; domain B (entity graphs) may be the stress case.

Risk: memory. Temporal batching on our largest internal snapshot exceeds single-node limits, so Bilal is sharding the loader; if that isn't done by Jun 12 we'll burn reserved capacity on smaller-than-planned runs. That's the June critical path.

Ondrej

subject: Re: Status: benchmark repro + June critical path
body:
Team — decisions for Friday's readout.

The June matrices came in on schedule and the story is clean: transfer works where structure is similar — on the session-graph domain, transferred models reach within a few points of per-domain training, good enough to kill cold-start training there — while the entity-graph domain shows the gap the benchmark warned about, so per-domain training stays.

Recommendation: a hybrid. Transfer-based TLP becomes the default for structurally similar onboarding domains, with a documented similarity check (Ondrej's criterion) deciding which path a new domain takes.

Bilal's sharded loader held up at full scale — worth writing up separately. Scope note: we are not proposing hub-style pretraining across all domains this year; that's a Q4 conversation with Eleni's org.

Readout deck reviews Thursday.

Anders

subject: Kickoff: fractal language metrics track
body:
Team — kicking off the fractal language metrics track.

The research establishes that language is self-similar and long-range dependent — Hurst parameter around H=0.70 — and, more usefully for us, that fractal parameters improve on perplexity-based bits-per-byte for predicting downstream performance. Product angle: a corpus-quality scoring service. If the self-similarity exponent S, Hurst exponent H, and Joseph exponent J computed over a candidate data mix predict downstream evals better than BPB, that changes how data-platforms prices and prioritizes corpora.

Plan: (1) reproduce the parameter-estimation pipeline from the released colab by Feb 27; (2) compute fractal parameters across five internal corpus slices in March; (3) a correlation study against our existing downstream eval suite in April; (4) readout and Q3 proposal by May 1.

Wei owns estimation, Rafael the correlation study, Gustavo pipelines, Amara data access. Daniela follows up on resourcing.

Priya

subject: Re: Kickoff: fractal language metrics track
body:
Priya — resourcing.

Staffing: Wei 50%, Rafael 40%, Gustavo 40%, Amara 30%.

Compute: parameter estimation needs LLM forward passes over large document collections — no training, but a lot of inference; I've sized it at 48 A100s best-effort on titan for the March runs.

The scheduling constraint is data access: our five corpus slices come through Corpus, and with the v2 migration freeze on 2026-07-10 we're planning all extraction against v1 now, with a re-validation pass on v2 before that date — Amara has the extraction jobs specced, and Jun Varga's team confirmed the freeze date when we asked last week.

Storage: 2TB for token-level log-likelihood dumps (the estimators need per-token increments, not just aggregate BPB). One ask: the April correlation study needs eval-suite results from Tomas's team — requesting now to avoid the end-of-quarter Evalline crunch.

Daniela

subject: Status: estimation pipeline live, H spread across slices
body:
Status.

The estimation pipeline is reproduced and productionized from the colab: we compute the self-similarity exponent S, Hurst exponent H, and Joseph exponent J per corpus slice using per-token log-likelihood increments from our reference model. Sanity checks pass — on general web text we estimate H around 0.70, right where the paper puts it.

The interesting spread: our five slices range from H of about 0.61 (transactional/short-form text) to 0.74 (long-form technical), matching the intuition that long-range dependence tracks document coherence. Gustavo's pipeline runs a full slice overnight on the current allocation.

Risk for April: the correlation study's power depends on how many model/eval pairs Tomas's team can supply — with fewer than a dozen pairs the BPB-versus-fractal comparison won't be conclusive and we'd frame the readout as directional. Rafael is drafting the analysis plan to make that call explicit.

Wei

subject: Re: Status: estimation pipeline live, H spread across slices
body:
Wei, all — decisions ahead of the May 1 readout.

Tomas came through with fourteen model/eval pairs, and Rafael's analysis holds up: fractal parameters (H and J jointly) predict downstream eval averages better than BPB alone on our internal pairs, consistent with the paper's claim — modest sample, but directionally solid and worth acting on.

The readout will propose a Q3 pilot: corpus-quality scoring integrated into data-platforms' intake flow, scored on v2 once the migration lands. Scope discipline: we are not claiming fractal metrics replace evals, only that they improve pre-training data triage; I'll keep the language tight.

Amara, please make sure the v1-extracted slices are queued for the v2 re-validation pass per Daniela's plan. Readout deck to me by Apr 29.

Excellent quarter, team.

Priya

subject: FAD productization — kickoff and Q2 milestones
body:
Hi Santiago,

Kicking off our productization of Frechet Audio Distance (FAD). The pitch: FAD is a reference-free evaluation metric for audio generation, particularly music enhancement, so we can score enhancement models without paired ground truth. I want this wrapped as a portfolio-standard metric service that every speech-audio launch review can cite.

Proposed milestones inside the Q2 window: port the Beam scoring pipeline by Apr 17, validate FAD against our internal listening-test panels by May 8, and take the metric service to Launch Review Board on May 22 (I have pinged Nadia to hold a slot).

Team: Hyun, Gustavo and Maren are the assigned contributors; Santiago owns feasibility. Can you come back with staffing fractions and compute asks by end of next week?

Thanks,
Goran

subject: Re: FAD productization — kickoff and Q2 milestones
body:
Hi Goran,

Staffing: Hyun 60%, Maren 50%, Gustavo 40% through May. Compute is modest — the VGGish embedding extraction runs comfortably on 64 A100s on titan-a100 best-effort, no reservation needed.

One structural call: for scoring, tracking and dashboards we are going to scope and staff an internal evaluation harness from scratch — batch scoring jobs, a metric registry, and regression dashboards. Maren will own the harness design doc, due Apr 3. Building it ourselves keeps us unblocked and gives us full control of the FAD-specific plumbing (VGGish checkpoint pinning, Beam pipeline configs).

Risks to flag early: the pinned apache-beam version still wants Python 2 for the pipeline, which is going to bite us during the port.

Santiago

subject: FAD status: Beam Python 2 blocker + panel validation
body:
Hi Santiago,

Status on the FAD port. The embedding path is done: we mirror the vggish_model.ckpt checkpoint internally and extraction matches the reference implementation bit-for-bit on our smoke set.

The blocker is the Beam pipeline: apache-beam at our pinned version does not support Python 3, so the whole scoring job runs in a Python 2 virtualenv. That is an EOL runtime and security will flag it at launch review.

Validation is encouraging — on our enhancement distortion suite, FAD ranks systems in agreement with the listening panel on 9 of 10 pairs, versus 6 of 10 for the SDR baseline.

Proposal: budget two extra weeks to rewrite the pipeline against a Python 3 capable Beam release. Maren has a spike branch already.

Hyun

subject: Re: FAD status: Beam Python 2 blocker + panel validation
body:
Team,

Decision from this morning's sync: we take the two weeks. The Python 2 pipeline does not go to Launch Review Board; Maren's Python 3 Beam rewrite is now on the critical path, with the LRB slot moving from May 22 to Jun 5 pending Nadia's confirmation.

Second decision: we ship v1 on the VGGish embedding model as-is. Swapping the embedding backbone is a Q3 conversation — it changes every historical score and the harness needs stable baselines first.

Hyun, please write up the 9/10 vs 6/10 panel-agreement result for the review packet; that is our headline number.

Thanks all — good, fast work this cycle.

Goran

subject: FVD workstream kickoff — one metric for video gen
body:
Hi Daniela,

Kickoff for the Fréchet Video Distance workstream. FVD gives us a single number for generative video quality: we embed real and generated clips with an I3D network (preprocessed to 224x224, loaded via tensorflow-hub) and compute the Fréchet distance between the two embedding distributions. Every video-gen effort in the vision portfolio is currently rolling its own eval, and I want FVD as the standard gate.

Milestones: metric library integrated with two internal model repos by Mar 13, variance and calibration study through the spring, and a large calibration sweep in early June so scores are comparable across model families before Q3 OKRs.

Quentin, Katya and Tereza are assigned. Daniela — staffing and compute plan when you can.

Best,
Lucia

subject: Re: FVD workstream kickoff — one metric for video gen
body:
Hi Lucia,

Plan: Quentin full-time on the metric library, Katya at 50% for model-repo integration, Tereza at 30% for infra.

Compute: day-to-day dev fits on titan-a100 best-effort. For the June calibration sweep we are covered — we hold the vulcan-h100 reservation for the week of 2026-06-08, 256 accelerators, which is sized for the full sweep across model families and seeds. I have put the reservation ID in the tracker; Ines, cc'ing you for awareness.

One dependency: the reference pipeline assumes clips shaped [NUMBER_OF_VIDEOS, VIDEO_LENGTH, 224, 224, 3] with values in 0-255; our internal stores are float-normalized, so Katya is writing a conversion shim first.

Daniela

subject: FVD status: variance study + memory risk
body:
Hi Daniela,

Status: the FVD library is integrated in both target repos and matches the open-source reference to four decimals on the smoke suite.

Finding from the variance study: at 512 videos per side, FVD moves about 3% across seeds — enough to flip rankings between checkpoints that are close. At 2048 videos the spread drops under 1%. Recommendation: standardize on 2048.

Risk: the I3D embedding step is memory-hungry for clips beyond 64 frames because the whole [N, T, 224, 224, 3] tensor is materialized before create_id3_embedding runs. I am chunking along the batch dimension, which drops peak memory roughly 4x, but the sweep budget needs to assume the slower chunked path.

Quentin

subject: Re: FVD status: variance study + memory risk
body:
Team,

Locking the calibration sweep plan: 4 model families x 3 seeds x 2048 videos per side, running in our vulcan-h100 week of Jun 8 on the 256-accelerator reservation. Quentin's chunked embedding path is the default.

Decision: 2048 videos per side is the portfolio standard from here on; any FVD number reported at launch review below that sample size gets flagged.

Note the vulcan maintenance window Jun 22-24 lands after our week, so no exposure there, but do not let the sweep slip — there is no second reservation this quarter.

Results readout Jun 16, invite to follow.

Lucia

subject: Fourier robustness heat maps — kickoff
body:
Hi Alina,

Kicking off the Fourier robustness work. The method generates Fourier heat maps of image classifiers: we add frequency basis vectors to input images and visualize how layer outputs and test error respond across the frequency spectrum. Product angle: a robustness report card that becomes part of the model release checklist for the vision portfolio — today we have no systematic view of which models fall over on high-frequency perturbations.

Milestones: wrap our classifiers behind the TensorFlowNeuralNetwork interface by Jun 12, heat maps for the flagship classifiers by mid-July, robustness readout to Hana's staff in early August.

Milan, Katya and Freya are assigned. Alina, over to you for staffing and the data plan.

Lucia

subject: Re: Fourier robustness heat maps — kickoff
body:
Hi Lucia,

Staffing: Freya 60% (analysis lead), Milan 50% (TensorFlowNeuralNetwork wrappers and batching), Katya 40% (eval sets). Compute: 32 A100s on titan best-effort covers heat map generation.

Data plan: we need our perturbed eval image sets living in Corpus before the v2 migration freeze. Corpus has the freeze landing 2026-07-24, so I am targeting Jul 17 for the last ingestion batch, one week of slack. Katya owns the ingestion pipeline and will version the Fourier basis perturbations alongside the clean sets.

One ask: can you confirm which classifiers count as flagship for the readout? Heat map cost scales linearly with the number of models.

Alina

subject: Heat map status: first results + cost risk
body:
Hi Alina,

Status: heat maps are done for the first two classifiers. Clear signal — test error is flat for low-frequency basis vectors but spikes above 30% for a band of high-frequency perturbations on the smaller model; the larger model is robust across most of the spectrum but has a narrow mid-frequency weakness we did not expect.

Cost risk: a full heat map means one clean-vs-corrupted evaluation per Fourier basis vector, comparing the tensor_list layer outputs each time, so a 224x224 input grid is tens of thousands of forward passes per model. Right now that is about 40 GPU-hours per model even with Milan's batched evaluation. If the flagship list grows past four models we blow the July timeline.

Freya

subject: Re: Heat map status: first results + cost risk
body:
Team,

Decisions from the review with Hana:

1. Flagship list is capped at three classifiers for the August readout. The long tail moves to Q4.
2. Freya's mid-frequency finding on the large model is the headline — please turn it into a one-pager with the heat maps.
3. Ingestion: we are tracking to the Jul 17 target Alina set against the Jul 24 corpus freeze; Katya confirmed the final perturbed sets go in this week.

Readout is Aug 6, 30 minutes. I will circulate the deck by Aug 3 for comments.

Thanks — this is shaping into the strongest robustness story in the portfolio.

Lucia

subject: FRMT kickoff — dialect quality as a launch gate
body:
Hi Ivo,

Kickoff for the FRMT workstream. FRMT is our benchmark for region-aware machine translation: a few thousand English Wikipedia sentences human-translated into Brazilian vs European Portuguese and Mainland vs Taiwan Mandarin. The clever part is the bucket design — the lexical bucket targets terms that translate differently by region, and the entity bucket is adversarial: a model should not switch to Portugal Portuguese just because Lisbon is mentioned.

Product framing: this becomes the dialect-quality gate for our translation features. Milestones: baseline evals by Mar 20, regional quality dashboard by Apr 24, Launch Review Board on May 15.

Milan, Vera and Yara are assigned. Ivo — staffing and budget when you can.

Priya

subject: Re: FRMT kickoff — dialect quality as a launch gate
body:
Hi Priya,

Staffing: Yara 60% as eval lead, Vera 50% on the dashboard, Milan 30% on data plumbing. That covers the Mar-May milestones.

Budget: good news — I spoke with Idris on Tuesday and he verbally earmarked $120k from Q3 discretionary compute budget line B-75 for our few-shot eval runs. That funds the exemplar-selection sweeps and the larger model comparisons without touching the portfolio baseline. I will get it in writing when the Q3 cycle opens, but we can plan against it now.

One dependency: the dataset splits are document-level (exemplar/dev/test), so the eval harness has to sample exemplars by document, not sentence. Yara has it.

Ivo

subject: FRMT baselines: entity bucket catches real drift
body:
Hi Ivo,

Baseline results are in. On the lexical bucket, our production model handles pt-BR vs pt-PT lexical choice reasonably (about 85% preferred-variant agreement) but the entity bucket exposes exactly the failure FRMT was designed to catch: on pages strongly tied to Portugal, the model drifts into European Portuguese for 18% of pt-BR requests. Mandarin shows the same pattern between Mainland and Taiwan variants, slightly milder.

Few-shot helps a lot — ten exemplars sampled at the document level cut entity-bucket drift roughly in half — but results are sensitive to which exemplar documents we pick, which is a reproducibility risk for the dashboard.

Proposal: fix a frozen exemplar set per language pair for dashboard runs.

Yara

subject: FSQ kickoff — simplifying the tokenizer stack
body:
Hi Santiago,

Kicking off the FSQ workstream. Finite Scalar Quantization replaces vector quantization in our VQ-VAE tokenizer stack: project the latent down to fewer than 10 dimensions, quantize each to a small fixed set of values, and the implicit codebook is the product of those sets. Same codebook sizes as VQ, but no codebook collapse and none of the machinery — no commitment losses, no reseeding, no entropy penalties.

Why the efficiency portfolio cares: a simpler tokenizer means fewer training pathologies across every downstream model. Milestones: MaskGIT image-generation repro by May 22, UViM dense-prediction repro by Jun 12, adopt/hold decision Jun 30.

Leilani, Carmen and Saoirse assigned. Staffing plan when you can.

Zofia

subject: Re: FSQ kickoff — simplifying the tokenizer stack
body:
Hi Zofia,

Staffing: Leilani 70% (tokenizer integration), Carmen 50% (MaskGIT and UViM repro), Saoirse 40% (training infra).

Compute: repro fits inside our existing titan allocation, but the Q3 comparison sweeps — FSQ vs VQ at matched codebook sizes across three downstream tasks — need dedicated budget. Idris has verbally earmarked $180k from Q3 discretionary compute budget line B-36 for this project, which covers the sweeps with roughly 15% margin. Planning against that figure now; paperwork lands when Q3 opens.

Flag: UViM panoptic segmentation is the heaviest of the dense-prediction tasks; if anything slips it will be that.

Santiago

subject: FSQ repro status: FID parity, 99% codebook utilization
body:
Hi Santiago,

Repro status. MaskGIT with FSQ matches the VQ baseline within 1.2 FID at the same effective codebook size — consistent with the paper's claim that the much simpler scheme stays competitive. The striking number is codebook utilization: FSQ sits near 99% while our VQ baseline idles at 71% with visible dead codes. No commitment loss, no reseeding, and training just runs.

UViM: depth estimation and colorization repro are done and within noise of the VQ numbers. Panoptic segmentation is behind — the head is trained but eval is two weeks out.

Risk: our chosen config (8 dimensions) underperforms on 512x512 inputs; we may need the larger-dimensionality variant for high-res work.

Carmen

Nice work everyone, this was a clean result.

Product goal: a clustering backbone for the retrieval stack that stays stable under updates. Milestones: C++ library hardened and benchmarked by May 15, integration prototype against a production update stream by Jun 26, go/no-go for Q3 adoption Jul 10.

body:

The library compiles clean with -O2 and we replicated the paper's headline: against greedy recomputation, the agreement-based algorithm gives comparable clustering cost with roughly 40x fewer recomputations on our sliding-window instances (sliding_window_size 100k, 10% of points as facilities, random_order on).

Parameter picks so far: num_levels_slack (the paper's beta) at 3 and epsilon (the lambda parameter) at 0.1 are the stability sweet spot; below that, assignments churn.

Kickoff for dynamic submodular maximization. Our open-source release implements fully dynamic algorithms for constrained submodular optimization with oracle access — the reference setting is graph coverage and influence maximization, which maps directly onto candidate selection freshness in the retrieval stack: we want the selected set to stay near-optimal as the underlying graph gets edge insertions and deletions, without recomputing from scratch.

Milestones: replicate the paper's experiments by Apr 24, port the oracle to our internal graph by Jun 5, freshness A/B design ready ahead of Q3 OKRs.

Giannis, Csilla and Bilal are assigned; Csilla is our submodularity depth. Staffing and compute over to you.

subject: Submodular status: enron replication done, influence-max 20x slower
body:

On the enron graph we match the paper's oracle-call counts exactly — the cross-platform-deterministic randomness makes this satisfying to verify — and the dynamic algorithm tracks the greedy baseline's objective within 5% across cardinality constraints k from 10 to 100, at a fraction of the oracle calls in the sliding-window setting.

The internal port is where the risk sits: the influence-maximization oracle is roughly 20x slower than plain coverage on our graph because of the sampling requirement. Coverage-only gets us the freshness win we actually care about for retrieval.

Recommendation: drop influence maximization from Q3 scope and keep it as a research thread.

subject: Fast Weight Layers kickoff — long-doc quality
body:

Kickoff for Fast Weight Layers. FWLs sit between the body of a Transformer decoder and the output softmax, and their parameters change based on observed tokens — the performance profile of dynamic evaluation, especially on long documents, but much faster and easier to deploy. Our EMNLP work showed the gains; now I want them in the long-document assistant, where quality visibly degrades past a few thousand tokens.

Milestones: production-shaped implementation evaluated by May 29, long-doc perplexity study by Jun 19, integration decision ahead of the July launch-planning cycle.

Gustavo, Quentin and Chiara are assigned. Staffing and budget please — I know the Q3 sweeps will need real money.

subject: FWL status: 6.1% long-doc perplexity gain, JAX gradient bug
body:
Hi Bruno,

Status. Both implementations are running. The fast weight block is as described — dense projection to 4x size, squared ReLU, projection back to size, layer norm — and on our 4096-token eval set, attn_chunks at 16 for the mixed chunk attention is clearly right; 4 loses most of the long-range benefit.

subject: GaterNet kickoff — input-conditional compute
body:

Kickoff for the GaterNet workstream. The idea from our CVPR release: a separate gater network looks at the input and selects which filters in the backbone CNN fire — dynamic, input-conditional filter selection, hence you look twice. We have released checkpoints for ResNet-20-Gated and ResNet-56-Gated on CIFAR-10 to build from.

Product angle for vision: input-conditional compute for our edge inference tier, where a static model burns the same FLOPs on easy and hard inputs alike.

Milestones: reproduce the released CIFAR-10 evals by Mar 20, gating study on an internal workload by Apr 30, scale decision in early June.

Rafael, Vera, Rosa and Umar assigned. Over to you.

Lucia

subject: Re: GaterNet kickoff — input-conditional compute
body:

Staffing: Rosa 60% (repro and eval), Vera 50% (internal workload port), Rafael 40% (analysis), Umar 20% (advisory).

subject: GaterNet status: exact repro, edge latency concern
body:

Status. Repro is exact: our eval of the released ResNet-20-Gated and ResNet-56-Gated checkpoints on CIFAR-10 matches the paper numbers, running main.py with backbone-depth 20 and 56 respectively.

The risk Rafael flagged: the architecture literally looks twice — the gater network runs a full forward pass before the backbone does, so wall-clock latency on our edge tier is worse than the static baseline even when FLOPs drop. subject: Gradient-based red teaming — kickoff
body:
Hi Ivo,

Kickoff for the gradient-based red teaming workstream, from our EACL 2024 release. Instead of hand-writing adversarial prompts, we optimize them: the EmbedTransformerLm variant accepts embeddings as inputs, simple_decode makes decoding differentiable with Gumbel softmax sampling between steps, and loss_fn scores the safety of the induced response by concatenating the SAFETY tokens and running one more decoding step. Gradients flow end to end, so unsafe-response-inducing prompts are found automatically.

Product goal: automated adversarial prompt discovery as a pre-launch gate for every language model release. Milestones: pipeline on an internal PAX LM by Mar 27, first full sweep Apr 30, gate proposal to LRB May 20.

Chiara, Fumiko and Halima assigned.

Priya

subject: Re: Gradient-based red teaming — kickoff
body:
Hi Priya,

Staffing: Halima 60% (red-team pipeline lead), Fumiko 50% (modeling), Chiara 40% (infra).

For running this as a launch gate we need real machinery around the core method, so we are scoping and staffing an internal evaluation harness from scratch — adversarial prompt corpus management, batch safety scoring, and regression dashboards that track model exposure over time. Halima owns the harness design doc, due Feb 27; Chiara builds. Roughly six engineer-weeks, but it is the piece that turns a paper into a gate.

Compute: modest — gradient attacks run on 32 A100s titan best-effort. The PAX LM checkpoint we target is the internal 8B, already trained with the SEP and SAFETY token conventions.

Ivo

subject: Red teaming status: pipeline live, mode collapse risk
body:
Hi Ivo,

Status. The pipeline runs end to end on the internal 8B PAX LM: prompt probabilities feed the LM, simple_decode runs the differentiable decoding, and safety scoring works through the SAFETY token path in a single decode when there is no separate classifier input.

Findings from the first partial sweep: the optimizer reliably finds prompts that flip the safety score, but they collapse into two low-diversity modes — near-duplicate token patterns. A diversity penalty in loss_fn helps, and the Gumbel temperature matters a lot (0.7 much better than 1.0 for us).

Risk: mode collapse means coverage claims for a launch gate are weaker than raw prompt counts suggest. Halima's harness will report distinct-mode counts, not just prompt counts.

Kickoff for the spectral energy distance TTS workstream. The method trains highly parallel speech models without an analytical likelihood: a generalized energy distance over magnitude-spectrogram distributions, a proper scoring rule that can be estimated without bias from minibatches, with a repulsive term over multi-scale spectrogram distances. Our release hit MOS 4.25 — competitive with autoregressive systems that need tens of thousands of sequential ops per second of generated audio.

Product goal: low-latency TTS on our serving hardware, where autoregressive sampling is the cost driver today. Milestones: training repro by Apr 24, internal-voice dataset run by Jun 12, production-scale training in July, MOS panel late July.

Kaia, Jorge, Gustavo and Chiara assigned.

subject: Generalized rate metrics — kickoff
body:
Hi Deshawn,

Kicking off the GIFT workstream. Platform customers keep asking why their classifiers decay as their data drifts, and the honest answer today is "retrain and hope." Our open-source GIFT work gives us something better: when intermediate distributions exist, iterative self-training forms an implicit curriculum and walks the model to the target; when they do not, GIFT manufactures virtual intermediate samples by interpolating source and target representations. That is the wedge - gradual adaptation without asking customers for labeled intermediate data.

Milestones: repro the natural-shift benchmark results by 4/24, integrate with one internal pipeline as a pilot by 5/29, decision review by 6/17.

Katya leads research, Amara pipeline integration, Saoirse the serving-side hooks. Ivo, can I get staffing confirmation plus a compute sketch by end of next week?

body:

Staffing confirmed: Katya 70%, Amara 60%, Saoirse 40%. Workable for the 6/17 review.

Compute: the iterative self-training loops are the cost center - every adaptation run is effectively N retrains, and the interpolation-step sweep (how far we push virtual samples toward target per iteration) multiplies that. I am estimating ~40 A100s sustained on titan-a100 through May, spiking for the benchmark repro.

Budget: Idris has verbally earmarked $120k from Q3 discretionary compute budget line B-75 for this project; the adaptation sweeps below are costed against that line. Idris - cc'd, would be good to get that confirmed in writing before Q3 OKRs lock on 6/26.

subject: Status: benchmark repro done; where GIFT wins and where it doesn't
body:
Hi both,

Repro is done on the natural-distribution-shift benchmark. Headline numbers: with intermediate data available, iterative self-training alone recovers most of the drop, confirming the implicit-curriculum effect from the paper. Without intermediates - the realistic customer case - plain self-training falls short, and GIFT's interpolated virtual samples buy us +2.3 points of target accuracy over it on our repro, in line with the published finding. Stacking GIFT on top of a standard domain-adaptation baseline also improved target accuracy, which is the config I want for the pilot.

Risk for the pilot: when source and target are too far apart, the interpolation curriculum needs more steps and cost grows roughly linearly - our worst sweep took 5x the compute of the best. Amara and I will publish a cost-vs-shift table next week so we can set customer expectations honestly.

subject: Kickoff: GON - auditable black-box optimization for trust-theory
body:
Hi Bruno,

Kicking off the GON workstream. Why trust-theory owns this: teams keep shipping black-box maximizers (ad budgets, dosing curves, threshold tuning) where nobody can certify the recommendation. A Global Optimization Network - any composition of an invertible function and a unimodal function - has a unique global maximizer recoverable in O(D) time, so the recommendation is auditable by construction. The unimodal half comes from lattice models with linear inequality constraints, which also gives us shape guarantees regulators like.

The published experiments show GON maximizers beat convex fits, GPR and DNNs on noisy real-world estimation problems, so we are not trading accuracy for auditability.

Milestones: repro of the simulation suite by 3/6, conditional-GON prototype on one internal tuning problem by 4/10, portfolio review 4/29.

Bruno - staffing plan when you can.

Ximena

body:

Staffing through the window and into the hardening phase after it:

- Gustavo 50% (simulation repro, done via `python -m gon.simulation` configs - already green as of last week)
- Umar 30% (theory review of the lattice constraint formulation)
- Yara 40% (conditional GON prototype)
- Chiara 50% (packaging + API)

For the hardening phase I have Linnea Yamada committed at 60% to this project for June 2026 - she is the only one of the five with production lattice-model experience, so please treat that allocation as load-bearing. If June slips, the productionization slips with it.

Compute is a non-issue: everything fits on a handful of CPUs plus 4 GPUs for the DNN baselines we compare against. No cluster reservations needed.

subject: Status: conditional GON prototype + a calibration trade-off
body:
Hi Ximena, Bruno,

Status ahead of the 4/29 review. The simulation repro confirmed the published pattern: GON maximizer estimates were statistically significantly better than the convex fit, GPR and DNN baselines on our noisy test functions, and recovering the maximizer really is O(D) - milliseconds even at D=64.

Yara's conditional GON prototype is running on the internal threshold-tuning problem: it finds a global maximizer conditioned on the customer-segment inputs, which is exactly the query shape the tuning team wants.

The trade-off to discuss: enforcing unimodality via the lattice linear-inequality constraints costs us fit quality when the true response surface is mildly multimodal. On one segment the constrained fit underestimates the peak by ~6%. We think that is the honest price of an auditable guarantee, but the review should say so explicitly rather than bury it.

Gustavo

Our open-source approach replaces that with tuning during training: hyperparameters get updated with the gradient on the tuning loss, and the implementation lets you pick any subset of hyperparameters to learn. If it holds up on our stack, that is a straight compute-cost reduction we can put a dollar figure on.

Grounding: the reference code is JAX/flax, trains Transformers on WMT translation data via TFDS, and ships a run.sh that starts with the Lithuanian-English pair on a tiny model - which is exactly where the repro starts.

body:

Status. The lt-en repro is green: run.sh end-to-end (data download, formatting, training) worked once we were on Halima's container instead of the pinned cuda11 jaxlib wheels. On the tiny config, learning the optimizer hyperparameters via the tuning-loss gradient matched the hand-tuned baseline BLEU within 0.3, with zero search runs.

The production-size comparison kicked off Friday on 32 GPUs (Bruno's memory flag was right - the meta-gradient step pushed us past 24). Csilla's eval protocol: same token budget for both arms, where the baseline arm's budget includes its historical search cost. That is the fair fight the adoption decision should hinge on.

Risk: learned learning-rate schedules occasionally spike early in training on the big config - two of five seeds needed a restart. Kaia suspects the tuning-loss batch is too small; she is doubling it. If instability persists into May, the recommendation gets a stability caveat.

Rosa

subject: Re: Status: lt-en repro green, production-size comparison running
body:
Team,

Adoption decision, settled a few days early:

1. ADOPT for optimizer hyperparameters (learning rate, warmup, decay) on the seq2seq stack. Csilla's token-budget accounting shows the learned arm reaching baseline BLEU with 28% less total compute once you charge the baseline for its search runs. That number goes to the portfolio review.
2. HOLD on learning regularization hyperparameters - the early-training spikes Kaia chased are mostly gone with the larger tuning-loss batch, but 1 in 5 seeds still restarts, and I will not put that into other teams' pipelines yet. Revisit as a Q3 item with the corpus regeneration work Bruno scheduled.
3. Rosa's container becomes the supported entry point; the raw pip route gets a deprecation note in the internal README.

Good, quantified work - this is the kind of decision memo I like writing.

Dmitri

subject: Kickoff: matrix compression for the serving fleet
body:
Hi Deshawn,

Kicking off the matrix compression workstream for efficiency. The library injects compression ops into the TensorFlow training graph so weight tensors are compressed while the model is being trained - not as a lossy afterthought at export time. The API surface is in good shape: MatrixCompressorInterface for the algorithm, CompressionOpInterface for the graph injection, and the ApplyCompression wrapper that walks layers and applies the chosen compression_option. Smoothed compression gives us a knob to trade accuracy against ratio during training.

Product target: cut serving memory for the three biggest internal models by 3-4x with under 1% quality loss, which Zeke's team can turn directly into fleet capacity.

Milestones: library integrated with one flagship model by 3/20, compression-vs-quality curves by 4/17, rollout recommendation by 5/15.

Yusuf leads research, Emeka tooling, Linnea training integration. Staffing and compute from you by Friday?

Zofia

subject: Re: Kickoff: matrix compression for the serving fleet
body:
Zofia,

Staffing: Yusuf 70%, Linnea 50%, Emeka 60%. Compute: retraining the flagship model with compression ops in the graph costs roughly 1.3x a normal training run, so I am asking for 48 A100s on titan best-effort for the March and April training cycles.

One scoping addition. Automated metrics will not settle the rollout question - for the ranking model especially, we need humans judging whether compressed-model outputs actually degrade. To close that gap we are scoping and staffing a human-rating annotation UI, built from scratch: Emeka owns it end to end (rater queue, side-by-side comparison view, rating storage), with a working version by end of April. I am budgeting Emeka's 60% around it, plus a rater pool booked through the vendor program.

That makes the 4/17 curves milestone automated-metrics-only, with human ratings following by 5/8. Still compatible with your 5/15 recommendation date.

Deshawn

subject: Status: compression curves ahead of the 4/17 gate
body:
Hi both,

Curves land on time. Headline: on the flagship ranking model, low-rank compression via ApplyCompression reaches 4x weight reduction at 0.4% metric loss when the ops run during training; the same ratio applied post-training costs 2.1%. That delta is the whole argument for the in-graph approach, so it goes on slide one.

Smoothed compression matters more than expected: ramping the compression fraction over the first third of training avoids the loss cliff we saw with an abrupt schedule. Linnea has the schedule hyperparameters documented in the shared config.

Risk: the embedding tables dominate memory but tolerate compression worst - past 2x, retrieval recall drops fast. Recommendation will likely be tiered: 4x on dense layers, 2x on embeddings. Also flagging that our second target model still runs TF1-style sessions and the CompressionOpInterface wiring there is fiddly; Emeka lost a week to it.

Yusuf

subject: Re: Status: compression curves ahead of the 4/17 gate
body:
Team,

Rollout recommendation is settled, three days ahead of the 5/15 gate:

1. Tiered compression ships: 4x on dense layers, 2x on embedding tables, exactly per Yusuf's curves. Zeke's capacity model says that frees the equivalent of ~140 serving hosts across the three flagship models.
2. Human ratings from Emeka's annotation UI backed the automated story - raters preferred the uncompressed model in only 51.8% of side-by-side comparisons, statistically a coin flip. The UI itself has held up well with the vendor rater pool; we will keep it running for future compression pushes.
3. The TF1-session model is deferred to Q3. Not worth the wiring cost this window.

Deshawn - please write up the smoothed-compression schedule as the recommended default in the library docs before we socialize this more widely.

Zofia

subject: Kickoff: uniform molecule sampling as a screening data product
body:
Hi Santiago,

Kicking off the graph sampler workstream. Screening partners keep asking for unbiased molecule libraries, and "unbiased" is the hard part: you cannot enumerate all molecules at a given size, so everyone samples from generative models with unknown bias. Our sequential importance sampling approach sidesteps that - enumerate stoichiometries for a given heavy-atom count, draw importance-weighted connected graphs per stoichiometry, reject to uniform, then aggregate into one provably uniform sample. Uniformity is the product.

Deliverables this window: pipeline hardened as a service (the enumerate_stoichiometries -> sample_molecules -> reject_to_uniform -> aggregate_uniform_samples chain), a reference library at C,N,O,F with up to 8 heavy atoms, and a scored variant using our property-prediction models.

Milestones: hardened pipeline 4/24, reference library 5/22, scored library + review 6/17.

Saoirse infra, Yara sampling correctness, Wanjiru pipeline. Compute plan from you when ready.

Anders

subject: Re: Kickoff: uniform molecule sampling as a screening data product
body:
Anders,

Resourcing.

Staffing: Saoirse 50%, Yara 60%, Wanjiru 70%. Good for all three milestones.

Compute splits in two. The sampling chain itself (stoichiometry enumeration, importance-weighted generation, rejection to uniform) is CPU-bound - we will run it on batch CPU quota, no accelerator ask. The scored library is different: property-scoring hundreds of millions of uniform samples is accelerator-heavy. For the property-scoring pass we hold the cirrus-tpu reservation - 128 accelerators - for the week of 2026-06-08, and I have built the eval schedule around that week. Ines, cc'd for awareness since Cirrus allocations are per-portfolio per quarter.

Risk to note early: rejection-to-uniform efficiency falls off as heavy-atom count grows; if acceptance rates at 8 heavy atoms are as low as Yara fears, the reference library may cap at 7. She will have measured acceptance curves by end of April.

Santiago

subject: Status: pipeline hardened, acceptance curves in, one cap decision needed
body:
Hi both,

Status. The hardened pipeline shipped on time: the full chain from enumerate_stoichiometries through reject_to_uniform and aggregate_uniform_samples now runs as a managed batch workflow with checkpointing per stoichiometry, and the stats_to_csv outputs feed a dashboard so we can watch acceptance rates live. Saoirse also added graphml validation between stages, which already caught two malformed batches.

Yara's acceptance curves are in: at C,N,O,F, rejection-to-uniform acceptance is comfortable through 6 heavy atoms, marginal at 7 (about 5x the CPU cost of 6), and genuinely bad at 8 - her projection says 8-heavy-atom uniformity would eat the entire remaining CPU budget for maybe 4% of the library.

Decision needed by 5/15: cap the reference library at 7 heavy atoms and document the cap, or descope elsewhere. Team recommendation is the cap.

Wanjiru

subject: Re: Status: pipeline hardened, acceptance curves in, one cap decision needed
body:
Team,

Confirming decisions ahead of scoring week:

1. The reference library caps at 7 heavy atoms. Yara's acceptance-curve analysis made this easy - we document the cap and the acceptance-rate rationale in the dataset card, and 8+ becomes a Q3 research question (importance distributions tuned per stoichiometry might move it).
2. Scoring runs next week as scheduled on the Cirrus reservation. Wanjiru, please have the uniform library staged and sharded by EOD Friday 6/5 so the accelerators are never idle - that week is the most expensive line item in this project.
3. The 6/17 review will present uniformity validation (Yara's importance-weight diagnostics), the C,N,O,F library through 7 heavy atoms, and the scored subset.

If staging slips even a day, tell Santiago immediately - we cannot shift that week.

Anders

subject: Kickoff: knowledge-graph-driven forecasting (graph temporal AI)
body:
Hi Bao,

Kicking off the graph temporal AI workstream. The gap we are attacking: existing forecasting offerings are passive - partners feed massive time-series data into complex models and get predictions back, with no way to inject what they actually know. Sector partners carry real domain knowledge (association rules, market principles, operation logistics) and today it goes unused.

Our approach integrates meta-data and user feedback as knowledge graphs inside the deep learning model, so the forecaster becomes adaptive and domain-specific rather than one-size-fits-all. Two partners in logistics have already agreed to pilot conversations if we can show a working feedback loop.

Milestones for this window: knowledge-graph encoder integrated with the base forecaster by 3/6, feedback-ingestion demo by 3/27, pilot-readiness review 4/15. Partner pilots themselves start in May, after the window.

Ondrej leads modeling, Hyun the graph encoder, Saoirse/Emeka/Paloma platform. Staffing from you this week?

Anders

subject: Re: Kickoff: knowledge-graph-driven forecasting (graph temporal AI)
body:
Anders,

Staffing for the window: Ondrej 70%, Hyun 40%, Saoirse 30%, Emeka 50%, Paloma 40%. That covers the encoder integration and the feedback-ingestion demo.

Looking past the window: Ondrej Bergstrom is committed at 60% to this project for May 2026 to carry the knowledge-graph encoder into the partner pilot, and my pilot plan assumes that allocation holds. He is the only person who understands both the encoder internals and the partner's association-rule format, so I want that in writing now rather than discovered in May.

Compute: modest - 16 A100s best-effort on titan for encoder training. The heavier cost is data engineering: partner meta-data arrives as three different graph schemas and Paloma needs to normalize them before Hyun can encode anything.

One calendar note: I want the pilot-readiness review before 4/15 if possible, since Q2 planning eats the following week.

Bao

subject: Status: encoder integrated, feedback loop demo on track, schema debt
body:
Hi both,

Status. The knowledge-graph encoder is integrated with the base forecaster as of 3/5 - a day early. On the internal logistics benchmark, conditioning on the meta-data graph cuts MAPE from 11.8% to 9.6% at the 2-week horizon; the win concentrates exactly where the partner's operation-logistics rules constrain the forecast, which is the story we wanted.

Feedback ingestion is on track for the 3/27 demo: a user correction becomes a graph edit, and Ondrej's incremental-update path retrains the affected embeddings in minutes, not hours.

The debt is schemas. Paloma normalized two of the three partner meta-data schemas; the third (the market-principles one) encodes rules as free text and needs a parsing step we did not scope. Recommendation: demo with two schemas and flag the third as a pilot-phase task with an owner, rather than rushing a fragile parser.

Hyun

subject: Re: Status: encoder integrated, feedback loop demo on track, schema debt
body:
Team,

Pilot-readiness review outcome (we squeezed it in 4/10 per Bao's calendar ask):

1. READY for the May pilot with the two normalized schemas. The 11.8% -> 9.6% MAPE improvement plus the minutes-scale feedback loop was the demo that landed - the partner rep literally asked when they could type in their own rules.
2. The free-text market-principles schema is formally deferred into the pilot phase, owned by Paloma with a design doc due 5/8. No fragile parser ships, agreed with Hyun's recommendation.
3. Pilot success criteria, agreed with the partner: MAPE parity or better vs their incumbent on 4 of 5 product lines, and at least one forecast correction round-tripped through the feedback loop per week.

Ondrej carries the encoder into the pilot per the staffing plan. Nice work all - this one reviewed itself.

Anders

subject: Kickoff: ARL - fairness without demographic labels
body:
Hi Ivo,

Kicking off the group-agnostic fairness workstream. The platform problem: customers want worst-group performance guarantees, but most of them cannot legally or practically collect demographic labels. Adversarially Reweighted Learning attacks exactly that - an adversary learns to upweight regions where the learner underperforms, improving the worst-off groups without ever seeing group membership.

Deliverables: ARL integrated into the model-quality tooling as an opt-in training mode, validated against the three benchmarks from the release (COMPAS, UCI Adult, and the Law School LSAC dataset), each of which has its own preprocessing notebook we need to port into the platform's ingestion path.

Milestones: benchmark repro by 4/17, tooling integration by 5/29, launch decision by 6/24 - I want this in front of the LRB before Q3 OKRs lock on 6/26.

Yara leads modeling, Kaia evals, Paloma ingestion, Emeka tooling. Staffing and compute from you next week?

Dmitri

subject: Re: Kickoff: ARL - fairness without demographic labels
body:
Dmitri,

Resourcing.

Staffing: Yara 60%, Kaia 40%, Paloma 50%, Emeka 40%. Compute is trivial for once - the ARL benchmarks are tabular, so we are talking a few GPUs on titan best-effort; the real cost is engineering time in the ingestion path.

Data plan: Paloma ports the COMPAS and UCI Adult preprocessing first (their notebooks are straightforward), then LSAC, which has the messiest licensing and format story. All three land in Corpus as versioned platform datasets. Per my notes the Corpus v2 migration freeze is 2026-07-24, so re-ingesting the benchmark datasets in mid-July still clears it with two weeks of slack. I have sequenced Paloma's work on that basis.

One flag: the reference code is TF1-era and the adversary/learner training loop needs a port to our current stack before Emeka can integrate it. Yara thinks two weeks; I budgeted three.

Ivo

subject: Status: benchmark repro complete, one honest caveat for the LRB
body:
Hi both,

Repro is complete on all three benchmarks. On COMPAS and UCI Adult, ARL improves worst-group AUC over the ERM baseline (+2.9 and +2.2 points respectively in our runs) with overall AUC essentially flat - matching the published pattern. LSAC took longer because of the preprocessing port Paloma flagged, but results there are consistent too. The TF1-to-current port cost us the full three weeks Ivo budgeted, not Yara's two, for the record - the adversary's gradient flow had a subtle stop-gradient bug that took days to find.

The caveat Kaia and I want stated plainly at the LRB: ARL improves worst-group outcomes for computationally-identifiable groups. When the disadvantaged group is not identifiable from features, ARL cannot find it. The tooling docs should say "improves" not "guarantees," and the eval report will include the synthetic case where ARL does nothing, so nobody oversells this.

Yara

subject: Re: Status: benchmark repro complete, one honest caveat for the LRB
body:
Team,

Decisions ahead of the 6/24 LRB slot (Nadia has us confirmed):

1. We present ARL as an opt-in training mode with the "improves, not guarantees" framing verbatim from Yara's note. The synthetic non-identifiable-group case goes in the appendix, not hidden - I would rather the board poke at it with us in the room.
2. Emeka's tooling integration is the launch surface: config flag, adversary architecture defaults from the paper, and the worst-group AUC panel in the standard eval report.
3. Scope cut: the customer-facing "fairness score" idea is dead for this cycle. It compresses exactly the nuance Yara warned about into one number.
4. Q3 OKR: extend validation beyond tabular to one text classification workload.

The +2.9/+2.2 worst-group AUC numbers with flat overall AUC are the headline. Good work getting the honest version to be also the compelling version.

Dmitri

subject: Kickoff: Gumbel-max causal gadgets -> counterfactual audit tooling
body:
Hi Bao,

Kicking off the causal gadgets workstream for trust-theory. The question every model audit ends with is counterfactual: would the system have made the same call if X had been different? Our open-source release gives us the machinery - JAX implementations of both Gadget 1 and Gadget 2 for learning generalized Gumbel-max causal mechanisms, where the learned coupling controls the variance of counterfactual estimates. Lower variance means fewer simulations per audit question, which is what makes an audit product economical.

Plan for the window: repro the Section 7.1 experiments and the first two Table 1 columns by 5/1, wrap the gadgets in an internal counterfactual-audit API by 6/5, then a pilot audit on one production decision system in July, review 7/9.

The tutorial.ipynb walkthrough is genuinely good onboarding - new folks should start there.

Wei leads research, Emeka the API, Giannis experiments. Staffing from you this week?

Ximena

subject: Re: Kickoff: Gumbel-max causal gadgets -> counterfactual audit tooling
body:
Ximena,

Staffing and resourcing.

Through June: Wei 50%, Emeka 40%, Giannis 60%. For the pilot month: Wei Ivanov is committed at 60% to this project for July 2026 - the counterfactual-audit pilot is scheduled entirely around his availability that month, so please protect the allocation. Nobody else on the roster can both interpret the learned couplings and talk to the decision-system owners in their language.

Compute: light. Coupling training for the Section 7.1 scale runs on 8 A100s best-effort; even the pilot's simulation batches are embarrassingly parallel CPU work. No reservations, no budget escalation - the constraint on this project is Wei's calendar, not hardware.

One dependency: the pilot needs read access to the decision system's logged inputs, which means a privacy review. Given the standard 2-3 week SLA I want the request filed by mid-May. Emeka will draft it.

Bao

subject: Status: repro done, variance wins hold, one scope boundary
body:
Hi both,

Repro status: done for Section 7.1 and the first two columns of Table 1, using paper_experiments.ipynb as the harness. The learned couplings from both gadgets beat the baseline couplings in coupling_util on counterfactual-estimate variance in our reruns - Gadget 2's advantage is largest exactly where the mechanism distributions are least uniform, matching the paper's story. Training was stable; the only surprise was how sensitive Gadget 1 is to temperature initialization, which Wei documented in the shared config notes.

Scope boundary to confirm: the last two Table 1 columns and the Section 7.3 experiments rely on the companion implementation from the second repository, which we deliberately did not port. Emeka's API therefore exposes Gadget 1 and Gadget 2 only. Fine for the pilot, but the review slide should say so explicitly so nobody expects the full table.

API integration is tracking to 6/5. Privacy request went to Kofi's queue 5/14.

Giannis

subject: Re: Status: repro done, variance wins hold, one scope boundary
body:
Team,

Decisions going into pilot month:

1. Pilot is GO for July. Privacy review cleared 6/24 with one condition - counterfactual queries run against a hashed snapshot, not live logs - which Emeka says costs us a day of plumbing. Acceptable.
2. Pilot scope: Gadget 2 only. Giannis's reruns show it dominating on the non-uniform mechanisms that actually occur in the decision system, and one gadget keeps Wei's July hours focused. Gadget 1 stays available in the API but out of the pilot report.
3. The audit report template will state the two-gadget scope boundary and cite the companion-repo limitation, per Giannis's note.
4. Review moves from 7/9 to 7/10 to avoid colliding with the portfolio all-hands.

Wei - the pilot is yours to run; everyone else protects your calendar. Let's find out if the variance numbers survive contact with a real audit question.

Ximena

subject: Kickoff: GWikiMatch as the standard long-document matching eval
body:
Hi Bao,

Kicking off GWikiMatch. The retrieval teams have no shared eval for long-form document matching - everyone measures content similarity between document pairs their own way, so numbers do not compare across teams. GWikiMatch fixes that: candidate pairs generated by label propagation over the English Wikipedia hyperlink graph (edge weights from directed hyperlink counts, each node initialized with its own URL as label), then every candidate pair annotated by 3 human raters with majority vote on a 0/1/2 similarity scale.

Deliverables this window: the dataset hosted internally with a documented eval protocol, two baseline systems scored on it, and adoption by at least two retrieval teams.

Milestones: hosted dataset + protocol by 5/29, baselines by 7/3, adoption review 8/5.

Quentin owns the eval protocol and baselines, Bilal data engineering, Oyin infrastructure. Staffing and any platform asks from you next week?

Anders

subject: Re: Kickoff: GWikiMatch as the standard long-document matching eval
body:
Anders,

Staffing: Quentin 50%, Bilal 60%, Oyin 50%. Compute is minor - scoring two baselines on long-document pairs needs maybe 16 A100s best-effort for a week each.
