The one platform dependency is storage — the precomputed Myrtle-10 kernels are large, and I'd rather mirror them once than have five people re-downloading. Halima will file the quota request this week. — Deshawn

subject: Re: Kickoff: infinite-width uncertainty & calibration audit
body: Status on the repro milestone. The ESS sampler is running under jax.vmap across 32 parallel chains; on the precomputed Myrtle-10 kernels we reproduce the paper's qualitative result — the NNGP posterior is markedly better calibrated than its finite-width analogue. On our CIFAR-10 subset (10k test) we're seeing ECE 0.019 for the NNGP with the softmax link vs 0.041 for the finite-width ensemble baseline. Two flags: (1) chain mixing degrades on the 45k-example kernel — we need roughly 3x more ESS iterations than budgeted, which pushes the full grid to ~4 days on best-effort titan; (2) the kernel mirror is 78 GB and the storage quota request is still pending with Corpus. Neither blocks the late-April report if the quota clears this week. — Halima

subject: Re: Kickoff: infinite-width uncertainty & calibration audit
body: Closing decision for this window. The calibration report went to Eleni's staff on Tuesday and the takeaway held up: NNGP plus ESS gives a defensible calibration reference, and the ECE gap vs finite-width is consistent across the Myrtle-10 grid. Decision: we are not standing up a live service this half. We ship the Colab notebooks as-is (ESS implementation plus kernel loaders), publish the internal report, and revisit the service question with the H2 GPC extension. Rationale: the mixing cost on large kernels makes on-demand runs too slow for a review-time tool; precomputing is the right shape, and that's an H2-sized job. Thanks all — clean landing, three days inside the window. Deshawn, keep the July staffing plan penciled in as discussed. — Ximena

subject: Kickoff: romanized language ID for ingestion routing
body: Team, kickoff for improving informally romanized language identification — the follow-on to our open-source release. Why data-platforms cares: a large share of user text in South Asian languages arrives romanized, and our ingestion pipelines currently misroute it. The method work sits on three resources: the Bhasha-Abhijnaanam (B-A) benchmark, the Aksharantar romanization lexicons, and the Dakshina dataset; part of the job is just making the identifiers line up (B-A uses Assamese, Aksharantar asm, and Dakshina bn-style codes exist only for a subset). Milestones: baseline LID repro on B-A by March 20; lexicon-augmented models by end of April; integration decision for the ingestion router by early June. Alina owns staffing; Rafael is tech lead. Please put risks in the tracker, not in hallway chats. — Dmitri

subject: Resourcing — romanized LID
body: Dmitri — resourcing picture. Current window: Rafael 50% (modeling), Leilani 40% (data conversion across the three resources), Milan 40% (router integration spike), Carmen 20% (eval design). Looking past the June decision point: the Aksharantar-driven expansion to the full 20+ language set is the obvious H2 continuation, and Rafael Duran is committed at 60% to this project for July 2026 — I've locked that in the allocation sheet so we don't lose him to whatever fire flares up next quarter. Compute is light (CPU plus a handful of titan-a100 GPUs for the transformer baselines). One dependency: keep the Corpus v2 migration freeze date (2026-07-10) on our radar — if the router integration slips past June it collides with the freeze window. — Alina

subject: Re: Kickoff: romanized language ID for ingestion routing
body: Status, week of April 20. Baseline repro done on B-A — our reimplementation matches the paper's reported setup within noise. The lexicon-augmented models are where the gains are: adding the Aksharantar romanization lexicons as training signal lifts macro-F1 by 3.4 points over the baseline, with the biggest jumps on the Hindi/Marathi/Nepali confusable cluster. Grunt-work note: the tooling assumes shared file root names (Assamese.tsv rather than asm.tsv), so Leilani wrote a normalization layer mapping B-A identifiers to Aksharantar codes and, where they exist, Dakshina codes. Open risk: Dakshina covers only a subset of the languages (no Bodo, Kashmiri, Maithili, Manipuri), so for those we have lexicons but no romanized supervision — accuracy there trails by ~6 F1. Proposal for the May review: a two-tier quality bar. — Rafael

subject: Re: Kickoff: romanized language ID for ingestion routing
body: Decision from Thursday's review: we integrate LID v1 into the ingestion router for the 12 languages where we have both Aksharantar lexicons and Dakshina supervision, and we hold the remaining languages behind a quality gate rather than shipping the ~6-point-worse tier. Milan's router spike showed the swap is low-risk (shadow mode first, two-week bake). Timeline: shadow deployment by May 29, decision review June 4, full cutover before the window closes June 8 — comfortably ahead of the Corpus v2 freeze on July 10. The B-A macro-F1 gains (+3.4) go in the OKR readout. Carmen, please finalize the eval dashboard so the shadow-mode diff is readable by non-team folks. Nice work all — this one's been unusually smooth. Dmitri

subject: IFEval kickoff — instruction-following as a release gate
body: Team — kicking off IFEval productization for the language portfolio. Base: our open-source instruction-following eval, which scores models on verifiable instructions ('write a 300+ word summary', 'answer in exactly three bullet points') from jsonl prompt/response pairs, reporting strict and loose accuracy at both prompt and instruction level. Goal: make IFEval a first-class gate in Evalline so every language-model release gets an instruction-following regression check — Tomas's team is expecting our integration spec. Milestones: harness integrated behind Evalline's runner API by June 5; baseline sweep across our current model fleet by June 19; Launch Review sign-off for gating by mid-July. Stretch goal we'll discuss at resourcing: using the eval as a training signal for improving small models, not just measuring them. Alina will send the staffing plan. — Priya

subject: IFEval staffing + distillation scope addition
body: Priya — staffing plus the scope addition we agreed at Thursday's sync. Core eval integration: Oyin 60% (Evalline runner API), Gustavo 30% (fleet sweep automation). The addition: the stretch goal is now in scope. There's nothing on the shelf internally for this, so we're scoping and staffing a distillation training recipe from scratch — teacher sampling, response filtering through the IFEval checker, and a finetuning loop that optimizes strict accuracy — with Yusuf at 60% and Rafael at 30% through June. First recipe milestone: an 8B student showing +5 points prompt-level strict accuracy by early July. Compute: titan-a100 best-effort suffices at 8B scale; no reservation ask. Dependency: the response-jsonl format from the fleet harness doesn't match evaluation_main's expected input yet — Oyin has a converter in review. — Alina

subject: Re: IFEval kickoff — instruction-following as a release gate
body: Status. Evalline integration is live in staging — IFEval runs behind the runner API, and Oyin's converter handles the fleet's response format (that mismatch cost us a week; watch for double-escaped newlines, they silently fail four instruction types). Baseline sweep: our 8B instruct model scores 58.9 prompt-level strict / 66.0 loose; the 34B scores 74.2 / 79.8. Distillation recipe: first end-to-end run finished — teacher sampling plus IFEval-filtered finetuning lifts the 8B to 62.1 strict (+3.2). Short of the +5 target, but the response filter is still crude (keeps only fully-compliant samples; we're testing per-instruction credit). Risk to flag: filtered data skews short — loose-accuracy gains lag strict, and MMLU dipped 0.4. Rafael is ablating filter strictness this week. — Yusuf

subject: Re: IFEval kickoff — instruction-following as a release gate
body: Decisions from Launch Review prep. (1) Gating: LRB signed off — IFEval strict accuracy becomes a blocking check in Evalline for language releases starting July 20, with thresholds set per model tier from Gustavo's sweep. (2) The distillation recipe stays funded in Q3 — it made the OKR list before the June 26 lock, scoped as 'recipe plus 8B reference student at +5 strict'. Yusuf's latest run is at +4.1 with per-instruction credit in the filter, so the target looks reachable. (3) Scope cut: we drop the 1B student from this half; the compliance data is too short-form to help at that scale, per the MMLU regression. Nadia will circulate the LRB minutes. Thanks all — this is the fastest an eval has gone from repo to gate. Priya

subject: Intent recognition kickoff — activity signals API
body: Team, kickoff for Intent Recognition in the data-platforms portfolio. We're productizing our sensor-ML tooling: models that infer user activities from device sensor streams. The pipeline stages are already defined in the open-source release — sensor data as AnnotatedRecordingCollections, mediapipe-based processing, conversion to SequenceExamples, then TensorFlow training and inference/metrics. Product target: an activity-signal API for two internal partners who today hand-roll their own classifiers. Milestones: ADL-dataset pipeline repro by end of April (the converter binary exists, so this is mostly build plumbing); partner-data pilot in June; go/no-go on the API for mid-July. Known annoyance up front: the whole thing builds under bazel with MEDIAPIPE_DISABLE_GPU=1 and C++17 flags, so getting CI green is a real task, not a checkbox. Alina owns staffing. — Dmitri

subject: Intent recognition — resourcing for the pilot
body: Dmitri — resourcing for the pilot phase. People: Nikhil 60% (pipeline + training), Fumiko 40% (modeling/metrics), Oyin 50%, Carmen 15% (advisory on eval design; she's heavily committed elsewhere). The new scope item: partner labels are too noisy to trust, so quality review needs humans in the loop, and there's no existing internal tool that supports span-level rating of sensor traces — so we're scoping and staffing a human-rating annotation UI from scratch: timeline visualization of recording collections, span labeling, and rater-agreement dashboards. Oyin owns it, design pass in June, first raters on it mid-July. Compute is trivial (CPU training, a few titan GPUs). Platform note: we'll host rater data in Corpus, and I've confirmed our schema lands before the v2 migration freeze on 2026-07-10. — Alina

subject: Re: Intent recognition kickoff — activity signals API
body: Status. Build: CI is green — took the full bag of tricks (--experimental_repo_remote_exec, pinned mediapipe commit, C++17 everywhere). ADL repro: the converter produces AnnotatedRecordingCollections cleanly; after mediapipe processing and SequenceExample conversion, the reference model trains in the colab notebook and we get 72.3% balanced accuracy across activity classes, in line with expectations for the sample configs. Partner pilot: first drop of partner sensor data is ingested; recording_collection fields were half-empty in ~18% of sessions, which the processing graph silently drops — Fumiko added a validation stage so we at least count what we lose. Risk: partner label noise is worse than assumed (kappa 0.41 between their two existing raters), which raises the stakes on Oyin's annotation UI landing on schedule. Mocks reviewed last week, backend scaffold up. — Nikhil

subject: Re: Intent recognition kickoff — activity signals API
body: Go/no-go outcome from Thursday: conditional go. The API ships to both partners in Q3, but gated on label quality — we will not train partner-specific models until their data passes a 0.6 kappa bar on re-rated samples. That makes the annotation UI the critical path; Oyin's beta goes to first raters July 13, and Fumiko will run the agreement study over the following two weeks. Scope cut to protect that: the second partner's custom activity taxonomy is deferred to Q4; both partners launch on the shared taxonomy. Also noting for the record: the pipeline itself is in good shape — the ADL numbers plus the validation stage were what convinced the review. OKR language went in before the June 26 lock, so no surprises there. Thanks all. Dmitri

subject: ROAR benchmark kickoff — scoring interpretability methods
body: Team, kickoff on the explainability-methods benchmark for data-platforms. We're standing up ROAR — RemOve And Retrain — as an internal service: it evaluates feature-importance estimators by removing the fraction of inputs each estimator ranks most important, retraining, and measuring the accuracy drop; the best estimator is the one whose removals hurt the most. Why it matters: three product teams are choosing interpretability methods for sensitive-domain work right now and are picking by vibes. Target: ROAR scores for our five candidate estimators on ImageNet-scale classification, delivered as an Evalline report. Milestones: pipeline repro by mid-April; full estimator sweep in early June; readout before end of June. Bruno — the retraining requirement is the whole cost story here (every estimator × removal fraction × seeds is a fresh ImageNet training), so let's get the compute plan pinned this month. — Dmitri

subject: ROAR sweep — vulcan compute plan
body: Ines — compute plan for the ROAR sweep; want to make sure the books agree with ours. The sweep is 5 estimators × 6 removal fractions × 3 seeds = 90 ImageNet retrainings, plus the base models. We hold the vulcan-h100 reservation for the week of 2026-06-01 — 256 GPUs — and the whole sweep is scheduled against that week: 90 trainings at ~14 h each on 16-GPU slices fits with margin if we keep utilization above 85%. Two asks: (1) confirm no preemption windows that week; (2) confirm the maintenance window we should plan around is still 2026-06-22 to 06-24 — we're deliberately a full three weeks ahead of it, but if June 1 slips we start eating into it. Dev work stays on titan best-effort meanwhile. — Bruno

subject: Re: ROAR benchmark kickoff — scoring interpretability methods
body: Status ahead of the sweep week. Pipeline repro is done: base ResNet-50s train to 76.0% top-1 on ImageNet in our setup, and the ROAR mechanics (rank inputs per estimator, remove the top fraction, retrain from scratch) are validated end-to-end on the 10%-removal slice. Early signal matches the paper's headline: gradient-based saliency barely beats a random-removal baseline once you retrain, while the ensemble variants degrade accuracy much faster — exactly the separation ROAR exists to expose. Ops notes: Leilani's launcher packs 16-GPU slices well (dry run hit 88% utilization), and checkpoint/removal artifacts land in Corpus without issues. Risk: estimator #5 (the SmoothGrad variant) is 3× slower at ranking than budgeted; Gustavo is precomputing its rankings this week so ranking never blocks a training slot during the June window. — Efe

subject: Re: ROAR benchmark kickoff — scoring interpretability methods
body: Wrap-up decisions from the readout. The sweep completed inside the June window and the report is in Evalline. Headline: two of the five estimators are defensible for sensitive-domain use; plain gradient saliency is formally indistinguishable from random removal at every fraction, and we're recommending teams stop using it for feature-importance claims. Decisions: (1) the ROAR report becomes a standing Evalline module — Tomas's team takes ownership of reruns, and we hand off by June 26; (2) we cut the planned CIFAR extension — ImageNet-scale evidence was the ask, and adding small-scale results doesn't change any decision; (3) Efe writes the one-page guidance doc for the three product teams. Handoff before the OKR lock keeps this off our Q3 plate entirely. Good, clean project. — Dmitri

subject: Kickoff: invariant explanations / meta-model audits
body: Team — kickoff for invariant-explanations in the vision portfolio. The core idea from our release: train meta-models that predict the predictions of an entire class of base-models trained under different hparam settings, without fully training those base-models. Covariates are either X,H (sample images plus hparams) or X,W@epoch (samples plus base-model weights at an early epoch); targets are the base-model predictions at the final epoch, 86, of the CNN zoo. Product angle: hparam-sensitivity audits — telling a vision team whether their model's behavior on a given input is stable across the hparam class, before they burn a training run. Milestones: repro on the accompanying sample weights/metrics by end of April; full-zoo training in May; audit-tool prototype decision by end of June. Ivo has the staffing pen. — Lucia

subject: Staffing & constraints — invariant explanations
body: Lucia — staffing and constraints. Allocations for the heavy month: Bilal Novak is committed at 60% to this project for May 2026 — he owns the covariate pipelines (X,H assembly and the W@epoch extraction, which is the fiddly one). Around him: Linnea 40% (meta-model training), Fumiko 30% (eval design), Vera 25% (infra), Yusuf 15% (advisory). Compute: the meta-models are small; the cost is I/O — the zoo's weight snapshots are ~2 TB and the train/test instance splits multiply fast (base models × samples per model), so we're asking Corpus for a fast-scratch mirror rather than GPU reservations. Titan best-effort covers training. One process note: if the audit prototype is a go, Launch Review will want the calibration story, so Fumiko's eval design should bake that in from the start. — Ivo

subject: Re: Kickoff: invariant explanations / meta-model audits
body: Status at the end of the heavy month. Full-zoo training is done for the X,H covariate setting: at train_fraction 0.8, the meta-model hits 87.9% test accuracy predicting base-model predictions, and accuracy is stable (±0.4) across the instance-split iterations — the invariance property we hoped to see. The X,W@epoch setting is running now; early epochs (≤10) barely beat X,H, which supports the cheap-covariates story for the audit tool. Per config.py conventions, every setup's train/test accuracy is saved out, so the aggregate plots regenerate automatically. Issues: the W@epoch extraction hit a snag — snapshot layouts differ across zoo generations, and Bilal lost most of a week normalizing them (this is the risk we flagged; his May allocation is what's absorbing it). The fast-scratch mirror from Corpus landed May 12 and I/O stopped being the bottleneck. On track for the June decision. — Linnea

subject: Re: Kickoff: invariant explanations / meta-model audits
body: Decision from Monday's review: the audit-tool prototype is a go, X,H covariates only. Rationale: X,H at train_fraction 0.8 delivers 87.9% with trivial storage, while W@epoch adds under a point at the epochs worth using but drags the 2 TB snapshot problem into every customer conversation — so W@epoch is cut from the product path and stays a research question. Q3 scope (locked in OKRs before June 26): prototype serving one pilot vision team, meta-model retrained weekly, audit report rendered through Evalline. Vera owns productionizing the covariate-pipeline handoff from Bilal as he rolls off; Fumiko's calibration section made the LRB pre-read and Nadia flagged no blockers. Nice work — this went from paper mechanics to a fundable tool in a quarter. — Lucia

subject: Invariant Slot Attention kickoff — unsupervised object inventories
body: Team, kickoff for Invariant Slot Attention productization. From our release: object discovery with slot-centric reference frames — slots carry their own position/scale frames, so the model discovers objects invariantly to translation and scale, built on the scenic codebase. Data-platforms angle: unsupervised object inventories over partner image feeds, no labels required. The repo ships configs and loaders for six datasets — Tetrominoes, Objects Room, MultiShapeNet-Easy, CLEVR, CLEVRTex, Waymo Open — with the first four runnable without manual downloads, so the ramp is: smallest model on Tetrominoes (the 512-example equiv_transl config) as a smoke test by April 10; CLEVR plus CLEVRTex quality runs in May; Waymo Open scale test in June; productization decision end of June. Ivo owns staffing and the compute ask — the June scale runs are the expensive part. — Dmitri

subject: ISA scale runs — cirrus reservation details
body: Ines — compute plan for the ISA scale runs. The small stuff (Tetrominoes/CLEVR configs) fits titan best-effort and is already running. The June push is the real ask: we hold the cirrus-tpu reservation for the week of 2026-06-01 — 384 accelerators — and both the CLEVRTex sweep and the Waymo Open scale test are scheduled against that week. The plan packs the sweep (12 configs × 3 seeds) into the first half of the week and the Waymo run into the back half, with checkpoints to Corpus every 2 h. Asks: (1) confirm the pod slice is contiguous — the Waymo input pipeline saturates host RAM if we're scattered; (2) a heads-up contact for that week in case we need a topology change on short notice. Dmitri's end-of-June decision depends directly on these runs landing. — Ivo

subject: Re: Invariant Slot Attention kickoff — unsupervised object inventories
body: Status before the June window. Smoke test: done long ago — the smallest ISA model on the Tetrominoes equiv_transl config trains cleanly (ARI 0.995, matching expectations). CLEVR: baseline vs invariant configs reproduce the expected gap; the invariant models hold ARI under object-translation shifts where baseline slot attention degrades ~15 points, which is the property the product story rests on. The yellow flag is data readiness for June: CLEVRTex and Waymo Open both require manual download and preprocessing per the datasets folder, and the Waymo preprocessing is heavier than estimated — Chiara's conversion job is ~60% through, and the licensing checklist with Kofi cleared only last week. If preprocessing isn't done by May 29 we should swap the run order (CLEVRTex first) rather than slip the week. Bilal's eval harness for object-inventory metrics is ready. — Maren

subject: Re: Invariant Slot Attention kickoff — unsupervised object inventories
body: Decisions from the post-mortem on the June runs. CLEVRTex sweep: landed, results strong — invariant reference frames keep ARI within 2 points of CLEVR performance on textured scenes, while the baseline drops 11. Waymo Open: we got a partial run only; preprocessing finished late (May 31) and the input pipeline underfed the accelerators for the first two days. Decision: Waymo scale validation moves to Q3 with the preprocessing done properly, and it goes into the OKRs before the June 26 lock. Productization: go for the object-inventory pilot on synthetic-plus-CLEVRTex evidence; the pilot partner's feed is closer to CLEVRTex statistics anyway. Chiara owns turning the conversion job into a maintained pipeline. Learning for the file: manual-download datasets get a two-week buffer, no exceptions. — Dmitri

subject: Kickoff: multilingual NMT representation analysis at scale
body: Team — kickoff on scaling up our multilingual-NMT representation analysis (the Investigating M4 line of work). The release ships the Colab and data for SVCCA-based analysis: model_scores.csv holds SVCCA similarity between language-pair activations across layers and checkpoints, and the finetuning files track relative BLEU change plus post-finetuning representation shift. The product question for the language portfolio: when we finetune our multilingual models for a priority language pair, which other pairs' representations move, and can we predict the BLEU regressions before they land? Milestones: repro the released plots by March 6; extend the SVCCA tooling to our current production multilingual model by mid-May; regression-prediction readout in July feeding H2 capacity planning. Alina will circulate staffing; Quentin is analysis lead. — Priya

subject: M4 analysis — July vulcan reservation
body: Ines — compute forecast for the M4 analysis so the July crunch doesn't surprise anyone. Activation extraction on the production multilingual model is the heavy step: full encoder/decoder activations per language pair, per layer, per checkpoint, for the SVCCA grid. We hold the vulcan-h100 reservation for the week of 2026-07-06 — 256 GPUs — and the full extraction plus SVCCA grid is planned against that week. Extraction fills roughly the first three days; the SVCCA computation itself is CPU-heavy, so days 4-5 are mostly staging results into Corpus while the GPUs run the finetuning probes. Asks: confirm the reservation shows on your side, and confirm the post-maintenance health checks from the 06-22 to 06-24 vulcan window won't spill into July. Dev-scale extraction runs on titan meanwhile. — Alina

subject: Re: Kickoff: multilingual NMT representation analysis at scale
body: Status. Repro milestone: done — Quentin regenerated the release plots from model_scores.csv and finetuned_model_scores.csv, and our reading matches the paper: encoder representations cluster by linguistic family, and the clustering sharpens with depth. Extension to the production model: the SVCCA pipeline now runs on our checkpoints; on the 12-pair pilot grid, high-resource pairs show layer-5 encoder similarity above 0.86 within family, and Nikhil's probe finetunes reproduce the expected asymmetry — finetuning a high-resource pair barely moves related-pair representations, while low-resource pairs shift broadly (matching the relative-BLEU-change pattern in the release data). Risks: (1) full activation dumps for the July grid project to ~38 TB — Csilla is negotiating retention with Corpus (dump, compute SVCCA, delete within 72 h); (2) checkpoint selection — production checkpoints aren't evenly spaced like the release data, which complicates the across-checkpoint axis. — Vera

subject: Re: Kickoff: multilingual NMT representation analysis at scale
body: Pre-flight decisions for next week's run. (1) Scope: the grid is frozen at 24 language pairs × 6 layers × 4 checkpoints — Quentin's power analysis says that's sufficient to rank finetuning-regression risk for every production pair we care about, and it keeps the dump inside the negotiated 72-hour retention window. (2) The regression-prediction readout moves from nice-slide to committed H2 deliverable — it went into the OKRs before the June 26 lock as the capacity-planning input for multilingual finetuning. (3) Contingency: if next week's runs slip badly, the fallback is the 12-pair pilot-grid results, which already support the family-clustering story. Csilla owns the go/no-go checklist Monday morning; Nikhil owns the finetuning probes. Fingers crossed for boring infrastructure. — Priya

subject: Kickoff: pretraining for irregular time series
body: Team, kickoff for pretraining on irregular time series. From our release: self-supervised pretraining for irregularly-sampled clinical time series, building on STraTS-style encoders, with geometric masking augmentations (pre-generated mask banks, since per-iteration mask generation proved too slow) and evaluation on PhysioNet Challenge 2012 — with MIMIC-III, eICU and the H&M retail dataset behind access agreements. Data-platforms angle: a pretraining recipe plus benchmark suite that health-science and commerce teams can reuse instead of hand-rolling encoders per dataset. Milestones: PhysioNet repro by April 10; pretraining-vs-scratch comparison across at least three datasets by mid-May; packaging decision by end of May. This is a short window, so scope discipline matters. Ivo owns staffing. Access paperwork for MIMIC-III/eICU starts today; it's the long pole. — Dmitri

subject: Staffing + leaderboard scope — irregular TS pretraining
body: Dmitri — staffing plus the one scope addition from Friday. Core: Freya 60% (pretraining recipes), Kaia 40% (clinical eval design), Maren 40% (data pipelines + mask caching), Saoirse 50%. The addition: for the benchmark suite to actually get adopted, teams need results they can see and submit to, and nothing internal does this today — so we're scoping and staffing a benchmark leaderboard service from scratch: run ingestion from the eval harness, ranking views per dataset and metric, and submission auth. Saoirse owns it within her 50%; Maren supports the ingestion path. Compute: titan best-effort is plenty (these models are small); the storage ask to Corpus for the pre-generated geometric mask banks (~400 GB) is filed. Risk on record: eICU access approval is still pending and historically takes 4-6 weeks — the three-dataset milestone may need H&M substituted for eICU. — Ivo

subject: Re: Kickoff: pretraining for irregular time series
body: Status. PhysioNet-2012 repro: done, and the headline result holds — pretraining with geometric masking lifts mortality-prediction AUROC to 0.852 vs 0.839 for the scratch-trained baseline, with the gain widening (+2.5 AUROC points) in the 10%-labels regime, which is the story that matters for adoption. The cached mask banks work as advertised: sampling from the pre-generated set instead of generating per-iteration cut step time about 35%. Dataset status: MIMIC-III access cleared April 28 and Maren's pipeline is converting it now; eICU is still in the approval queue (as predicted), so the mid-May comparison will run PhysioNet + MIMIC-III + H&M. One technical wrinkle: the imported STraTS modules needed the smart_cond shim from TF 2.12 to run on our stack — Kaia has the fix documented. Leaderboard: Saoirse has ingestion working end-to-end against the eval harness; ranking UI in review. — Freya

subject: Re: Kickoff: pretraining for irregular time series
body: Packaging decision from yesterday's review: ship it. The recipe goes out as an internal package (pretraining configs + mask banks + STraTS-compatible encoder), and the benchmark suite launches with PhysioNet-2012, MIMIC-III and H&M — the three-dataset evidence was convincing, with pretraining winning on all three and the low-label gains (+2.5 AUROC on PhysioNet at 10% labels) doing the persuading. Saoirse's leaderboard goes live to the two pilot teams June 8 with submission auth on; eICU gets added whenever the approval clears, as a fast-follow rather than a blocker. Deferred: the retail-specific augmentation ideas — interesting, but Q3 material, and they would have blown the window. Kaia writes the model card and access-requirements page (the DUA constraints need to be impossible to miss). Clean landing, three days early. — Dmitri

subject: ISL kickoff — causal explainability for tabular models
body: Team, kickoff for ISL — Invariant Structure Learning — in data-platforms. From our release: ISL learns causal structure that stays invariant across environments, improving generalization and giving causal explanations; the codebase covers environment construction for synthetic and real data (Boston Housing, Insurance, Sachs) and both supervised and self-supervised settings. Product angle: a causal-explainability toolkit for tabular models — partner teams keep asking which features actually drive a model and getting correlational answers. Milestones: repro on the shipped datasets by May 22 (synthetic env generation is scripted — e.g., 3 environments × 100 samples per graph); self-supervised mode evaluated on one partner tabular dataset by mid-June; toolkit go/no-go by early July. Alina owns staffing; Csilla is tech lead. Reminder that Q3 OKR planning locks June 26 — if this is a go, the ask needs to be written by then. — Dmitri

subject: ISL staffing + leaderboard scope
body: Dmitri — staffing and scope. Core: Csilla 50% (ISL modeling), Linnea 40% (partner-dataset evaluation), Rafael 30% through June (self-supervised setting). The addition we agreed: adoption needs a visible comparison surface — there's no internal service for this, so we're scoping and staffing a benchmark leaderboard service from scratch for structure-learning evals: run submission, SHD and edge-F1 rankings per dataset, and per-environment breakdowns. Jorge owns it at 60%. Compute: negligible (CPU plus occasional titan GPUs). Dependencies: partner tabular data goes through Corpus, and their schema intake pauses for the v2 migration freeze on 2026-07-10 — Linnea's ingestion request is filed this week to stay ahead of it. Privacy review for the partner dataset started Monday; the 2-3 week SLA fits if nothing bounces. — Alina

subject: Re: ISL kickoff — causal explainability for tabular models
body: Status. Repro: complete on all three real datasets plus the synthetic grids. On Sachs, ISL's supervised setting recovers the consensus network at SHD 12 vs 19 for our NOTEARS baseline, and on synthetic graphs (3 envs × 100 samples) the invariance penalty reliably kills the spurious edges that single-environment fitting keeps. Self-supervised mode: running on the partner tabular dataset since June 9; early edge-F1 is promising (0.71) but stability across bootstrap resamples is worse than on the shipped datasets — Rafael suspects the partner data violates the environment-separation assumption (their environments are time slices with drift). Mitigation being tested: coarser environment binning. Leaderboard: Jorge demoed submission-to-ranking end-to-end Friday; per-environment breakdown views land this week. Privacy review cleared June 11. On track for the go/no-go. — Csilla

subject: Re: ISL kickoff — causal explainability for tabular models
body: Go/no-go outcome: go, with one scope adjustment. The toolkit ships in Q3 for supervised ISL plus the leaderboard — that combination is defensible today (Sachs SHD 12, partner edge-F1 0.71, and a comparison surface teams can check). The self-supervised setting is held back from the toolkit until the environment-binning work stabilizes bootstrap variance; it stays a research track. This matches what we wrote into the Q3 OKRs before the June 26 lock, so no re-litigation needed. Assignments: Jorge hardens the leaderboard for a second team's datasets; Linnea documents the environment-construction requirements (the time-slice caveat goes in bold); Csilla owns the v1 API surface. Launch Review pre-read due to Nadia by July 23 for the early-August board. Solid quarter's work, everyone. — Dmitri

subject: ABC factor isolation kickoff
body: Team — kickoff for the ABC factor-isolation project in vision. From our release (Learn your ABCs): approximate bijective correspondence isolates factors of variation using set supervision — train on image sets grouped by a shared factor, and the representation isolates the complementary factors. The repo gives us three tracks: Shapes3D training with mutual-information measurement via MINE to quantify exactly which generative factors the representation captures; the MNIST digit-style notebook; and pose-estimation evaluation in both dictionary-lookup and regression scenarios. Product angle: controllable-representation building blocks for the vision portfolio's editing pipeline — isolate pose from identity, style from content. Milestones: Shapes3D repro with MI measurements by May 8; pose-estimation evaluation by mid-June; integration recommendation by end of June (window closes July 6). Santiago owns staffing and the compute ask. — Lucia

subject: ABC sweeps — vulcan compute plan
body: Ines — compute plan for the factor-isolation sweeps. The Shapes3D experiment grid is wide (set-supervision settings × factor groupings × seeds — train.py makes this cheap to launch and expensive to run), and the pose-estimation training adds a second wave. We hold the vulcan-h100 reservation for the week of 2026-06-01 — 256 GPUs — and both waves are packed into that week: the Shapes3D grid across the first three days, pose models the back two. The MINE information estimates run alongside on the same slices (they're light). Asks: (1) confirm the reservation on your books; (2) we plan to be well clear before the 06-22 to 06-24 vulcan maintenance, but if our week slips please tell us early — the end-of-June recommendation has no slack behind it. Dev runs continue on titan best-effort. — Santiago

subject: Re: ABC factor isolation kickoff
body: Status from inside the compute week. Shapes3D grid: ~70% complete and reproducing the paper's core claim — with set supervision on a single shared factor, the ABC objective isolates the complementary factors cleanly; MINE estimates show the isolated representation carrying high mutual information with the target factors and near-zero with the supervised one. The factor-grouping ablations are the interesting product signal: pose/identity-style groupings isolate as well as the easy color factors do. Pose wave starts tomorrow, one day early. Issues: (1) tensorflow_datasets auto-download of Shapes3D failed on the cluster's egress rules — Oyin mirrored it into Corpus, ten-minute fix, noting for the runbook; (2) MINE training is finicky on two factor pairs (estimator variance blows up) — Carmen suggests the standard bias-corrected variant, testing today. No risk to the week's plan. — Giannis

subject: Re: ABC factor isolation kickoff
body: Integration recommendation, as promised by end of June: adopt, narrowly. The pose-estimation results are the deciding evidence — in the dictionary-lookup scenario the ABC representations retrieve correct poses at parity with the supervised baseline, and the regression scenario lands within 8% of it with zero pose labels, which is the cost story the editing-pipeline team cares about. Recommendation shipped to their leads today: use ABC-style set supervision for the pose/identity split in the editing pipeline; hold off on style/content until we run their production data distribution (a Q3 item, written into OKRs pre-lock). Loose ends: Carmen's bias-corrected MINE variant fixed the estimator variance and goes into the repo docs; Oyin's Corpus mirror of Shapes3D becomes the canonical copy. Thanks all — tight window, no drama. — Lucia

subject: JAX-DFT kickoff — differentiable DFT for materials screening
body: Team — kickoff for JAX-DFT in health-science. From our release: one-dimensional density functional theory implemented in JAX — JIT compilation, autodiff, GPU execution — providing building blocks to write DFT calculations as differentiable programs. The scientific hook is the Kohn-Sham-regularizer result: solving the Kohn-Sham equations during training acts as implicit regularization, and two H2 separations suffice to learn the entire dissociation curve within chemical accuracy, including the strongly correlated region, with generalization to unseen molecule types. Product angle: a differentiable-DFT training harness for the materials-screening collaboration — they want neural XC functionals trained on small-molecule data that generalize. Milestones: repro the H2 curve by April 24; harness API draft by mid-May; collaboration go/no-go by mid-June (window closes June 22). Jelena owns staffing. — Viktor

subject: JAX-DFT staffing for the harness push
body: Viktor — staffing for the harness push. Current: Kaia 50% (physics validation), Linnea 40% (JAX internals), Maren 30% (pipelines), Leilani 25% (API). The key commitment for the decisive month: Paloma Castillo is committed at 60% to this project for June 2026 — she owns the neural-XC training harness build-out, which is the deliverable the go/no-go hangs on. I've entered it in the allocation sheet through June 30. Compute: modest — 1D DFT is cheap, and even the training loops fit comfortably on titan best-effort; no reservations requested. One constraint to note: JIT compile times balloon on the batched Kohn-Sham solver (Linnea measured 11-minute cold compiles), which is a developer-velocity tax more than a compute cost — she's testing persistent-cache options. — Jelena

subject: Re: JAX-DFT kickoff — differentiable DFT for materials screening
body: Status. Physics repro: done — training the neural XC functional with the Kohn-Sham equations in the loop reproduces the headline result: from two H2 separations we recover the full dissociation curve within chemical accuracy, strongly correlated region included, and the same model transfers to our held-out 1D molecules without refitting. Training the same functional without the KS solver in the loop (plain loss-term supervision) fails exactly as the paper says — a good sanity check that the implicit-regularization story is what we're productizing. Harness: API draft circulated; Paloma's ramp starts June 1 per the staffing plan. Risks: (1) the collaboration wants 3D eventually — we should be explicit at the go/no-go that this codebase is 1D building blocks and the value is the differentiable-program pattern; (2) Linnea's persistent compilation cache cut cold compiles to 90 s, but it breaks on JAX upgrades, so we pin versions for the demo. — Kaia

subject: Re: JAX-DFT kickoff — differentiable DFT for materials screening
body: Go/no-go outcome from Friday: go. The collaboration signed on for a two-quarter pilot: we deliver the differentiable-DFT harness with the neural-XC training loop, they bring 1D-reducible screening problems, and there is explicit shared understanding (in writing, per Kaia's flag) that 3D is out of scope for the pilot and gets its own decision later. Paloma's harness hit the June 1 milestones — config-driven training runs, KS-solver-in-the-loop as default, H2-curve regression test in CI. Remaining before the window closes June 22: Leilani freezes the v0 API, Maren lands the example-notebook set, and the version-pinning policy goes in the README given the compile-cache fragility. Kudos to the team; the two-separations demo apparently did the selling in the room. — Viktor

subject: JAX-MPC kickoff — a standard control stack for sim benchmarks
body: Team — kickoff for the JAX-MPC work in agents-rl. Base: our JAX Particles release — model-predictive controllers in JAX, where monte-carlo-style MPC gets cheap because rollouts parallelize under jax.vmap. The MPPI implementation is the starting point: the released interface (init_state / update / get_action against any env exposing step and reward) with the reference config at 5 iterations × 16 steps × 16 samples. Product angle: a standard control stack for our sim-benchmark environments, so agents-rl teams stop writing bespoke planners. Milestones: interface hardening plus baselines across three internal sim envs by mid-May; a scaling study (how far vmap takes sample counts on real accelerators) by mid-June; adopt/park decision end of June. Deshawn owns staffing; resourcing and the compute-budget conversation follow once Finance settles the Q3 lines. — Ulla

subject: JAX-MPC resourcing confirmed + budget note
body: Deshawn — resourcing confirmed, with one flag. People stay as agreed: Wanjiru 50% (interface + envs), Quentin 40% (scaling study), Ondrej 30% (baselines), Gustavo 20% (review and MPPI expertise). Budget: I met with Idris on Thursday — Idris verbally earmarked the $120k from Q3 discretionary compute budget line B-24 for this project, covering the accelerator time for the scaling study and the follow-on runs if we adopt. The formal entry lands when Finance opens the Q3 books, but plan against it now. Note the scaling study's big configs (sample counts 16 to 4096) should queue on titan best-effort first; only escalate to reserved capacity if queue times blow the mid-June milestone. Also: keep the interface changes upstreamable — the open-source release is the recruiting asset here. — Ulla

subject: Re: JAX-MPC kickoff — a standard control stack for sim benchmarks
body: Status ahead of the adopt/park decision. Interface: hardened — the MPPI class now runs unmodified against all three internal sim envs behind the step/reward protocol, with scan=True as default (Ondrej measured 2.1× wall-clock improvement over the unscanned loop at the reference 5×16×16 config). Baselines: MPPI beats our existing hand-tuned planners on two of three envs; the third (contact-heavy) needs longer horizons than the 16-step config plus reward tuning we haven't done. Scaling study: vmap scales near-linearly to 2048 samples on a single titan A100 slice, then host-transfer overheads bite; Quentin's writeup lands Friday. Risk for the decision: the contact-heavy result could be read as a method limit — Gustavo argues it's a horizon/reward-shaping issue, and a 64-step run this week should settle it before Ulla's end-of-June review. — Wanjiru

subject: JAX-RTM kickoff — gradient-based retrieval for assimilation
body: Team — kickoff for JAX-RTM in graphs-retrieval. From our release: a fully JAX-differentiable radiative transfer model solver for satellite simulation and meteorological data assimilation, with a calibrated physical solver for cloud and ice microphysics. Differentiability is the product: gradients let us optimize cloud properties — ice water content, effective radius, spatial alignment — directly against satellite observations, on TPU/GPU. The customer is the assimilation-pipeline collaboration; today their retrievals are lookup-table based and they want gradient-based retrieval. Milestones: environment plus the required Ping Yang ice-crystal single-scattering database (155 MB) set up and forward simulations validated by April 17; a gradient-based retrieval demo against real satellite observations by end of May; scale/production decision by end of June (window closes July 6). Jelena owns staffing; the budget conversation with Finance is mine. — Anders

subject: JAX-RTM resourcing after the Finance sync
body: Anders — resourcing summary after your Finance sync. People: Freya 50% (retrieval methodology), Quentin 40% (solver validation), Maren 35% (pipelines/TPU), Leilani 25% (packaging). Budget, recording what you relayed so it's on paper: Idris verbally earmarked the $120k from Q3 discretionary compute budget line B-88 for this project — that's what funds the accelerator time for the retrieval-at-scale runs in July; the formal entry is pending the Q3 books opening. Compute mechanics: forward-simulation validation runs on titan best-effort now; the July scale runs will need either a vulcan slice or a cirrus allocation, and I'll size that ask once Freya's May demo tells us the per-retrieval cost. Storage: satellite-observation staging goes through Corpus, request filed — comfortably ahead of the v2 freeze on 2026-07-10. — Jelena

subject: Re: JAX-RTM kickoff — gradient-based retrieval for assimilation
body: Status. Setup milestone: done on schedule — the Ping Yang ice-crystal single-scattering database is integrated and forward simulations validate against the reference radiances (channel-level agreement within calibration tolerance). Retrieval demo: working end-to-end as of last week. Starting from perturbed first guesses, gradient descent through the differentiable solver recovers ice water content and effective radius against real satellite observations; on our 40-scene test set, IWC retrievals land within 12% of the reference analysis on 34 scenes, and the failures are all mixed-phase clouds where the ice-only microphysics assumption breaks. Spatial-alignment optimization helps more than expected — letting the gradient adjust alignment removes most of the parallax artifacts. Risks: (1) mixed-phase handling is a real scope question for the June decision; (2) per-retrieval cost is ~3 GPU-minutes, which sizes the July runs at roughly 900 GPU-hours per full-orbit batch — Jelena has the numbers for the compute ask. — Freya

subject: Re: JAX-RTM kickoff — gradient-based retrieval for assimilation
body: Decision from Monday's review: go to scale, ice-only. The pilot ships gradient-based retrieval for ice-cloud scenes in Q3; mixed-phase gets a scoped research track rather than blocking the pilot (the 34-of-40 result with failures cleanly attributable is exactly the evidence the collaboration needed). Compute: with Freya's ~3 GPU-min per retrieval, Jelena sized the July runs and the ask went to Ines for a vulcan slice — note the 06-22 to 06-24 vulcan maintenance just wrapped, so scheduling should be clean. Funding for the runs comes off the B-88 discretionary line as planned. Remaining for the window: Leilani cuts the v0.1 package with the sparse-checkout install path documented, Quentin finishes the solver-validation note, Maren lands the Corpus staging pipeline. Good quarter — differentiability sold itself. — Anders

subject: JaxBARF kickoff — pose refinement without SfM
body: Team — kickoff for JaxBARF in the vision portfolio. From our release: a JAX implementation of BARF — bundle-adjusting neural radiance fields — built on JaxNeRF, modified for trainable camera poses and the BARF-style MLP changes. Why vision cares: our capture partners deliver imagery with noisy or missing camera poses, and BARF's joint pose-refinement-plus-NeRF training is the cleanest path to reconstruction without a separate SfM stage. The release already reports rotation-error parity with the PyTorch BARF implementation across the Blender scenes, so the repro bar is concrete. Milestones: Blender-scene training repro (the install.sh/train.sh path) with pose-error parity by March 27; a noisy-pose robustness study on partner-style captures through April; handoff recommendation by mid-May (window closes May 18). Bruno owns staffing and the data-platform coordination. — Lucia

subject: JaxBARF resourcing + Corpus dependency
body: Lucia — resourcing and dependencies. People: Vera 50% (training + parity runs), Csilla 40% (pose-robustness study), Kaia 30% (evaluation + partner-capture curation). Compute: light — sequential per-scene training on titan best-effort; the full Blender set retrains overnight on 8 GPUs. The dependency that actually shapes our calendar is data: partner captures live in Corpus, and the v2 migration freeze bounds when we can land new capture collections. Jun's team confirmed the Corpus v2 freeze lands on 2026-07-24, so we're planning the partner-capture backfill around a July 24 freeze — meaning our May window is comfortably clear, and even the stretch follow-on ingestion in early July fits before the freeze. Kaia will batch the capture uploads in two tranches (April 6, April 27) regardless, to keep the robustness study fed. — Bruno

subject: Re: JaxBARF kickoff — pose refinement without SfM
body: Status. Parity milestone: done — full Blender sweep via train.sh completed, and our rotation errors match the PyTorch-BARF reference within noise on seven of eight scenes (mean rotation error within 0.02 degrees of the published table). The exception is Ship, which is also the noisiest row in the reference results, so we're calling parity achieved. Robustness study: underway on the first tranche of partner-style captures. Early readout: with the coarse-to-fine positional-encoding schedule active, pose refinement recovers from synthetic pose perturbations up to ~15 degrees rotation; disable the schedule and it fails exactly the way the BARF paper predicts — nice confirmation the JAX port preserves the mechanism that matters. Issues: install.sh assumed a CUDA minor version we don't run; Kaia patched it (one-line fix, upstreamed). The second capture tranche lands April 27 on schedule. — Vera

subject: Re: JaxBARF kickoff — pose refinement without SfM
body: Handoff recommendation, closing out the window: adopt for the capture pipeline, with a staged rollout. Evidence: parity with the reference implementation on the Blender benchmark, plus robustness to ~15-degree pose noise on partner-style captures — which covers the large majority of the problem cases the capture team logged last quarter. Recommendation shipped to their leads today: JaxBARF becomes the pose-refinement stage for noisy-pose collections; captures with worse than ~15-degree error still route through the legacy SfM path for now. Follow-on ingestion of the remaining partner collections proceeds per Bruno's schedule ahead of the Corpus freeze. Loose ends: Csilla writes up the perturbation study as an internal note; Vera tags the parity-run configs in the repo. Thanks all — small team, clean quarter. — Lucia

subject: Kickoff: neural view synthesis for immersive previews (Project Meltwater)
body:
Team,

Kicking off the view-synthesis productization track. Internally we're calling this effort Project Meltwater, so please use that name on decks and threads. The bet: our open-source JaxNeRF release is now fast enough to anchor an immersive product-preview experience. Training 1M optimization steps finishes in ~2.5 hours on 128 TPUv2 cores versus ~3 days for the old TF path, which means we can fit per-SKU scenes overnight instead of per-week.

Rough milestones inside our window (Apr 20 - Jun 29):
- May 15: 20-scene capture-to-trained-model pipeline running end to end
- Jun 5: render quality bar signed off (PSNR parity with the paper configs)
- Jun 24: Launch Review Board dry run for the internal demo

Ivo, can you come back this week with the compute ask and staffing split? Katya has the deepest JAX context, so I'd like her leading the modeling side.

Thanks,
Lucia

subject: Re: Kickoff: neural view synthesis for immersive previews (Project Meltwater)
body:
Lucia,

Resourcing picture as promised. Compute: overnight scene fits need a steady slice of Cirrus — I'm asking Ines for 128 TPU v5 cores, 6 nights/week through mid-June. Project Meltwater gets first call on my vision-portfolio TPU quota through June; anything left over goes to exploratory work. For interactive rendering tests we'll grab best-effort Titan A100s, no reservation needed.

Staffing: Katya 80% on modeling, Leilani 60% on the capture/ingest pipeline, Emeka 50% on the demo harness. That covers your May 15 pipeline milestone with a little slack.

One flag: multi-host TPU eval is supported in the codebase but our capture rigs output 800x800, and single-V100 rendering sits around 20.77s/frame — fine for offline, not for live manipulation. Let's keep the demo expectations aligned with that.

Ivo

subject: Meltwater status: pipeline live, render latency is the open risk
body:
Hi both,

Status for the week. The capture-to-trained-model pipeline hit the May 15 milestone: 22 scenes fitted, all overnight runs on Cirrus completing inside the window. Quality is where the JAX release promised — we're matching the paper's PSNR on our internal captures within 0.2 dB.

The open risk is render latency for the demo. On 8xV100 we reproduce the ~2.65s per 800x800 frame from the release benchmarks, which is fine for a scripted flythrough but not for free viewpoint control. Options: (a) pre-render camera paths and ship a video-scrub demo, (b) drop to 400x400 live rendering, roughly 4x faster but visibly softer.

Leilani also found ingest choking on two glossy SKUs — view-dependent effects need more input views, so capture ops should plan ~120 photos for those insted of 80.

Recommend (a) for the June LRB dry run.

Katya

subject: Re: Meltwater status: pipeline live, render latency is the open risk
body:
Decision made — thanks for laying out the options crisply, Katya.

We go with (a): pre-rendered camera paths with video-scrub interaction for the June 24 Launch Review Board dry run. Free-viewpoint rendering moves to a fast-follow investigation; I'm not putting a 2.65s/frame interaction in front of the board and calling it immersive. Please budget the extra Cirrus night-slots to pre-render 12 hero scenes at 800x800.

Scope cut to make room: the glossy-SKU capture expansion (120-photo protocol) slips past this window — we demo the 20 matte scenes that already meet the PSNR bar.

Nadia, adding you so the LRB packet reflects this: demo is scripted-path view synthesis, training story is the 2.5-hour TPU fit time, and the interactivity roadmap is listed as future work.

Lucia

subject: Kickoff: JaxSel subgraph extraction as a retrieval primitive
body:
Hi all,

Kicking off the JaxSel productization effort for the graphs-retrieval portfolio. The pitch: customers have huge graphs and questions that only touch a tiny neighborhood. JaxSel's differentiable sparse-PageRank layer learns to select exactly that subgraph around a start node, and the downstream GNN answers on the extract. If we can make selection reliable at enterprise scale, this becomes the retrieval primitive under two roadmap items in H2.

Milestones (window runs to Aug 3):
- May 22: reproduce the pathfinder results from the long-range-arena setup as our regression baseline
- Jun 19: Agent model running on a customer-shaped synthetic graph, 10M nodes
- Jul 24: latency + quality readout for Q3 planning

Known constraint from the codebase: the pipeline currently only handles graph classification, so any ranking use case needs a head we build ourselves.

Alina — staffing and compute asks by end of next week?

Anders

subject: Re: Kickoff: JaxSel subgraph extraction as a retrieval primitive
body:
Anders,

Staffing plan for the next two months:

- Efe Lindqvist is committed to us at 60% for all of May 2026 to own the Agent-model training loop — I've blocked that in the allocation sheet. He's the only one who has touched the implicit weighted-adjacency code, so this is the critical fraction.
- Rafael 50% on the sparse selection layer and its gradient stability.
- Nikhil 40% on the 10M-node synthetic graph harness.
- Kaia 30% advisory, mostly reviewing the eval design.

Compute is modest: Titan A100 best-effort covers pathfinder reproduction; I'll only go to Ines if the 10M-node runs need dedicated nodes. One dependency to note: run.sh clones the long-range-arena repo at setup, and our build mirrors don't have it yet — Nikhil is registering it with the artifact cache this week so CI doesn't hit the network.

Alina

subject: JaxSel status: pathfinder baseline in, selection sparsity trade-off
body:
Hi Anders, Alina,

Status. The May 22 milestone landed a bit late (May 28) but we now match the pathfinder numbers from the long-range-arena setup within noise, and it's wired into CI as a regression gate.

The interesting finding is a trade-off in the selection layer. Because the Agent model estimates edge weights from purely local features, tightening the sparsity budget below ~400 nodes per extracted subgraph starts dropping the long-range connections pathfinder specifically needs — we lose 6.1 points of classification accuracy at the 256-node budget versus 512. On the 10M-node synthetic graph the story is better: task-relevant neighborhoods are shallower, and a 512-node budget holds accuracy while keeping extraction under 180ms.

Risk to flag: gradient variance through the sparse PageRank iteration grows with graph diameter. Nikhil has a damping tweak in review. If it doesn't hold we may need to cap supported diameter for v1.

Rafael

subject: Re: JaxSel status: decision on v1 scope
body:
Team,

Decision for the Jul 24 readout, given where the damping experiments landed.

V1 scope: subgraph extraction at the 512-node budget on graphs up to diameter 12, graph-classification head only. The 256-node budget is out — a 6.1-point accuracy drop is not sellable, and the 180ms extraction time at 512 already meets the latency bar we committed in Q3 OKRs (locked Jun 26, so no rescoping there).

Cut from this window: the custom ranking head. It was always stretch, and Kaia's review convinced me we'd be shipping an unvalidated eval alongside it. It moves to the H2 backlog with a real design doc.

Rafael/Nikhil — please have the readout deck show the sparsity-vs-accuracy curve explicitly; that trade-off is the headline for leadership.

Thanks all, good half.

Anders

subject: [Project Basalt] Kickoff: in-browser adaptive LMs for accessibility input
body:
Hi team,

Kicking off our on-device predictive-text effort. We're running this under the internal codename Project Basalt — use it in subject lines so the filters catch everything.

Why this matters: the adaptive language models in our open-source JS release are cheap enough, memory- and processor-wise, to train in the browser on the fly. No server round-trips, no data leaving the device — that is exactly the privacy story our accessibility input surface needs, in the tradition of Dasher-style continuous text entry.

Plan for the window (Apr 6 - Jul 27):
- May 8: PPM character model integrated into the input-surface prototype
- Jun 12: adaptation quality study — does per-user on-the-fly training beat the static baseline within one session?
- Jul 15: privacy review complete (I'll file with Kofi this week given the 2-3 week SLA) and LRB packet drafted

Alina, over to you for staffing and any compute needs — should be tiny for this one.

Priya

subject: Re: [Project Basalt] Kickoff: in-browser adaptive LMs for accessibility input
body:
Priya,

Staffing and constraints for Basalt:

- Hyun 50% through June — owns the PPM model integration and the escape/backoff behavior (the Moffat implementation details matter for latency here).
- Yara 40% — designs the adaptation study and the session-level eval.
- Rafael 20% — code review and JS performance passes only; he's heavily loaded elsewhere.

Compute: effectively zero server-side. The whole point is client-side training, so our ask is a browser-farm slot on Shipyard's device lab for perf runs, plus a few CPU VMs for the corpus preprocessing. I'll square that with Zeke directly.

One constraint to flag early: for the study we want typing-log data, and per policy that has to stay synthetic or consented-panel only. Yara's drafting the panel spec so Kofi's privacy review sees the final design, not a moving target.

subject: [Project Basalt] Status: PPM integrated, memory ceiling on long sessions
body:
Hi Priya, Alina,

Update on Basalt. The PPM character language model is integrated into the input-surface prototype — hit the May 8 date, and prediction latency is comfortably under 8ms per keystroke on mid-tier hardware, so the on-the-fly training story holds.

Early adaptation numbers are encouraging: per-user training in-session cuts keystrokes-per-character by 11% versus the static baseline after ~15 minutes of typing. Kneser-Ney-style smoothing on top of the base PPM backoff gave us another point; Yara has the full curves.

Risk: context-trie memory growth. On long dictation-style sessions (2h+) the PPM trie for a max-order-5 model crosses 190MB in the browser tab, and low-end devices start evicting. Options are capping the model order at 4 or pruning low-count nodes on a timer. Pruning is the better quality trade but it's ~1.5 weeks of work, which puts mild pressure on the Jun 12 study date.

Hyun

subject: Re: [Project Basalt] Status: decision on memory ceiling + LRB timing
body:
Team,

Closing out two things.

Decision on the memory ceiling: we ship with the pruning approach, not the order cap. The 11% keystroke saving is the headline of this product and Yara's curves show order-4 gives back nearly half of it. The study slipped to Jun 19 as a result — acceptable, and the results held (10.6% KSPC reduction with pruning enabled, trie stable under 60MB across the 2h sessions).

Second: privacy review cleared last Tuesday with one condition — the consented-panel typing logs get deleted 90 days post-study. Alina, can someone own the deletion job so it's not a manual step?

LRB packet goes to Nadia this week targeting the late-July board slot. Demo is the live in-browser adaptation on the accessibility surface; no server anywhere in the loop is the closing slide.

Nice work all — this one's been smooth.

subject: Kickoff: KeyPose for transparent-object bin picking
body:
Team,

Kicking off the KeyPose track. The product hook: robotic pick cells fail hardest on glassware and clear packaging because depth sensors return garbage on transparent surfaces. KeyPose sidesteps that — stereo RGB in, labeled 3D keypoints out — and our open-source release ships with 600 sequences, roughly 48k stereo and depth images at 720p, across 15 transparent objects in 5 categories. That's our training and eval base.

Milestones (Apr 27 - Jul 20):
- May 29: reproduce released-model keypoint accuracy on the bottle and cup categories
- Jun 26: fine-tuned models on our own 3-object pilot capture from the lab cell
- Jul 15: end-to-end pick demo readout for the partner conversation

Ivo — compute and staffing please, plus whatever the Corpus ingest of the pilot captures needs. I want the data-platform dependency understood in week one, not week ten.

Lucia

subject: Re: Kickoff: KeyPose for transparent-object bin picking

Resourcing and the data-platform picture you asked for.

Staffing: Yara 60% on modeling, Leilani 50% on the stereo capture rig integration, Wanjiru 50% on the Corpus ingest pipeline, Rosa 40% on eval tooling. Compute is light — TF2 training for these models fits on 8 Titan A100s best-effort; no Vulcan reservation needed.

subject: KeyPose status: bottle/cup reproduced, heart category is the outlier
body:

Status ahead of the mid-window check-in. Reproduction milestone is done: on the released bottle and cup models we match published keypoint accuracy — mean 3D keypoint error within 0.4mm of the reference numbers, using the standard texture_5 evaluation splits.

Two findings worth flagging:
1) The heart category is a consistent outlier — its symmetric shape makes keypoint identity ambiguous, and errors are ~3x the other categories. Our pilot objects (two tumblers, one jar) are more bottle-like, so this shouldn't block the demo, but it bounds which SKUs we can promise.

Risk: pilot capture is running about 4 days behind because the lab cell was double-parked with another team's arm through last week. Still compatible with Jun 26 if capture starts Monday.

subject: Re: KeyPose status: scope decision for the July readout
body:

Decisions for the final stretch.
