subject: Kickoff: dataset distillation (KIP) as a data-platform service
body:
Hi all,

Kicking off the dataset-distillation track for the data-platforms portfolio. The core tech is the Kernel Inducing Points (KIP) and Label Solve (LS) algorithms from our open-source release — meta-learn a tiny synthetic training set from kernel ridge-regression, so downstream teams can iterate on models against a few hundred distilled examples instead of hauling full corpora around. Two product angles: fast CI-style training loops, and a data-minimization story for datasets we'd rather not replicate broadly.

Milestones (Apr 20 - Jul 27):
- May 22: reproduce the released distilled-set results using the infinitely-wide ConvNet kernels; finite ConvNet transfer check
- Jun 19: distill one internal tabular corpus end to end, quality delta documented
- Jul 20: platform integration readout — distilled sets as first-class Corpus artifacts

Bao — resourcing please. Kernel computations at this scale are not cheap, so let's get the compute ask right early.

Dmitri

subject: Re: Kickoff: dataset distillation (KIP) as a data-platform service
body:
Dmitri,

Resourcing picture:

Compute: KIP with convolutional kernels was originally done with large-scale distributed resources, and that's what our reproduction needs too. Ask is 64 Titan A100s in sustained best-effort for the kernel computations through May, then bursts for the internal-corpus distillation in June. If Titan preemption bites we escalate to a small Vulcan slice, but I'd rather not burn a reservation on this.

Staffing: Kaia 60% (kernel methods lead), Yara 40% (eval + finite-network transfer, she'll own the ConvNet training checks), Chiara 50% (pipeline + Corpus artifact plumbing).

Platform dependency: we're planning around the Corpus v2 migration freeze on 2026-07-10 — all distilled-set artifacts have to be registered in v2 before that date, or the Jul 20 integration readout demos against a frozen platform. Jun, cc'd so you can flag if the artifact-registration API won't be stable in time.

Bao

subject: KIP status: reproduction done, transfer gap on finite networks
body:
Hi Dmitri, Bao,

Status. Reproduction milestone closed May 26: we regenerate distilled sets with the infinitely-wide ConvNet kernels and match the released numbers within 0.3% test accuracy. The Label Solve variant is also wired in — it's much cheaper when we only re-solve labels on a fixed support set, which is likely the mode platform users actually want.

The honest caveat: the kernel-to-finite-network transfer gap. Training a finite ConvNet on a distilled set (per the release's nn_training flow) costs us 4-6% accuracy versus the kernel regime, and on our internal tabular corpus the early gap is nearer 8%. For CI-loop use that's fine; for the data-minimization pitch it needs to be front and center in the quality-delta doc.

On track for Jun 19 on the internal corpus. Chiara's artifact schema went to Jun's team for review last week — no response yet, gentle nudge needed given the freeze.

Kaia

subject: Re: KIP status: positioning decision + freeze-week logistics
body:
Team,

Two calls ahead of the Jul 20 readout.

1) Positioning: v1 is the fast-iteration/CI story only. With a 4-6% finite-network gap (8% on our tabular corpus), I'm not standing behind data-minimization claims this quarter — that pitch returns when the gap narrows or when Label Solve on a curated support set closes it for specific corpora. Yara, one slide quantifying LS-vs-KIP cost and quality would really help here.

2) Freeze logistics: Chiara got the schema approved and registered the first three distilled sets in Corpus v2 yesterday — one day inside the freeze, closer than I'd like but done. Remaining sets are read-only demos so they can wait out the freeze window.

Readout invite going out today; Bao, please sanity-check the compute-cost appendix, the A100-hour numbers are doing a lot of work in the ROI slide.

Dmitri

subject: Kickoff: reference-less MT evaluation (Project Obsidian)
body:
Hi team,

Kicking off the KoBE productization. Codename for this effort is Project Obsidian — please tag docs and dashboards with it.

The product problem: our localization customers want translation quality scores for language pairs where no human references exist. KoBE is reference-less — it links entity mentions in the source and the candidate translation against a large-scale multilingual knowledge base and uses matched entity counts as the quality signal. The released annotations give us a serious eval base: 425k sentences across 18 language pairs from 262 MT systems, with 1.8M entity mentions over 28k distinct entities.

Milestones (window ends May 25):
- Mar 20: reproduce the WMT19 metrics-track correlations from the released annotations
- Apr 17: KoBE scoring behind an internal Evalline endpoint
- May 18: pilot with the localization team on two no-reference language pairs

Deshawn — staffing and the entity-linking dependency question are yours. That's the piece we don't have in-house today.

Priya

subject: Re: Kickoff: reference-less MT evaluation (Project Obsidian)
body:
Priya,

Staffing for Obsidian: Wei 60% as research lead, Saoirse 50% on the Evalline endpoint and serving path, Emeka 40% on data plumbing for the released annotations. Compute is trivial — CPU scoring, a couple of standard VMs.

The real constraint is the one you named: there's no open-source multilingual KB + entity-linking stack, which is exactly why the release ships pre-computed annotations instead of a linker. So we split the work: the Mar 20 reproduction and the May pilot both run on the released annotation files, while Wei scopes a replacement linker for candidate translations (that's the part we must run live at scoring time; source-side entities can be cached). His current candidate is a lightweight multilingual linker fine-tuned on our own KB snapshot — realistically a Q3 build, not this window.

Tomas cc'd: we'd like Evalline to treat KoBE as a metric plugin, same contract as the existing BLEU/chrF runners.

Deshawn

subject: Obsidian status: correlations reproduced, entity-sparsity caveat
body:
Hi Priya, Deshawn,

Status. Reproduction is done — we match the published WMT19 metrics-track system-level correlations from the released annotations across the 18 language pairs. Saoirse has the Evalline endpoint in staging as of Monday, slightly ahead of the Apr 17 date; scoring 10k segments takes ~40s on one VM.

The caveat we need to carry into the pilot: KoBE's signal comes from matched entity counts, so it degrades on entity-sparse text. On our internal conversational-support sample, 31% of segments have zero linked entities and the metric is essentially uninformative there. On entity-rich domains (news, product catalogs) segment coverage is 85%+ and correlations hold. Recommendation: pilot on the catalog localization pairs, and report KoBE alongside a fluency-oriented metric rather than alone.

Also, small thing — the annotation files use the release's per-system file layout, and Emeka's loader now handles all 262 systems without the manual renames we were doing in March.

Wei

subject: Re: Obsidian status: pilot decision
body:
Team,

Decision on the pilot, based on Wei's coverage analysis.

We run the May 18 pilot on the two catalog localization pairs only, and KoBE ships as part of a composite: entity-grounding score from KoBE plus the existing fluency metric, never KoBE alone. The conversational-support domain is explicitly out of scope — 31% zero-entity segments means we'd be selling noise, and I'd rather tell the localization team that plainly now.

Also agreed with Deshawn: the in-house linker build goes into Q3 planning as Obsidian phase 2, since the live candidate-side linking is what unlocks arbitrary customer content instead of pre-annotated sets. Wei, please write the half-page scoping note by Friday so it lands before OKR discussions heat up.

Saoirse — endpoint to prod behind the pilot flag by Thursday, please.

Thanks all,
Priya

subject: Kickoff: KwikBucks clustering for platform-scale dedup
body:
Hi all,

Kicking off the KwikBucks track. The dedup problem in the data platform is exactly the paper's setting: we have a cheap-weak signal (embedding similarity) for every record pair, and an expensive-strong signal (a cross-encoder judgment) we can only afford on a small budget of pairs. KwikBucks does correlation clustering that spends the strong-query budget where it matters — the core is the qwick_cluster_using_ordering routine in model_utils.py, and the released baselines give us honest comparisons.

Milestones (Mar 2 - Jun 22):
- Apr 3: reproduce paper results on the released datasets
- May 15: dedup prototype on one internal record corpus, budget-vs-quality curve
- Jun 15: readout with a go/no-go on platform integration for Q3

Daniela — staffing and infra ask when you can. The strong-signal service is the piece that needs real engineering.

Dmitri

subject: Re: Kickoff: KwikBucks clustering for platform-scale dedup
body:
Dmitri,

Staffing and infra:

- Carmen 50% as algorithm lead — she owns the reproduction and the budget-vs-quality analysis.
- Yara 30% on eval design, shared with her vision commitments.
- Oyin Iversen is locked in at 60% on this project for May 2026 to build the strong-signal query service — that allocation is confirmed on my side. April he's at 30% ramping the service design.
- Paloma 40% on the weak-signal embedding pipeline, Rosa 30% on the internal-corpus extraction.

Compute: modest. The clustering itself is CPU; the cross-encoder strong queries need 4-8 Titan A100s best-effort during the May prototype, nothing reserved. The released datasets are already mirrored internally, so the Apr 3 reproduction has no external dependencies.

One ask back: the internal record corpus needs a data-access ticket — can you sponsor it this week so Rosa isn't blocked mid-April?

Daniela

subject: KwikBucks status: reproduction done, weak-signal quality drives everything
body:
Hi Dmitri, Daniela,

Status update. Reproduction closed on Apr 6 (three days late, dataset mirroring hiccup): KwikBucks matches the paper's numbers on the released datasets and beats every baseline in the repo at equal strong-query budget, as expected.

Main finding as we move to the internal corpus: the budget-vs-quality curve is extremely sensitive to weak-signal quality. With Paloma's current embedding pipeline, we reach 0.91 F1 on the labeled dedup sample using strong queries on just 2.3% of candidate pairs. But when we swapped in the older embedding model as a stress test, the same budget only gets 0.78 — the ordering the algorithm consumes really matters, not just the budget.

Risk: the cross-encoder service Oyin is building has a 40ms p50 per pair; at prototype scale fine, but platform-scale nightly runs will need batching work we haven't scoped. Flagging now so Jun 15 go/no-go includes it.

Carmen

subject: Re: KwikBucks status: go/no-go outcome
body:
Team,

Outcome from yesterday's readout: conditional GO for platform integration in Q3.

The May prototype numbers carried the room — 0.91 F1 at a 2.3% strong-query budget on the labeled sample is a clear win over the current rules-based dedup (0.84 with far higher compute). Conditions attached by the platform side:

1) Batched cross-encoder serving lands before integration; Oyin's estimate of 3 weeks is in the Q3 plan (his allocation drops after June, so Daniela is finding the follow-on owner).
2) An embedding-quality regression gate, per Carmen's finding — if the weak signal degrades, the budget math silently rots. Carmen writes the gate spec.
3) Dedup runs stay advisory (flag, don't merge) for the first month in prod.

Q3 OKR language was locked ahead of the Jun 26 lock with exactly these conditions, so no surprises there. Thanks everyone — strong half.

Dmitri

subject: Kickoff: streaming keyword spotting for the wake-word stack (Project Riverbed)
body:
Hi team,

Kicking off the streaming KWS effort. We're tracking this internally as Project Riverbed — that's the codename on the roadmap and in the OKR tooling.

What we're building on: our open-source streaming-aware release solves the exact problem killing our current wake-word latency. Instead of waiting for a whole 1-second window, the streaming wrappers let the model consume 20ms audio chunks incrementally and emit classifications in real time. The clever bit is the dynamic topology — one architecture for training (non-streaming), a different one for inference (streaming), converted by the keras wrappers.

Milestones (Apr 27 - Aug 3):
- May 29: reproduce reference accuracy for two model families in both modes
- Jun 26: streaming conversion validated bit-exact against non-streaming on our internal keyword set
- Jul 24: on-device latency readout on the target DSP-class hardware

Alina — staffing and device-lab needs when you can.

Priya

subject: Re: Kickoff: streaming keyword spotting for the wake-word stack (Project Riverbed)
body:
Priya,

Riverbed resourcing:

Staffing: Linnea 60% as tech lead on the streaming wrappers and conversion path; Vera 50% on training runs and eval; Giannis 40% on the device-lab harness; Rafael 15% advisory only — he's spread across two other language efforts, so please don't route review load his way.

Compute: training is small-model work — 8-16 Titan A100s best-effort covers the model-family sweeps. No reservations. The scarce resource is the device lab: we need recurring slots on the DSP-class boards for the July latency readout. Zeke, cc'd — can Shipyard give us two half-days a week from mid-June?

Technical constraint to note: the functional Keras API path doesn't support the dynamic train/inference topologies, so we standardize on the subclassing route the release recommends. That constrains how we export to the on-device runtime, and Linnea wants a spike week in May to de-risk the conversion before we promise bit-exactness.

Alina

subject: Riverbed status: conversion validated, one stateful-layer gotcha
body:
Hi Priya, Alina,

Status. May 29 milestone done: both model families reproduce reference accuracy in non-streaming training mode, and Vera's runs are within 0.1% absolute of the published numbers on the keyword benchmark.

Conversion milestone is effectively done ten days early, with one asterisk. For the convolutional family, streaming inference on 20ms chunks is bit-exact with the non-streaming model over our full internal keyword set. The gotcha is the recurrent family: state resets between utterances weren't handled in our harness (not the release's fault — our bug), which produced a phantom 2% accuracy drop that cost us a week. Fixed; now matching.

Risk for the Jul 24 readout: first numbers off the DSP boards put the conv model at 14ms per 20ms chunk — real-time with margin — but memory on the smallest target board is tight, 480KB against a 512KB budget. If quantization doesn't buy headroom, we may need to drop the largest conv variant from the device matrix.

Linnea

subject: Re: Riverbed status: device-matrix decision ahead of the readout
body:
Team,

Decision ahead of Friday's latency readout, so the deck states it rather than debates it.

Device matrix for v1: the two smaller conv variants only. The large conv variant is cut from the smallest board — post-quantization it still sits at 496KB against the 512KB budget, and 16KB of headroom is not something I'll defend in a launch review. It stays in the matrix for the mid-tier board where it clears easily. The recurrent family ships nowhere in v1; it's accuracy-competitive but the state-management complexity Linnea hit is exactly the class of bug we don't want in a wake-word path.

Headline numbers for Nadia's packet: 14ms processing per 20ms chunk on-device, 0.1% of published accuracy, bit-exact streaming conversion. LRB slot requested for the Aug 6 board — window closes Aug 3 so all artifacts need to be in by then.

Priya

subject: Kickoff: label-bias correction as a pipeline pre-processing stage
body:
Hi team,

Kicking off the label-bias track for trust-theory. The premise from our open-source release: datasets carry biases because labelers — modeled as an agent intending accuracy but biased against certain groups — overwrite the unknown, unbiased labels. The method's punchline is that you can correct this by re-weighting data points without changing any labels, with theoretical guarantees that training on the re-weighted set corresponds to training on the unbiased labels.

Productization goal: a drop-in pre-processing stage any Meridian pipeline can enable, plus a report artifact for model cards.

Milestones (Mar 2 - Jul 6):
- Apr 10: reproduce the paper's results on the standard fairness benchmarks across the supported fairness notions
- May 22: pipeline-stage API in review; two internal teams identified for pilots
- Late June: full re-weighting sweep across our model families, then a decision memo for the LRB

Deshawn — resourcing please, including the June sweep compute which is the big-ticket item.

Ximena

subject: Re: Kickoff: label-bias correction as a pipeline pre-processing stage
body:
Ximena,

Resourcing:

Staffing: Rosa 50% as tech lead, Farah 40% on the re-weighting implementation and its convergence behavior, Emeka 40% on the pipeline-stage API, Bilal 30% on benchmark harnessing. The method itself is cheap — it's the validation sweep that costs.

Compute: the fairness-benchmark reproduction runs on a handful of Titan A100s, nothing to plan around. The June validation sweep is different: re-training every supported model family with and without re-weighting, across the fairness notions, is a big fan-out. We hold the cirrus-tpu reservation — 512 accelerators — for the week of 2026-06-22, which covers the full re-weighting sweep across all model families. I sized it with 30% headroom, so if the sweep grows we still fit inside the week.

One planning note: Q3 OKR lock is Jun 26, so the sweep results land just in time to ground whatever we commit for Q3. Tight but workable.

Deshawn

subject: Label-bias status: benchmarks reproduced, weight-drift question for pilots
body:
Hi Ximena, Deshawn,

Status. Reproduction milestone closed Apr 9: on the standard fairness datasets we match the paper — the re-weighting method outperforms the standard baselines on demographic parity and equalized odds while holding accuracy within 0.5%. Bilal's harness runs all fairness notions from one config, which the pilot teams will like.

API review for the pipeline stage started last week; main open comment is whether weights are recomputed per training run or cached per dataset version. Farah's convergence experiments say recomputation is cheap (the iterative weight solve converges in under 20 iterations on every benchmark), so we're leaning per-run for correctness.

Risk for pilots: on one internal dataset with heavy class imbalance, the learned weights concentrate hard on a small minority slice — technically correct per the method, but it amplifies label-noise sensitivity exactly where labels are worst. We think this needs a weight-cap option plus a warning in the report artifact. Adds ~1 week to the API work.

Rosa

subject: Re: Label-bias status: decisions before the sweep week
body:
Team,

Locking decisions before next week's validation sweep so nothing changes mid-flight.

1) Weight-cap option: approved, ship it in the stage API with the warning in the report artifact. Rosa's imbalance finding is exactly the kind of thing the trust portfolio exists to catch — I'd rather ship a capped, explained method than an uncapped surprising one. The one-week slip is absorbed; pilots start Jul 1 instead of Jun 24.

2) Sweep config freezes Friday: all model families, both fairness notions in the pilot scope (demographic parity, equalized odds), with/without re-weighting, capped and uncapped. Anything not in Friday's config waits for Q3.

3) Kofi — cc'ing you because the report artifact surfaces per-group statistics; want your read on whether that needs privacy review before pilot teams see it. The 2-3 week SLA means we need your answer routed this week.

Decision memo drafts right after sweep results land.

Ximena

subject: Kickoff: LAMP as an interpretable sequential-recs baseline
body:
Hi all,

Kicking off the LAMP evaluation track. Context: platform customers keep asking why their sequential recommendations do what they do, and our neural stack can't answer cheaply. Linear Additive Markov Processes are the counter-bet — a model that combines history states through an explicit linear mixture, so every prediction decomposes into readable per-step contributions. If LAMP holds up within a few points of the neural baseline, we ship it as the default interpretable tier.

Milestones (Feb 9 - May 25):
- Mar 13: reproduce the paper's experiments, starting with the Brightkite check-ins dataset per the released setup
- Apr 17: LAMP vs neural baseline on one internal sequential corpus, quality and cost side by side
- May 18: recommendation memo — adopt, adapt, or drop

Bao — staffing and any build-infra needs. It's a C++ codebase with gflags, so someone needs to own getting it into our bazel monorepo cleanly.

Dmitri

subject: Re: Kickoff: LAMP as an interpretable sequential-recs baseline
body:
Dmitri,

Resourcing for LAMP:

- Fumiko 50% as research lead through the window; she owns the reproduction and the mixture-weight interpretability analysis.
- Nikhil 30% on the bazel port — the release builds with gflags and plain make, so he'll wrap it rather than rewrite it.
- Yusuf 30% on dataset prep; Brightkite and the other public check-in sets first, then the internal corpus extraction.
- Farah Haddad is committed here at 60% for May 2026 to drive the internal-corpus evaluation and the production-readiness pass — I've confirmed the allocation. Through March/April she's at 20% doing early harness work.

Compute: negligible — this is CPU-bound C++; a couple of 64-core VMs cover every experiment, incl. the max-iter/max-order sweeps the paper recommends starting small on. No cluster asks, which makes a nice change.

Bao

subject: LAMP status: reproduction done, internal-corpus gap is real but small
body:
Hi Dmitri, Bao,

Status. Reproduction closed Mar 11 — on the Brightkite check-ins data our runs match the paper's perplexity curves, and Nikhil's bazel wrapper builds clean on linux; the mac gflags dylib dance from the README is thankfully not our problem in CI.

Internal-corpus results (first cut, Apr 10): LAMP sits 4.2% behind the neural baseline on hit@10 for next-item prediction, at roughly 1/40th the serving cost and with fully decomposable predictions — the mixture weights over history positions are exactly the explanation surface we hoped for. Interesting detail: learned weights put 71% of mass on the last 3 positions for this corpus, which itself is a finding product can use.

Risk/trade-off: LAMP degrades on long-gap sessions (users returning after 30+ days), where the linear history mixture can't capture the reset. If those sessions matter for the platform tier, we should scope a hybrid fallback rather than stretch LAMP.

Fumiko

subject: Re: LAMP status: recommendation memo decision
body:
Team,

Decision for the May 18 memo (going out today, one day late — my fault, launch review week).

Recommendation: ADAPT. LAMP becomes the interpretable tier for short-horizon sequential recs, with an explicit carve-out: long-gap sessions (30+ days) route to the existing neural path. 4.2% hit@10 behind at 1/40th serving cost, plus per-position explanations, is a trade plenty of platform customers will take — Farah's production-readiness pass confirmed sub-millisecond scoring on the standard serving VMs.

What we are NOT doing: extending LAMP itself to model session resets. Fumiko's analysis convinced me that's fighting the model's shape. The hybrid routing is Farah's design doc, due before window close on May 25 so it can feed Q3 planning.

Thanks all — this was a well-run evaluation, exactly what the memo process is for.

Dmitri

subject: Kickoff: KnowNo-style uncertainty alignment for agent workflows
body:
Hi team,

Kicking off the uncertainty-alignment track. The pain point: our agent workflows either barrel through ambiguous instructions (bad) or ask clarifying questions constantly (worse). The KnowNo framework from our open-source release is the principled middle path — conformal prediction over the planner's options gives statistical guarantees on task completion while minimizing how often we ask a human for help. Crucially it works with LLMs out of the box, no fine-tuning, which keeps us off the training-compute treadmill.

Milestones (Apr 6 - Jul 13):
- May 8: reproduce the released calibration flow on the demo settings
- Jun 12: KnowNo wrapped around one production agent workflow in shadow mode, with our own calibration set
- Jul 8: readout — help-rate vs completion-rate curves, and a ship/hold call

Ivo — staffing and any serving-side needs, please. The calibration-set build is the real work here.

Priya

subject: Re: Kickoff: KnowNo-style uncertainty alignment for agent workflows
body:
Priya,

Staffing and infra:

- Vera Egede is allocated at 60% to this project for May 2026 — she owns the calibration-set construction and the conformal threshold tuning, and I've locked that in the staffing plan. April she's at 40% while she closes out a previous commitment.
- Rosa 40% on the shadow-mode integration with the production agent workflow.
- Wanjiru 30% on logging/telemetry — help-rate and completion-rate need clean instrumentation or the Jul 8 curves are fiction.
- Farah 25% on the option-generation prompt harness.

Compute/serving: inference-only, so no cluster reservations. We do need a dedicated eval quota on the internal LLM endpoint — calibration involves scoring full option sets per task, and I don't want us rate-limited mid-run. I'll size the ask once Vera counts tasks; ballpark 200k scored options for a 1,000-task calibration set.

One dependency: shadow mode needs sign-off from the workflow's owning team; Rosa is setting that up this week.

Ivo

subject: KnowNo status: calibration reproduced, ambiguity-mix caveat for our workflows
body:
Hi Priya, Ivo,

Status. The May 8 milestone closed on time — we reproduced the released calibration flow on the demo setting and get the expected behavior: prediction sets grow exactly when the instruction is ambiguous, and the conformal guarantee holds at our 90% target completion level on held-out tasks.

Our own calibration set now stands at 1,150 tasks drawn from real (anonymized) workflow traces. Early threshold tuning shows a wrinkle the paper's settings didn't stress: our ambiguity distribution is lumpy — about 20% of tasks are numeric-quantity ambiguities where the option generator produces near-duplicate plans, inflating prediction sets and triggering unnecessary help requests. Farah's dedup pass in the option harness cuts the spurious help-rate from 23% to 14% at the same coverage target.

Risk: if the workflow's task mix shifts after calibration, the guarantee quietly weakens. We'll propose a monthly recalibration job as part of the ship criteria.

Vera

subject: Re: KnowNo status: shaping the Jul 8 ship/hold call
body:
Team,

Ahead of the Jul 8 readout, here's where I've landed so we can pressure-test it together.

Shadow-mode numbers Rosa pulled Friday: at the 90% completion target, the wrapped workflow asks for help on 13.8% of tasks versus the 31% clarification rate of the current heuristic — a better experience AND a formal guarantee behind it. That's a ship story.

Proposed ship criteria (the decision I'll take into the room):
1) Ship to the one calibrated workflow only. Every new workflow gets its own calibration set — no guarantee transfer, full stop.
2) Vera's monthly recalibration job is a launch blocker, not a fast-follow. A silently weakening guarantee is worse than no guarantee.
3) Help-request UX copy goes through the trust review since we're now telling users "the system is unsure."

If anyone disagrees with 2 being a blocker, bring data Thursday. Otherwise this goes in as written.

Priya

subject: Kickoff: generalized inlier voting for the localization core
body:
Hi team,

Kicking off the inlier-voting evaluation for the efficiency portfolio. Our AR anchoring pipeline spends most of its localization budget on RANSAC-style hypothesize-and-verify, and it falls over at high outlier ratios. The general voting approach from our open-source release is the alternative: the core algorithm in general_voter.h is application-independent, and the released 6DoF example solves calibrated-camera posing directly — exactly our anchoring problem shape.

Milestones (Mar 30 - Jun 22):
- Apr 24: build + reproduce the paper's tables (the repo ships create_table_2.sh / create_table_3.sh, so this should be mechanical)
- May 22: 6DoF posing on our own map data, accuracy vs the current RANSAC stack
- Jun 12: efficiency readout — latency, memory, and robustness at outlier ratios up to 95%

Ivo — resourcing please. Note the June benchmark sweep is the compute-heavy piece.

Zofia

subject: Re: Kickoff: generalized inlier voting for the localization core
body:
Zofia,

Resourcing for the voting track:

Staffing: Umar 50% as algorithm lead (he knows the 6dof example code already), Yara 30% on accuracy evaluation against the RANSAC stack, Ondrej 40% on the map-data adaptation, Farah 30% on build/CI — the bazel + OpenCV3 dependency needs pinning in our monorepo, the WORKSPACE path tweak the README mentions is exactly the kind of thing that rots.

Compute: day-to-day development is CPU. For the pre-readout benchmark sweep we're covered: we hold the cirrus-tpu reservation — 256 accelerators — for the week of 2026-06-01 to run the full localization benchmark sweep before the readout. That sizes for the 95%-outlier-ratio grid across all map regions with margin; sweep configs freeze May 27.

One flag: our map tiles are bigger than anything in the paper's tables, so memory behavior of the voting structure at our scale is a genuine unknown until Ondrej's adaptation lands.

Ivo

subject: Voting status: tables reproduced, memory scaling is the watch item
body:
Hi Zofia, Ivo,

Status. Reproduction closed Apr 22: tables 2 and 3 regenerate from the released scripts and match the paper, and the 2D line-fitting example (the paper's Figure 2 setup) is our smoke test in CI. Farah's bazel pinning means builds are hermetic now — c++17 flag and all.

Our-data results are promising: on the mid-density map region, the 6DoF voter matches the RANSAC stack's pose accuracy (median error 3.1cm vs 3.3cm) and is 2.7x faster at the 80% outlier ratio. At 90%+ outliers RANSAC's accuracy collapses while the voter degrades gracefully — that's the headline.

The watch item Ivo predicted: memory. The voting structure on our largest map tile peaks at 41GB, versus ~6GB for the paper-scale problems. Ondrej has a tile-partitioning scheme that trades ~4% recall on tile-boundary anchors for a 4x memory cut. We need a call on whether that trade is acceptable before the sweep configs freeze May 27.

Umar

subject: Re: Voting status: decisions going into the Jun 12 readout
body:
Team,

Closing the loop before Friday's readout.

1) Partitioning decision (made May 26, recording it here for the record): we took Ondrej's tile-partitioning trade. 41GB per tile was never going to fly on the serving fleet; a 4% boundary-recall cost with a 4x memory cut is the right shape, and Yara's follow-up showed half the recall loss disappears with a 10m tile overlap.

2) Sweep results are in from the benchmark week: the voter holds median pose error under 3.5cm up to 92% outlier ratio across all map regions; RANSAC exits the acceptable band at 85%. Latency p95 is 2.4x better. Those are the readout headlines.

3) Recommendation going to the room: adopt as the localization core for AR anchoring, staged rollout by region density, RANSAC retained as fallback for two quarters. If the room agrees, engineering handoff plan lands before window close on Jun 22.

Zofia

subject: Kickoff: Lasagna layer-stacking for the translation tier
body:
Hi all,

Kicking off the Lasagna evaluation. The bet: our translation tier runs a uniform transformer stack, but the Lasagna work shows you can do better by choosing which layer type sits at each position in the encoder and decoder — mixing Light and Dynamic convolutions with attention where each earns its keep. If the paper's quality-at-lower-cost story transfers to our language pairs, this is a straight serving-cost win for the platform.

Milestones (Feb 9 - Jun 15):
- Mar 13: fairseq-based training path standing, incl. compiling the CUDA kernels for the Light/Dynamic conv layers
- Apr 24: Lasagna configs vs our production transformer baseline on two internal language pairs
- Early June: final architecture sweep, then the adopt/drop readout on Jun 12

Santiago — staffing and the compute plan please. The June sweep is real GPU money, so let's get the reservation sorted well ahead.

Dmitri

Kaia 40% on architecture-search design — which layer-type-per-position configs we actually sweep, since exhaustive is hopeless. Milan 40% on the eval harness and baseline parity.

Compute: interim experiments fit on 64 Titan A100s best-effort. subject: Lasagna status: first head-to-heads in, decoder is where the win lives
body:
Hi Dmitri, Santiago,

Status. Training path has been stable since mid-March (fp32 auto-regressive, matching the release's supported configuration — we deliberately didn't stray into mixed precision to keep comparisons clean).

First head-to-head results on the two internal pairs, at matched parameter count and the release's inverse_sqrt schedule with 4k warmup:
- A Lasagna config with conv layers in the lower decoder and attention on top gets +0.4 BLEU on pair A and +0.1 on pair B versus the production transformer, with 18% faster decode.
- Encoder-side mixing has been neutral-to-negative for us so far. The win concentrates in the decoder, which is convenient — decode cost dominates serving.

Risk/trade-off for the sweep: Kaia's config space is now decoder-focused (16 configs, down from 24). That fits the reserved week with more retries slack, but means if encoder mixing matters for other pairs we won't know this window. We think that's the right cut — flagging for visibility.

subject: Re: Lasagna status: sweep week + readout framing
body:
Team,

Quick alignment now that the sweep week is underway.

Decision on scope, confirming what we discussed: decoder-focused sweep, 16 configs, both pairs — encoder mixing is formally deferred to a Q3 exploration if the readout lands adoption. I'll own writing that deferral into the readout so nobody reads it as a finding of "encoder mixing doesn't work."

Framing for Jun 12: if the sweep confirms the +0.4/+0.1 BLEU at 18% faster decode, the recommendation is staged adoption on pair A first (bigger quality delta, higher traffic), pair B follows once serving telemetry from A looks clean for two weeks. Milan's harness numbers become the before/after baseline of record.

Santiago — please confirm mid-week that all runs will clear the reservation window; if anything looks like it slips past Friday I want to know before it does, not after.

subject: Kickoff: Latent Programmer for example-driven pipeline synthesis
body:
Hi all,

Kicking off the Latent Programmer evaluation. Platform users keep writing the same data-transformation pipelines by hand from a few input/output examples; program synthesis is the obvious assist. The Latent Programmer approach is attractive because it doesn't decode a program token-by-token blind — it first predicts discrete latent codes as a coarse plan, then decodes the program conditioned on that plan, which the paper shows beats the plain Transformer baseline on synthesis benchmarks.

Milestones (Feb 23 - May 25):
- Mar 27: baseline Transformer (train.py) and latent model (train_latent.py, latent_vocab_size=30 with the 10k-step latent pretraining) both reproducing on the released benchmark setup
- Apr 24: synthesis accuracy on our internal transformation DSL, top-1 and top-10
- May 20: readout with a Q3 scale-up recommendation and its budget ask

Bruno — staffing and compute please. Keep it lean; the big spend, if any, is a Q3 question.

Resourcing:

subject: Latent Programmer status: internal-DSL results + what the readout should say
body:
Hi Dmitri, Bruno,

Status rolling into the readout.

Reproduction closed in March: latent model beats the baseline Transformer on the released benchmark, consistent with the paper. On our internal transformation DSL (Ondrej's 40k-task dataset): top-1 synthesis accuracy 34% for the latent model vs 27% baseline, top-10 is 61% vs 52%. The latent codes are doing real work — inspection shows they cluster by transformation family (joins vs aggregations vs string ops), which also gives us a plausible UI hook: show the user the plan before the program.

The honest trade-off: at top-10, a user still has to pick among candidates, and 39% of tasks have no correct candidate at all. So the readout should pitch this as an assist with example-checking in the loop (we auto-run candidates against the user's examples and only surface ones that pass — that filter takes effective accuracy to 71% of tasks with at least one verified program).

Recommend scale-up: more data helps monotonically in our ablations, and the May 20 memo will size the Q3 ask against exactly that curve.

Efe

subject: Kickoff: latent subgroup shift adaptation for platform models
body:
Hi all,

Kicking off the latent-shift-adaptation track. The recurring incident pattern on platform models: an unobserved subgroup's prevalence shifts between training and deployment and accuracy quietly craters for that slice, with nothing in the observed features to alert on. The AISTATS work we open-sourced tackles exactly this — adapting to latent subgroup shifts using concept and proxy variables, with both a discrete eigendecomposition approach and continuous spectral / WAE variants.

Milestones (Mar 30 - Jun 29):
- Apr 24: replicate the synthetic-data experiments (Tables 1 and 2 from the released notebooks)
- May 29: apply to one historical platform incident where we have the post-hoc subgroup labels — can the method see the shift we missed?
- Jun 24: readout with a Q3 productionization recommendation

Santiago — staffing/compute please, and start the Q3 budget conversation early; if May works out, the validation runs get expensive.

Dmitri

subject: Latent-shift status: replication done, incident study needs proxy quality
body:
Hi Dmitri, Santiago,

Status. Replication closed Apr 22 — Quentin reproduced the synthetic-data results from the released notebooks: the discrete eigendecomposition numbers match Table 1, and the 10-seed model comparison matches Table 2 within seed noise. His shift-strength sweeps also reproduce the figures for both the WAE method and the continuous spectral method, so we trust the codebase end to end.

Incident study (the interesting part): on the historical incident, the method recovers the latent subgroup structure and — had it been running — would have flagged the prevalence shift 9 days before our on-call did. That's the headline for Jun 24.

The caveat: it only works when the proxy variables actually carry subgroup signal. Freya ran an ablation degrading proxy quality; below a measurable threshold the recovered subgroups go to mush, silently. So the productionization story must include a proxy-strength diagnostic as a gate — otherwise we'd be shipping false confidence, which is worse than the status quo.

Kaia

subject: Re: Latent-shift status: readout framing + Q3 commitment
body:

Locking the Jun 24 readout framing.

The "9 days before on-call" result is the story — we sell early detection, and the adaptation step stays human-approved for at least two quarters. Freya's proxy-strength diagnostic is a hard gate in the design: no proxy signal, no subgroup claims, and the dashboard says so explicitly.

subject: Re: BLT status: decisions locked for sweep week + readout

Risk/trade-off: the third target has sharp discontinuities and the residual-correction pass (step 3) is eating most of the error budget before commands are even extracted, so the "interpretable" story gets weaker exactly where customers would want it most. Options: constrain that target's domain, or present interpretability coverage honestly as partial. We'd like a steer before the June review — recommend we discuss at the decision review rather than expanding scope now.

Tereza

subject: Kickoff: LEGO multi-hop KGQA on the entity graph
body:

Milestones:

subject: Re: Kickoff: LEGO multi-hop KGQA on the entity graph

Per-hop accuracy, latency percentiles, and regression tracking across graph snapshots. It's roughly 40% of our eng budget this quarter but everything downstream depends on trustworthy evals.

subject: Re: Kickoff: LEGO multi-hop KGQA on the entity graph — status + risk
body:
Priya, Deshawn,

Status for the April milestone:

Risk for the go/no-go: latent execution keeps intermediate reasoning in embedding space, so when a traversal goes wrong we can't show a customer *where*. For support-facing use that's a real explainability gap. Proposal: scope v1 to 2-hop queries only and present 3-hop as research-continuing. I'll bring eval plots to the May 29 review.

Rafael

subject: Kickoff: Light Field Neural Rendering productization

subject: Kickoff: Lighthouse relighting primitive
body:

subject: Kickoff: LDS clustering for telemetry streams
body:

Milestones:

subject: Kickoff: linear-eval as the portfolio's representation check
body:
Hi all,

Kicking off the linear-eval standardization effort. Our open-source tooling does linear evaluation on fixed embeddings in JAX using L-BFGS, and the one-call convenience function — tune_hparams_and_compute_test_accuracy — handles the train/val split, distributes across devices, retrains at the optimal L2, and reports test accuracy. Right now every embedding team in graphs-retrieval hand-rolls this differently, which makes model comparisons across teams basically meaningless.

Goal: by mid-June, linear-eval is the blessed representation-quality check wired into Evalline, with three embedding teams migrated.

Milestones: Mar 20 library hardened + Evalline integration design; Apr 24 first team migrated; Jun 12 all three, plus a comparison dashboard.

Jelena owns staffing; Efe is tech lead. Tomas Fofana's team has the Evalline review slot on Mar 12.

Anders

subject: Re: Kickoff: linear-eval as the portfolio's representation check
body:
Anders,

Plan on my side:

- Efe Lindqvist 40%, Linnea Yamada 30% on Evalline integration, Paloma Castillo 40% on the migration tooling and dashboard. Compute is negligible — L-BFGS on fixed embeddings runs on a handful of accelerators; we'll use titan-a100 scraps.
- Scope addition we discussed Tuesday, now formal: the same embedding teams keep asking how to shrink their encoders without losing representation quality. Since nothing like it exists internally, we're scoping and staffing a distillation training recipe from scratch — Efe at 40% owning the recipe, Paloma supporting the training loop — so teams can compress models and immediately verify the students with linear eval. It pairs naturally with this project since linear eval is the acceptance test.

That takes us to ~1.5 FTE total. Flag now if the recipe should wait for Q3.

Jelena

subject: Re: Kickoff: linear-eval as the portfolio's representation check — status
body:
Hi Anders, Jelena,

Status:

- First team migrated Apr 22 (two days early). Their old hand-rolled logistic-regression eval disagreed with linear-eval by up to 1.9pp on the same embeddings — traced to them never tuning L2; our optimal_l2_reg search settles it. Good ammunition for the standardization story.
- One subtlety worth documenting: when embedding counts aren't divisible by device count, the library zero-pads and relies on the train mask, but the migrating team's custom loader dropped the mask and quietly trained on padding. Linnea added a validation check that hard-fails on unmasked padding.

Risk: the distillation recipe is going slower than the eval work — my first students verify fine on linear eval but the recipe isn't turnkey yet, and 40% of my time is proving thin. May need Jelena to rebalance if Jun 12 is to include a distillation quickstart.

Thanks all — the 1.9pp discrepancy find alone justified this project.

subject: Re: Kickoff: TextGenSHAP explanation service for RAG answers — status
