Toolkit defaults can't ask users to hand-set the band, so I'm deriving it from a cheap pilot chain. Adds ~10% runtime, removes the sharpest edge. Will have numbers next status.

Umar

subject: Re: NeuTra kickoff — release decisions
body:
Team,

Decisions for the 06-08 release, from today's review:

1. Ship with Umar's pilot-chain auto-banding as the default tuner path. The 10% runtime tax is the right trade for not exposing step-size bounds to users; power users can still set the band manually via config.
2. Benchmark suite ships with funnel + calibration posterior #1. Posterior #2 goes in as "experimental" — the tuner fix works but has only a week of soak on it, and I'd rather label honestly than slip the date.
3. Tereza's final data refresh is confirmed for this week per the March plan, so we release against the current pre-freeze Corpus snapshot with plenty of runway before the migration freeze.

Docs review Thursday; Vera and Tereza, please have the affine-vs-IAF guidance section ready by then.

Nice quarter for a small team.

Zofia

subject: Project Kestrel kickoff — LLM-generated parallel data beats web crawl
body:
Hi Daniela,

Kicking off the NewsPaLM effort — internal codename is Project Kestrel, please use it in docs and OKR entries so the workstream is trackable across the portfolio.

Basis: our open-source NewsPaLM MBR/QE release. The dataset is LLM-generated parallel data for en-de and de-en, produced three ways — MBR-decoded, QE-reranked, and greedy-decoded — at both sentence level and multi-sentence blob level. The headline claim we're operationalizing: this curated generated data outperforms traditional web-crawled parallel data for training.

Kestrel deliverables: (1) reproduce the data-quality claim inside our training stack, (2) a decision memo on replacing a slice of our web-crawled de-en corpus with MBR-decoded data, (3) a recipe for extending beyond en/de. Milestones: eval harness by mid-March, ablations by end of April, memo before 05-25.

Staffing note from you when ready.

Dmitri

subject: Re: Project Kestrel kickoff — staffing + compute
body:
Dmitri,

Kestrel staffing and compute:

Staffing — Linnea leads the training-stack integration and the ablation matrix; Ondrej owns eval methodology (he wants BLEURT as primary metric with chrF as the sanity check, matching how the release was validated); Kaia handles the blob-level vs sentence-level comparison, which is the part most relevant to our document-translation customers; Maren builds the corpus-mixing tooling.

Compute — training runs for the ablation matrix (3 decoding strategies x 2 granularities x 2 directions, plus web-crawl baselines) fit within our standing titan-a100 share if we serialize; ~5 weeks of queue time. I considered asking for a vulcan slot to parallelize but the serialization actually matches our milestone spacing, so no reservation and no discretionary budget ask this half.

Data is already mirrored internally from the release zip; tsv parsing was trivial.

Daniela

subject: Re: Project Kestrel — ablation status
body:
Hi both,

Kestrel ablation status, halfway through the matrix:

- Core claim reproducing so far: models trained on the MBR-decoded de-en set beat the size-matched web-crawl baseline by +2.1 BLEURT on our news holdout. QE-reranked lands at +1.4, greedy-decoded at +0.3 — the ordering from the release holds in our stack.
- Kaia's granularity result is the surprise: blob-level (multi-sentence) data gives a further +0.8 BLEURT on the document-translation eval even though the sentence-level sets are cleaner to mix. That materially strengthens the case for our doc-translation customers.
- chrF agrees directionally everywhere, so no metric-gaming concerns yet.

Risk: the en-de direction is running ~2 weeks behind because the web-crawl baseline corpus needed dedup against the NewsPaLM sources (Maren caught overlap that would have flattered the baseline). Worth the delay for a defensible memo, but it eats our April buffer.

Linnea

subject: Re: Project Kestrel — memo decision + scope call
body:
Team,

Decisions for the Kestrel close-out:

1. The decision memo recommends replacing 30% of the web-crawled de-en training slice with MBR-decoded NewsPaLM data, blob-level where the downstream task is document translation. The +2.1 BLEURT with a dedup-hardened baseline is a defensible number, and Ondrej's methodology section makes that case explicitly.
2. Scope call: the en-de direction ships in the memo as preliminary (the dedup delay means only half its ablation cells finish by 05-25). I'd rather flag it than pad the timeline. Full en-de results become a Q3 fast-follow.
3. The beyond-en/de recipe ships as an appendix — Kaia's granularity finding is the piece I want quoted when other portfolios pick this up.

Memo review Tuesday, final to Hana's staff by 05-22, closing Kestrel on schedule.

Excellent work, all.

Dmitri

subject: N-Grammer kickoff — efficiency lever for language models
body:
Hi Daniela,

Kickoff for N-Grammer. Our open-source release augments the Transformer with n-grams constructed from a discrete latent representation of the sequence — a cheap architectural add-on that outperformed both Transformer and Primer baselines on C4 language modeling and SuperGLUE classification. Given how much of the language portfolio's budget goes to training and inference, this is our most credible near-term efficiency lever.

Deliverables for the window (04-20 to 07-20): (1) reproduce the C4 and SuperGLUE results in our stack, (2) quantify the quality-per-FLOP win on one production-adjacent model config, (3) ship the promised Jax APIs for flax and haiku as a maintained internal library, tracking the open-source release.

Milestones: repro by end of May, FLOP study by end of June, API release mid-July. Staffing from you please — I know this team is popular.

Priya

subject: Re: N-Grammer kickoff — staffing plan
body:
Priya,

Staffing, with the July crunch in mind:

- Gustavo: C4/SuperGLUE reproduction now, then the FLOP study. 80% through June.
- Rosa: training-stack integration and benchmark plumbing, 50%.
- Rafael Duran: committed at 60% to N-Grammer for July 2026 to lead the flax/haiku API release — he wrote our internal Jax API guidelines, so the mid-July library milestone is his to land. Before July he's advisory at ~15% while Gustavo runs the repro.

You're right that the team is popular, so I've written those numbers into the resourcing sheet — July especially is load-bearing: if Rafael's allocation slips, the API release moves to August past your window.

Compute: repro and FLOP study fit titan-a100 best-effort; the C4 runs are the big line but they serialize fine. No reservation ask.

Daniela

subject: Re: N-Grammer kickoff — repro done, FLOP study early read
body:
Hi both,

Status:

- Reproduction milestone met (late by a week — C4 queue times on titan, not model issues). N-Grammer beats our Transformer baseline on C4 perplexity at matched parameter count and edges the Primer config we run internally; SuperGLUE classification shows the same ordering. The release's claims hold up in our stack.
- FLOP study early read: at matched quality, the n-gram-augmented config needs roughly 0.85x the training FLOPs of the baseline, and the latent n-gram lookup adds under 2% inference overhead. The interesting knob is the discrete latent vocab size — too small and the n-grams stop helping, too large and embedding memory becomes the cost. We're mapping that curve now; it will be the centerpiece of the June readout.
- Risk: SuperGLUE fine-tuning variance is high on small tasks, so I'm running 5 seeds before quoting deltas. Might push the FLOP report to 07-03.

Rafael's API work spins up next week per plan.

Gustavo

subject: NNGP-NAS kickoff — cheap architecture pre-screening
body:
Hi Bao,

Kickoff for the NNGP-NAS effort. Our open-source release shows you can compute NNGP validation accuracy for a NAS-Bench-101 model on a subset of CIFAR-10 and use it as a performance predictor — no training loop at all — and it ships the metrics to judge predictor quality: Kendall's Tau, correlation coefficient, PQETP (prediction quality for exceedance of threshold performance), and discovered performance.

Product: an architecture pre-screening service. Teams running searches burn full-training budget on candidates a cheap NNGP score would have rejected; we want screening to cut those wasted runs meaningfully.

Deliverables in the short window (02-02 to 05-04): (1) release notebook turned into a batch scoring service, (2) validation on an internal search workload, not just NAS-Bench-101, (3) a calibration study of when the predictor is trustworthy. Resourcing next, please.

Anders

subject: Re: NNGP-NAS kickoff — resourcing + annotation UI build
body:
Anders,

Resourcing:

- Freya: predictor methodology and the calibration study.
- Jorge: batch scoring service (the NNGP kernel computation batches nicely; CIFAR-10 subsets keep each score under a minute on an A100).
- Maren: data plumbing and the internal-workload integration.

One addition to scope, and it needs your blessing on cost: the calibration study needs expert judgments — engineers rating whether the predictor's accept/reject calls match their read of an architecture before ground-truth training lands. There's no tool for collecting that, so we're scoping and building a human-rating annotation UI from scratch: Jorge and Maren split a 5-week build for rating queues, side-by-side comparisons, rater agreement stats, and CSV export for analysis. It's generic enough that we'll reuse it every time we validate a predictor.

Compute is trivial otherwise — titan best-effort covers everything.

Bao

subject: Re: NNGP-NAS kickoff — March status + a calibration finding
body:
Hi both,

Status:

- Scoring service: Jorge's batch path is live internally. Scoring the full NAS-Bench-101 sample we use takes about 90 minutes on 8 A100s; per-architecture cost is small change vs a full training run.
- Replication: our Kendall's Tau between NNGP score and trained accuracy matches the release's reported range, and PQETP is the metric that actually predicts screening value — Tau alone flatters the predictor in the mid-pack where nobody cares.
- Calibration finding worth flagging: the predictor is reliable at the top and bottom deciles but noisy in between, and it systematically underrates architectures with unusual skip-connection patterns. So v1 policy should be "screen out the bottom 40%" rather than "rank everything" — that's where the PQETP numbers say we're trustworthy.
- Annotation UI: rating queues and agreement stats are working; Maren demos the comparison view Friday. First real rating round starts next week feeding my study.

Freya

subject: Re: NNGP-NAS kickoff — close-out decisions
body:
Team,

Decisions for the 05-04 close:

1. v1 ships as a bottom-40% screening filter, per Freya's calibration study. We are explicitly not shipping a ranker — the mid-pack noise and the skip-connection blind spot make that a credibility risk. The service docs state the operating envelope in exactly those terms.
2. The internal-workload validation stays in scope: Maren's integration shows screening would have saved roughly a third of full-training runs in the last search the graphs team ran, at zero missed top-decile candidates. That's the adoption pitch, and it goes in the readout.
3. The annotation UI ships as an internal tool alongside the service — the rater-agreement data made Freya's study materially stronger, and I want it maintained, not orphaned. Jorge owns it through Q3.

Readout to Eleni's staff 04-30. Good, tight project.

Anders

subject: Kickoff: worst-case recall training for long-tail classification
body:
Hi Deshawn,

Kickoff for the non-decomposable objectives effort. Our NeurIPS 2021 release implements worst-case recall maximization (Algorithm 1) using a logit-adjusted cost-sensitive loss, with three baselines in the box: standard ERM, the balanced logit-adjusted loss, and a re-weighted cost-sensitive loss.

Why it matters: data-platforms customers with long-tail label distributions keep discovering that average accuracy hides catastrophic recall on rare classes. "No class left behind" as a training objective is a sellable, auditable guarantee.

Deliverables: (1) reproduce the paper's results on the CIFAR-10/100 long-tail datasets, (2) validate on one internal long-tail workload, (3) integrate the loss into the platform trainer with sane defaults. Milestones: repro by end of April, internal validation by mid-June, integration readout by 06-29.

One planning note: our internal workload's tfrecords live in Corpus, so migration timing affects us — details with your resourcing pass.

Dmitri

subject: Re: Kickoff: worst-case recall — resourcing + Corpus deadline
body:
Dmitri,

Resourcing:

Staffing — Umar leads methodology and the repro (the codebase branches from our logit_adjustment release, which he knows well); Carmen runs the internal-workload validation; Paloma does the trainer integration and data plumbing.

Compute — light. CIFAR-10/100 long-tail runs are single-node jobs; the internal workload needs a few dozen A100s at peak. Titan best-effort throughout, no reservation, no discretionary budget ask.

On your Corpus note: confirmed with Jun's team — the Corpus v2 migration freeze is 2026-07-10. Our window closes 06-29, but the internal workload's long-tail tfrecords must be re-registered under the v2 schema before that freeze or the Q3 retraining pipeline inherits a broken path. Paloma is doing the re-registration in early June alongside the validation work, so we're clear of the deadline with margin rather than discovering it in July.

Deshawn

subject: Re: Kickoff: worst-case recall — repro done, internal validation early read
body:
Hi both,

Status:

- Repro milestone met. On CIFAR-100 long-tail, Algorithm 1 lifts worst-case (minimum per-class) recall by a wide margin over standard ERM, and beats both the balanced-loss and re-weighted baselines, at a modest cost to average accuracy — the same trade the paper reports. The release's test mode made the setup verification painless.
- Internal workload early read: on our long-tail workload (about 400 classes, heaviest-to-lightest ratio ~900:1), worst-case recall goes from 0.12 under ERM to 0.41 with the cost-sensitive loss, average accuracy down 1.8 points. That trade needs a product conversation — some customers will take it instantly, others won't.
- Risk: convergence. The per-class multiplier updates oscillate on classes with <20 examples; Umar is damping the update rate, which stabilizes things at the cost of ~15% more epochs. Needs to settle before Paloma freezes trainer defaults.

On plan for mid-June.

Carmen

subject: Re: Kickoff: worst-case recall — decisions for close-out
body:
Team,

Decisions from today's review, ahead of the OKR lock next week:

1. The trainer integration ships with TWO presets: "balanced" (the logit-adjusted baseline) and "worst-case" (Algorithm 1 with Umar's damped multiplier updates). The 0.12 → 0.41 worst-case recall result is the headline, and offering the milder preset answers the average-accuracy objection without a custom-config support burden.
2. Umar's damping lands in the defaults; the 15% epoch overhead is acceptable and we document it.
3. Paloma confirmed the v2 re-registration of the long-tail tfrecords completed 06-09, so we're fully clear of the Corpus freeze and Q3 retraining is unblocked.
4. Q3 OKR filed: worst-case preset adopted by 2 platform customers, with a published trade-off note.

Readout on 06-25; window closes clean on 06-29. Thanks all.

Dmitri
